items.title: llm-vram-calc: zero-dependency CLI VRAM + KV-cache calculator for LLM quantizations
items.author: DangerousANEN
items.body_excerpt:
## llm-vram-calc

A zero-dependency Python CLI that answers the #1 question in local inference: **"will this quantization fit in my VRAM?"** — before the 40GB download.

```bash
pip install https://github.com/DangerousANEN/llm-vram-calculator/releases/download/v1.1.0/llm_vram_calculator-1.0.0-py3-none-any.whl
llm-vram-calc
```

### What it does
- 10+ model presets (Qwen 2.5/3, Llama 3.x, DeepSeek R1/V3, Phi-3, Gemma 2, Mistral)
- Quantizations from q2_k to f16 with per-model bit-precision maps
- Q8_0 auto-detection with llama.cpp fallback defaults
- Batch comparison across multiple configs
- **Offload layers calculator**: how many GPU layers fit when VRAM is short and system RAM picks up the rest
- **KV-cache estimator**: max context length for a given VRAM budget
- Verdict output: `fits` / `OOM` with exact MB breakdown (weights / KV-cache / overhead)

### Live interactive web version
https://ai.zxc1x1.ru/tools/vram/

### Russian-language deep-dives on the math behind VRAM estimation
Telegram: @llm_hubs — weekly LLM digest, benchmarks, no hype.

**Source code:** https://github.com/DangerousANEN/llm-vram-calculator
**Release (wheel + sdist):** https://github.com/DangerousANEN/llm-vram-calculator/releases/tag/v1.1.0

items.title: [good-first-issue] tests: make flaky vllm_bench throughput comparisons reproducible
items.author: maobaolong
items.body_excerpt:
Parent tracker: #5313 · Onboarding: #3372

## Confirmed flaky behavior

`k3-multiprocess-test / vllm / vllm_bench / zmq` changes its throughput verdict without a source update:

| Build #5340, September 29, 2026 (UTC) | Result |
| --- | --- |
| [Original job](https://buildkite.com/lmcache/k3-multiprocess-test/builds/5340#01a0eab1-a517-4a38-8163-b0ec7cfaff63) | LMCache throughput **7.34% slower** than baseline; fails the 5% limit |
| [Retry](https://buildkite.com/lmcache/k3-multiprocess-test/builds/5340#01a0eaba-4671-4f79-a910-4a02cfa0cadf) | LMCache throughput **0.62% faster** than baseline; passes |

Both are `dev` builds of **`9e8226dd49728769843bf6f586b00b33ab616125`**, with no PR-base merge, vLLM **`0.30.1rc1.dev244+g0da126676`**, and torch **`2.13.0+cu130`**. Both baseline and LMCache completed all 50 requests with 500400 input tokens. This is an intermittent benchmark verdict, not an installation failure.

The inputs are not reproducible across those attempts: the original uses seed `1790644335`, the retry `1790645482`. Each attempt uses the same seed for its own baseline/LMCache pair, but the default `RANDOM_SEED` comes from `date +%s`. The seed change is a confirmed confounder; it is **not proven to be the sole cause** of the throughput fluctuation.

## Bounded good-first task

Make this benchmark's inputs reproducible across retries, and make the comparison auditable. This is the first test-harness improvement for the confirmed flake, not a production performance optimization.

1. Replace the clock-derived default seed with a documented stable default; continue honoring an explicit `RANDOM_SEED` override.
2. Save a small comparison manifest next to `baseline.json` and `lmcache.json`: effective seed, model, request count and lengths, actual checkout SHA, installed vLLM/torch versions, and the two throughput values/verdict. Keep any new diagnostics local to this workload.
3. Preserve separate attempt results when used in CI. Follow the existing result-directory/cleanup conventions, and ensure the manifest is accessible in the job log or a public Buildkite artifact rather than merely naming a container-local file.
4. Add focused CPU-only regression coverage using stub benchmark commands: default seed is repeatable, both sides receive it, an override is honored, and success/failure summaries retain the actual numbers.

Keep the 5% throughput limit, request/token checks, and cache-retrieval validation. Do not add blanket retries, remove assertions, or present a fixed seed as proof of a resolved performance issue. #5227 already added retry mitigation; this task addresses reproducibility within the workload.

Starting points, checked at `42be9c7439a1eb0b17bf6b7565a894a9743fd052`:

- [Workload seed and result comparison](https://github.com/LMCache/LMCache/blob/42be9c7439a1eb0b17bf6b7565a894a9743fd052/.buildkite/k3_tests/multiprocess/scripts/workloads/vllm/vllm-bench.sh).
- [Result cleanup/copying](https://github.com/LMCache/LMCache/blob/42be9c7439a1eb0b17bf6b7565a894a9743fd052/.buildkite/k3_tests/multiprocess/scripts/cleanup.sh).
- [Buildkite step and existing retry policy](https://github.com/LMCache/LMCache/blob/42be9c7439a1eb0b17bf6b7565a894a9743fd052/.buildkite/k3_tests/multiprocess/pipeline.yml).

## Acceptance

- [ ] Default inputs are identical across attempts; explicit overrides still work.
- [ ] A reviewer can recover both results, the effective inputs, versions, and verdict from public job output/artifacts.
- [ ] Stubbed CPU coverage exercises default/override and passing/failing results.
- [ ] GPU validation reports first-attempt results with a fixed seed; remaining fluctuation is reported as unresolved rather than hidden.
- [ ] Existing behavioral assertions and thresholds remain effective.

## Reproduce the CI workload

The evidence below comes from CI; this issue does not claim a local GPU reproduction. Use a dedicated Linux x86_64 GPU test host with Docker and NVIDIA Container Toolkit, two available CUDA GPUs capable of running separate `Qwen/Qwen3-14B` servers, sufficient host RAM for the default 80 GiB LMCache buffer (plus the mock L2 storage for the L2 case), and disk/network access for the image, wheels, and model. CI uses CUDA 13.0, Python 3.12, and a 1 GiB `/dev/shm`. A maintainer can run the GPU validation for a contributor who only has a CPU machine.

These commands build the public CI image recipe, explicitly start Bash, and pin the historical LMCache and vLLM revisions. They are a reproduction recipe, not a fully locked copy of every historical dependency or GPU scheduling condition. Run from a fresh directory; make the actual PR against current `dev`.

```bash
git clone https://github.com/LMCache/LMCache.git
cd LMCache
git checkout 9e8226dd49728769843bf6f586b00b33ab616125
docker build -t lmcache-flake-ci \
  -f .buildkite/k3_harness/ci-base.Dockerfile .
docker run --rm --gpus '"device=0,1"' --shm-size=1g \
  --entrypoint bash \
  -v "$PWD:/workspace/LMCache" -w /workspace/LMCache \
  -e MAX_JOBS=1 \
  -e INFERENCE_ENGINE=vllm \
  -e LMCACHE_REQUEST_TRANSPORT=zmq \
  -e LMCACHE_PR_BASE_MERGE=never \
  -e PINNED_VLLM_VERSION=0.30.1rc1.dev244+g0da126676 \
  -e PINNED_VLLM_ARCHIVE_INDEX_URL=https://wheels.vllm.ai/0da126676e38f5dc1b02b2c4f48dc85f90f5a79f/cu130 \
  lmcache-flake-ci -c '
    set -e
    source /opt/venv/bin/activate
    command -v git uv python3 nvcc gcc g++
    nvidia-smi
    git config --global --add safe.directory /workspace/LMCache
    .buildkite/k3_tests/multiprocess/run.sh vllm_bench
  '
```

Use the linked failed and passed jobs as the initial reproduction pair. For subsequent GPU runs, record the actual checkout SHA, installed package versions, GPU model, input settings, and first-attempt result. A green retry alone does not show that the underlying fluctuation was fixed.

`k3-multiprocess-test / vllm / long_doc_qa / zmq` intermittently fails its time-to-first-token (TTFT) threshold on unchanged code:

| Build #5294, September 26, 2026 (UTC) | LMCache TTFT | Baseline TTFT | Verdict (at least 60% faster) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [Original job](https://buildkite.com/lmcache/k3-multiprocess-test/builds/5294#01a0ddba-52b3-4ed4-8c7b-556bc2e41819) | 0.6464 s | 1.3012 s | **50.3% faster — FAIL** |
| [Retry](https://buildkite.com/lmcache/k3-multiprocess-test/builds/5294#01a0ddd3-60b4-40e2-aeda-af965c02a2b0) | 0.3950 s | 1.3337 s | **70.4% faster — PASS** |

Both jobs test `dev` commit **`dc68527c76fd08c5501e19097973938143f06348`**, without a PR-base merge, and install vLLM **`0.30.1rc1.dev193+gddd6fbca1`** and torch **`2.13.0+cu130`**. The query round-time check passes in both attempts.

There is a second independent same-build pair: [#5291 original](https://buildkite.com/lmcache/k3-multiprocess-test/builds/5291#01a0db7c-b789-4b24-bb2f-963ca51b94fd) gives 51.4% TTFT improvement, while [its retry](https://buildkite.com/lmcache/k3-multiprocess-test/builds/5291#01a0db9f-e858-4549-af74-a2f240bc0bf7) gives 72.6%. Both use `dev` commit `9a7b60501bc8ac3d0ab33b11dfd962ccfd02a5ae` and vLLM `0.30.1rc1.dev142+g3a58aeb1a`.

These pairs confirm an intermittent test verdict. They do **not** establish whether the cause is cache readiness, runtime scheduling, or a performance defect.

## Bounded good-first task

Preserve separate per-request timings for the baseline and LMCache phases so this flake can be investigated without rerunning an entire GPU job blindly.

The benchmark currently writes `warmup_round.csv` and `query_round.csv` to its working directory. The wrapper launches baseline and LMCache sequentially in the same directory, so the second invocation overwrites the first phase's raw timings. The wrapper retains aggregate JSON but loses that raw comparison.

1. In the **L1 `long-doc-qa.sh` wrapper**, give baseline and LMCache separate output/working directories under the workload's existing `RESULTS_DIR`. Preserve each phase's CSVs, aggregate JSON, and text output on both success and threshold failure. Keep paths absolute when changing the child process's working directory.
2. Add a compact diagnostic summary that identifies the phase, effective workload settings, sample/success counts, and available timing distribution information. Keep the existing aggregate calculation and threshold semantics.
3. Make both phases' diagnostics accessible in public job output/artifacts. A container-local path by itself is not sufficient. Keep any artifact rule narrow to this workload; avoid a repository-wide artifact refactor.
4. Add CPU-only coverage with a stub benchmark writing distinguishable phase CSVs. Prove the baseline files survive the second invocation, and a failing threshold still leaves both phases inspectable and returns failure.

This is a diagnostic first step, not a claim that preserving CSVs fixes the TTFT variation. Do not loosen the 60% TTFT / 15% round-time requirements, add retries, or change cache semantics. Keep the L2 wrapper out of this issue so the sibling task remains independently claimable.

Starting points, checked at `42be9c7439a1eb0b17bf6b7565a894a9743fd052`:

- [L1 workload wrapper](https://github.com/LMCache/LMCache/blob/42be9c7439a1eb0b17bf6b7565a894a9743fd052/.buildkite/k3_tests/multiprocess/scripts/workloads/common/long-doc-qa.sh).
- [Benchmark raw CSV output and aggregate calculation](https://github.com/LMCache/LMCache/blob/42be9c7439a1eb0b17bf6b7565a894a9743fd052/benchmarks/long_doc_qa/long_doc_qa.py#L551).
- [Existing result cleanup/copying](https://github.com/LMCache/LMCache/blob/42be9c7439a1eb0b17bf6b7565a894a9743fd052/.buildkite/k3_tests/multiprocess/scripts/cleanup.sh).

## Acceptance

- [ ] Baseline and LMCache raw timings coexist and are clearly attributed.
- [ ] CPU regression coverage proves phase isolation and preservation on failure.
- [ ] A GPU job exposes both phases' data through public output/artifacts, including a failing comparison.
- [ ] Threshold failures retain a nonzero exit status; no assertion is removed or weakened.
- [ ] The PR distinguishes completed diagnostics from any remaining cause of the intermittent timing result.

Use a dedicated Linux x86_64 GPU test host with Docker and NVIDIA Container Toolkit, two available CUDA GPUs capable of running separate `Qwen/Qwen3-14B` servers, sufficient host RAM for the default 80 GiB LMCache buffer (plus the mock L2 storage for the L2 case), and disk/network access for the image, wheels, and model. items.title: [good-first-issue] tests: retain L2 diagnostics when flaky TTFT checks fail
items.author: maobaolong
items.body_excerpt:
Parent tracker: #5313 · Onboarding: #3372

## Confirmed flaky behavior

`k3-multiprocess-test / vllm / long_doc_qa_l2 / zmq` changes its L2 time-to-first-token (TTFT) verdict on a same-source retry:

| Build #5287, September 26, 2026 (UTC) | Query speedup | TTFT speedup | Verdict |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [Original job](https://buildkite.com/lmcache/k3-multiprocess-test/builds/5287#01a0db08-cd08-4819-aafd-3b1599eed368) | 1.46x | **1.49x** | Fails the 1.5x TTFT requirement |
| [Retry](https://buildkite.com/lmcache/k3-multiprocess-test/builds/5287#01a0db28-e4d4-4a86-96f8-6923e870be90) | 1.43x | **1.54x** | Passes |

Both jobs test `dev` commit **`002693d8aa5ba8ead0d67922540e4ad4ba6fb3d3`**, without a PR-base merge, and install vLLM **`0.30.1rc1.dev142+g3a58aeb1a`** and torch **`2.13.0+cu130`**. The retry additionally reports 1190 successful L2 stores, 95 prefetch lookups, 2340 prefix hits, and 2340 loaded keys.

The failed attempt exits before the L2 data-flow checks, so we cannot tell from those checks whether it exercised the same successful cache path. That diagnostic gap must not be treated as evidence of broken L2 retrieval, or as proof that the fluctuation is harmless noise.

## Bounded good-first task

Ensure a performance-threshold failure still captures and checks L2 data-flow evidence before the workload exits.

In `long-doc-qa-l2.sh`, `set -e` is active. Step 3's Python threshold verifier exits nonzero, so Step 4's Prometheus scrape and L2 store/prefetch validation never run on the failing path. This is a small shell control-flow and test-diagnostics task.

1. Retain the performance verification status instead of immediately exiting. Run the existing bounded metrics collection while the L2 server is still alive.
2. Report **both** performance and data-flow outcomes, save the metrics snapshot, then return failure if either outcome fails. A metrics timeout/missing snapshot must remain visible and must not mask the original performance failure.
3. Make the snapshot and summary accessible in the public job log or a job artifact. Keep the change local to the L2 workload and any narrowly needed artifact rule.
4. Add CPU-only coverage with stubbed verifier/scrape commands for: both pass, only performance fails, only metrics/data-flow fails, and both fail. Assert bounded behavior, metrics collection after a performance failure, and the final exit status.

Keep the existing 1.3x query-speedup, 1.5x TTFT-speedup, 1.2x warmup-overhead limits and positive L2 data-flow assertions. Do not add blanket retries, reduce thresholds, or redesign storage policy. This completes the missing diagnostics for a confirmed flake; it does **not** by itself establish that the GPU timing instability is fixed. Keep the L1 wrapper outside this task.

Starting points, checked at `42be9c7439a1eb0b17bf6b7565a894a9743fd052`:

- [L2 workload: threshold verifier followed by metrics checks](https://github.com/LMCache/LMCache/blob/42be9c7439a1eb0b17bf6b7565a894a9743fd052/.buildkite/k3_tests/multiprocess/scripts/workloads/common/long-doc-qa-l2.sh#L229).
- [Result cleanup/copying](https://github.com/LMCache/LMCache/blob/42be9c7439a1eb0b17bf6b7565a894a9743fd052/.buildkite/k3_tests/multiprocess/scripts/cleanup.sh).
- [Buildkite workload step](https://github.com/LMCache/LMCache/blob/42be9c7439a1eb0b17bf6b7565a894a9743fd052/.buildkite/k3_tests/multiprocess/pipeline.yml#L173).

## Acceptance

- [ ] A forced performance failure still collects bounded L2 diagnostics before cleanup.
- [ ] All four outcome combinations have regression coverage and correct final exit status.
- [ ] A failed GPU comparison exposes the available store/prefetch counters, or an explicit collection error, in public output/artifacts.
- [ ] Existing thresholds and data-flow assertions remain effective.
- [ ] The PR reports remaining timing instability separately from completed diagnostic hardening.

## Reproduce the CI workload

The evidence below comes from CI; this issue does not claim a local GPU reproduction. Use a dedicated Linux x86_64 GPU test host with Docker and NVIDIA Container Toolkit, two available CUDA GPUs capable of running separate `Qwen/Qwen3-14B` servers, sufficient host RAM for the default 80 GiB LMCache buffer (plus the mock L2 storage for the L2 case), and disk/network access for the image, wheels, and model. CI uses CUDA 13.0, Python 3.12, and a 1 GiB `/dev/shm`. A maintainer can run the GPU validation for a contributor who only has a CPU machine.

These commands build the public CI image recipe, explicitly start Bash, and pin the historical LMCache and vLLM revisions. They are a reproduction recipe, not a fully locked copy of every historical dependency or GPU scheduling condition. Run from a fresh directory; make the actual PR against current `dev`.

```bash
git clone https://github.com/LMCache/LMCache.git
cd LMCache
git checkout 002693d8aa5ba8ead0d67922540e4ad4ba6fb3d3
docker build -t lmcache-flake-ci \
  -f .buildkite/k3_harness/ci-base.Dockerfile .
docker run --rm --gpus '"device=0,1"' --shm-size=1g \
  --entrypoint bash \
  -v "$PWD:/workspace/LMCache" -w /workspace/LMCache \
  -e MAX_JOBS=1 \
  -e INFERENCE_ENGINE=vllm \
  -e LMCACHE_REQUEST_TRANSPORT=zmq \
  -e LMCACHE_PR_BASE_MERGE=never \
  -e PINNED_VLLM_VERSION=0.30.1rc1.dev142+g3a58aeb1a \
  -e PINNED_VLLM_ARCHIVE_INDEX_URL=https://wheels.vllm.ai/3a58aeb1a13e7447da3037608d6489da7e7f22a2/cu130 \
  lmcache-flake-ci -c '
    set -e
    source /opt/venv/bin/activate
    command -v git uv python3 nvcc gcc g++
    nvidia-smi

items.title: [good-first-issue] logging: convert top-level LMCache utility logging to %-format
items.author: maobaolong
items.body_excerpt:
Follow-up for #5118 after #5125.

#5125 enabled Ruff `G004` repo-wide and added temporary `per-file-ignores` for the files/directories that still build logging messages with f-strings. This issue is one small slice of that cleanup queue.

Claiming: please comment `/claim` and wait for assignment so we avoid duplicate PRs.

## Scope

Convert only the logging f-strings in:

- `lmcache/observability.py` (2 G004 findings)
- `lmcache/sdk/context.py` (1 G004 findings)
- `lmcache/utils.py` (1 G004 findings)

Counts above were measured on `dev` at `dd5dfca` with `ruff check --isolated --select G004`.

## Expected change

- Replace logging f-strings with lazy `%`-style logging arguments, for example `logger.info("loaded %s tokens", num_tokens)`.
- Preserve the rendered log text and behavior.
- Do not change non-logging f-strings or unrelated control flow.
- Remove the matching `G004` ignore entry/entries from `pyproject.toml` once the listed paths are clean.

Matching ignore entry/entries:

- `"lmcache/observability.py" = ["G004"]`
- `"lmcache/sdk/context.py" = ["G004"]`
- `"lmcache/utils.py" = ["G004"]`

For a `**` directory ignore, delete the directory entry only when the whole listed directory is clean. If a merge conflict leaves other unmigrated files in that ignored directory, replace the broad `**` entry with explicit file-level entries for the leftovers.

## Verification

```bash
ruff check --isolated --select G004 lmcache/observability.py lmcache/sdk/context.py lmcache/utils.py
ruff check --select G004 lmcache/observability.py lmcache/sdk/context.py lmcache/utils.py pyproject.toml

items.title: [Bug]: FP8 KV cache startup can OOM because CUDA graph memory is omitted from the cache budget
items.author: the-Shallow
items.body_excerpt:
### Your current environment
The output of python collect_env.py ```text vLLM 0.28.0 on Linux with an NVIDIA GPU ```
### 🐛 Describe the bug On a 24 GiB GPU, `LLM(..., kv_cache_dtype="fp8")` is accepted but fails during startup with an out-of-memory error, while the identical engine using the default KV cache dtype answers successfully. ```python from vllm import LLM, SamplingParams llm = LLM( model="Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B", kv_cache_dtype="fp8", ) print(llm.generate( ["Hello, my name is"], SamplingParams(max_tokens=8), )) ``` Observed failure: ```text torch.OutOfMemoryError: CUDA out of memory. Tried to allocate 150.00 MiB. GPU 0 has a total capacity of 23.49 GiB of which 122.00 MiB is free. ... RuntimeError: Engine core initialization failed. See root cause above. ``` The startup accounting allocates about 19.93 GiB to the KV cache after subtracting a near-zero CUDA graph estimate. CUDA graph capture happens afterwards and consumes about 0.80 GiB in the FP8 case, pushing actual usage beyond the memory reserved by `gpu_memory_utilization`. Reducing `gpu_memory_utilization` avoids the failure. ### Expected behavior KV cache sizing should reserve the actual CUDA graph memory so an accepted configuration does not exceed its memory budget during graph capture or the first sampling allocation. If vLLM cannot fit the configuration, it should fail early with an actionable error. ### Suggested fix Make `profile_cudagraph_memory()` account for the actual graph capture cost, including its dependence on the number of KV blocks, or adjust the KV cache after graph capture when measured use exceeds the requested budget. ### Before submitting a new issue... - [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.

items.title: MP-mode component-level K/V tier placement for asymmetric (FP16-K / FP8-V) serde
items.author: mcgrof
items.body_excerpt:
# [Feature] MP-mode component-level K/V tier placement for asymmetric (FP16-K / FP8-V) serde

**Label**

Please label this issue with `new feature` (and `MP` / `enhancement` if available) so it can be categorized under [LMCache Onboarding](https://github.com/LMCache/LMCache/issues/1882).

**Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe.**

PR #3277 landed the CPU-side building blocks for asymmetric K16/V8 serde — the multi-output `Serializer`/`Deserializer` extension, the `AsymK16V8` codec (exact BF16 K, FP8 V with self-describing scale metadata + magic/version/CRC header), and unit tests. But those are just the *codec*: there is currently **no MP-mode storage path that actually places K and V on different tiers**.

Concretely, in MP mode today a chunk is serialized/deserialized as a single logical object through one L2 adapter; there is no way to say "keep exact K in the fast host tier (L1) and route only the compressed V (+scales) to L2/NVMe." So the storage win the asymmetric codec is designed for — and the V-only split-tier policy in particular — can't be realized end-to-end in MP mode. The serde can produce the bytes, but the `StorageManager` → L2 path can't split them into typed, independently-placed/evicted components.

For context on what the codec buys once placement exists:

| Mode | K | V | Storage bytes vs FP16 KV |
|---|---|---|---|
| Asymmetric, all-L2 | FP16 → L2 | FP8 → L2 | ~0.75× |
| **V-only split-tier** | FP16 → **L1 (host)** | FP8 → **L2 (NVMe)** | **~0.25× of FP16 NVMe bytes** |

The V-only mode needs component-level placement; it cannot be expressed at all with the current single-object MP storage path.

**Describe the solution you'd like**

Add **typed, component-level K/V placement** on top of LMCache's existing tiered (L1/L2) storage path: exact K retained in the fast host tier, compressed V (+ self-describing scales) routed to L2, both addressable via one logical key, integrated with the **existing write-behind drainer** (not a new write-back mechanism).

Proposed pieces (a prototype exists, see Additional context):

- Dispatch a multi-output serde through the L2 adapter wrapper (`SerdeL2AdapterWrapper`) so store/load/lookup operate on derived per-component child keys.
- A "KV-component-groups" L1 layout policy that splits the packed `[2, …]` K|V staging tensor into separate typed K and V component groups (no-op for the default packed layout; total bytes unchanged).
- A split-tier placement mode + child-key derivation (K-child retained in L1, V-child stored to L2), with a small `SplitTierManifest` state machine that marks an entry `COMPLETE` only when the K-child is present in L1 **and** the V-child is present in L2.
- Lifecycle correctness: pair L1 K-child eviction with L2 V-child cleanup, guard against evicting a K-child whose L2 V store is still in flight, and (perf) parallelize the per-key K-child copy / serve K-child buffers from a slab pool / release the logical L1 entry early via a V scratch copy.
- Read-side: reassemble the full logical object from the two children on load; refuse to serve a cross-mode blob (e.g. a V-only deserializer must reject a storage-only blob rather than mis-decode) — the codec's magic/version/CRC + codec-hash header already fails closed on mismatch.

The caller-facing API stays logical-key based; the component split is internal to the storage layer.

**Describe alternatives you've considered**

- **Asymmetric all-L2 (Mode 1), already supported by the #3277 codec.** Stores both K and V to L2 at ~0.75× FP16. Useful, but it does not give the larger host-tier/endurance reduction that K-in-L1 / V-only-to-L2 provides, and it doesn't need this feature.
- **Whole-KV offload** (e.g. vLLM's `v1/kv_offload`, FlexKV-style multi-tier): offloads KV as whole blocks, with no K/V component split — so it can't express "exact K hot, compressed V cold."
- **Strict write-back caching.** Not proposed: LMCache MP already does write-behind (the store controller asynchronously drains L1 → L2 after writes complete). This feature composes *component placement* on top of that existing path rather than introducing write-back.
- **Prior art for K/V component placement exists** (e.g. ShadowKV keeps low-rank K and offloads V), so this is not "first to split K/V across tiers" — the delta here is a reusable typed-output placement layer integrated with LMCache's existing L1/L2 model, with the asymmetric V-only codec as the first consumer.

**Additional context**

- Builds on PR #3277 (asymmetric serde building blocks): https://github.com/LMCache/LMCache/pull/3277
- A working prototype of the storage wiring lives on `mcgrof:serde-multi-output-mp-contract` (split-tier manifest, store/load/lookup composition, paired L1/L2 eviction, in-flight guard, slab pool, integration tests), including the **multi-output MP contract test** requested in the #3277 review (confirming `AsyncSerdeProcessor` round-trips a multi-output group through the MP path).
- The async serde drainer default of `max_workers=4` for the asym serdes was chosen because a single drainer thread becomes the codec bottleneck at load; with 4 the codec is hidden behind the write-behind drain at normal serving rates.
- Note on rebasing: the prototype predates a large MP refactor on `dev` (e.g. `multiprocess/server.py` was substantially restructured and several hooks moved out of it), so landing this is a deliberate forward-port onto the current MP architecture rather than a straight cherry-pick. Happy to split it into reviewable PRs:
  1. multi-output dispatch through the L2 wrapper + KV-component-groups L1 layout,
  2. split-tier placement mode + manifest + store/load/lookup,
  3. paired L1/L2 eviction + in-flight guard + perf (slab pool, early release),
  4. tests (contract + split-tier integration).
- What this does **not** cover: numeric quantization correctness (lives in the codec, already tested), CUDA/torch kernels, or the GPU-side connector path (a separate API, deliberately out of sco

From the perspective of bench_serving, estimating token throughput using TPOT (Time Per Output Token) provides a comprehensive evaluation over the entire testing period. On the other hand, the throughput printed in the engine log refers to the number of tokens generated within a single logging interval (which can be understood as the time for 40 consecutive decodes) divided by the time taken. comments.body:
I think I've found the cause. In multiple tests, when the backend is specified as "sglang," the `flush_cache` function is called to clear the cache.

 If `flush_cache` is executed successfully, there will be an inconsistency in the Decode Throughput between `bench_serving` and `engine logs`, specifically, `bench_serving` will be lower than `engine logs`. 

If `flush_cache` fails, the difference in Throughput between the two is within an acceptable range.

I speculate that the time loss caused by the successful execution of `flush_cache` might be the reason. The Decode Throughput in `engine logs` is not affected by this, but `bench_serving` is. I'm still not sure how to fix it. Does anyone have any suggestions?

When the backend is specified as "sglang," the following code is called to flush the cache，code in [here](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/blob/9cf407729441a18561ee5a8b2c1e3e535ba817f9/python/sglang/bench_serving.py#L961):
```python
# Flush cache
if "sglang" in backend:
    requests.post(base_url + "/flush_cache")
```

The specific implementation of `flush_cache` can be found [here](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/blob/9cf407729441a18561ee5a8b2c1e3e535ba817f9/python/sglang/srt/managers/scheduler.py#L1677):
```python
def flush_cache(self):
    """Flush the memory pool and cache."""
    if len(self.waiting_queue) == 0 and (
        self.running_batch is None or len(self.running_batch.reqs) == 0
    ):
        self.tree_cache.reset()
        self.tree_cache_metrics = {"total": 0, "hit": 0}
        if self.grammar_backend:
            self.grammar_backend.reset()
        self.req_to_token_pool.clear()
        self.token_to_kv_pool.clear()

        if not self.spec_algorithm.is_none():
            self.draft_worker.model_runner.req_to_token_pool.clear()
            self.draft_worker.model_runner.token_to_kv_pool.clear()

        self.num_generated_tokens = 0
        self.forward_ct_decode = 0
        self.spec_num_total_accepted_tokens = 0
        self.spec_num_total_forward_ct = 0
        torch.cuda.empty_cache()
        logger.info("Cache flushed successfully!")
        if_success = True
    else:
        logging.warning(
            f"Cache not flushed because there are pending requests. "
            f"#queue-req: {len(self.waiting_queue)}, "
            f"#running-req: {0 if self.running_batch is None else len(self.running_batch.reqs)}"
        )
        if_success = False
    return if_success
```

comments.author: ptimizeroracle
comments.body:
I went through both sides of this with the current code (main @ 99b9109). Happy to turn any of it into a fix if wanted, but evidence first.

**The two numbers are different estimators, not two measurements of the same thing:**

| | bench_serving | engine log |
|---|---|---|
| definition | TPOT-derived, per request: `(latency − ttft)` over `output_len − 1`, averaged across the whole run, client-side | `num_generated_tokens / gap_latency` where `gap_latency` is the time since the previous log line (`scheduler_components/metrics_reporter.py:799,894`) |
| window | entire run: queueing, any cold start, `[DONE]` tail included | one reporting interval, near-instantaneous |

So bench < engine is expected whenever the run has any ramp-up: the engine line reads close to a short-window peak, the bench number is a whole-run average.

Three smaller things verified along the way (all `python/sglang/benchmark/serving.py` unless noted):

1. TPOT arithmetic is the standard upstream vLLM formula (`(latency − ttft)/(output_len − 1)`, `:1136`): sound.
2. `itl` is recorded per stream **event**, not per token (`:334-337`, `:466+`). Events carrying several tokens (stream-interval batching, speculative decoding) contribute one itl sample, so `len(itl) < output_len − 1` and ITL percentiles conflate event latency with token latency. A retokenized correction already exists, but only for the `sglang-oai` backends (`:1131-1135`, `:1145-1155`); the completions/chat paths don't get it. I wrote CPU unit tests pinning this behavior (sum(itl) + [DONE]-tail == latency − ttft exactly; mean(ITL) > TPOT for the same request from denominators alone). Happy to PR them.
3. `should_flush_cache` is `("sglang" in backend AND SGLANG_IS_IN_CI) or --flush-cache` (`:1467-1471`), not default-on, so the cold-start mechanism discussed earlier in this thread needs CI or the explicit flag to apply to a default run.

If it's useful, the options I see: (a) a note in the bench output clarifying the window difference vs engine logs, (b) an engine-side long-window average for apples-to-apples runs, (c) extending the retokenized ITL path to the other backends. Which, if any, would you want?

items.title: [Feature] Expose the effective `max_running_requests` (after the mamba/linear-attention state-cache cap) in `/get_server_info`
items.author: fredchu
items.body_excerpt:
### Checklist
- [x] This is a feature request, not a general question.
- [x] English.

### Motivation
On hybrid (mamba / Gated DeltaNet) models, `KVCacheConfigurator.resolve_max_num_reqs` (`python/sglang/srt/mem_cache/kv_cache_configurator.py`, v0.5.19) can cap concurrency well below the CLI value and only says so in the log:

```
max_running_requests is capped to 9 by the mamba state cache (max_mamba_cache_size=47, 5 state slots per request). To raise it: increase --mamba-full-memory-ratio or --max-mamba-cache-size, or halve the state size with --mamba-ssm-dtype bfloat16.
```

`GET /get_server_info` keeps returning the CLI value (`"max_running_requests": 32` in our runs), and the ready-summary line (`max_total_num_tokens=... max_running_requests=9 ...`) is again log-only.

Concrete impact: we drove a concurrency benchmark through the OpenAI-compatible API on `Jackrong/Qwopus3.6-27B-v2-FP8` (Qwen3.5-27B hybrid, RTX 6000 Ada 48 GB, `--max-running-requests 32`, default radix cache) across three rentals, believing the server ran 16–32 concurrent requests. It ran 9 and queued the rest. Every "N=16/24/32" number measured the queue, not the engine, and the inflated per-request latency looked like retraction until we read the container log. With `--disable-radix-cache` the per-request slot count drops from 5 to 1 (`_calculate_mamba_ratio`) and the cap disappears — again only visible in the log.

Proposal:
- Add `effective_max_running_requests` to `/get_server_info` (keep the CLI value as-is for compatibility), populated from the value `resolve_max_num_reqs` returns.
- Optionally expose the inputs (`max_mamba_cache_size`, mamba slots per request) so clients can explain the cap, and a gauge in `/metrics` (e.g. `sglang:max_running_requests_effective`).

### Related resources
- `kv_cache_configurator.py::resolve_max_num_reqs` (warning text above) and `_calculate_mamba_ratio` (ratio 3 + 2 with radix cache + overlap schedule; 1 with `--disable-radix-cache`).

items.title: [RFC] Dynamic Latent Consensus Governor for DeepSeek-R1 to Reduce KV-Cache Holding Time by 4.5x.
items.author: Arnab758
items.body_excerpt:
## Motivation

Reasoning models like `DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-32B` generate long chains-of-thought that place severe pressure on SGLang's RadixAttention memory pools.

In our empirical profiling on an NVIDIA A100-SXM4, we observed that in ~40% of coding and algorithmic tasks, models reach the correct deduction within the first 80–120 tokens, but spend an additional 1,000–1,500 tokens in repetitive self-verification loops ("Wait, let me double check...").

This holds RadixAttention KV-cache allocations for ~150 seconds per query, creating a major throughput bottleneck in multi-tenant serving.

## Proposed Solution: SubNeutralize Latent Governor

We propose an opt-in runtime governor based on latent trajectory dynamics at the model's cognitive bottleneck layer (layer 32 on 32B models, layer 14 on 7B models):

1. **Directional Velocity:** `v_t = 1 - cos(h_t, h_{t-1})`
2. **Scale-Free Momentum:** `R_t = v_t / EMA_t(v_t)` (alpha=0.10)
3. **Consensus Trigger:** When `R_t < 0.82` for 2 consecutive decode steps, consensus equilibrium is certified, early-terminating the reasoning loop and transitioning to emission.

## Empirical Benchmark (A100-SXM4, DeepSeek-R1-32B)

Tested on complex backend coding tasks under a 1,500 token ceiling:
* **Tokens Consumed:** 5,698 -> 1,261 (**77.9% reduction**)
* **Wall-Clock Latency:** 596.1s -> 132.3s (**4.51x speedup**)
* **Unit Test Accuracy:** 4/4 PASS (**100% preserved**)
* **Kernel Overhead:** < 15 µs per decode step (< 0.05% overhead)

## Reference & Paper
* **Paper (Zenodo DOI):** https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22941619
* **Reference Implementation:** https://github.com/Arnab758/subneutralize
* **Related vLLM RFC:** https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/58909

We would love to discuss with SGLang maintainers how to cleanest integrate this into SGLang's scheduler/worker decoding loop.

items.title: [Bug] `--enable-unified-memory` on a hybrid-SWA model kills the scheduler, `alloc_token_slots` raises "Out of memory"
items.author: Yunzez
items.body_excerpt:
### Checklist

- [x] I searched related issues but found no solution.
- [x] The bug persists in the latest version.
- [x] Issues without environment info and a minimal reproducible demo are hard to resolve and may receive no feedback.
- [x] If this is not a bug report but a general question, please start a discussion at https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/discussions. Otherwise, it will be closed.
- [x] Please use English. Otherwise, it will be closed.

### Describe the bug

`openai/gpt-oss-20b` (hybrid sliding-window attention) runs with `--enable-unified-memory`. After a few minutes of mixed
traffic, the scheduler process dies:

```
Out of memory. Try to lower your batch size.
Try to allocate 2389 tokens.
Available full tokens: 4799 (full_available_size=4658 + full_evictable_size_=141)
Available swa: 5822 (available_size=4658 + component_evictable_size_=1164)
Scheduler hit an exception: Traceback (most recent call last):
  ...
  File ".../sglang/srt/managers/scheduler.py", line 4108, in _get_new_batch_prefill_raw
  File ".../sglang/srt/managers/schedule_batch.py", line 2793, in prepare_for_extend
  File ".../sglang/srt/mem_cache/allocation.py", line 396, in alloc_for_extend
  File ".../sglang/srt/mem_cache/allocation.py", line 169, in alloc_token_slots
RuntimeError: Out of memory. Try to lower your batch size.
```

The allocator's own report says the allocation fits:

- The joint available size (`UnifiedSWATokenToKVPoolAllocator.available_size()`, already expressed in tokens that each take one FULL and one SWA page) is **4,658**. The request is **2,389**.
- **141** FULL and **1,164** SWA tokens are evictable on top of that.

Even so, `evict_to_free_tokens` → `reclaim_plan` evicts nothing, `allocator.alloc(2389)` returns `None`, and the scheduler raises. No retract or fallback runs, so the server stops answering. On an A100-40GB the same failure appeared as `allocate 4096` with `full_available_size=8116` plus 2,082 evictable, five times out of five runs.

The same server without `--enable-unified-memory` serves the identical request stream to the end.


### Reproduction

nvironment: SGLang v0.5.21 (source build), 1x RTX 4090 24 GB; the A100-SXM4-40GB runs failed the same way.
Model: `openai/gpt-oss-20b`.

Start the server. Run it once with `--enable-unified-memory` and once without:

```bash
python -m sglang.launch_server --model-path openai/gpt-oss-20b --served-model-name openai/gpt-oss-20b --port 30000 \
    --context-length 8192 --mem-fraction-static 0.85 --swa-full-tokens-ratio 0.8 --max-total-tokens 12000 \
    --enable-cache-report --chunked-prefill-size 4096 --attention-backend triton --enable-metrics \
    --enable-unified-memory
```

Replay the attached request stream (`request_stream.jsonl`) with the attached client (`repro_wire_log_replay.py`). The stream holds 1,437 requests with their recorded start offsets:
[repro_wire_log_replay.py](https://gist.github.com/Yunzez/e125ead2b431dc2a85f355ae59dc12d4#file-repro_wire_log_replay-py)

- `/v1/completions`, `/generate` and `/v1/chat/completions` requests, some streamed and some cancelled mid-flight;
- `/flush_cache` and `/reset_prefix_cache` calls;
- `/metrics` and `/v1/loads` polls.

The client re-sends each request at its original offset, cancels the cancelled ones at their original time, and reports whether the server still answers `/health` afterwards:

```bash
python repro_wire_log_replay.py request_stream.jsonl http://127.0.0.1:30000
```

Results, same card, same build, same flags apart from the one under test:

| | `--enable-unified-memory` | without |
|---|---|---|
| requests replayed | 1,437 | 1,437 |
| answered | 1,193 (32 cancelled on schedule) | 1,405 (32 cancelled on schedule) |
| failed | 212: every request after the scheduler died | 0 |
| `Out of memory` in the server log | 2 (`allocate 2389`, joint available 4,658) | 0 |
| `/health` after the replay | connection refused | 200 |

The bug was first found by a fuzzing cell that ran this configuration against gpt-oss-20b on an A100-SXM4-40GB. It died at iteration 15 or 16 in 5 of 5 runs across two seeds. The same cell without `--enable-unified-memory` ran 133 iterations. Replaying only the generation requests did not reproduce the crash. The `/flush_cache` and `/reset_prefix_cache` calls in the stream appear to be needed. They empty the radix tree while pages stay allocated at both ends of the shared buffer. This has not been reduced further.

items.title: [Feature]: Add a 2-bit KV-cache quantisation backend from Together AI
items.author: zhangj1an
items.body_excerpt:
### 🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch

## Purpose

Integrate a new INT2 KV-cache quantisation backend.

Paper:**OSCAR** ([arXiv:2605.17757](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.17757)). 
Code: https://github.com/FutureMLS-Lab/OSCAR 
(500+ stars, proved to be working on Qwen3-32B, GLM-4.7-FP8.)
Website: https://oscar-quantize.github.io/

vLLM already has TurboQuant, a data-free Hadamard-rotation KV-cache quantizer. Oscar is similar, but has better accuracy. If we apply the most aggresive quantisation method in TurboQuant, (`turboquant_3bit_nc`), the accuracy will drop by 20%. But with Oscar, for Qwen3-32B and GLM-4.7-FP8 respectively, the mean gap to BF16 is −0.02, and +0.27 points while reducing KV memory by ~8× and increasing large-batch throughput by up to ~7×. 

The main idea is, before applying clipped INT2 scalar quantization, we first apply a per-layer covariance-aware orthogonal rotation to distribute the values evenly, so they can be later de-quantised with higher precision. 

To use this feature, just need to load the original model checkpoints, and download a small per-layer rotation file
(`[head_dim, head_dim]` orthogonal matrices, a few MB), published in the [OSCAR RotationZoo](https://huggingface.co/Zhongzhu/OSCAR-RotationZoo).

## CC List
Paper author: @zzz0906
vLLM maintainer: @mgoin, @robertgshaw2-redhat 

## Implementation Details
- We stored rotation matrix for K and V. 
- Then, we use the same fp16 `(scale, zero)` parameter for each vector. We then store these values by re-using TurboQuant's `TQFullAttentionSpec` in a Combined `[key_packed | value_packed]` slot (72 B/token/kv-head
  at `head_dim=128`). 
- We also introuced 3 additional triton kernels for this feature. Fused Triton store (quant + pack + scatter) and split-KV decode attention (INT2 unpack + online softmax + AV), plus a full-dequant kernel for the continuation-prefill path.

We will mainly change these files:
- `vllm/model_executor/layers/quantization/oscar/`: config,  rotation loading.
- `vllm/v1/attention/backends/oscar_attn.py`: prefill (BF16 attention + INT2 store), decode (rotate-Q → INT2 score/AV → `R_vᵀ` output).
- `vllm/v1/attention/ops/triton_oscar_{store,decode}.py`: fused Triton INT2 pack/store and split-KV decode-attention kernels.

Usage:

```bash
export VLLM_OSCAR_K_ROTATION_PATH=.../Qwen3-32B/.../k_rotation_qqt_r_h_pbr.pt
export VLLM_OSCAR_V_ROTATION_PATH=.../Qwen3-32B/.../v_rotation_sst_r_h_pbr.pt
export VLLM_OSCAR_K_CLIP_RATIO=0.96 VLLM_OSCAR_V_CLIP_RATIO=0.92
vllm serve Qwen/Qwen3-32B --kv-cache-dtype oscar_int2
```

## Reduce in KV-cache memory

As reported by paper, at `head_dim=128`, per token per KV head:

| Scheme | bytes | bits/elem | ratio |
|---|---|---|---|
| BF16 (K+V) | 512 | 16.0 | 1.0× |
| OSCAR INT2 slot | 72 | 2.25 | **7.11×** |
| OSCAR effective (4/64 layers BF16) | 99.5 | 3.11 | **5.15×** |

## Test plan

1. **Kernel correctness**: `tests/quantization/test_oscar.py`: INT2 store→dequant round-trip vs a PyTorch reference quantizer, and the fused INT2 decode kernel vs reference attention over the dequantized cache.
2. **End-to-end coherence**: Qwen3-32B, `--kv-cache-dtype oscar_int2` with the RotationZoo rotations.
3. **Accuracy**: GPQA-Diamond, BF16 vs OSCAR INT2, Qwen3-32B (thinking enabled).


## Not a duplicate

Checked before opening (please re-run; `gh` was unavailable in the dev sandbox):
```
gh pr list --repo vllm-project/vllm --state open --search "OSCAR"
gh pr list --repo vllm-project/vllm --state open --search "INT2 KV cache"
gh issue list --repo vllm-project/vllm --search "OSCAR 2-bit KV"
```
No existing OSCAR / INT2-KV-cache backend in `main`; the only adjacent work is TurboQuant (3-bit, data-free), which this complements at the 2-bit frontier.


### Alternatives

- Use `turboquant_3bit_nc`. It would incur ~50% larger KV than OSCAR INT2 and performs worth on reasoning at the 2-bit frontier, as stated by the paper.
- Per-tensor INT2 without calibrated rotation. The model will just collapse (verified on my local test. identity-rotation INT2 on Qwen3 produces incoherent text).

### Additional context

High accuracy, low-bit quantisation method is becoming increasing important in production use, such as autoround in `llm-compressor`.  So we believe this algo will be a valuable add. 

### Before submitting a new issue...

- [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.

items.title: [RFC]: Streaming Derender for Disaggregated Serving
items.author: hickeyma
items.body_excerpt:
### Motivation.

The batch derender endpoints (`/v1/chat/completions/derender`, `/v1/completions/derender`) landed in #43606 (detokenization) and #45919 (non-streaming reasoning/tool parsing). They consume `GenerateResponse` and emit a complete `ChatCompletionResponse`.

Many real world disaggregated consumers cannot use a batch only post processing tier:

- **Interactive serving** (llm-d, Dynamo) returns tokens to end clients as they are generated. Streaming is a **hard gating requirement** (ref: @bbrowning in https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/42729#issuecomment-4631310758).
- The producer side already streams e2e. `/inference/v1/generate` returns an SSE `StreamingResponse` when `request.stream` is set (`scale_out/token_in_token_out/api_router.py`), emitting `GenerateStreamResponse` chunks whose `GenerateResponseStreamChoice` carries the delta token IDs per step (`scale_out/token_in_token_out/serving.py`). `/render` already forwards `stream` / `stream_options`. **It therefore needs to be implemented on the  derender side.**

This RFC specifies a streaming derender that is the inverse of the streaming render path.

Partial:
- #34407
- #22817

Companion to:
- #42729

#### Why is this not a flag on the derender batch endpoint?

1. **Different input type.** The batch path (#42729) consumes a complete `GenerateResponse`. Streaming consumes `GenerateStreamResponse` *deltas*. It is therefore a distinct request shape and not a parameter on the existing endpoint.
2. **Incremental detokenization is stateful.** `IncrementalDetokenizer` carries `prefix_offset` / `read_offset` / prior tokens across `update()` calls. A naive per chunk `tokenizer.decode()` produces wrong spacing and can split multi-byte characters (see #44620). The per step delta `token_ids` are the right incremental input. `GenerateStreamResponse` however does **not** carry the detokenizer offsets and that state has to come from somewhere.
3. **Streaming parsers are stateful too.** Reasoning/tool parsers maintain incremental parse state across deltas (the reasoning to content/tool transition, partial tool call JSON). This compounds the state transport question below.

### Proposed Change.

#### New endpoints

| Method | Path | Input | Output |
|--------|------|-------|--------|
| `POST` | `/v1/chat/completions/derender` (`stream: true`) | `DerenderChatStreamRequest` | JSON `{ "chunk": ChatCompletionStreamResponse, "stream_state": DerenderStreamState }` |
| `POST` | `/v1/completions/derender` (`stream: true`) | `DerenderCompletionStreamRequest` | JSON `{ "chunk": CompletionStreamResponse, "stream_state": DerenderStreamState }` |

> [!NOTE]
> Streaming reuses the same `derender/` path with a `stream: true` flag, mirroring the producer (`/inference/v1/generate`). FastAPI validates a typed union discriminated on the `stream` literal and the handler dispatches with `isinstance`. The existing non-streaming types keep `generate_response` required.

Both endpoints run on the existing render server (GPU-free, only the `Renderer`/tokenizer) and are **stateless**.

#### Response format: plain JSON per call, not SSE

The derender is a **stateless per chunk translator**: one request in to one `{ "chunk", "stream_state" }` out. SSE out was rejected because it requires either a long lived connection or buffering all chunks before calling derender. This both conflict with the stateless design (Option A). The SSE protocol lives on the generate side and the final usage chunk are the client's responsibility.

#### Core design decision: incremental state (Option A, stateless)

The server returns updated state in each chunk. The client echoes it back on the next chunk. Server stays stateless and idempotent. There is no `request_id` keyed session and no lifecycle/eviction on the render tier.

Other design decision considered:

- **Option B (server-side session keyed by `request_id`)**: rejected because it breaks statelessness and adds session lifecycle + eviction + memory pressure.
- **Option C (shm state transport)**: deferred as a future optimization for large round tripped state on long generations. Only consider after Option A's payload cost is measured.

#### Parser state: replay (no opaque serialization)

Tool parsers hold internals we can't cheaply round trip (`prev_tool_call_arr`, `current_tool_id`, `streamed_args_for_tool`, engine lexer buffers). Rather than serialize them, the streaming chat derender **rebuilds a fresh parser each chunk by replaying the output tokens through it**, then feeds the new chunk and emits whatever the parser hands back.

Replay keeps the producer's chunk boundaries. `stream_state` carries `output_chunk_lens` (the token count of each chunk as it arrived) next to `output_token_ids`. Every chunk, replayed or live, goes through one `parse_delta` call. That matches standard serving which calls `parse_delta` once per engine step, so a multi-token step (e.g. speculative decoding) rebuilds the same parser state. Per token replay could diverge because some parser state (e.g. `history_tool_call_cnt`) advances once per `parse_delta` call. Text comes from a throwaway incremental detokenizer with `skip_special_tokens=False`, so the parser sees `</think>` / `<tool_call>` markers exactly as generate emits them.

Here are a few things to be aware of:

- **Cost:** transport is O(n) per chunk → O(n²) over a generation. Replay is one `parse_delta` call per prior chunk → O(n²) calls over a generation. `parse_delta` is itself O(n) for parsers that re-scan the accumulated text (Hermes tool call JSON, DeepSeek-R1 reasoning), so compute is O(n³) character work. `prompt_token_ids` is also sent and re-scanned on every chunk, so on long prompts it dominates the payload. Prompt + history + delta is bounded by `max_model_len` and rejected past it. Replay runs off the event loop on the renderer's executor (`renderer_num_workers`, default `1`), so size it for concurrent parser configured streams. Documented in `derenderer.md`.
- **Measured

~~~

The output above is from the container that served the failing request. Very long CPU flag/vulnerability lines were omitted because they are unrelated; full non-secret collect_env.py output can be provided if needed.
</details>

### 🐛 Describe the bug

## Summary

With Qwen3.8-27B NVFP4 served by vLLM 0.27.1 using the Qwen3 reasoning parser, streaming OpenAI-compatible Chat Completions, strict response_format.type=json_schema with a top-level array schema, and DSpark speculative decoding K=7, XGrammar repeatedly logged Failed to advance FSM.

Most calls completed normally, but one call returned HTTP 200 with an incomplete JSON array followed by 249,698 whitespace characters. The vLLM container remained healthy and did not restart.

This looks related to #52852, #53181, #53777 and the accepted-block validation discussed in #52452, but this report adds a separately observed environment and a preserved client-visible failure mode: RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell, DSpark K=7, Qwen3 reasoning, explicit JSON Schema array, concurrent streaming, and a roughly 250k-character whitespace tail.

## Related issues / PRs already checked

- #43338 appears to be the same broad structured-output/speculative-decoding family, but focuses on multi-token GPT-OSS reasoning boundaries and reports Qwen3 as its working control.
- #52852 is the closest prior report: Qwen3.8 NVFP4 + streaming + XGrammar with token 271 FSM failures.
- #53181 reports recurrence after the fix referenced when #52852 was closed.
- #53777 reports a similar failure with DFlash2 and json_object.
- #52805 stops XGrammar token batches at grammar termination.
- #52452 validates speculative accepted blocks before commit, explicitly covers reasoning-boundary/grammar-termination invariants, and mentions DSpark K5 qualification.

Please close this as a duplicate if one of those fully covers this path. I am filing it because this is a new DSpark K7 + json_schema top-level array reproduction with a saved malformed response and detailed runtime statistics.

## Effective server launch

The private registry hostname is omitted. The container reports the upstream base tag shown in the environment section. The effective vLLM command was:

~~~bash
vllm serve /model/Qwen3.8-27B-NVFP4-unsloth --served-model-name /model/Qwen3.8-27B-FP8 --language-model-only --reasoning-parser qwen3 --enable-prefix-caching --gpu-memory-utilization 0.55 --port 80 --max-model-len 262144 --kv-cache-dtype fp8 --max-num-seqs 12 --max-num-batched-tokens 24576 --enable-auto-tool-choice --tool-call-parser qwen3_coder --speculative-config '{"method":"dspark","model":"/model/Qwen3.8-27B-DSpark-RadixArk","num_speculative_tokens":7,"draft_sample_method":"probabilistic"}'
~~~

The startup wrapper maps the draft model architecture name DSparkDraftModel to Qwen3DSparkModel before exec'ing vllm serve. No vLLM Python source files are patched.

## Request shape

The real extraction text is private, so it is redacted below. This is the exact API/options/schema shape, but not yet a deterministic public minimal prompt:

~~~python
from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(base_url="http://<vllm-endpoint>/v1", api_key="<redacted>")

response_format = {
    "type": "json_schema",
    "json_schema": {
        "name": "business_database_extraction",
        "strict": True,
        "schema": {
            "type": "array",
            "items": {
                "type": "object",
                "properties": {
                    "field_key": {"type": "string"},
                    "value": {"type": "string"},
                    "chunk_id": {"type": "string"},
                    "confidence": {
                        "type": "number",
                        "minimum": 0,
                        "maximum": 1,
                    },
                },
                "required": [
                    "field_key",
                    "value",
                    "chunk_id",
                    "confidence",
                ],
                "additionalProperties": False,
            },
        },
    },
}

stream = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="/model/Qwen3.8-27B-FP8",
    messages=[
        {"role": "system", "content": "Return only JSON matching the supplied schema."},
        {"role": "user", "content": "<redacted private extraction text>"},
    ],
    max_tokens=25000,
    temperature=0.1,
    top_p=0.95,
    presence_penalty=0.5,
    stream=True,
    stop=[],
    reasoning_effort="medium",
    response_format=response_format,
    extra_body={
        "top_k": 20,
        "repetition_penalty": 1.0,
        "chat_template_kwargs": {
            "enable_thinking": True,
            "preserve_thinking": False,
        },
    },
)
~~~

No tools were requested in these calls. The top-level array schema was accepted by vLLM and normally produced valid arrays in the other calls.

## Reproduction workload

- 10 application-level runs
- concurrency: 2
- each run split the same request into 3 model calls (12, 12 and 5 expected items)
- one downstream repair call after the malformed result
- 31 total model calls in the test
- 30 primary calls used the same private source text and field definitio

comments.author: jahnclawdmonet
comments.body:
From the source at your build (`6e448d0ea9bf`, the v0.27.1 tag), not from running your workload: it lacks #52805's in-batch termination checks. `accept_tokens()` updates `_is_terminated` only after the loop, and `validate_tokens()` has no termination check at all ([backend_xgrammar.py#L152-L188](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/6e448d0ea9bf3d88d898b65449ca6dc2aec170ac/vllm/v1/structured_output/backend_xgrammar.py#L152-L188)). The `grammar_matcher.cc:612` warning in your log is consistent with that: once a batch terminates mid-loop, both functions keep feeding tokens to a finished matcher.

#52805 (`12f64b39d292`) moves the check inside `accept_tokens()`'s loop, adds one to `validate_tokens()`, and makes an accept after termination return True instead of False ([backend_xgrammar.py#L157-L201](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/12f64b39d29282437e35be9aa5db432fb2a1a6e6/vllm/v1/structured_output/backend_xgrammar.py#L157-L201)). As of today no stable release contains that commit: v0.28.0 (`2cf0a6915ce5`) still has the old loops, and the earliest tag carrying it is `v0.28.1rc0` ([`v0.28.1rc0`](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/79651d6085885cf2842baf85526ece7afa87c87d/vllm/v1/structured_output/backend_xgrammar.py#L157-L201)).

The FSM log alone is ambiguous, because two paths in serving hit the same `logger.error` at `backend_xgrammar.py:162`. Your build's `StructuredOutputManager.grammar_bitmask()` calls `accept_tokens()` while simulating speculative candidates after a reasoning boundary, tolerates rejection there, and rolls back successful advances ([structured_output/__init__.py#L308-L350](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/6e448d0ea9bf3d88d898b65449ca6dc2aec170ac/vllm/v1/structured_output/__init__.py#L308-L350)); every tolerated rejection still prints that line, and #53046 (`c6e19b3be243`, same RC boundary) puts a `validate_tokens()` check in front of that accept to stop them ([structured_output/__init__.py#L320-L342](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/c6e19b3be24338759a443e03c8325d76da9ee202/vllm/v1/structured_output/__init__.py#L320-L342)).

The other path is the scheduler rejecting already committed output; that one also logs `Unexpected: grammar rejected tokens ... Terminating request.` and sets `FINISHED_ERROR` ([scheduler.py#L1807-L1843](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/6e448d0ea9bf3d88d898b65449ca6dc2aec170ac/vllm/v1/core/sched/scheduler.py#L1807-L1843)), which the serving layer turns into an error chunk in the stream and a `Request ... failed with an internal error during generation` line ([serving.py#L170-L187](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/6e448d0ea9bf3d88d898b65449ca6dc2aec170ac/vllm/entrypoints/generate/base/serving.py#L170-L187)). Grep the server log from that window for the `grammar rejected tokens` line. If it isn't there, the FSM lines alone don't show the response broke its grammar. One more cheap check on the bad response: the `finish_reason` of its last chunk. Whitespace between array elements is legal under the compiled grammar unless `disable_any_whitespace` is set, so a model that degenerates into spaces can run to `max_tokens` without the grammar rejecting anything, and `length` there would point away from a desync.

#52452 (open, head `fa0777ff775a`, in no tag) works at the scheduler commit point instead: it filters accepted multi-token speculative blocks before `_update_request_with_output()` and keeps only the grammar-valid prefix ([scheduler.py#L1873-L1911](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/fa0777ff775a870a5d6a6ff187f769e50b38c4ad/vllm/v1/core/sched/scheduler.py#L1873-L1911)). Its base already contains #52805. For your second question: right area, but the diff alone doesn't tell me whether it covers your K7 case, and whether the combination is meant to be supported is a maintainer call. Those two answers settle which path you were on.

comments.author: Recursive-Logic-Core
comments.body:
This failure mode perfectly illustrates the architectural tax of token-level grammar enforcement (FSM masking) on reasoning models with speculative decoding.

When an FSM desyncs at a boundary condition, an unconstrained whitespace production rule becomes an infinite sink. Emitting 249,698 trailing spaces over 646 seconds with HTTP 200 is the ultimate symptom of over-constraining the model at the wrong abstraction layer.

While patching accept_tokens() loop invariants in XGrammar (#52805) addresses the immediate engine crash, relying on rigid, nested JSON schemas for extraction pipelines remains structurally fragile:

Syntax-to-payload overhead: 30–50% of the token budget is burned purely on structural ballast (quotes, commas, closing delimiters).

Speculative decoding breakdown: Strict regex/FSM masks drastically reduce draft acceptance rates across token boundaries.

For tabular/database extraction like business_database_extraction, an architectural alternative is bypassing JSON entirely in favor of a deterministic, single-pass line protocol:

-record_01
.field:f13
.chunk:chunk_a
.confidence:0.98
.value:extracted_string

Using a prefix-deterministic grammar (such as SLAP — Structural Line Algorithm Path) eliminates bracket-balancing, lookaheads, and whitespace sinks completely. It cuts payload size by >50% while allowing unconstrained greedy/speculative decoding without risking FSM deadlocks.

comments.author: jahnclawdmonet
comments.body:
The negative has a second difference from the report, in the code path this bug was traced to.

In the reporter's build (`6e448d0ea9bf`), `vllm/v1/structured_output/backend_xgrammar.py` sets `_is_terminated` at line 170, after the accept loop has finished, and `validate_tokens` at 173 carries no termination guard at all. In yours (`a8d1aa9c9`), `accept_tokens` sets and checks it inside the loop at 176 and 177, and `validate_tokens` guards on entry at 187 and calls `matcher.is_terminated()` in its own loop at 194. Those are the in-batch termination checks absent from the reporter's build.

So the runs differ in both draft acceptance rate and the XGrammar termination path.

If you want to separate the two variables, attempt 3 against a build from before those checks landed would do it without changing the harness. If the whitespace tail appears at 92 percent acceptance, prompt strength was not the variable.

All 60 calls returned HTTP 200, `finish_reason="stop"`, `[DONE]`, valid JSON matching the schema, the expected field set, and **zero trailing whitespace**.

items.title: [Performance]: spec-decode boot-to-boot throughput dispersion on L4 (CV up to 13.92%), resolved in 0.30.0
items.author: akshathtiwari
items.body_excerpt:
### Proposal to improve performance

Not a proposal so much as a measurement suggestion. Speculative-decoding throughput on this stack is boot-dependent to a degree a single-boot benchmark cannot see: on 0.29.0 / L4, twelve boots of a byte-identical configuration gave CV 13.92% in one container and 3.73% in another. Anything comparing speculative configurations from one boot each is partly measuring which boot it got.

0.30.0 looks much better on this axis (0.99% and 1.61% across two containers on different physical cards), so this may already be resolved. I am reporting it mainly because the mechanism is not what I assumed, and the protocol seems worth having on record either way.

### Report of performance regression

Reporting this because 0.30.0 appears to resolve it, and the obvious explanation turns out to be wrong, so something else changed and I would like to know what.

**Setup.** Qwen3-4B target, `z-lab/Qwen3-4B-DFlash-b16` drafter, 5 speculative tokens, bf16 weights, `--kv-cache-dtype auto`, FlashInfer pinned. GSM8K, concurrency 1, one fixed prompt set replayed on every boot. 12 boots per arm inside a single container, one physical GPU per session (UUID recorded). The harness speaks HTTP only and never imports vLLM.

Throughput at concurrency 1, output tokens/s:

| card | engine | session | default | --enforce-eager | ratio | default CV |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| L4 (SM89) | 0.29.0 | A | 39.2 | 80.5 | **0.487** | **13.92%** |
| L4 (SM89) | 0.29.0 | B | 61.2 | 79.7 | **0.768** | **3.73%** |
| L4 (SM89) | 0.30.0 | C | 82.8 | 81.6 | **1.014** | 0.99% |
| L4 (SM89) | 0.30.0 | D | 78.2 | 77.0 | **1.017** | 1.61% |
| A10 (SM86) | 0.29.0 | E | 132.6 | 138.3 | 0.959 | 2.08% |

Each ratio is the default arm divided by the eager arm measured in the same container, so session and card effects cancel. On 0.29.0/L4 the CUDA-graph path runs at 49% and 77% of the eager path; on 0.30.0 it reaches parity. Acceptance length is flat throughout (tau 4.11-4.15), so this is throughput rather than a change in what the drafter gets accepted.

### Misc discussion on performance

Two observations, one related issue, and a question.

**1. The CUDA-graph fallback still fires on 0.30.0.** I had assumed the improvement was the speculative path gaining full graphs. It is not. The warning is byte-identical on both versions and capture proceeds under PIECEWISE in each:

> CUDAGraphMode.FULL_AND_PIECEWISE is not supported with spec-decode for attention backend FlashInferBackend (support: AttentionCGSupport.UNIFORM_SINGLE_TOKEN_DECODE); setting cudagraph_mode=PIECEWISE

Backend selection is unchanged too: both versions log FLASHINFER for the target and FLASH_ATTN for the second selection. So neither graph mode nor backend choice explains the difference.

**2. On 0.29.0 the dispersion magnitude is itself not reproducible.** Two twelve-boot measurements of the identical configuration gave CV 13.92% and 3.73%, with means 39.2 and 61.2 tok/s. The effect is present in both; its size is not a property of the configuration. The eager arm is stable across every session measured (80.5, 79.7, 81.6, 77.0 on L4; 138.3 on A10), which is what makes it usable as a control.

**Related, but I do not think it is the same thing: #58677.** That reports the draft model's torch.compile cache identity flipping between exactly two values across restarts with byte-identical argv, attributed to the shared VllmConfig being mutated in-place during the main model's warmup and CUDA-graph-capture phase, before the draft head compiles. Two differences: the symptom there is startup recompile cost rather than steady-state throughput, and it reports 0.27.1 affected with 0.29 appearing immune, whereas what I measure is on 0.29.0.

Still, the shape is close enough that I would rather ask than assume: **if VllmConfig is mutated in place during graph capture and that mutation reaches what the draft compiles to, could the same mechanism produce a steady-state throughput difference and not only a cache-key difference?** My measurements begin after the server reports healthy, so any recompilation has finished by then.


**The question.** What changed between 0.29.0 and 0.30.0 on this path, given the fallback and the backend selection are identical in both? If a specific PR is responsible I would rather cite it than guess. I looked at #53867, #51700, #54646 and #52228 and could not attribute it from the release notes alone.

**Possibly relevant.** The effect is much weaker on an A10 (ratio 0.959) than on an L4 (0.487 and 0.768) at the same engine version. The A10 has 24 GiB against the L4's 22.03 GiB usable, and this configuration sits close enough to the memory ceiling that --enforce-eager alone decides whether an fp8_e4m3-KV variant boots at all. So capacity pressure may matter more here than architecture. I have not separated the two.

**Reproduction.** Harness, raw append-only records, analysis scripts and the engine logs are at https://github.com/akshathtiwari/spec-fp8-study (archived at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23033168). The boot-variance runs are one command each and the per-session numbers regenerate from the stored records. Happy to run further configurations if a specific one would help; the full sweep is a couple of GPU-hours.

### Your current environment (if you think it is necessary)

Not `collect_env.py` output: the engine runs in an ephemeral container on a rented GPU, so this machine's environment is not the one under test. These are the fields the harness records per measurement, read from nvidia-smi and from the running server.

```text
GPU         NVIDIA L4 (SM89, 22.03 GiB usable) and NVIDIA A10 (SM86)
            one physical card per session, gpu_uuid recorded per record
driver      580.95.05
CUDA        13.0
torch       2.13.0+cu130
vLLM        0.29.0 and 0.30.0, pinned by image digest. Version is read from
            the server's /version endpoint and checked against the declared
            value before any measu

comments.author: akshathtiwari
comments.body:
Correction to the "possibly relevant" paragraph in my original post.

I wrote that the A10 has 24 GiB against the L4's 22.03 GiB usable, and offered memory capacity as the likelier of two readings for why the deficit is weak on the A10. **That is wrong.** Both cards report **22.5 GiB** in my own records, and I had never checked the field before writing it. Capacity is not the difference between them.

What does differ, from the same records:

| | VRAM | arch | max SM clock | power limit |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| L4 | 22.5 GiB | SM8.9 | 2040 MHz | **72 W** |
| A10 | 22.5 GiB | SM8.6 | 1695 MHz | **150 W** |

So the card showing the deficit has less than half the power budget. That is a better fit for the symptom than capacity ever was: CUDA graphs run the work faster, faster work draws more power, and a 72 W part can hit its cap and clamp — variably, depending on thermal history, which would also explain why the dispersion magnitude itself does not reproduce between sessions. The eager arm runs slower, stays under the cap, and is stable in every session measured.

I want to be clear that this is a hypothesis and **my data cannot test it.** I was recording `clocks.max.sm` and `power.limit`, which are what the card is permitted to do, not what it did. A throttling explanation is precisely what configured limits cannot see.

I have since added sampling of achieved SM clock, power draw and `clocks_throttle_reasons.*` across the measurement window, and a run is in flight. If `sw_power_cap` is active during the default arm and not during the eager arm, that is the driver answering the question directly rather than me inferring it from a clock curve. I will post the result either way, including if it kills the hypothesis.

The throughput numbers and the ratio table in the original post are unaffected by this — they are measured, and the correction is to an explanation I attached to them.

items.title: [good-first-issue] tests: stabilize flaky CI tests from recent PRs
items.author: maobaolong
items.body_excerpt:
Part of #3372. This is a community tracker for small, independently claimable improvements to flaky tests.

## The problem

Recent PR CI contains assertions that race background work and an intermittent hang that can occupy a runner for almost six hours. These failures consume contributor time and make unrelated PRs harder to validate.

The initial triage reviewed GitHub Actions `Test` runs from September 13-23, 2026 and recent `k3-unit-tests` failures. These are selected examples, not a complete inventory or a measured repository-wide flake rate. The test code was checked against `dev` at [21571dae80c6](https://github.com/LMCache/LMCache/commit/21571dae80c64ab4d141be571744494995270160).

The initial tasks cover:

- **Health-monitor exit:** a fixed 200 ms sleep precedes a thread-exit assertion; two PRs have same-checkout failed/passed attempts.
- **Health-monitor fallback/recovery:** a fixed 200 ms sleep precedes a state assertion; failure logs show fallback completing after the assertion.
- **RESP wait diagnostics:** a same-checkout rerun passes after an almost-six-hour hang near the RESP test boundary. The exact blocked operation remains unproven; this task adds bounded waits and diagnostics, not a speculative production fix.

## Initial tasks

- [x] #5314: Synchronize health-monitor exception-driven exit
- [ ] #5315: Synchronize health-monitor fallback/recovery phases
- [ ] #5316: Bound RESP waits and add stalled-operation diagnostics

## September 22–29 follow-up tasks

The follow-up scan covered **September 22, 2026 04:31 UTC through September 29, 2026 04:31 UTC**. It inspected 1,338 GitHub Actions run records across `Test`, `CPU Device Tests`, and `Operator: CI`, and 2,106 Buildkite build records across the active LMCache pipelines, then examined relevant failed jobs and retry logs. These inventory counts are not a repository-wide flake rate or a claim that every failed log was exhaustively analyzed.

Each new task below includes a failed/passed pair within the **same `dev` Buildkite build**, with the same LMCache checkout and vLLM/torch versions. PR-head-only matches with an unverified base merge, dependency/version changes between attempts, and one-off failures were not used as confirmation.

- [ ] #5402: Make `vllm_bench` inputs reproducible across retries and retain the comparison settings/results. Build #5340 changes from 7.34% slower than baseline to 0.62% faster without a source change.
