items.title: [Onboarding 2026] Good first issues — start contributing to LMCache in one PR
items.author: maobaolong
items.body_excerpt:
👋 Welcome to LMCache! This umbrella issue is the **single entry point** for first-time
contributors. If you've never sent a PR to LMCache before, start here.

> If you're looking for the older onboarding thread, see #627. This 2026 version
> focuses on smaller, well-scoped tasks with a friendly step-by-step PR workflow.

---

## 0. Before you start

- Read [`CONTRIBUTING.md`](../blob/dev/CONTRIBUTING.md). The most important parts:
  - Base branch is `dev`. Open PRs against `dev`, not `main`.
  - Every Python file starts with `# SPDX-License-Identifier: Apache-2.0`.
  - Imports are grouped as `# Standard / # Third Party / # First Party / # Local`.
  - Line length is **88**, formatter is `ruff format`, lint is `ruff check`.
  - Never access `_private` members of other classes (SLF rule).
  - Public functions/methods need **type hints** + **docstring**.
- Set up the environment:
  ```bash
  uv venv --python 3.12 && source .venv/bin/activate
  uv pip install -e . --no-build-isolation
  uv pip install -r requirements/test.txt
  pre-commit install
  ```

## 1. How to claim a task

These tasks are mainly for new contributors to learn the LMCache issue-to-PR workflow. Please claim **only one good-first issue at a time**. If you already have an assigned good-first issue or an open good-first PR, finish that work before taking another one, and leave the remaining tasks for other newcomers.

1. Pick **one** sub-issue below that has no assignee and no `🔒 claimed` comment.
2. Comment exactly: `/claim` (or `I'd like to work on this 🙋`).
   A maintainer will assign it to you within ~2 business days.
3. If you go silent for 7 days we'll un-assign so others can pick it up — totally fine,
   just leave a comment if you need more time.

## 2. Branch & commit

```bash
git checkout dev && git pull
git checkout -b gfi/<issue-number>-short-slug
# ... do the work ...
git commit -s -m "short imperative summary"   # -s is required (DCO)
```

- **Sign-off is required** (`-s`). PRs without DCO sign-off cannot be merged.
- Keep the PR small: one issue = one PR.

## 3. Local checks (must pass before pushing)

```bash
pre-commit run --all-files
pytest -xvs tests/<the_file_you_touched>.py    # if applicable
```

## 4. Open the PR

**PR title format** (please follow):

```
[good-first-issue] <area>: <imperative summary>  (#<sub-issue-number>)
```

Examples:
- `[good-first-issue] docs: fix broken link in quickstart (#1801)`
- `[good-first-issue] tests: add unit test for FooBar.flush (#1802)`
- `[good-first-issue] lint: add SPDX header to scripts/foo.py (#1803)`

**PR description** — please use this template (the repo's PR template already
gives you the skeleton; just fill it in):

```markdown
**What this PR does / why we need it**:
Closes #<sub-issue-number>
Refs #<this umbrella issue number>

<one or two sentences describing the change>

**Special notes for your reviewers**:
- This is my first PR to LMCache 🙇 please be gentle.
- I ran `pre-commit run --all-files` locally — all green.
- I ran `pytest -xvs tests/...` — all green.

**If applicable**:
- [ ] this PR contains user facing changes - docs added
- [ ] this PR contains unit tests
```

> Tip: writing `Closes #1234` in the description auto-closes the sub-issue when the
> PR is merged. Keep `Refs #<umbrella>` so the umbrella stays linked.

## 5. Finding a reviewer

You don't need to find one yourself — `.github/CODEOWNERS` will auto-request
the right people based on the files you changed. If the PR sits idle for **3 working
days**, leave a polite comment like:

> Friendly ping — PTAL when you have a moment 🙏 cc @<one CODEOWNER from the file you changed>

If you really can't tell who to ping, default to:
- Tests / CI / packaging → @hickeyma @sammshen @ApostaC @deng451e
- Docs / examples → @sammshen @deng451e
- Storage backends → @maobaolong @sammshen @chunxiaozheng
- Core engine / memory → @ApostaC @YaoJiayi @sammshen
- Multiprocess → @ApostaC @OasisGit @hlin99

(See [`.github/CODEOWNERS`](../blob/dev/.github/CODEOWNERS) for the full map.)

## 6. Responding to review comments

This is the part most newcomers miss — please follow it, it makes everyone happier:

1. **Address every comment.** For each thread:
   - If you agree → push a fix and reply `Done in <commit-sha>`.
   - If you disagree → explain politely, propose an alternative.
   - If you don't understand → ask! Reviewers expect questions.
2. **Don't force-push** during review (it loses inline-comment context). Just add
   commits; we'll squash on merge.
3. **Re-request review explicitly** once all threads are resolved:
   > Addressed all comments, PTAL again 🙏 @reviewer1 @reviewer2

   `PTAL` = "Please Take Another Look". Tag every reviewer who left comments.
4. If CI is red, fix it before pinging — reviewers will skip red PRs.


---

## 7. How to create and claim a sub-issues

- You can extend the new cli commend line tools, ref to https://github.com/LMCache/LMCache/pull/3719 and https://github.com/LMCache/LMCache/pull/3678

---

Stuck? Drop a message in the `#contributors` channel of our
[Slack](https://join.slack.com/t/lmcacheworkspace/shared_invite/zt-3g8e6xzz8-KzS_HI8bPERGFK5PTB~MYg)
or comment here. We're happy to help. 🙌


**Maintainers**: please update this checklist as sub-issues are filed.

items.title: [Bug][MP] Failed prefetch cleanup can publish invalid L1 data
items.author: ae86zhizhi
items.body_excerpt:
**Label**

`bug`

**Describe the bug**

In MP mode, `PrefetchController` cleans up the L1 destination of an L2 load that failed (the adapter reported the key as not loaded) with two calls in this order:

```python
l1_mgr.finish_write(failed_keys)
l1_mgr.delete(failed_keys)
```

(`lmcache/v1/distributed/storage_controllers/prefetch_controller.py`, "Clean up failed keys" in the load-completion handler; the same pair runs in `_cleanup_in_flight_requests` on `stop()` for every request still in its load phase.)

`finish_write` makes the destination readable and notifies the write-finished listeners even though the load has not been confirmed successful; its contents may be incomplete or uninitialized. `StoreController`'s listener enqueues the key and its loop calls `reserve_read` on it, which now succeeds. If the store controller acquires and still holds that read lock when the `delete` runs, the `delete` returns `KEY_IS_LOCKED` and the entry stays; the destination is then stored to the policy-selected L2 adapters under a valid key, and a later lookup returns it as a hit.

The shutdown path has the same shape without needing a failed load: every in-flight request's `write_reserved_keys` goes through the same two calls while the store controller's loop is still running.

Even when the `delete` wins the race, the key is announced to every `L1ManagerListener` as write-finished, and `finish_write` publishes `L1_WRITE_FINISHED`, so metrics and coordinator cache events report an unconfirmed destination as a completed write.

**To Reproduce**

With the regression test of the linked pull request (`tests/v1/distributed/test_prefetch_failed_load_cleanup.py`), against `dev`:

1. Store one key in a `MockL2Adapter` and wrap it in `FaultInjectL2Adapter(gap_indices=(0,))`, so the key is present at lookup and its load is reported as failed.
2. Register an `L1ManagerListener` that records `on_l1_keys_write_finished`, and start a `StoreController` with a second, empty `MockL2Adapter` as its target.
3. Submit a prefetch for the key and wait for its result (0 retained keys).
4. The recording listener has received the failed key as write-finished (`assert key not in listener.write_finished_keys()` fails). Depending on scheduling, the empty adapter may also receive a store of the destination.

The second test checks L1 absence and listener silence when `stop()` interrupts an unfinished load (an adapter that accepts a load which then stays pending); it fails on `dev` for the same reason.

**Expected behavior**

A reservation whose load failed or was cancelled is removed while it is still write-locked. The key never becomes readable, is never announced to the write-finished listeners, and no store task is created for it. `reserve_read` on the key returns `KEY_NOT_EXIST`.

`L1Manager.delete(keys, force=True)` already does this; the fix is to call it instead of the `finish_write` + `delete` pair at both sites. A pull request with the change and the two tests follows.

**Environment**

- LMCache `dev` at 45e019df (2026-09-08); the same two call sites are in v0.5.4.
- Linux x86_64, Python 3.12, torch 2.13.0. The tests use the pinned-memory L1 and no model.

items.title: [Feature] support `gather` instead of `all_gather` when gathering the logits
items.author: chunyuan-w
items.body_excerpt:
### Checklist

- [x] 1. If the issue you raised is not a feature but a question, please raise a discussion at https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/discussions/new/choose Otherwise, it will be closed.
- [x] 2. Please use English, otherwise it will be closed.

### Motivation

We noticed that in the `_get_logits` function of vllm, `gather` instead of `all_gather` will be used under certain conditions (the main condition is that for non-tpu devices):
Code link:

- [logits = tensor_model_parallel_gather(logits)](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/6e1fc61f0fb90c37f0d4a1a8f76235a6e4e1103c/vllm/model_executor/layers/logits_processor.py#L101C22-L101C50)

- [condition of whether using `all_gather` or `gather`](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/6e1fc61f0fb90c37f0d4a1a8f76235a6e4e1103c/vllm/model_executor/layers/logits_processor.py#L53-L57)

The change from using `all_gather` to `gather` is initially added in this PR for your reference: https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/2221.

While in SGLang, we see currently `all_gather` is always used:
https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/blob/e868d0b60eb2d435c5599165f787bca06bdc9c3d/python/sglang/srt/layers/logits_processor.py#L246

Does SGLang have the plan to add `gather` instead of only `all_gather` when gathering the logits? Per the practice in vllm, using `gather` seems to have better performance than `all_gather` on devices which have `gather` support.

items.title: [Performance] NVFP4 KV cache regresses Qwen4Exp decode ~29% on DGX Spark (SM121) vs fp8_e4m3 — consider arch-gating the default
items.author: leego
items.body_excerpt:
# [Performance] NVFP4 KV cache regresses Qwen4Exp decode ~29% on DGX Spark (SM121) vs fp8_e4m3

## Summary
`--kv-cache-dtype nvfp4` (the new default, `NVFP4_KV_CACHE=1`) costs **~29% single-stream
decode throughput** for Qwen4Exp-style models (QSA sparse attention) on GB10/SM121,
versus fp8_e4m3 KV. The FP4 packed-KV path's gather-side dequant is expensive on this
silicon; on datacenter parts the tradeoff may differ, but on Spark the pool-size win
is pointless (262K native context already fits with fp8) and the decode cost is real.

## Data (2× DGX Spark TP=2, NEXTN 3/1/4, decode CUDA graphs on, n=7-10 median)
| KV dtype | single-stream decode | notes |
|---|---|---|
| nvfp4 (default since the NVFP4-KV change) | 44.0 tok/s | also occasional deep dips |
| **fp8_e4m3** (`NVFP4_KV_CACHE=0`) | **56.8-58.6 tok/s** | stable |
| bf16 | 54-59 (more variance) | |

Same cluster, same weights (RadixArk/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-NVFP4), same bench
(`completion_tokens`-based streaming, 400-token runs).

## Suggestion
- Gate `NVFP4_KV_CACHE` default by arch: keep 1 on SM100+, default 0 on SM120/121 for
  QSA models (or autotune at first capture).
- Alternatively add a fused gather+dequant path for FP4 KV in the QSA Triton varlen
  fallback kernel (`qsa_fa_fallback.py` pattern used on SM121).

## Environment
Image lmsysorg/sglang:qwen38flashnext (+SM121 QSA fallback), 2×GB10, RoCEv2 TP2.
Full methodology: MiaAI-Lab/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-Dual-DGX-Sparks → OPTIMIZATION-2026-08-28.md.

items.title: [Bug] HiCache backup thread dies on any storage backend exception; queued backups and their host memory are never released
items.author: qidaye
items.body_excerpt:
### Checklist

- [x] I searched related issues but found no solution.
- [x] The bug persists in the latest version.
- [x] Issues without environment info and a minimal reproducible demo are hard to resolve and may receive no feedback.
- [x] If this is not a bug report but a general question, please start a discussion at https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/discussions. Otherwise, it will be closed.
- [x] Please use English. Otherwise, it will be closed.

### Describe the bug

`HiCacheController.backup_thread_func` (and the `HybridCacheController` override) only catches `queue.Empty`:

```python
while not self.storage_stop_event.is_set():
    try:
        operation = self.backup_queue.get(block=True, timeout=1)
        if operation is None:
            continue
        if not self.backup_skip:
            self._page_backup(operation)
        self.ack_backup_queue.put(operation)
    except Empty:
        continue
```

Any exception raised by the storage backend while writing a page (I/O error, timeout, malformed response from a remote store such as Mooncake / NIXL / 3FS / HF3FS / file backends) escapes the loop and kills the daemon thread. From that point on:

- every backup operation stays in `backup_queue` forever and is never written to L3;
- `ack_backup_queue` never drains, so `HiRadixCache` / `UnifiedRadixCache` never release the host memory held by those operations (`entry.release_host()` in the backup drain path);
- the only visible symptom is host pool exhaustion much later. There is no log line pointing at the dead backup thread, and `hicache_*` metrics keep reporting as if backups were in flight.

A backend that returns `False` from `batch_set` already stops the current operation, but the acked `StorageOperation` carries no information about the failure, so the ack consumer cannot distinguish a partial or failed write from a complete one.

Expected: a failing backup should be logged, the operation should still be acked (so host memory is released and the queue keeps draining), and the ack should say what went wrong.

### Reproduction

Drives the production `backup_thread_func` with a controller stub whose backend raises once. No GPU or model needed.

```python
import threading
from queue import Empty, Queue
from unittest import mock

import torch

from sglang.srt.managers.cache_controller import HiCacheController, StorageOperation

controller = mock.MagicMock()
controller.storage_stop_event = threading.Event()
controller.backup_skip = False
controller.page_size = 16
controller.backup_queue = Queue()
controller.ack_backup_queue = Queue()

calls = [0]
def page_backup(operation):
    calls[0] += 1
    if calls[0] == 1:
        raise RuntimeError("storage backend I/O error")  # e.g. remote store timeout
    operation.completed_tokens = 16 * len(operation.hash_value)
controller._page_backup = page_backup

def make_op(n):
    return StorageOperation(torch.zeros(n * 16), list(range(n * 16)), hash_value=[f"h{i}" for i in range(n)])

controller.backup_queue.put(make_op(4))
controller.backup_queue.put(make_op(2))

t = threading.Thread(target=HiCacheController.backup_thread_func, args=(controller,), daemon=True)
t.start()
t.join(timeout=3)
print("backup thread alive:", t.is_alive())
acked = []
try:
    while True:
        acked.append(controller.ack_backup_queue.get(timeout=1).id)
except Empty:
    pass
print("acked operations:", acked, "(2 expected)")
print("still queued:", controller.backup_queue.qsize())
```

Output on `main` (2358916d5a):

```
Exception in thread Thread-1 (backup_thread_func):
Traceback (most recent call last):
  ...
  File ".../sglang/srt/managers/cache_controller.py", line 1289, in backup_thread_func
    self._page_backup(operation)
RuntimeError: storage backend I/O error
backup thread alive: False
acked operations: [] (2 expected)
still queued: 1
```

The same happens in a real deployment whenever the L3 backend raises during `batch_set` (observed with a remote storage backend timing out under load): the backup thread disappears and host memory is never reclaimed.

In a server the trigger is any exception from the configured `--hicache-storage-backend` during a write; e.g. `--enable-hierarchical-cache --hicache-storage-backend <backend>` with a backend that becomes unreachable.

### Environment

Reproduction above is CPU-only and does not depend on the accelerator.

```
sglang: main @ 2358916d5a (editable install from source)
python: 3.12.13
torch: 2.13.0+cpu
OS: Ubuntu 24.04, Linux 7.0.0-30-generic
```

`python3 -m sglang.check_env` currently fails on a CPU-only host with `NameError: name 'env' is not defined` (no branch in `check_env.py` for the CPU case), so the versions above were collected manually.

A fix is in #38427.

items.title: [Bug] HiCache write_through does not fully persist first-seen prefixes before eviction
items.author: donghyq
items.body_excerpt:
# [SGLang] HiCache `write_through` does not fully persist first-seen prefixes before eviction

## Summary

When `--hicache-write-policy write_through` is used with Mooncake Store, a first-seen prefix can be evicted from L1/L2 before all of its KV is backed up to storage. Replaying that prefix after eviction restores only part of it from L3; the rest is recomputed.

Using `--hicache-write-policy write_back --hicache-storage-prefetch-policy wait_complete` on the same workload restores the full prefix from Mooncake Store, so the storage backend and restore path are functional.

## Environment

- SGLang commit: `bdf8886ad3`
- Branch: `main`
- Model: Qwen3-4B
- GPU: 1 × NVIDIA H20-3e
- Attention backend: Triton
- HiCache:
  - `--enable-hierarchical-cache`
  - `--hicache-size 4`
  - `--hicache-write-policy write_through`
  - `--hicache-storage-backend mooncake`
  - `--hicache-storage-backend-extra-config '{"standalone_storage": true, "client_server_address": "127.0.0.1:50300", "enable_group_semantics": false}'`
- Mooncake Store:
  - master/client started independently
  - `root_fs_dir` and `cluster_id` configured
  - global segment size: 16 GiB
- Prompt: 5 distinct 16,011-token prefixes, `max_new_tokens=1`
- L1 capacity: 42,763 tokens
- L2 capacity: 27,127 tokens

## Reproduction

1. Start SGLang with the `write_through` configuration above.
2. Flush the cache.
3. Send five distinct 16,011-token prefixes sequentially.
4. Replay prefix A after prefixes B–E have displaced it from L1/L2.

## Expected

Prefix A should be restored from Mooncake Store with roughly:

```json
{
  "cached_tokens": 16010,
  "cached_tokens_details": {
    "device": 0,
    "host": 0,
    "storage": 16010,
    "storage_backend": "MooncakeStore"
  }
}
```

## Actual

Prefix A restores only part of the KV from storage:

```json
{
  "cached_tokens": 2551,
  "cached_tokens_details": {
    "device": 0,
    "host": 0,
    "storage": 2551,
    "storage_backend": "MooncakeStore"
  }
}
```

A second replay then reports a full device hit:

```json
{
  "cached_tokens": 16009,
  "cached_tokens_details": {
    "device": 16009,
    "host": 0,
    "storage": 0,
    "storage_backend": "MooncakeStore"
  }
}
```

## Control experiment

The same workload with:

```text
--hicache-write-policy write_back
--hicache-storage-prefetch-policy wait_complete
```

returns:

```json
{
  "cached_tokens": 16010,
  "cached_tokens_details": {
    "device": 0,
    "host": 0,
    "storage": 16010,
    "storage_backend": "MooncakeStore"
  }
}
```

This indicates that Mooncake Store can persist and restore the full prefix when the write path is forced.

## Possible cause

In `python/sglang/srt/mem_cache/hiradix_cache.py`:

- `_inc_hit_count()` at line 926 skips chunked requests.
- `write_backup()` at line 856 is only called after `hit_count` reaches `write_through_threshold`.
- For a first-seen prefix, the leaf node may therefore not be backed up before eviction.
- `write_backup()` also requires the parent node to already be backed up, so a long first-seen prefix may only be partially persisted.
- `_evict_write_back()` at line 1105 shows the working control path: it stages the node to host, waits for the backup, and then writes storage.

## Suggested fix

One of the following would make the behavior clearer:

1. Add a true “write-through on insert” mode that persists the full prefix chain when a request finishes.
2. Document that `write_through` means “second-hit persistence” rather than “insert-time persistence”.
3. Keep the current optimization, but add a warning when a first-seen prefix is evicted before its backup completes.

## Impact

This affects long first-seen prompts that are evicted before a second request arrives. It can silently reduce L3 hit rate and make shared-cache routing less effective.

items.title: [Bug] Large HiCache UCX startup timeout on downstream build; not reproduced on v0.5.20
items.author: ByronHsu
items.body_excerpt:
### Result

**Not reproduced on the latest upstream image (v0.5.20).** A large HiCache pool triggered a UCX startup timeout on our earlier downstream build, but both HiCache and no-HiCache starts passed with the unmodified upstream image.

| Build | HiCache per rank | UCX initialization, all 8 ranks | Server ready |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Downstream `869abc0605`, NIXL 1.3.0 / UCX 1.21.0 | 234 GB | Six ranks explicitly timed out at 60s; none completed | No |
| Same downstream build, no HiCache | 0 | 3–4s | Yes |
| **Upstream v0.5.20, NIXL 1.4.1 / UCX 1.22.0** | **234 GB** | **~2s** | **234s after launch** |
| Same upstream image, no HiCache | 0 | ~2s | 62s after launch |

Each HiCache/control pair ran on the same eight-H200 node with fresh processes. The upstream pair used a different physical node from the downstream pair, and multiple software components changed: this does **not** identify a fix or prove the cause. Only startup was tested, with no inference requests. Both upstream runs registered all eight KV buffers, passed passive `/ready` checks for 30 seconds, and exited cleanly.

### Reproduction settings

8 H200s, approximately 2014 GiB host RAM; public `deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V2-Lite` real weights, revision `604d5664dddd88a0433dbae533b7fe9472482de0`.

Upstream image: `lmsysorg/sglang:latest` resolved to **v0.5.20**, source `94602c9c2b7cbdb8efd5c52802dac6a1c180089e`. Tested amd64 image digest:

```text
lmsysorg/sglang@sha256:b27fce60bc5494c118c4910702812bcfa8cee67abcdd1ff8b0902f21647552f4
```

No source overlay, serving patches, or dependency replacements. Download the model revision above into `$MODEL_DIR`, then run:

```bash
export SGLANG_DISAGGREGATION_ENGINE_INIT_TIMEOUT=60
export SGLANG_NCCL_ALL_GATHER_IN_OVERLAP_SCHEDULER_SYNC_BATCH=1
export SGLANG_FORCE_STREAM_INTERVAL=1
export SGLANG_FORCE_CPU_IMAGE_PREPROCESSING=0

python -m sglang.launch_server \
  --model-path "$MODEL_DIR" --trust-remote-code \
  --host 127.0.0.1 --port 30000 \
  --tp-size 8 --dp-size 8 --ep-size 8 --enable-dp-attention \
  --disaggregation-mode prefill --disaggregation-transfer-backend nixl \
  --mem-fraction-static 0.7 --dtype bfloat16 --kv-cache-dtype bf16 \
  --page-size 64 --tokenizer-worker-num 4 \
  --context-length 150000 --max-running-requests 1024 \
  --skip-server-warmup --log-level debug --decode-attention-backend fa3 \
  --enable-hierarchical-cache --hicache-size 234 \
  --hicache-write-policy write_through \
  --hicache-mem-layout page_first --hicache-io-backend kernel
```

Remove the five HiCache options for the control. CUDA graphs stay enabled; NIXL is the PD transport, not L3 storage. Actual pool allocation: **234,001,612,800 bytes per rank**, about **1.872 TB total**. Size is per rank and requires sufficient host/cgroup headroom.

### Original failure

The downstream run failed **during UCX backend creation, before KV registration**:

```text
RuntimeError: NIXL create_backend('UCX', {'num_threads': '8'}) did not return within 60s
```

Five seconds before failure: **141.6 GiB host headroom**, **39.2–39.4 GiB free per GPU**, no host OOM-counter increase or CUDA OOM. Host memory pressure and compaction were high. No native stack inside UCX was captured. A later audit found rank 0 in a debugger tracing stop at 21:29:30 UTC, inside the 60-second UCX window, as well as earlier allocation-stage attachments. The retained samples do not establish total pause duration. Other ranks also timed out without a recorded tracing stop, but this run was not free of measurement interference. A telemetry gap further limits the evidence.

The upstream HiCache run kept at least **120 GiB host headroom**, logged no OOM, and completed UCX startup quickly. The underlying reason for the older failure remains unresolved.

<details>
<summary>Upstream runtime</summary>

Python 3.12.3; PyTorch 2.13.0+cu130; NIXL/nixl-cu13 1.4.1; bundled UCX 1.22.0; CUDA 13.0; driver 595.71.05; Linux 6.8.12; FlashInfer 0.6.18; Transformers 5.12.1. THP mode remains `madvise`. The 60-second UCX deadline and eight prefill backend threads were unchanged.

</details>

### Follow-up: the extra host memory is DC receive buffers

On one exclusive node, with the same upstream source/image and **232 GB/rank** HiCache, we compared fresh server processes:

| Native backend | DC interfaces | Receive-buffer chunks | Scheduler anonymous huge pages | UCX startup span |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| NIXL 1.4.1 / UCX 1.22 | 0 | 288 | 12.498 GiB | 2s |
| NIXL 1.3.0 / UCX 1.21 | 288 | 576 | 23.188 GiB | 4s |
| Same 1.3.0 package, only `UCX_TLS=^dc_mlx5` added | 0 | 288 | 12.502 GiB | 3s |

All three initialized all eight ranks, registered KV buffers, and held passive readiness for 30 seconds. No compaction stalls, THP fallbacks, or OOM occurred. No inference or PD transfers were tested. The third case is a diagnostic intervention, **not a verified timeout fix**.

UCX debug logs and per-scheduler memory maps identify the difference: **8 ranks × 9 workers × 4 ports = 288 DC interfaces**, each eagerly allocating a **38 MiB** receive buffer through `rc_recv_desc`. Those extra buffers account for **10.6875 GiB** of huge pages. Excluding only DC on the old package removes them and matches the newer package. Actual loaded UCX versions were verified in server logs.

The old binary includes DC; the new wheel omits it. [NIXL PR 1708](https://github.com/ai-dynamo/nixl/pull/1708) disables DC in the manylinux build. The v1.3.0 source tag also contains that flag despite the tested wheel including DC, so we report observed binary features rather than infer build history from tags.

During the **original failing UCX initialization window**, kernel counters rose by **10,496 compaction attempts, 10,492 failures, 3,407 THP fallbacks, and 3,668 direct-reclaim stalls**. They were flat just before UCX started. The examined SGLang NIXL startup and host-pool files are byte-identical between the downstream and upstream revisions.

This supports a host-memory compact

items.title: llama-quantize: GGML_ASSERT(size mismatch) when quantizing mmproj files containing 3D conv tensors (gemma4v audio conv1d)
items.author: mrBenBern
items.body_excerpt:
Quantizing the gemma-4-E2B combined mmproj (vision+audio, gemma4v/gemma4a projectors) from F16 to Q8_0 aborts with:

  llama-quant.cpp:1365: GGML_ASSERT(gguf_get_tensor_size(...) == new_size) failed

Repro:
  llama-quantize --allow-requantize mmproj-F16.gguf out.gguf Q8_0

Fails at tensor `a.conv1d.0.weight` — shape [3,3,1,128] (3D conv1d from the audio encoder). The f32→f16 conversion changes the tensor size, and the split-output writer asserts on the mismatch. Every subsequent 3D tensor fails the same way (a.conv1d.1.weight [3,3,128,32], ...).

Workaround (verified): keep 3D tensors in f32 via tensor-type overrides —
  llama-quantize --allow-requantize \
    --tensor-type "a.conv1d.0.weight=f32" \
    --tensor-type "a.conv1d.1.weight=f32" \
    mmproj-F16.gguf mmproj-F16-q8_0.gguf Q8_0

This works and the resulting Q8_0 mmproj is functionally correct on-device (Android, llama.cpp 4ebdf2c): vision outputs verified same-in-quality as F16 (sign-text reading), encode on a Helio G99 CPU improved 6.4x vs BF16 (37s -> 5.8s for a 91-token image).

Expected behavior: either skip/conversion-preserving handling for N-D tensors whose element count doesn't allow requantization, or a clean error message listing the offending tensors instead of an assert.

items.title: [Bug]: `validate_regex_is_buildable` (outlines backend) misses `\b` and backreferences inside groups
items.author: the-Shallow
items.body_excerpt:
### Your current environment
The output of python collect_env.py ```text vLLM 0.30.0 (the latest release) and 0.28.0, CPU, Python 3.12, Ubuntu 24.04, x86_64 ```
### 🐛 Describe the bug `vllm.v1.structured_output.backend_outlines.validate_regex_is_buildable` rejects regex features that `outlines_core` cannot build (word boundaries, backreferences, look-arounds), but its helper `_check_unsupported` recurses only into `BRANCH` and `MAX_REPEAT` nodes, not into `SUBPATTERN` (group) nodes. Recursing into `SUBPATTERN` (`tval[3]`), as `_prefix_needs_context` in the same file already does, fixes it. ### Expected Patterns with an unsupported feature are rejected wherever the feature appears. ### Before submitting a new issue... - [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.

items.author: the-Shallow

### Your current environment

### 🐛 Describe the bug `MambaStateShapeCalculator.mamba2_state_shape` supports `n_groups` values that are not divisible by the tensor-parallel world size by extending the groups assigned to head shards. Passing the resulting state shape to `append_replayssm_ring`, however, calls `divide(n_groups, tp_world_size)` on the original group count and raises an assertion. ```python from vllm.model_executor.layers.mamba.mamba_utils import ( MambaStateShapeCalculator as C, ) base = C.mamba2_state_shape( tp_world_size=2, intermediate_size=256, n_groups=1, num_heads=4, head_dim=64, state_size=128, conv_kernel=4, ) C.append_replayssm_ring(base, 1, 2, 16) ``` This raises: ```text AssertionError: 1 is not divisible by 2 ``` ### Expected behavior `append_replayssm_ring` should use the same group-extension rule as `mamba2_state_shape`, so a state shape accepted by the calculator can have a ReplaySSM ring appended without an assertion. ### Suggested fix Extend `n_groups` for the tensor-parallel head shards before dividing it, matching the logic already used by `mamba2_state_shape`. ### Before submitting a new issue... - [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.

items.title: [Bug]: tool_choice="required"` streaming drops tool calls when one delta completes more than one call
items.author: the-Shallow
items.body_excerpt:
### Your current environment
The output of python collect_env.py ```text vLLM 0.30.0 (the latest release) and 0.28.0, CPU, Python 3.12, Ubuntu 24.04, x86_64 ```
### 🐛 Describe the bug With `tool_choice="required"` the model writes a JSON array of tool calls, and the serving layer streams it through `extract_required_tool_call_streaming` (`vllm/tool_parsers/streaming.py`). The helper looks only at the last object of the partially parsed array (`obj[-1]`) and returns at most one tool call per delta. When a delta completes more than one call, the earlier calls are never streamed: ```python import json from vllm.tool_parsers.streaming import extract_required_tool_call_streaming text = json.dumps([{"name": "get_weather", "parameters": {"city": "Dallas"}}, {"name": "get_time", "parameters": {"tz": "UTC"}}]) previous, returned = "", False for delta in (text[:1], text[1:]): message, returned = extract_required_tool_call_streaming( previous_text=previous, current_text=previous + delta, delta_text=delta, function_name_returned=returned, tool_call_idx=0, tool_call_id_type="random") previous += delta if message: print([(c.index, c.function.name, c.function.arguments) for c in message.tool_calls]) # [(1, 'get_time', '{"tz": "UTC"}')] <- get_weather (index 0) is never sent ``` The non-streaming path returns both calls for the same text. Streamed one character at a time, both calls arrive, so the result depends on how the text is cut. Deltas of several tokens are what `--stream-interval` above 1 produces. ### Expected behavior Every call of the array is streamed with its name and its arguments, whatever the size of the deltas. The helper would need to go over every object of the array that still has something unsent, with the "name sent" state kept per index instead of in one boolean. ### Before submitting a new issue... - [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.

items.title: [RFC]: CPU backend support for the vLLM connector + Mooncake Store L2 for multi-instance CPU serving
items.author: amd-lalithnc
items.body_excerpt:
## 1. Summary

This RFC proposes upstreaming two related contributions that enable **LMCache on the vLLM CPU backend** and make **cross-instance KV reuse** work for CPU serving:

1. **A CPU GPU-connector** (`VLLMCPUConnector`): a pure-torch gather/scatter path between vLLM's paged CPU KV cache and an LMCache `MemoryObj`, handling vLLM's 4D fused K/V CPU layout. This is the missing piece that lets LMCache run at all on `device=cpu`.
2. **Fixes to the Mooncake Store L2 connector** so it works on the CPU backend and shares KV **across instances** (fork-safe per-process client init, a correct `exists()`/lookup path, and a config-key alias).

Together these let multiple vLLM CPU instances behind a load balancer share one KV cache (SHM on a single box, or Mooncake Store over TCP across a cluster), instead of each instance recomputing the same prefixes.

Note that the CPU connector (contribution 1) is **backend-agnostic**: it is the shared foundation that unlocks the *entire* LMCache backend ecosystem on CPU (local DRAM L1, the shared SHM server, pickle, and remote L2s). Contribution 2 is one representative distributed L2 (Mooncake). We enable and validate **both** the default (SHM) and Mooncake paths because they target different deployment scopes (see §3.4).

We propose **two stacked PRs** (CPU connector, then Mooncake-on-CPU) plus this RFC to tie them together.

## 2. Motivation

- **CPU inference is growing** (cost, availability, disaggregated/CPU-tier deployments), and vLLM has a maturing CPU backend.
- **Multi-instance CPU serving needs *shared* KV.** vLLM's Automatic Prefix Caching (APC) is **per-instance**: behind a load balancer, instance B cannot reuse instance A's prefix KV, so shared system prompts / few-shot / documents are recomputed on every instance.
- **LMCache already solves cross-instance reuse**, but had **no CPU connector**, so it could not run on vLLM CPU at all; and the **Mooncake Store L2** path did not work on CPU or across instances (fork-safety + lookup bugs).
- **Measured impact** (Section 5): on a single-socket AMD EPYC, an external shared KV cache gives **+27-31% aggregate throughput at 3 instances** and **-28%/-34% p95/p99 tail latency** vs APC.

## 3. Design

### 3.1 Topology

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    LB[NGINX load balancer] --> V1[vLLM CPU inst 1]
    LB --> V2[vLLM CPU inst 2]
    LB --> V3[vLLM CPU inst 3]
    V1 <-->|store / load KV| L[(LMCache)]
    V2 <-->|store / load KV| L
    V3 <-->|store / load KV| L
    L <-->|put / get| S{{Shared KV: SHM  or  Mooncake Store L2 / TCP}}
```

### 3.2 CPU connector (`VLLMCPUConnector`)

**Why a CPU connector is needed.** Every existing GPU connector relies on CUDA custom ops (`c_ops`) and CUDA streams and assumes the GPU KV memory layout. None of that exists on CPU, so LMCache previously could not run on vLLM's CPU backend at all. `VLLMCPUConnector` fills that gap.

**What it implements.** The same connector interface, using **plain PyTorch tensor operations** (indexing + copy) with no CUDA kernels or streams:

- `from_gpu(...)` (**STORE / gather**): copy the KV for tokens `[start, end)` out of vLLM's paged CPU buffer into a contiguous `MemoryObj`.
- `to_gpu(...)` (**LOAD / scatter**): copy KV from a `MemoryObj` back into vLLM's paged buffer, placing each token's K/V into the slot given by vLLM's slot mapping.
- `batched_from_gpu(...)` / `batched_to_gpu(...)`: batched variants that handle several token ranges in one call.

**Handling vLLM's CPU KV layout.** vLLM's CPU backend stores each layer's cache as a single **4D fused K/V tensor** (K and V packed together), which is laid out differently from the GPU cache. For each layer the connector derives logical views shaped `[num_blocks, block_size, num_heads, head_size]` for K and for V (`_kv_token_views`), then uses the request's block/slot offsets to move exactly the right rows. This keeps gather/scatter correct without copying the whole buffer.

**Selection.** The connector is picked automatically when the device is CPU (`torch_device_type == "cpu"` in `CreateGPUConnector`), so no user config change is required.

**Plugging in as a `GPUConnectorInterface`.** So the CPU connector can subclass `GPUConnectorInterface` without importing the CUDA-heavy `gpu_connectors`/`utils` modules (which import `c_ops`, absent in NO_GPU_EXT builds), the interface ABC is extracted into a small `c_ops`-free `interface.py` that `gpu_connectors.py` re-exports. Existing GPU connectors are unaffected.

### 3.3 Mooncake Store L2 on CPU

The Mooncake client (Go runtime + multithreaded C++) is **not fork-safe**, and vLLM forks its scheduler/worker processes. Fixes:

- **Fork-safe, lazy per-process init**: the store/lookup client is created inside each process on first use (`_ensure_store()`), never inherited across a fork.
- **Correct lookup path**: `exists()`/`exists_sync()` now call `_ensure_store()` first (the contains/lookup path can run before any put/get on an instance) and compare `is_exist() == 1` (it returns `1/0/-1`) so an error never reads as a cache hit. Without this, cross-instance lookups were swallowed as misses and the instance recomputed.
- **Config-key alias**: accept `master_server_address` as an alias for `master_server_addr` in dict-based setup.

**Cross-instance key consistency (usage requirement, not connector code):** for a prefix computed on instance A to be found by instance B, the KV keys must hash identically across processes. Python's default randomized hashing breaks this; deployments must use a stable algorithm (e.g. `LMCACHE_PRE_CACHING_HASH_ALGORITHM=sha256` with `PYTHONHASHSEED=0`). This will be documented.

### 3.4 Why enable both paths (default SHM and Mooncake L2)

The CPU connector is transport/backend-agnostic, so a natural question is *why validate two L2 paths instead of one*. Because they are **complementary, not competing**: the right choice is dictated by deployment topology, and we want CPU users to be able to pick either without changing the connecto

items.title: [RFC][MP] Hidden-state caching
items.author: Vivo50E
items.body_excerpt:
Cache a model's per-token hidden states alongside the KV they were produced with, so a consumer that conditions a downstream stage on them can still be fed after a KV hit skips prefill.

## Background

A multi-stage model can condition a later stage on an earlier stage's hidden states. In vLLM-Omni the talker is conditioned on the thinker's hidden states; Qwen3-Omni additionally uses intermediate layers named by `talker_config.accept_hidden_layer`.

KV offload breaks that. When LMCache serves a prefix, the engine skips prefill for those tokens, so no hidden states are produced for them. The talker is handed a suffix and the audio degrades — with no error anywhere, because from the KV path's point of view everything succeeded.

The fix is to cache the hidden states under the same keys as the KV they ride with, and restore them on a hit. This is implemented in-process today (`HiddenStateStore`, `lmcache/v1/hidden_state_store.py`, consumed by vllm-project/vllm-omni#1330) and does not exist in MP mode at all.

That PR would be the first consumer of an MP implementation too. The design below is written against its requirements, and we would do the port — so a first version gets exercised end to end rather than only specified.

## What the in-process implementation got wrong

Three properties this design has to have, each learned by shipping a bug without it:

**Keys must be derived exactly as the KV keys are.** Hidden states are only useful when they land under the same chunk hash as the KV for the same tokens, multimodal spans included — `mm_hash_to_token_values` substitution and all (`docs/design/integration/vllm/multimodal_cache_keying.md`). Deriving them separately produces a store that never hits, or worse, hits under the wrong identity. MP gets this for free if hidden states go through the same key derivation rather than a parallel one.

**Coverage must reach the scheduler.** In-process, hidden states live in a second pool with its own capacity and its own LRU, so the two quantities drift: the shipped defaults size them at 2 GB against 5 GB of KV, and a KV hit routinely outruns what hidden states can supply. Nothing detects it until the worker, by which point the prefill has already been skipped. The scheduler needs to commit to `min(KV, HS)` at `get_num_new_matched_tokens`, not to KV alone. LMCache#4824 adds this to the in-process lookup; the MP equivalent is the substance of this RFC's second half.

**Absolute token positions must survive a non-aligned hit.** Storage is chunk-aligned but a hit is not: a full-prompt hit leaves the engine recomputing the last token, so the first rows a worker produces after a restore start mid-chunk. Filing them at the rounded-down boundary stores them under earlier positions than they hold.

## Design

Hidden states are transient per-token activations with no paged home, and MP puts a process boundary between where they are produced and where they would be stored. Two ways across; the cheap one is good enough to start, and the other is below as a later optimization.

### Transport: a handler pair that ships bytes

`EngineDrivenTransferModule.commit_store` is the shape to copy — worker sends CPU bytes, server writes them, `prepare_retrieve` mirrors it:

```python
def commit_store(self, key: IPCCacheServerKey, instance_id: int,
                 cpu_data: bytes) -> bool:
    """Commit serialized CPU chunks to storage.
       cpu_data: Pickled list of CPU tensors produced by the worker."""
```

Copy the shape, not the handlers. `commit_store` opens with `entry, strategy = self._resolve_for_transfer(instance_id)`, which finds the engine-driven context the worker registered — and a CUDA deployment whose KV runs lmcache-driven never registered one. Reusing them would make the hidden state path inherit the KV path's transport mode, or force a second registration.

It does not need to. The transfer strategy exists to gather and scatter paged KV across block lists. Hidden states are a contiguous run of rows per request: there is nothing to gather. So the proposal is **a handler pair of its own — `store_hidden_states` and `retrieve_hidden_states` — taking and returning CPU bytes, resolving keys, and writing through the storage manager, with no transfer strategy involved**. CUDA and non-CUDA deployments take the same path, and whichever mode KV uses is not this path's concern.

The reason a copy is affordable here is size. A token of KV is `2 * num_layers * num_kv_heads * head_size` elements; a token of hidden state is `hidden_size`. On the Qwen2.5-Omni thinker that is `2 * 36 * 2 * 128 = 18,432` against a hidden size in the low thousands — **roughly a tenth**, or a third of it with three layers captured. The KV already crosses this boundary in an engine-driven deployment; a tensor a tenth its size does not change the shape of the cost.

### Keys

MP addresses objects with `ObjectKey`, not the in-process `CacheEngineKey`:

```python
class ObjectKey:
    chunk_hash: bytes
    model_name: str
    kv_rank: int
    object_group_id: int = 0
    cache_salt: str = ""
```

The chunk hash comes from `TokenHasher.compute_chunk_hashes`, so hidden states calling it on the same token ids land under the same hash as the KV — which is also how the `mm_hash_to_token_values` substitution comes along for free rather than being reimplemented.

The hashes have to be computed in a session of the hidden path's own, not the KV path's. `Session.set_tokens` replaces the token list while `get_hashes` memoizes the chunks it has already hashed, so two callers sharing one session and passing different token lists quietly serve each other's chunk hashes. Suffixing the request id is enough to separate them, and the session manager's TTL reaps the extra entry.

What is left is telling the two apart. `object_group_id` is taken: it indexes KV kernel groups and carries a layout descriptor per group, which hidden states do not have. That leaves `model_name`, which is what Q already uses (`<model>##q

- #29476 "vulkan: Tune GDN kernel" — measured on Intel Arc (+26-38% PP) and AMD Pro VII (neutral); the regressed workload here is exactly GDN-hybrid prefill

items.body_excerpt: ## Introduction To address the issue where all metadata is lost after a master service failure and recovery, this solution proposes a **hot-standby synchronization mechanism** and a **hybrid approach** combining hot standby with snapshots, ensuring rapid data recovery following a master service failure. ## Motivation The current HA (High Availability) mode only supports rapid restart of the master service after a failure but cannot guarantee fast data recovery. The pain points of the current HA mode are as follows: | Issue | Impact | Severity | | -------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------ | ---------- | | **Complete loss of metadata after Leader failure** | All KV cache location information is lost and must be rebuilt | 🔴 Critical | | **Follower lacks data pre-warming** | After successful election, the new Leader must start serving from scratch | 🟠 Medium | | **Long recovery time** | Relies on clients to re-register; may take several minutes to tens of minutes | 🟠 Medium | | **Service unavailability window** | Requests cannot be processed during Leader failover | 🟡 Low | ## Goals: 1. **Near-zero RPO**: Minimize the data loss window 2. **Fast failover**: Achieve second-level RTO (Recovery Time Objective) 3. **Data consistency guarantee**: Ensure correct synchronization between primary and standby 4. **Verifiability**: Include mechanisms to validate data integrity 5. **Low performance overhead**: Avoid impacting normal business operations ## Proposal ### 1. Core Design Approach **Use etcd as an intermediate reliability component to implement OpLog primary-standby synchronization**: - **OpLog Mechanism**: Primary Master records all state change operations to OpLog - **etcd Storage**: OpLog is written to etcd, leveraging etcd's strong consistency and persistence capabilities - **Watch Mechanism**: Standby Master receives OpLog in real-time through etcd Watch mechanism - **Ordering Guarantee**: Guarantee operation order through global sequence_id and key-level key_sequence_id ### 2. Architecture Design #### (1) Overall Architecture The overall architecture diagram shows the interaction relationships between Primary Master, etcd Cluster, and Standby Master: **Architecture Description**: - **Primary Master**: Handles client requests, records OpLog and writes to etcd - **etcd Cluster**: Acts as intermediate storage, providing strong consistency and Watch mechanism - **Standby Master**: Receives OpLog in real-time by watching etcd and applies to local metadata store #### (2) Data Flow Diagram The data flow diagram shows the complete flow from Client request to Standby synchronization: **Flow Description**: a. Client sends `PutEnd` request to Primary Master b. Primary Master records operation through `OpLogManager`, generating sequence_id c. `EtcdOpLogStore` writes OpLog to etcd d. etcd notifies Standby Master through Watch mechanism e. `OpLogWatcher` receives events and passes to `OpLogApplier` f. `OpLogApplier` checks order and applies to Standby's metadata store #### (3) Failover Sequence The failover sequence diagram shows the complete process from Primary failure to Standby promotion to Primary: **Flow Description**: a. **Normal Operation**: Primary maintains Lease, Standby continuously synchronizes OpLog through Watch b. **Primary Failure**: Primary's Lease expires, etcd notifies Standby c. **Standby Promotion**: Stop Standby service, initialize Lease, clean expired metadata, start leader election ### 3. Core Component Design #### (1) OpLogManager (Primary Side) **Responsibilities**: - Record all state change operations (PUT_END, PUT_REVOKE, REMOVE) - Generate global sequence_id and key-level key_sequence_id - Maintain memory buffer (for fast queries) **Key Methods**: ```cpp class OpLogManager { uint64_t Append(OpType type, const std::string& key, const std::string& payload = ""); std::vector GetEntriesSince(uint64_t since_seq_id, size_t limit = 1000) const; uint64_t GetLastSequenceId() const; }; ``` #### (2) EtcdOpLogStore (Primary Side) **Responsibilities**: - Write OpLog to etcd - Update latest sequence_id - Record snapshot corresponding sequence_id - Clean up old OpLog **etcd Key Design**: - OpLog Entry: `mooncake-store/oplog/{cluster_id}/{sequence_id}` - Latest Sequence ID: `mooncake-store/oplog/{cluster_id}/latest` - Snapshot Sequence ID: `mooncake-store/oplog/{cluster_id}/snapshot/{snapshot_id}/sequence_id` #### (3) OpLogWatcher (Standby Side) **Responsibilities**: - Watch etcd OpLog changes - Read historical OpLog (for initial synchronization) - Process Watch events and pass to OpLogApplier **Key Methods**: ```cpp class OpLogWatcher { void Start(); void Stop(); bool ReadOpLogSince(uint64_t start_seq_id, std::vector& entries); }; ``` #### (4) OpLogApplier (Standby Side) **Responsibilities**: - Apply OpLog Entry to local metadata store - Check global and key-level order - Handle sequence number discontinuities and out-of-order cases - Periodically clean up key_sequence_map_ (memory optimization) **Key Methods**: ```cpp class OpLogApplier { bool ApplyOpLogEntry(const OpLogEntry& entry); bool CheckSequenceOrder(const OpLogEntry& entry); void CleanupStaleKey

comments.body: ### 1. Problem & Assumptions #### 1.1 Problem After a `Delete` (or eviction) on the primary master: - The primary frees a replica’s memory (returns buffer to allocator’s free list). - The `Delete` event is **not** replicated to the standby master. - The primary then crashes; the standby is promoted to new master. - The new master still believes that this replica exists, and returns its address to clients. - That buffer may already have been **reused by another object**, or may still contain **logically deleted data**. We must **never** return data that belongs to some other key/object/tenant due to buffer reuse, even if we allow some metadata loss. #### 1.2 Accepted Semantic Constraints We explicitly accept the following semantics: - **Metadata / delete operations may be lost across failover**: - A delete acknowledged by the old master may be “rolled back” after failover. - That is acceptable because the KV cache can be recomputed. - **Hard safety requirement**: - It is strictly forbidden to read data that **belongs to another key/object/tenant** as if it were the requested key. - In other words: buffer reuse must not cause **cross-key contamination**. Under these constraints, it is acceptable that: - A key that was “deleted” on the old master may reappear after failover (logical delete rolled back). - But it is **not** acceptable to read someone else’s data due to buffer reuse. --- ### 2. Idea We upgrade each replica from a “raw pointer” into a **versioned capability**: - In-memory layout of a replica buffer becomes: - The master generates a **64-bit version** for each successful `Put` of a key. - This `version` is stored: - In `ObjectMetadata` on the master. - In the `ReplicaDescriptor` returned to clients. - In the first 8 bytes of the actual buffer in the KV store. - On **Get**, the client always verifies: - Read the first 8 bytes of the buffer. - Compare with the expected version from `ReplicaDescriptor`. - If versions match → buffer still belongs to this key/epoch → safe to read payload. - If versions differ → buffer was reused by someone else → mark this replica invalid, do not use it. Thus, even if the physical address is reused for a different object, the client will detect it and reject the replica. --- ### 3. Data Model Changes #### 3.1 Version Type ```cpp using Version = uint64_t; ``` Version can be constructed as: - High bits: timestamp (e.g., microseconds since epoch). - Low bits: per-node monotonic sequence ID. Requirements: - For a single master process, each successful `Put` for a given key gets a **unique, monotonically increasing** version. - Version collisions are practically impossible within a process lifetime. #### 3.2 Replica Descriptor Extension Extend `Replica::Descriptor` (or equivalent) to carry version information: On `PutStart`, the master generates `version`, stores it in metadata, and includes it in each replica descriptor. --- ### 4. Write Path (Put) Design #### 4.1 Master: PutStart 1. Client invokes `Put(key, slices, config)`. 2. `MasterService::PutStart(key, slice_lengths, config)`: - Validates input. - Allocates replicas as it does today (segments, buffers, etc.). - Generates a new `Version version = MakeVersion()` for this key. - Stores `version` in `ObjectMetadata` for this key. - Fills `ReplicaDescriptor.version = version` for each allocated replica. - Returns the list of descriptors to the client. All replicas of the same key for this `Put` share the same version. #### 4.2 Client: Writing to Store We enhance `TransferWrite` to enforce the following **write order** per replica: 1. Write **8-byte version header** at `buffer_address`. 2. Write **payload** at `buffer_address + 8` for length `size`. There are two implementation options: - **Option A: Two-step write** (simpler): - First,

comments.author: ykwd
comments.body:
Thanks for sharing the proposal. Unfortunately, this approach is not safe and does not actually guarantee the hard safety requirement you described, for two reasons:

First, RDMA reads and writes do not provide ordering and atomicity guarantees, which breaks the version-only validation scheme. In your design, correctness relies on the assumption that the first 8 bytes (the version) and the payload are written and observed atomically and in order. That assumption does not hold.

Second, the allocator does not guarantee alignment between successive allocations, which makes the embedded-version assumption invalid. Your scheme assumes that when a buffer is freed and later reused, the next allocation will reuse the same start address and layout, so that the version stored in the first 8 bytes corresponds exactly to the logical object boundary.

### Changes proposed

#  Explicit Context Caching — Guaranteed KV Cache Eviction Protection

## Summary

Introduce a `guaranteed_until` timestamp mechanism in Mooncake Store to implement Explicit Context Caching:

1. **Eviction protection**: Users mark `cache_control: {"type": "ephemeral"}` in `messages`, and the corresponding prefix KV Cache is marked as guaranteed (non-evictable within TTL) in the Store. After expiration, objects automatically degrade to regular objects
2. **Passive expiration**: Uses an absolute `guaranteed_until_` timestamp — BatchEvict naturally skips unexpired objects; expired objects automatically become eviction candidates. Zero new RPCs, crash-safe by design
3. **Zero state on inference engine side**: All guaranteed lifecycle management resides on the Master side. Inference engines (SGLang, vLLM, etc.) do not track or manage guaranteed cache; radix tree nodes require no new fields

## 1. Background and Motivation

### Problem 1: High-Value Prefixes Lack Eviction Protection

Mainstream inference engines (SGLang, vLLM, etc.) reuse KV Cache through prefix matching (RadixAttention / Automatic Prefix Caching). Shared prefixes (system prompts, RAG documents, few-shot examples) are frequently hit. The current eviction strategy in Mooncake Store sorts purely by lease timeout — least recently accessed objects are evicted first. This means:

- Under memory pressure, high-value long prefixes (e.g., a 4K-token system prompt) may be evicted first (because they may not have recent writes)
- After eviction, the next request requires full recomputation, causing P99 latency spikes and GPU compute waste

### Problem 2: OpenAI-Compatible cache_control Semantics Have No Backend Support

The OpenAI API introduced `cache_control: {"type": "ephemeral"}` markers, allowing users to declare "this prefix is important, don't evict it" in message content blocks. Frontend frameworks (e.g., LangChain, VLLM) widely support this semantic, but Mooncake Store has no corresponding eviction protection mechanism, rendering the marker effectively inert.

### Problem 3: Design Gap Between Explicit and Implicit Caching

Alibaba Bailian adopts a standalone CacheIndex + 20-block lookback window approach (multi-tenant cloud service), but this introduces a complex indexing system and inference-engine-side lifecycle management. For single-cluster self-deployment scenarios, we need a lighter approach.

**Goals**: Provide deterministic eviction protection (hard guarantee) for prefixes marked with `cache_control`. After TTL expiry, objects automatically degrade to regular objects. Zero new state on inference engine side. Zero regression risk.

## 2. Core Design

### Tiered Architecture

| Tier | Location | Role in Explicit Caching | Guarantee Level |
|------|----------|-------------------------|-----------------|
| L1 (GPU) | Inference engine Worker (local) | Temporarily held during inference, normal eviction | No guarantee |
| L2 (CPU) | Inference engine Worker (local) | Speedup on same-engine hit (bonus) | No guarantee |
| L3 (Mooncake Store) | Distributed storage | **Deterministic guarantee tier** | Hard guarantee |

L1/L2 do not participate in guarantees: requests may be routed to any engine instance, and L2 is only available on the local instance. Binding guarantees to L2 would require forced routing to a specific instance, breaking load balancing. L3 is shared across all engines, naturally supporting cross-engine reuse.

### Architecture Diagram

```
  Client (messages with cache_control markers)
       │
       ▼
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Inference Engine API Server          │
  │  - Parse cache_control → token offsets│
  └──────────────┬───────────────────────┘
                 │
                 ▼
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Inference Engine Worker Instance     │
  │  ┌──────────────────────────────┐    │
  │  │ HiCache Controller (no change)│   │
  │  │ - radix tree normal prefix   │    │
  │  │   matching                   │    │
  │  │ - On write: check cache_     │    │
  │  │   control → write_through    │    │
  │  │   with guaranteed param      │    │
  │  │ - On read: check cache_      │    │
  │  │   control → GetReplicaList   │    │
  │  │   with guaranteed param      │    │
  │  └──────────────────────────────┘    │
  └──────────┬───────────────────────────┘
             │
  ┌──────────▼───────────────────────────┐
  │  Mooncake Store (L3)                │
  │  - guaranteed_until_ timestamp guard │
  │  - BatchEvict skips unexpired objs  │
  │  - GrantLease auto-renewal          │
  │  - Guaranteed capacity limit+fallback│
  │  - SSD Offload priority protection  │
  └─────────────────────────────────────┘
```

### Design 1: guaranteed_until_ Timestamp Scheme

Add `guaranteed_until_` (`SteadyClock::time_point`) to `ObjectMetadata`, defaulting to epoch (no guarantee). At PutStart, if `ReplicateConfig.guaranteed_until_ms > 0`, the Master converts it to an absolute timestamp.

**Core semantic**: `guaranteed_until_` unexpired → object is non-evictable (equivalent to hard pinned); expired → automatically degrades to a regular object.

**Why timestamps over reference counting / lease renewal**:

| Approach | New RPCs | Crash recovery | Complexity |
|----------|----------|----------------|------------|
| Reference counting | Requires ReleaseGuaranteed | Must clean residual counts | High |
| Lease renewal | Requires RenewGuaranteed | Depends on TTL patches | Medium |
| **guaranteed_until timestamp** | **Zero** | **Natural expiration, no orphans** | **Low** |

### Design 2: Zero State on Inference Engine Side

Inference engines (SGLang, vLLM, etc.) hold no guaranteed state. All lifecycle management is on the Master side:

- **Write path**: HiCache checks whether the current block falls within `cache_control`-marked token range → if yes, write_through to L3 with `guaranteed_until_ms`
- **Read path**: When a request carries `cache_control`, pass `guaranteed_ttl

items.title: response_format + tools on glm47: tool calls silently dropped, model invents a JSON answer
items.author: justicel
items.body_excerpt:
## What happens

On v0.5.21 (and on main as of today) with `--tool-call-parser glm47`, a request that carries both callable tools and a JSON `response_format` never calls a tool. The model answers the format immediately with invented content.

We serve GLM-5.3 and GLM-5.3-Flash behind a gateway and hit this through codex, which sends its `--output-schema` as `response_format` on every request of an agent turn. Every run came back with a schema-shaped answer having done no work. A PR reviewer reported "no findings" on a diff it had never opened.

Minimal repro against the engine, temperature 0, same prompt both times ("use read_file on note.txt, then report the secret word in it"):

```
# tools only
finish_reason: tool_calls
tool_calls: [read_file({"path": "note.txt"})]

# same request + response_format: {"type": "json_schema", "json_schema": {..."word"...}}
finish_reason: stop
tool_calls: []
content: {"word": "note.txt"}
```

The word is invented. The file was never read. Same result with `json_object`, on both models, streaming and not.

## Why

`to_sampling_params` in `python/sglang/srt/entrypoints/openai/protocol.py` drops the tool-call constraint with a warning when the request also carries a format, then compiles the format grammar over the whole answer. That grammar forbids every tool-call token and even the thinking-close token, so the only legal output is a bare JSON object. The model complies, and makes up content to fill it.

#34881 made `required` + format a 400, which is fair. But `auto` still warn-and-drops, and glm47 is exempt from even that because its constraint is a `full_assistant_ebnf`, so on glm47 the combination silently fabricates. #5178 asked for real support back in late 2024 and was auto-closed for inactivity.

## A fix that works

The glm47 parser already generates a full-assistant EBNF covering the whole turn. The format can be merged into that grammar instead of dropping the tool side:

```
assistant_turn ::= thinking_block ( tool_call_blocks+ | final_json_answer )
```

`final_json_answer` is the response format's JSON grammar. The rule set in `glm4_moe_detector.py` already carries JSON value rules for tool arguments (`_GLM_XML_GRAMMAR_RULES`), so typing object properties reuses the same machinery. `serving_chat.py` passes the format into `get_structure_constraint` and clears `request.response_format`, so `to_sampling_params` applies the merged grammar through the existing `full_assistant_ebnf` path. `protocol.py` needs no changes.

One catch we found the hard way: the grammar alone is not enough. With just the merged grammar, the model re-calls the tool forever. Three rounds, no answer. Prose is masked, and it never finds the JSON branch. The fix also needs to state the requirement in the prompt, that the final answer must be the JSON and nothing else. The instruction alone is not enforcement. Both together, measured on both models:

```
round 0: finish_reason tool_calls, read_file
round 1: finish_reason stop, content {"word": "quokka-a6f5ca"}   # the real word, from the tool result
```

Requests with tools only, or a format only, behave exactly as before. With no format present the generated grammar is byte-identical to today's, so there is no regression path for existing traffic.

Two smaller things worth knowing if anyone picks this up. `JsonSchemaResponseFormat.schema_` is `Field(alias="schema")`, so `model_dump_json()` emits `schema_` unless you pass `by_alias=True`, and anything downstream reading `"schema"` silently gets None and falls back to a looser grammar. And the shallow schema typing matches how tool arguments are typed today, so exotic schemas degrade to any-JSON-object rather than erroring.

We're running this as a source patch on both models in production now and it has been clean. Happy to turn it into a PR if the approach sounds right, or to reshape it to fit whatever direction the maintainers prefer.

## Environment

sglang v0.5.21 (also verified on the 2026-09-25 nightly and on main), GLM-5.3 and GLM-5.3-Flash, `--tool-call-parser glm47 --reasoning-parser glm45`, TP 4 and TP 8.

items.title: [Bug] /update_weights_from_disk: is_async / keep_pause / token_step have no effect, num_paused_requests is always 0
items.author: apex-mochen
items.body_excerpt:
On current main (`1818db4e54`), four parameters of `/update_weights_from_disk` are part of the API and documented in `docs/docs/advanced_features/sglang_for_rl.mdx`, but nothing in the tree reads them:

| name | kind | declared | documented as | who reads it |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `is_async` | request | `io_struct.py:1879` | "Perform weight load asynchronously." (`sglang_for_rl.mdx:172`) | — |
| `keep_pause` | request | `io_struct.py:1883` | "Keep scheduler paused after update." (`:184`) | — |
| `token_step` | request | `io_struct.py:1887` | "Trainer step id for rollout bookkeeping." (`:196`) | — |
| `num_paused_requests` | response | `io_struct.py:1898` | "Number of paused requests during update." (`:241`) | only the producer, which hardcodes `0` (`scheduler_components/weight_updater.py:152`) |

For the three request fields the only occurrences in the whole tree are the declarations themselves and the docs rows (checked with `git grep`; unrelated hits: `is_async` in the flash-attn copy utils / marlin templates / tracing, and the `token_steps` sampling field). `num_paused_requests` is plumbed all the way into the HTTP/gRPC response (`http_server.py:1252,1258`, `grpc_bridge.py:571`, `tokenizer_manager.py:2210,2274,2283`), so callers do receive the field — it just can never be non-zero. (In DP>1 it comes back as a per-rank list of zeros while the documented type is `int` — `tokenizer_manager.py:2283`.)

I could not find a version where these were consumed either: the same greps on `v0.5.12.post1` and `v0.4.9` show no readers in the scheduler/tokenizer files that would have to read them, and no in-tree code sends them. So this looks like long-standing documentation/API drift rather than a fresh break.

### Impact

RL clients that follow the guide will pass `keep_pause` / `is_async` / `token_step` and silently get behavior other than what is documented, and `num_paused_requests` cannot be used to tell "nothing was paused" from "the counter is not wired".

### Proposed fix — happy to send a PR for whichever direction you prefer

- **A. Remove** the three request fields and their docs rows, and drop `num_paused_requests` from the response/docs. The pause lifecycle is caller-driven now (`/pause_generation` + `/continue_generation`, plus the begin/end weight-update session), so the async/keep-pause semantics have no home; removal converts a silent no-op into a loud error for out-of-tree callers.
- **B. Keep them for wire compatibility** but document them as deprecated no-ops.
- **C. Re-wire them**, if there is a live plan — e.g. `token_step` next to `weight_version`, and `num_paused_requests` sourced from the existing scheduler counter (the `sglang:num_paused_reqs` gauge, `observability/metrics_collector.py:493`).

items.title: [RFC]: Limit the use of envvars in vLLM
items.author: zhuohan123
items.body_excerpt:
### Motivation.

vLLM's envvars are on the edge of getting out of control. There are many envvars should instead be configs. Like the attention backend, all2all kernel backend, and even there is a flag to control KV cache layout. envvars are evil because:

1. It is equivalent of using global variables everywhere in the code, which is a bad programming practice.
2. envvars have no advanced structure like, hierarchy, typechecks, etc. 

In summary, I think envvars are the kind of thing that is very easy to add so people tend to add envvars as the shortest path to implement their feature, but this can quickly becomes unmanageable and makes the project very hard to use. 

### Proposed Change.

I think we should:

1. Spend some effort on reviewing the current envvars and move many of them to configs.
2. Have very strict bar on what can be an envvar and question every new envvars in vllm.

items.title: [Docs] Document NIXL KV connector metrics aggregation semantics
items.author: NickLucche
items.body_excerpt:
## Summary

The NIXL KV connector logs transfer metrics periodically:

```
KV Transfer metrics: Num successful transfers=4, Avg xfer time (ms)=1.381, P90 xfer time (ms)=2.601, Avg post time (ms)=0.672, P90 post time (ms)=0.801, Avg MB per transfer=2.25, Throughput (MB/s)=1629.549, Avg number of descriptors=72.0
```

Currently there is no documentation explaining what these metrics represent, especially in the context of **multi-rank (TP > 1) deployments**. This has already caused confusion among users.

## Current behavior

All metrics are **aggregated across all TP ranks** before summary stats are computed:

1. Each TP rank independently records per-transfer telemetry (`transfer_duration`, `post_duration`, `bytes_transferred`, `num_descriptors`) via `NixlKVConnectorStats.record_transfer()` in [`stats.py`](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/main/vllm/distributed/kv_transfer/kv_connector/v1/nixl/stats.py).
2. Stats from all ranks are concatenated via `aggregate()` (`list.extend()`).
3. `reduce()` computes averages, percentiles, and throughput over the **combined** pool of observations from all ranks.

This means:
- **"Num successful transfers"** is the total count across all ranks, not per-rank.
- **"Avg MB per transfer"** is the average over all individual rank-level transfers, not the total bytes moved for a single KV cache transfer operation.
- **"Throughput (MB/s)"** is `total_MB_all_ranks / total_time_all_ranks` — effectively an average per-rank throughput, not the aggregate system throughput.
- **Percentiles (P90)** are computed over the combined distribution of all ranks' transfer times.

This is unintuitive because users may expect metrics to reflect per-engine totals or aggregate system throughput.

## What needs to be documented

1. **Docstrings in `stats.py`**: Add clear documentation to `NixlKVConnectorStats` explaining that stats are aggregated across all TP ranks and what each metric represents in that context.
2. **Inline comments in `reduce()`**: Clarify the semantics of throughput and averages — that they are per-rank averages over the combined observation pool.
3. **Docstrings in `metrics.py`**: Document the `observe()` → `aggregate()` → `reduce()` → `log()` pipeline and the fact that stats arrive pre-aggregated across workers.
4. **(Optional) Docs page**: Add a section to the disaggregated serving documentation explaining how to interpret the KV Transfer metrics log line.

## Relevant files

- `vllm/distributed/kv_transfer/kv_connector/v1/nixl/stats.py` — `NixlKVConnectorStats` (recording, aggregation, reduction)
- `vllm/distributed/kv_transfer/kv_connector/v1/metrics.py` — `KVConnectorLogging` (observe/log pipeline), `KVConnectorStats` (base class)

## Context

See related discussion: metrics are aggregated across ranks rather than reported per-rank or per-engine. This is a deliberate design choice (fire-and-forget from workers), but it needs to be clearly documented so users can correctly interpret the numbers.

items.title: [Feature]: Per-request prefix-cache miss attribution (prompt divergence vs. eviction)
items.author: sachinworks
items.body_excerpt:
### 🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch

Automatic prefix caching is one of the biggest cost and latency wins for RAG and agent workloads, where every request re-sends a long, mostly identical scaffold (system prompt, tool schemas, few-shot examples).

vLLM already reports per-request cached tokens (`num_cached_tokens`, `usage.prompt_tokens_details.cached_tokens`), so you can tell roughly *where* the cache hit ended. What you can't tell is *why* it ended there. That matters because the fix is completely different:

- **The prompt changed.** A timestamp or request ID in the system prompt, tool definitions serialized in a different order, a user name injected near the top. Each one invalidates every block after it. The fix is in the application.
- **The block was evicted.** The prefix was cached earlier but got pushed out under memory pressure. The fix is capacity, routing or cache offload, not the prompt.

Today both look identical from the outside: a short cache hit. Telling them apart means diffing tokenized prompts by hand and guessing about eviction.

**Proposal:** optional per-request diagnostics, disabled by default:

- a **miss reason** for the first uncached block after the longest hit: `evicted` (its hash was cached recently and evicted, tracked with a small bounded set of recently evicted hashes) or `no_match` (no matching block key was seen recently). `no_match` covers both changed prompt tokens and changed extra keys mixed into the block hash (`cache_salt`, LoRA adapter, multimodal inputs), so on its own it is not proof that the text changed.
- the **kinds of extra keys** included in that block's hash (e.g. `cache_salt`, `lora`, `mm`), names only and never values, so users can rule out salt or adapter differences first
- optionally, an opt-in **comparison against a reference request** that returns a short decoded snippet around the first differing token, off by default for privacy

_Updated after discussion below: renamed `not_cached` to `no_match` and added extra-key kinds, following the `cache_salt` edge case raised in the comments._

These could be surfaced in debug-level logs and/or request-level metrics.

**Why it helps:** teams could catch cache-hostile prompt construction in CI or staging, and tie TTFT regressions to the right cause: a prompt change versus cache pressure in the serving stack.

### Alternatives

- Diffing tokenized prompts by hand against a known-good request. Works for divergence, but is slow, needs the exact tokenized input, and says nothing about eviction.
- Correlating with KV cache events (block stored / removed) externally. Possible, but requires running an event consumer and joining block hashes to requests outside vLLM.
- Re-hashing prompts client-side. This duplicates vLLM's block-hashing logic and drifts whenever that changes (block size, hash function, multimodal or LoRA extra keys).

### Additional context

Related: #43711 proposed a lower-level debug event at the lookup point (`KVCacheManager.get_computed_blocks`, right after `find_longest_cache_hit`). It was closed for inactivity without maintainer feedback. That lookup point looks like the natural place to compute the miss reason above.

Happy to work on a PR if maintainers agree on the approach.

items.title: [Performance][ROCm] KV connectors rule out ROCM_ATTN, so PD workers decode on ROCM_AITER_UNIFIED_ATTN (1.9–3.2x the per-token time for Qwen3 models on MI355X)
items.author: chunfangamd
items.body_excerpt:
### Your current environment

- vLLM `0.30.1rc1.dev396+gac68c3087` (the ROCm nightly image `vllm/vllm-openai-rocm:nightly-ac68c3087215e0a4f3cdfa218508c6aada57235d`), MI355X, one GPU per instance (TP1).
- Models: `Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B`, `Qwen/Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507` and `Qwen/Qwen3-30B-A3B` (bf16), `openai/gpt-oss-20b` and `openai/gpt-oss-120b`. All with `--compilation-config '{"cudagraph_mode":"PIECEWISE"}' --max-model-len 16384`; `--gpu-memory-utilization` was 0.3 for Qwen3-0.6B in runs A and B below, 0.35 for the other models without AITER, and 0.5 for every model with `VLLM_ROCM_USE_AITER=1`.
- The image's defaults otherwise: it sets no `VLLM_ROCM_*` variables, so `VLLM_ROCM_USE_AITER` is off and `ROCM_AITER_FA` is not a candidate. For the Qwen3 models, vLLM logs `potential backends: ['ROCM_ATTN', 'ROCM_AITER_UNIFIED_ATTN', 'TRITON_ATTN']` without a connector and `['ROCM_AITER_UNIFIED_ATTN', 'TRITON_ATTN']` with one.

### Describe the performance issue

An instance with any KV connector cannot use `ROCM_ATTN`: `RocmAttentionBackend.supports_kv_connector()` returns `False` (`vllm/v1/attention/backends/rocm_attn.py` L210–214, "incompatible with KV connectors that require blocks-first layout"), so backend selection picks `ROCM_AITER_UNIFIED_ATTN` with the LBHNC layout instead. For the three Qwen3 models we measured (0.6B, 4B and 30B-A3B), decode on that backend takes 1.9–3.2x the per-token time of `ROCM_ATTN` at ~3,900 tokens of context. Every PD worker has a KV connector, so PD on ROCm pays this on every decode step, with NixlConnector and MoRIIOConnector alike.

The connector itself is not the cost: for Qwen3-0.6B, an instance without any connector but with `--attention-backend ROCM_AITER_UNIFIED_ATTN` is just as slow. Models that cannot use `ROCM_ATTN` anyway are not affected: gpt-oss uses attention sinks, which `ROCM_ATTN` does not support (`supports_sink()` returns `False`, `rocm_attn.py` L199–204), so its instances run `ROCM_AITER_UNIFIED_ATTN` with or without a connector.

With `VLLM_ROCM_USE_AITER=1`, instances without a connector keep `ROCM_ATTN`, while connector instances get `ROCM_AITER_FA`; the gap narrows to 1.1–1.4x but does not close.

### Measurements

Each configuration ran alone on one MI355X, on the same GPU, with the flags above. 16 prompts (8 of ~3,000–3,900 tokens, 8 short) were sent straight to the instance (no PD, no transfer), each generating exactly 32 tokens (`ignore_eos`). The tables give the median decode time per token from `vllm:request_decode_time_seconds`, from two passes in opposite orders, and in parentheses the ratio to the instance without a connector in the same run.

| A | `MoRIIOConnector`, `kv_producer` | `ROCM_AITER_UNIFIED_ATTN`, LBHNC | 5.04 / 5.01 ms (2.04) | 3.77 / 3.73 ms (1.54) |
| A | No connector, `VLLM_KV_CACHE_LAYOUT=LBHNC` | `ROCM_ATTN`, LBHNC: "Cannot use ROCm custom paged attention kernel, falling back to Triton implementation" | 9.09 / 9.09 ms (3.70) | 3.59 / 3.54 ms (1.46) |
