items.title: `tt.scan`/`tl.cumsum` hits an internal `AddPartialReduce` assert when `num_ctas > 1`
items.author: dequeueing
items.body_excerpt:
Launching a kernel that runs `tl.cumsum` (any `tt.scan`) under a multi-CTA layout (`num_ctas >= 2`) triggers an internal consistency assertion in the scan lowering:

```
triton-opt: .../lib/Conversion/TritonGPUToLLVM/ScanOpToLLVM.cpp:157:
void AddPartialReduce(...):
Assertion `numScanBlocks * numParallelBlocks * parallelElementsPerThread *
scanElementsPerThreads == srcValues.size()' failed.
```

**Expected**: either a clean diagnostic telling the user that scan is not supported under multi-CTA layouts, or correct codegen.
**Actual**: the internal assert fires. On a bare `triton-opt` run this is a `SIGABRT`; through the Python frontend the same assertion is surfaced as an opaque `RuntimeError: PassManager::run failed` after the assert text is printed, rather than a user-facing diagnostic.

The assert exists to catch a block-count mismatch, and it does — but the failure mode gives the user no hint that `num_ctas` is the problem.

This is **not** the same defect as the batched-dot `num_ctas` crash fixed by #11811 / reported in #11808. That bug lived in `TritonNvidiaGPUAssignCGALayoutsPass` (a rank mismatch while *assigning* the CGA layout). The IR reproducer below never runs that pass — the `CGALayout` is already written into the encoding and it crashes later, inside `ConvertTritonGPUToLLVM`'s scan lowering. On the Python frontend the same kernel does go through `AssignCGALayouts` successfully and only aborts at lowering. So this survives the #11811 fix; I have not rebuilt past that commit to confirm on current `main`, but the failing code path (`ScanOpToLLVM`, not `AssignCGALayouts`) is untouched by it.

## Reproducer 1 — `tl.cumsum` + `num_ctas=2`

```python
import torch, triton, triton.language as tl

@triton.jit
def scan_k(x_ptr, o_ptr, M: tl.constexpr, N: tl.constexpr, AX: tl.constexpr):
    om = tl.arange(0, M); on = tl.arange(0, N)
    x = tl.load(x_ptr + om[:, None] * N + on[None, :])
    r = tl.cumsum(x, axis=AX)
    tl.store(o_ptr + om[:, None] * N + on[None, :], r)

x = torch.randn(32, 32, device="cuda", dtype=torch.float32)
o = torch.empty(32, 32, device="cuda", dtype=torch.float32)
scan_k[(1,)](x, o, 32, 32, 0, num_ctas=2)   # <- num_ctas=2 triggers it
```

Output (the assert message is emitted, then the pipeline reports a generic failure):

```text
python: .../ScanOpToLLVM.cpp:157: ... AddPartialReduce(...):
Assertion `numScanBlocks * numParallelBlocks * parallelElementsPerThread *
scanElementsPerThreads == srcValues.size()' failed.
...
RuntimeError: PassManager::run failed
```

`num_ctas=1` compiles and runs correctly. The crash is independent of the scan axis and of which tensor dimension the CGA layout splits.

## Reproducer 2 — `triton-opt` (offline, no GPU)

`repro.mlir`:

```mlir
#b = #ttg.blocked<{sizePerThread=[1,1],threadsPerWarp=[1,32],warpsPerCTA=[4,1],
                  order=[1,0], CGALayout=[[1,0]]}>
module attributes {"ttg.num-ctas"=2:i32,"ttg.num-warps"=4:i32,
                   "ttg.threads-per-warp"=32:i32} {
  tt.func @p(%v:tensor<32x32xf32,#b>) {
    %r = "tt.scan"(%v) <{axis = 0 : i32, reverse = false}> ({
    ^bb0(%a:f32,%b:f32):
      %s = arith.addf %a, %b : f32
      "tt.scan.return"(%s) : (f32) -> ()
    }) : (tensor<32x32xf32,#b>) -> tensor<32x32xf32,#b>
    tt.return
  }
}
```

```text
$ triton-opt repro.mlir --allocate-shared-memory-nv \
    --convert-triton-gpu-to-llvm=compute-capability=90 -o /dev/null
triton-opt: .../ScanOpToLLVM.cpp:157: ... AddPartialReduce(...):
Assertion `numScanBlocks * numParallelBlocks * parallelElementsPerThread *
scanElementsPerThreads == srcValues.size()' failed.
(SIGABRT, exit 134)
```

## Controls

- **`num_ctas=1`** (drop the `CGALayout`): compiles cleanly (rc 0).
- **`tt.reduce` with the same 2-CTA `CGALayout`**: compiles cleanly **and produces numerically correct output** (`tl.sum` + `num_ctas=2` matches the reference). Reduction lowering accounts for the CTA dimension; scan lowering does not.
- The assert fires for every scan configuration I tried: any scan axis, 2D or 3D tensors, `num_ctas=2` or `4`, and CGA splits on either dimension. The gap is systemic to `tt.scan` under multi-CTA, not tied to one config.
  - The **same assertion text is reached at two sites**, chosen by how many warps carry unique data along the scan axis (`axisNumWarps`). With the layouts Triton picks for the Python reproducer, `axis=0` goes through `AddPartialReduce` at `ScanOpToLLVM.cpp:157`, while `axis=1` on a 2D tensor (and the scan axis of a 3D tensor) takes the `axisNumWarps==1` fast path and fires the identical assert inside `AddPartialReduceOneWarp` at `ScanOpToLLVM.cpp:263`. A hand-written layout that puts several warps on the scan axis hits `:157` instead — so the site is decided by `axisNumWarps`, not by rank. Both come from the same `ScanLoweringHelper` block-count math, so the suggested fix below covers both.

<details>
<summary>Relevant native stack frames (triton-opt)</summary>

```text
#17 AddPartialReduce(...)
      .../lib/Conversion/TritonGPUToLLVM/ScanOpToLLVM.cpp:184:63
#21 (anonymous namespace)::ScanOpConversion::emitFastScan(
      mlir::triton::ScanOp, ..., mlir::triton::TargetInfoBase const&) const
      .../lib/Conversion/TritonGPUToLLVM/ScanOpToLLVM.cpp:522:3
#22 ConvertOpToLLVMPattern<mlir::triton::ScanOp>::matchAndRewrite(...)
#27 (anonymous namespace)::OperationLegalizer::legalize(mlir::Operation*)
```
</details>

Note on the two line numbers: the assert that fails is at **`ScanOpToLLVM.cpp:157`** (the `numScanBlocks * ... == srcValues.size()` check). The `#17` frame prints `184:63` because `-O2` attributes the inlined cold `__assert_fail` block to the next source line — the `__assert_fail` call is preceded by `mov $0x9d, %edx` (`0x9d = 157`), confirming the assert's own line argument is 157. The `#18–#20` frames are inlined `SmallVector` destructors on the same PC, not real calls.

## Root cause

`AddPartialReduce` (`ScanOpToLLVM.cpp:157`) asserts:

```cpp
assert(numScanBlocks * numParallelBlocks * parallelE

comments.author: he-yufeng
comments.body:
Verified against current main (`aad2a60d9`, local `triton-opt` built with `TritonRelBuildWithAsserts`, pinned LLVM 24.0.0git): this is fixed by #11990.

Running the exact pipeline from the report (`--allocate-shared-memory-nv --convert-triton-gpu-to-llvm=compute-capability=90`):

| config | result |
|---|---|
| repro as posted (scan axis 0, `CGALayout=[[1,0]]`, split along the scan axis) | clean `error: TODO: unsupported scan layout`, exit 1, no assert |
| scan axis 1, split along axis 1 | same clean error |
| scan axis 0, `CGALayout=[[0,1]]` (split along the non-scan axis) | compiles, exit 0 |
| scan axis 1, split along axis 0 | compiles, exit 0 |
| `num_ctas=1` control | compiles, exit 0 |

No SIGABRT anywhere. The two assert sites (`ScanOpToLLVM.cpp:157` and `:263`) are still in the tree but no longer reachable from these inputs. The mechanism matches the #11990 description: scan-axis CTA splits now fail `ScanLoweringHelper::isSupported()` via `getCTASplitNum(...)[axis] != 1`, and non-scan-axis partitions use the per-CTA shape in `getNonAxisNumBlocks()` / `getAxisBlockStride()`, which is what the assert's block-count product needed.

One observation in case anyone touches this code: the rejection text is the pre-existing placeholder `TODO: unsupported scan layout`, which does not tell the user that `num_ctas` is the trigger. Not worth a PR on its own, but if the scan-axis case is meant to stay unsupported, naming the cause there would save the next person a source build.

Suggest closing this as fixed by #11990.

items.title: [BUG] CuTe DSL >= 4.6: FlashAttention-4 SM100 backward with block-sparse masks spills registers, up to 1.8x slower than 4.5.3 (same kernel source)
items.author: janhuenermann
items.body_excerpt:
### Which component has the problem?

CuTe DSL

### Bug Report

**Describe the bug**

With the same kernel source, CuTe DSL 4.6.0.dev0 and later generate PTX for the FlashAttention-4 SM100 backward kernel (`flash_attn.cute.flash_bwd_sm100.FlashAttentionBackwardSm100`) that spills registers. The spills appear when the kernel is specialized for block-sparse attention with a `mask_mod`. That is the path `torch.nn.attention.flex_attention(..., kernel_options={"BACKEND": "FLASH"})` takes. With CuTe DSL 4.5.3, the same source compiles to PTX with no spills, or almost none. The kernel is at the 128-register cap (512 threads per CTA), so the extra pressure becomes local-memory traffic. On B200 the backward kernel is 22% slower with a sliding-window mask and 82% slower with a document mask. The dense, causal, GQA and native `window_size` specializations of the same kernel are not affected.

This looks like the backward counterpart of #3701 (forward kernel, 4.7/4.8 vs 4.5.1), and it narrows down where the regression landed. 4.5.3 is fine. 4.6.0.dev0 already regresses, and it is the first release whose PTX header says `Based on NVVM 23.0.0` (4.5.3: `NVVM 20.0.0`).

**Backward kernel GPU time**, ms (B200, bf16, head dim 128, 16 heads; median of 50; main backward kernel only, from the torch profiler; a repeat run agrees within 1% for the block-sparse rows and within 5% for the others)

| attention | 4.5.3 | 4.6.0.dev0 | 4.8.0 ¹ |
|---|---|---|---|
| full, batch 2 × 8192 | 2.039 | 2.010 (−1%) | 2.084 |
| causal, 2 × 8192 | 1.121 | 1.140 (+2%) | 1.177 |
| GQA causal (32 q / 4 kv heads), 2 × 8192 | 2.287 | 2.266 (−1%) | 2.366 |
| native sliding window 1024 (`window_size`), 2 × 16384 | 0.714 | 0.713 (0%) | 0.756 |
| **block-sparse `mask_mod`: sliding window 1024**, 2 × 16384 | 0.858 | **1.045 (+22%)** | **1.027 (+20%)** |
| **block-sparse `mask_mod`: document mask** (causal within random-length documents), 1 × 32768 | 1.279 | **2.329 (+82%)** | **2.209 (+73%)** |

The 4.5.3 and 4.6.0.dev0 columns run the same FA4 source (b20, see "Same source" below).
¹ The 4.8.0 column runs FA4 4.0.0b32, the latest release at the time of testing (b33 has a byte-identical backward kernel). FA4 changed between b20 and b32, so this column shows that the regression persists; it is not a clean A/B.

**The same PTX files assembled by one ptxas** (CUDA 13.0, V13.0.88, `ptxas -arch=sm_100a -O3 -v`)

| backward specialization | PTX from | spill stores / loads | SASS instr. | IMAD | STL / LDL |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| causal | 4.5.3 (CUDA 12.9 / NVVM 20.0.0) | 0 / 0 B | 3496 | 242 | 0 / 0 |
| causal | 4.6.0.dev0 (CUDA 13.3 / NVVM 23.0.0) | 0 / 0 B | 3360 | 216 | 0 / 0 |
| sliding window `mask_mod` | 4.5.3 | 0 / 0 B | 3800 | 294 | 0 / 0 |
| sliding window `mask_mod` | 4.6.0.dev0 | 124 / 228 B | 4528 | 703 | 31 / 57 |
| sliding window `mask_mod` | 4.8.0 (CUDA 13.4 / NVVM 23.0.0) ¹ | 260 / 264 B | 4192 | 318 | 65 / 55 |
| document `mask_mod` | 4.5.3 | 28 / 16 B | 4512 | 653 | 7 / 4 |
| document `mask_mod` | 4.6.0.dev0 | 204 / 204 B | 5952 | 1049 | 51 / 42 |
| document `mask_mod` | 4.8.0 ¹ | 184 / 184 B | 5456 | 968 | 46 / 37 |

All of these are at 128 registers (`.reqntid 512`), with warp-specialized budgets (`setmaxnreg.inc` 136/152, `setmaxnreg.dec` 88/24). The PTX files have no `.local` declarations, so ptxas introduces the spills from register pressure in the NVVM 23 PTX. The SASS that 4.8.0 ships through its own ptxas has 50 STL / 42 LDL for the document mask and 35 / 26 for the sliding window (causal: 2 / 2).

**Likely pressure region.** `CUTE_DSL_COMPILER_OPT="remarks{ptx}" CUTE_DSL_LINEINFO=1` on 4.8.0 marks `flash_attn/cute/block_sparse_utils.py:1564` in `get_block_sparse_iteration_info_bwd`. items.title: [Bug] CuTe DSL HCA (DeepSeek V4 sparse MLA) produces non-finite output on SM107: arch dispatch covers only sm_100/sm_103
items.author: Vinnie6167
items.body_excerpt:
# CuTe DSL HCA (DeepSeek V4 sparse MLA) produces non-finite output on SM107 — arch dispatch covers only sm_100/sm_103

**Component:** `flashinfer/cute_dsl/attention/dsa/hca_fp8.py` (`BlackwellHeavilyCompressedAttentionForwardFP8`), wrapper `flashinfer/cute_dsl/attention/wrappers/batch_hca.py`, entry `trtllm_batch_decode_sparse_mla_dsv4(backend="cute-dsl")`.
**Author / owner:** @myu-guo (#3943, #4368).
**Affects:** SM107 (Rubin). SM100/SM103 unaffected.

## What happens

`batch_hca.py:220` and `:436` reject anything but `(10, 0)/(10, 3)`, so today HCA simply raises on SM107 (5 test cases in `tests/attention/test_cute_dsl_hca_dsv4.py` skip). Widening those two checks compiles and launches the kernel on an SM107 part, but every case fails:

```
AssertionError: Tensor-likes are not close!            (test_cute_dsl_hca_dsv4.py:868, :1072)
assert torch.isfinite(out).all()  -> False
```

## Why — the kernel body's arch arms don't include SM107

With `nvidia-cutlass-dsl >= 4.8.0.dev0` the DSL knows `sm_107a` natively, so `require_cute_dsl_arch()` does **not** fall back to the `sm_100f` family target and the kernel is compiled for `sm_107a`. The softmax stage then dispatches on the compile arch:

```python
# hca_fp8.py ~L3045
arch = BaseDSL._get_dsl().get_arch_enum()
if cutlass.const_expr(Arch.sm_100 <= arch <= Arch.sm_100f):      # plain tmem_load + masked row-max
    ...
elif cutlass.const_expr(Arch.sm_103 <= arch <= Arch.sm_103f):    # LdRed32x32bOp / TmemLoadRedOp.MAX
    ...
# no arm for sm_107*
```

`sm_107a` satisfies neither range, both arms are `const_expr`, so the accumulator TMEM→register load and the row-max are compiled out — the softmax runs on uninitialised registers, hence the non-finite output. (`arch_str = "sm_100"` at `:130` is only the SMEM/TMEM-capacity lookup key and does not steer codegen.)

## Questions for the author

1. Which arm should SM107 take? Rubin has `tcgen05.ld.red` (PrimTS selects its LDTM.STAT path on SM107 for that reason), so the SM103 `LdRed…MAX` arm is probably the fast choice; the SM100 plain-load arm is the safe first step. Adding `or Arch.sm_107 <= arch <= Arch.sm_107f` to one of them is the minimal change.
2. `dsa/gather4_utils.py:46,48` pins `GatherScatterTmaLoadEnum.sm_100` / `sm_100_2sm` for the Gather4 TMA atom; the enum has no `sm_107` member in DSL 4.8.0. Is the sm_100 atom valid on Rubin, or does Gather4 need a Rubin variant?
3. Anything else in the kernel sized against SM100 (TMEM columns, SMEM budget from `get_smem_capacity_in_bytes("sm_100")` = 232448 — equal to Rubin's opt-in max, so probably fine)?

## Repro

SM107 part, cu134 nightly image + `nvidia-cutlass-dsl[cu13]==4.8.0.dev0`, widen the two `((10, 0), (10, 3))` checks in `batch_hca.py` and run `pytest tests/attention/test_cute_dsl_hca_dsv4.py -k "correctness or partial_head"` → 5 failures with non-finite output. The other DSv4 path (trtllm-gen sparse MLA) passes 119/119 on the same part (#5391), so a working HCA would complete DSv4 on Rubin.

items.title: [SM120] sparse MLA MG prefill kernel races on `w_head_sc_all` in released versions (fixed on main by #5197, please backport)
items.author: gavinkvx
items.body_excerpt:
**Affected:** `sparse_mla_prefill_mg_kernel` (SM120 sparse MLA prefill, more than 64 query tokens, models without V rope such as the DSv3.2 path) in v0.6.18 and v0.7.0.post1.

**Cause:** each KV tile's XV MMA reads the per-head V scales in `sm.w_head_sc_all`. Nothing makes the next tile wait for those reads before it zeroes the buffer and rebuilds it.

- In 0.6.18, the SG kernel has the barrier: `if constexpr (!KV::V_HAS_ROPE) bar_sync_t<2, MATH_THREADS>();` at `prefill_kernel.cuh:513`. The MG kernel has no equivalent before its `bar_arrive_alt` (`:1517`).
- On main, after #5197, the reset is preceded by `RoleSync<MATH>::wait()` ("All prior XV readers retired"). That fixes it, but no release includes it.

**Evidence** (RTX 5090, CUDA 13.0, torch 2.13, flashinfer 0.6.18; I also checked the v0.7.0.post1 source, which has the same pattern):

- compute-sanitizer racecheck reports ≥9.9M hazards, with the write at `prefill_kernel.cuh:936` (zeroing) and the read at `:1454` (XV MMA). With the barrier there are 0.
- With `kv_scale_format="pow2_fp32"`, 2000 out of 2000 identical calls give a different result from the first call: about 74 rows × 8–16 heads differ, relative error around 0.1. With the barrier, 0 out of 2000 differ.
- The barrier costs about 1.5% in kernel time.

**Repro**

```python
import torch, flashinfer
from flashinfer.mla import trtllm_batch_decode_with_kv_cache_mla
torch.manual_seed(0); dev = "cuda"; T, CTX, H, K, P = 2048, 24576, 64, 2048, 64
nope = torch.randn(CTX, 4, 128, device=dev) * 0.5
sc = torch.exp2(torch.ceil(torch.log2(nope.abs().amax(-1, keepdim=True).clamp(min=1e-4) / 448)))
kv = torch.cat([(nope / sc).to(torch.float8_e4m3fn).view(torch.uint8).reshape(CTX, 512),
                sc.reshape(CTX, 4).contiguous().view(torch.uint8),
                (torch.randn(CTX, 64, device=dev) * 0.5).to(torch.bfloat16).view(torch.uint8)], 1)
kv = kv.view(CTX // P, 1, P, 656)
pos = torch.arange(CTX - T, CTX, device=dev)
key = torch.rand(T, CTX, device=dev); key[torch.arange(CTX, device=dev)[None] > pos[:, None]] = 2
idx = key.topk(K, 1, largest=False).indices.sort(1).values.int()
q = (torch.randn(T, 1, H, 576, device=dev) * 0.5).bfloat16()
ws = torch.zeros(128 << 20, dtype=torch.uint8, device=dev)
run = lambda: trtllm_batch_decode_with_kv_cache_mla(
    query=q, kv_cache=kv, workspace_buffer=ws, qk_nope_head_dim=128, kv_lora_rank=512,
    qk_rope_head_dim=64, block_tables=idx.unsqueeze(1), seq_lens=torch.full((T,), K, dtype=torch.int32, device=dev),
    max_seq_len=K, sparse_mla_top_k=K, bmm1_scale=576 ** -0.5, backend="sparse", kv_scale_format="pow2_fp32")
ref = run().clone()
print(sum(not torch.equal(run().view(torch.int16), ref.view(torch.int16)) for _ in range(200)), "/ 200 runs differ")
```

**Ask:** please backport the `w_head_sc_all` reset ordering from #5197 to the release branch, or cut a patch release that includes it.

items.title: server: tool_choice: "required" accepted but not enforced on templates with supports_preserve_reasoning=true
items.author: lmbagley
items.body_excerpt:
# `tool_choice: "required"` is accepted but not enforced on templates with `supports_preserve_reasoning: true`

### Name and Version

```
build_info: b330-84e908c62
```
Built locally for CUDA 13.0, `-DGGML_CUDA=ON -DCMAKE_CUDA_ARCHITECTURES=121 -DCMAKE_CUDA_FLAGS="-O2"`.

### Operating systems

Linux (aarch64, NVIDIA GB10 / sm_121)

### Which llama.cpp modules do you know to be affected?

`llama-server`, and the chat/grammar layer under `common/` (`chat-auto-parser-generator.cpp`).

### Command line

```
llama-server -m qwen36-NVFP4-MTP-HQ.gguf --host 0.0.0.0 --port 11435 \
  -c 131072 --jinja -ngl 999 -fa on -ctk q8_0 -ctv q8_0 --spec-type draft-mtp
```

### Problem description

`llama-server` accepts `"tool_choice": "required"` on `/v1/chat/completions` without error or
warning, and then does not enforce it, on models whose chat template llama.cpp classifies with
`supports_preserve_reasoning: true`.

Instead of being constrained to emit a tool call, the model generates freely until `max_tokens`
is exhausted. The request returns `finish_reason: "length"` with `predicted_n` equal to the full
budget and no `tool_calls`. In the runs I inspected the tail of the output had degenerated into a
repeating emoji sequence, which is consistent with generation being unconstrained rather than
grammar-limited.

The failure is **silent and expensive**: a caller that relies on `required` for structured output
receives ordinary prose, no error, and pays the maximum token cost of the request every time.

Two servers on the same host, same binary, same build string, both `--jinja`, differ only in the
model/template:

| | fast lane | smart lane |
|---|---|---|
| model | Qwen3.6-35B-A3B (NVFP4, MTP) | Qwen3-Next-80B-A3B-Instruct (Q4_K_M) |
| `supports_tool_calls` | true | true |
| `supports_parallel_tool_calls` | true | true |
| `supports_object_arguments` | true | true |
| **`supports_preserve_reasoning`** | **true** | **false** |
| `tool_choice: "required"` | **ignored** | honoured |

`supports_preserve_reasoning` is the only differing capability in `/props → chat_template_caps`.

**On reproducing this without my exact file:** the GGUF above is a local conversion and is not
something you can download, so please do not treat the filename as the repro target. The trigger
appears to be the *chat template* — specifically whichever templates llama.cpp classifies
`supports_preserve_reasoning: true`, i.e. a `<think>`-style reasoning template. Any model whose
`/props → chat_template_caps` reports that flag together with `supports_tool_calls: true` should
show it. `repro.sh` prints both flags up front so it is obvious at a glance whether a given server
is a candidate. I am happy to attach the exact template text if that helps.

### What is NOT the cause (ruled out by measurement)

- **The model.** An identical hand-written GBNF grammar posted to `/completion` forces a perfect
  tool call on both servers, from a prompt with no intent to call anything. Section B of the
  reproducer is this control.
- **Grammar sampling generally.** `root ::= "BANANA"` is honoured on the affected server.
- **Speculative decoding.** The control above succeeds with `--spec-type draft-mtp` active.
- **Reasoning parsing.** Sending `"reasoning_format": "none"` does not change the behaviour.
- **Token budget.** Identical failure at `max_tokens` 500 / 1500 / 3000 / 5000 — all fully
  consumed, `reasoning_content` exactly 801 chars each time.
- **The tool-call syntax.** Both templates emit `<tool_call>…</tool_call>` with `<|im_start|>`.

### Why this looks like a defect rather than unsupported behaviour

`common/chat-auto-parser-generator.cpp` appears to intend enforcement on this path:

```cpp
// ~line 84
bool include_grammar = has_response_format || (has_tools &&
        ((inputs.tool_choice == COMMON_CHAT_TOOL_CHOICE_AUTO && !trigger_marker.empty()) ||
          inputs.tool_choice == COMMON_CHAT_TOOL_CHOICE_REQUIRED));

// ~line 89 — REQUIRED yields a NON-lazy (eager) grammar
data.grammar_lazy = !has_response_format && inputs.tool_choice == COMMON_CHAT_TOOL_CHOICE_AUTO;

// ~line 369 and ~line 500 — for REQUIRED the tool calls are NOT made optional
if (!require_calls) { tool_calls = p.optional(tool_calls); }
```

So a grammar is built, marked eager, and tool calls are non-optional — yet generation is
evidently unconstrained. I have not isolated the specific line where enforcement is lost; that
likely needs a debug build dumping the emitted GBNF for the two templates.

### Steps to Reproduce

Full script at the bottom of this issue. `./repro.sh <host:port>` exits **1** when the bug reproduces and **0**
when `required` is honoured — it was verified to discriminate between the two servers above.

```bash
curl -s http://HOST:PORT/v1/chat/completions -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{
  "model":"local",
  "messages":[{"role":"user","content":"Hello, how are you today?"}],
  "tools":[{"type":"function","function":{"name":"get_disk_free",
    "parameters":{"type":"object","properties":{"host":{"type":"string"}},"required":["host"]}}}],
  "tool_choice":"required","max_tokens":2000,"temperature":0}'
```

Expected: a `tool_calls` response. Actual on an affected template: `finish_reason: "length"`,
`predicted_n` == `max_tokens`, no `tool_calls`.

### Relevant log output

```
finish_reason : length
predicted_n   : 2000
tool_calls    : NONE
content tail  : '🎗️🎗️🎗️🎗️🎗️🎗️🎗️🎗️🎗️🎗️🎗️🎗️🎗️🎗️🎗️🎗️🎗️🎗️🎗️🎗️…'

# control, same server, hand-written grammar via /completion:
'<tool_call>{"name": "get_disk_free", "arguments": {"host": "beta"}}</tool_call>'
```


### Possibly related open issues

- **#26781** — *"enable_thinking forced true in jinja/caps.cpp capability probe leaks into
  non-DeepSeek templates"*. Same model family (Qwen3.6-35B-A3B), same subsystem, and a very
  similar end state: budget consumed inside `reasoning_content`, no `tool_calls`, a silent dead
  end for an API consumer. **Differences:** that report needs ~38-41 turns of accumulated co

items.title: [Feature Request]: Hierarchical Eviction with Assign / Evict / Fallback
items.author: kanceler
items.body_excerpt:
### Describe your feature request

# Discussion Draft: Hierarchical Eviction with Assign / Evict / Fallback

## Background

The current [type-aware eviction PR](https://github.com/kvcache-ai/Mooncake/pull/2746) shows that Mooncake Store needs a way to distinguish eviction semantics across object data types. For example, Hidden State and KV Cache differ in cache granularity, reuse interval, recomputation cost, and serving impact. They should not always be ranked by the same global lease-time ordering.

However, if each new policy is implemented directly inside `MasterService`, the master service will become increasingly complex as we add tenant-aware, type-aware, cost-aware, or other future eviction policies.

One possible direction is to model eviction policy as a small set of composable operations rather than as policy-specific branches embedded in `MasterService`.

## Core Idea

The policy layer can be expressed using three basic operations:

```text
Assign
Evict
Fallback
```

These operations are policy-side planning operations. They do not directly mutate metadata or remove replicas. `MasterService` remains responsible for safe execution.

### Assign

`Assign` partitions a candidate set by some dimension and assigns an eviction target to each child scope.

The partition dimension can be tenant, object data type, model, priority, namespace, or another future policy dimension.

For example:

```text
global_scope
-> Assign(by tenant)
   -> tenant A scope + A_evict_ratio + A_evict_ratio_lowerbound
   -> tenant B scope + B_evict_ratio + B_evict_ratio_lowerbound
```

Inside each tenant, the policy can continue partitioning by object data type:

```text
tenant B scope
-> Assign(by type)
   -> tenant B / KV Cache scope + KV_evict_ratio + KV_evict_ratio_lowerbound
   -> tenant B / Hidden State scope + Hidden_evict_ratio + Hidden_evict_ratio_lowerbound
```

In this model, tenant and type are not hard-coded hierarchy levels in the framework. They are just different ways to use `Assign`.

The assigned target can be represented as a ratio or as bytes. For memory pressure, bytes are often the more natural responsibility unit, while ratios are useful for compatibility with the current `BatchEvict` semantics.

### Evict

`Evict` selects victims within the current scope according to that scope's ranking policy.

It does not cross the scope boundary. For example, when running inside `tenant B / Hidden State`, it only selects victims from Hidden State candidates belonging to tenant B.

Different scopes can use different ranking policies:

- KV Cache can use a lease/LRU-like policy.
- Hidden State can use a policy that accounts for longer reuse intervals and higher recomputation cost.
- Unknown or general types can use the default lease-based policy.

`Evict` only produces a planned victim list. It does not modify metadata, release quota, remove replicas, or interact with offload state.

### Fallback

`Fallback` is used when child scopes fail to satisfy the lowerbound target of their parent scope. It selects additional victims inside the parent scope while relaxing the child partition boundaries.

For example, if type-scoped eviction inside a tenant cannot satisfy that tenant's lowerbound target, the policy should first fall back within that tenant rather than immediately shifting pressure to other tenants:

```text
tenant B scope
-> Fallback(tenant scope)
```

This means the policy can select from all remaining candidates in tenant B, without strictly preserving the original type-level split.

If all tenant scopes together still cannot satisfy the global lowerbound target, the policy can then use a global fallback:

```text
global_scope
-> Fallback(global scope)
```

Global fallback should not degenerate into raw lease-time ordering. It should still be able to consider tenant pressure and type pressure, so that fallback does not systematically punish scopes that are not the main source of memory pressure.

Fallback only relaxes policy partition boundaries. It does not relax execution safety boundaries. Hard pin, soft pin, group semantics, offload behavior, replica refcount, quota accounting, and metadata correctness are still enforced by `MasterService` during execution.

## Composed Flow

Using these three operations, a hierarchical eviction policy can be expressed as:

```text
global_scope
-> Assign(by tenant)
-> for each tenant_scope:
     -> Assign(by type)
     -> for each type_scope:
          -> Evict(type policy)
     -> Fallback(tenant scope)
-> Fallback(global scope)
```

This flow expresses several principles:

1. Assign responsibility before selecting victims.
2. Prefer eviction inside more specific scopes first.
3. If child scopes cannot satisfy the parent target, fall back within the parent scope first.
4. Only when the parent scope still cannot satisfy the target should the policy fall back to a higher-level scope.

## Relationship With MasterService

`MasterService` does not need to understand each policy's internal rules. It only needs to provide the mechanism around policy planning:

1. Build a lightweight candidate view.
2. Execute the policy's plan with revalidation.
3. Report actual eviction progress back to the policy flow.

The candidate view can be produced by the existing metadata scan. It should contain object identity and a small set of policy-relevant attributes, such as tenant, data type, memory footprint, lease state, and pin state.

The candidate view should not be a full metadata snapshot. It should not copy complete `ObjectMetadata`, replica lists, group membership, or segment state.

When executing eviction, `MasterService` uses the candidate reference to locate the real metadata again, revalidates whether the object is still evictable, and then handles group eviction, offload-on-evict, quota release, replica removal, metrics, and metadata erase.

Therefore, the policy layer owns decision-making, while `MasterService` owns mutation and correctness.

## Execution Feedba

items.author: gilfree
items.body_excerpt:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

`torch.fx.Tracer` has a `record_stack_traces` member. It does not give the correct stack trace, starting with torch  2.4 RC.

I am not sure it is part of the external API, but it was nice to have. The following is working in 2.3, but broken in 2.4RC


```python
import torch.fx
class M1(torch.nn.Module):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        self.linear = torch.nn.Linear(1, 1)
    def forward(self, x):
        return x + self.linear(x)
class M2(torch.nn.Module):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        self.m1 = M1()
    def forward(self, x):
        return x + self.m1(x)
m = M2()
tracer = torch.fx.Tracer()
tracer.record_stack_traces=True
graph = tracer.trace(m)
sym=torch.fx.GraphModule(m,graph)
print(sym.print_readable())
assert 'code: return x + self.linear(x)' in sym.print_readable()
assert 'code: return x + self.m1(x)' in sym.print_readable()
```

It was broken in this PR: https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/121449/ where you stopped using the find_user_frame (or an equivalent function) to filter non user stack traces.

Something along these lines can be probably used as a fix:

```python
    def create_proxy(self, kind, target,args, kwargs, name, type_expr = None, proxy_factory_fn = None):
....
     if self.record_stack_traces and not proxy.node.stack_trace:
            proxy.node.stack_trace = _find_user_frame2_4(''.join(CapturedTraceback.extract().format()))


    def _find_user_frame2_4(self, stack_trace):
        stack_trace=stack_trace.split('\n')
        if 'torch/fx/proxy.py' in stack_trace[-3]:
            stack_trace=stack_trace[:-1]
            while len(stack_trace)>2 and '/fx/' in stack_trace[-2]:
                stack_trace=stack_trace[:-2]
        return '\n'.join(stack_trace)
```

Notes:
- I am not sure why you don't see the effect in `torch.export.export`.
- `torch.export.unflatten` looses stack trace for collapsed modules.

items.title: [Bug] NVGPUWarpSpecialization: `Unexpected op` in backward-slice when `tl.gather` feeds `tl.dot` (sm90)
items.author: dequeueing
items.body_excerpt:
## Summary
A `tl.gather` result used as a `tl.dot` operand inside `tl.range(..., warp_specialize=True)` aborts the `NVGPUWarpSpecialization` pass at `WSDataPartition.cpp:330` (`llvm_unreachable("Unexpected op")`) during backward-slice partitioning — `tt.gather` is not in the op whitelist. `num_ctas=1`, `num_warps=4`.

## Reproducer
Save the following script as `repro.py` and run with `python repro.py`:

```python
import torch, triton, triton.language as tl

@triton.jit
def k(a_ptr, b_ptr, c_ptr, M: tl.constexpr, N: tl.constexpr, K: tl.constexpr):
    om = tl.arange(0, M); on = tl.arange(0, N); ok = tl.arange(0, K)
    acc = tl.zeros([M, N], dtype=tl.float32)
    for i in tl.range(0, 4, warp_specialize=True):
        a = tl.load(a_ptr + om[:, None] * K + ok[None, :] + i * M * K)
        b = tl.load(b_ptr + ok[:, None] * N + on[None, :] + i * K * N)
        idx = tl.full([M, K], 1, tl.int32)
        a = tl.gather(a, idx, axis=1)          # gather result feeds tl.dot
        acc += tl.dot(a, b)
    tl.store(c_ptr + om[:, None] * N + on[None, :], acc)

M = N = K = 128
a = torch.randn(4 * M * K, device="cuda", dtype=torch.float16)
b = torch.randn(4 * K * N, device="cuda", dtype=torch.float16)
c = torch.empty(M * N, device="cuda", dtype=torch.float32)
k[(1,)](a, b, c, M, N, K, num_ctas=1, num_warps=4)
```

## Crash
Expected: the kernel compiles and runs (as it does when `warp_specialize=True` is removed), or fails with a user-facing diagnostic. Actual: compiler crashes with an internal assertion/error.

```
UNREACHABLE executed at <triton_src>/third_party/nvidia/hopper/lib/Transforms/WarpSpecialization/WSDataPartition.cpp:330!
```

## Root cause
`getBackwardSliceToPartition`'s op whitelist does not include `tt.gather`; reaching it hits `llvm_unreachable` rather than a graceful "unsupported" diagnostic. The identical kernel compiles and runs normally when `warp_specialize=True` is removed.

## Environment
Triton `42c5e89c3` (2026-09-11, `TritonRelBuildWithAsserts`), NVIDIA H800 (sm_90a), `num_ctas=1`, `num_warps=4`. Deterministic.

items.title: [Bug] NVGPUWarpSpecialization: `Unexpected asyncTaskIds.size()` with `tl.atomic_add` after `tl.dot` (sm90)
items.author: dequeueing
items.body_excerpt:
## Summary
`tl.atomic_add` on the dot accumulator written **after** `acc += tl.dot` inside `tl.range(..., warp_specialize=True)` aborts at `WSDataPartition.cpp:775` (`llvm_unreachable("Unexpected asyncTaskIds.size()")`) — the atomic carries a task-id count the sliceOp dispatch does not handle. `num_ctas=1`, `num_warps=4`.

## Reproducer
Save the following script as `repro.py` and run with `python repro.py`:

```python
import torch, triton, triton.language as tl

@triton.jit
def k(a_ptr, b_ptr, c_ptr, M: tl.constexpr, N: tl.constexpr, K: tl.constexpr):
    om = tl.arange(0, M); on = tl.arange(0, N); ok = tl.arange(0, K)
    acc = tl.zeros([M, N], dtype=tl.float32)
    for i in tl.range(0, 4, warp_specialize=True):
        a = tl.load(a_ptr + om[:, None] * K + ok[None, :] + i * M * K)
        b = tl.load(b_ptr + ok[:, None] * N + on[None, :] + i * K * N)
        acc += tl.dot(a, b)
        tl.atomic_add(c_ptr + om[:, None] * N + on[None, :], acc)   # atomic AFTER dot, on acc
    tl.store(c_ptr + om[:, None] * N + on[None, :], acc)

M = N = K = 128
a = torch.randn(4 * M * K, device="cuda", dtype=torch.float16)
b = torch.randn(4 * K * N, device="cuda", dtype=torch.float16)
c = torch.empty(M * N, device="cuda", dtype=torch.float32)
k[(1,)](a, b, c, M, N, K, num_ctas=1, num_warps=4)
```

## Crash
Expected: the kernel compiles and runs (as it does when `warp_specialize=True` is removed), or fails with a user-facing diagnostic. Actual: compiler crashes with an internal assertion/error.

```
UNREACHABLE executed at <triton_src>/third_party/nvidia/hopper/lib/Transforms/WarpSpecialization/WSDataPartition.cpp:775!
```

## Root cause
Inside `WSDataPartition.cpp`'s `sliceOp`, the per-task-id dispatch assumes a fixed set of `asyncTaskIds.size()` values; the atomic-on-accumulator produces a count outside the handled set and hits `llvm_unreachable`. The kernel compiles and runs normally when `warp_specialize=True` is removed.

## Environment
Triton `42c5e89c3` (2026-09-11, `TritonRelBuildWithAsserts`), NVIDIA H800 (sm_90a), `num_ctas=1`, `num_warps=4`. Deterministic.

items.title: [RFC]: Control-plane orchestration of vLLM sleep mode and kvcached for warm standby and multi-model GPU pooling
items.author: Jeffwan
items.body_excerpt:
### Summary

AIBrix scales replicas as 0-or-N and only *observes* engine memory state; it never drives it. Two engine-side mechanisms now make GPU memory reclaimable at runtime — vLLM **sleep mode** (park a whole idle model's weights+KV) and **kvcached** (elastically shrink/grow a model's KV so several models share one GPU) — but both are mechanism-only, with no control plane. This RFC proposes AIBrix own the *policy*: a control-plane-driven "warm/asleep" tier between one replica and zero, plus KV-budget arbitration across co-resident models. The result: multi-minute cold starts become second-scale wakes, and one GPU can densely host many long-tail models.

### Motivation

Scaling is binary today. To reclaim a GPU we either keep a replica running (burning HBM while idle) or delete the pod and pay a multi-minute cold start (weight load + CUDA graph capture) when traffic returns. Neither fits bursty or long-tail traffic.

The engine now exposes the levers, but not the policy:

| | vLLM sleep mode | kvcached (github.com/ovg-project/kvcached) |
|---|---|---|
| Scope | whole model (weights + KV) | KV cache only (weights allocated outside it) |
| Granularity | all-or-nothing, single process | page-level elastic, cross-process co-residency |
| Target | a fully **idle** model | several **active** models sharing a GPU |
| Mechanism | CUDA VMM; `/sleep` `/wake_up`; level 1 weights→CPU, level 2 discard | CUDA VMM; per-process `cudaMemGetInfo` headroom + `/dev/shm` budget via `kvctl` |
| Control | manual API only; `VLLM_SERVER_DEV_MODE`-gated; no autoscaling | decentralized by design; no scheduler/admission/cross-node; `controller/` is a demo |

They are complementary: kvcached handles elastic KV among active co-resident models; sleep parks idle models' weights. Both are VMM actuators that enforce/observe — neither *decides*. The missing piece is a control plane that decides **which** model sleeps/wakes and **when**, **how much** KV budget each co-resident model gets, **admission** when a GPU is oversubscribed, and **routing/readiness** as models move between awake / warm / asleep. AIBrix already scrapes `vllm:engine_sleep_state` but never acts on it, and has no notion of co-resident KV budget — so it is the natural owner.

### Proposed Change

(Sketch only; full design — CRD, state machine, budget algorithm, agent protocol — to follow in a complete doc.)

1. A **warm/asleep lifecycle state** between `minReplicas` and zero: low traffic → `POST /sleep?level=1&mode=wait` (graceful drain); traffic returns → `/wake_up` (seconds). Pod/IP/endpoint persist.
2. A **KV-budget arbiter** across co-resident models, driving `kvctl` limits by policy (per-model min/max/share, priority) with cost-asymmetric reclaim — shrink KV first (cheap), sleep weights only when protected floors don't fit (expensive).
3. A **decide/execute split**: a Go controller (placement, admission, sleep/wake & budget policy, status) over a pod-side agent (kvcached engine, `kvctl`, sleep).
4. **Required couplings:** invalidate the prefix index on sleep (KV is wiped — see the sleep/prefix-index bug), exclude asleep pods from routing/readiness, and document the `VLLM_SERVER_DEV_MODE` requirement.

### Alternatives Considered

- **HPA scale-to-zero** (`minReplicas=0`): already supported, but pays the full cold start and has no warm tier.
- **Leave it to kvcached's decentralized scheme:** works on a single node but has no admission/priority/cross-node policy and no sleep orchestration — precisely the demo `controller/` AIBrix would replace.
- **Token-level time-sharing** (swap at request granularity): higher utilization ceiling but far more complex/intrusive; this RFC targets model-granularity pooling.

items.title: [Bug]: AutoDeploy logger treats verbose and internal_error as info
items.author: adenzhou1350
items.body_excerpt:
### System Info

- TensorRT-LLM main at `b8e337d939cde1b7aa65feb5287e5bdefa02154b`
- Python 3.12 and 3.14
- Reproduced on Linux and Windows
- CPU-only; no GPU or model is involved

### Who can help?

_No response_

### Information

- [ ] The official example scripts
- [ ] My own modified scripts

### Tasks

- [ ] An officially supported task in the `examples` folder (such as GLUE/SQuAD, ...)
- [ ] My own task or dataset (give details below)

### Reproduction

`ADLogger` defines AutoDeploy-specific severities and maps `verbose` to `logging.DEBUG` and `internal_error` to `logging.CRITICAL` in `log()`. The environment-variable path and `set_level()` instead use `getattr(logging, ...)`, so these same public severity names silently fall back to INFO.

```python
import logging
from tensorrt_llm._torch.auto_deploy.utils.logger import ADLogger

logger = ADLogger()
logger.set_level("verbose")
print(logger._logger.level)  # 20 (INFO), expected 10 (DEBUG)

logger.set_level("internal_error")
print(logger._logger.level)  # 20 (INFO), expected 50 (CRITICAL)
```

The same mismatch occurs when `AUTO_DEPLOY_LOG_LEVEL` is set before importing the module. Standard levels such as `warning` work as expected.

### Expected behavior

All public AutoDeploy severity names should resolve consistently in `log()`, `set_level()`, and `AUTO_DEPLOY_LOG_LEVEL`: `verbose` should select DEBUG and `internal_error` should select CRITICAL. Unknown strings can continue to fall back to INFO.

### actual behavior

Both AutoDeploy-specific names resolve to INFO in `set_level()` and the environment-variable initialization path, so verbose logs stay hidden and internal errors lose their intended severity.

### additional notes

I searched open and closed issues/PRs and did not find an exact duplicate. A minimal fix can reuse `_SEVERITY_TO_LEVEL` for all three paths and add a CPU-only regression test. I have reproduced the baseline/fix differential on current main and can submit the patch if this issue is approved, per the contribution policy. The behavior remains present even though AutoDeploy is being redirected toward the standalone backend.

### Before submitting a new issue...

- [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and checked the [documentation](https://nvidia.github.io/TensorRT-LLM/) and [examples](https://github.com/NVIDIA/TensorRT-LLM/tree/main/examples) for answers to frequently asked questions.

items.title: [New Model]: Apertus (swiss-ai/Apertus-8B-Instruct-2509, swiss-ai/Apertus-v1.5-8B)
items.author: maxwbuckley
items.body_excerpt:
### The model to consider.

`swiss-ai/Apertus-8B-Instruct-2509` (`ApertusForCausalLM`) and the text path of `swiss-ai/Apertus-v1.5-8B` (`Apertus1p5ForConditionalGeneration`), from the Swiss AI initiative. Both are fully open models supporting more than 1,800 languages.

### The closest model TensorRT-LLM already supports.

Llama / Qwen3: a Llama-style dense decoder with per-head QK-norm (as in Qwen3) and llama3 RoPE scaling.

### What's your difficulty of supporting the model you want?

- A non-gated MLP with the xIELU activation ([arXiv 2411.13010](https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.13010)), which has two coefficients learned per layer.
- The existing fused QK-norm + RoPE kernel doesn't implement llama3 scaling.
- Apertus 1.5 ships as a multimodal checkpoint (decoder under `model.language_model.`). Its input embedding is larger than its output head, and its config type isn't in the pinned transformers.

An implementation is in #19735, with an optional CUDA xIELU op in #19737.

### The model to consider.

aleph-alpha/kolibri-1 ( Kolibri1ForCausalLM ), from Aleph Alpha. 

It's an open, modern fine-grained Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model.


### The closest model TensorRT-LLM already supports.

- **4-Norm Sandwich Structure**: Each decoder layer applies sandwich RMSNorms after attention (`post_attn_norm`) and after MoE (`post_ffn_norm`) before residual accumulation.
- **Fine-Grained MoE**: 384 routed experts (top-6 activated per token) + 1 shared expert, with intermediate size 512.

An implementation is prepared in a linked Draft PR.

items.title: pycute left_inverse returns a different canonical layout than CuTe C++
items.author: VaggelisGian
items.body_excerpt:
### Which component has the problem?

pycute (`python/pycute`, the pure-Python reference implementation), not the CuTe DSL

### Describe the bug

`pycute.left_inverse` returns a different canonical layout than `cute::left_inverse` in `include/cute/layout.hpp` for non-contiguous and hierarchical inputs. Both results are valid left inverses on the image of the layout (applying them to `layout(i)` recovers `i`), so this is a fidelity gap between the Python reference and the C++ implementation rather than a broken inverse. Anyone using pycute to cross-check CuTe semantics gets different shapes/strides exactly in the interesting cases.

`python/pycute/layout.py` implements

```python
def left_inverse(layout):
  ...
  return right_inverse(make_layout(layout, complement(layout)))
```

while the C++ side uses a dedicated sort-by-stride algorithm (`left_inverse` at `include/cute/layout.hpp`, with a divisibility static assert and an explicit stride-0 skip).

### Steps to reproduce

Python (main):

```python
from pycute import *
print(left_inverse(Layout(4,2)))
print(left_inverse(Layout((4,2),(1,16))))
print(left_inverse(Layout(((2,2),(2,2)),((1,4),(8,32)))))
```

C++ (host-only, g++ against include/):

```cpp
#include <cute/tensor.hpp>
#include <iostream>
using namespace cute;
int main() {
  print(left_inverse(Layout<Shape<_4>,        Stride<_2>>{}));        print("\n");
  print(left_inverse(Layout<Shape<_4,_2>,     Stride<_1,_16>>{}));    print("\n");
  print(left_inverse(Layout<Shape<Shape<_2,_2>,Shape<_2,_2>>,
                        Stride<Stride<_1,_4>,Stride<_8,_32>>>{}));    print("\n");
}
```

Comparison gathered on main:

| input | C++ `left_inverse` | pycute `left_inverse` |
|---|---|---|
| `4:1` | `_4:_1` | `4:1` (agree) |
| `4:2` | `(_2,_4):(_0,_1)` | `(2,4):(4,1)` |
| `1:0` | `_1:_0` | `1:0` (agree) |
| `(8,4):(1,8)` | `_32:_1` | `32:1` (agree) |
| `(8,4):(4,1)` | `(_4,_8):(_8,_1)` | `(4,8):(8,1)` (agree) |
| `(2,4,6):(1,2,8)` | `_48:_1` | `48:1` (agree) |
| `(2,4,6):(4,1,8)` | `(_4,_2,_6):(_2,_1,_8)` | `(4,2,6):(2,1,8)` (agree) |
| `(4,2):(1,16)` | `(_16,_2):(_1,_4)` | `(4,4,2):(1,8,4)` |
| `(2,5):(5,1)` | `(_5,_2):(_2,_1)` | `(5,2):(2,1)` (agree) |
| `((2,2),(2,2)):((1,4),(8,32))` | `(_4,_8,_2):(_1,_2,_8)` | `(2,2,4,2,2):(1,16,2,32,8)` |

The C++ output for `4:2` contains an explicit leading stride-0 mode that the Python result lacks entirely, and the hierarchical case differs in both rank and strides.

### Expected behavior

`pycute.left_inverse` should return the same canonical layout as `cute::left_inverse`, matching shape and stride structure, so the Python reference can be used to verify CuTe behavior. Alternatively, if the two algorithms are intentionally allowed to differ, the divergence should be documented in the pycute sources.

### Environment details

- Bare metal Windows host; C++ side compiled host-only with g++ against `include/cute/layout.hpp` from current `main`
- Pure Python comparison needs no GPU

items.body_excerpt:
### Which component has the problem?

CUTLASS C++ - `include/cutlass/transform/threadblock/predicated_tile_access_iterator.h` and siblings

### Describe the bug

`add_tile_offset(TensorCoord const &tile_offset)` moves the iterator by whole tiles along both ranks. When a caller passes a non-zero `contiguous()` component while advancing along the strided rank (or vice versa), that cross-term must be scaled by the element size because the iterators keep byte-based pointers. The residue-handling branch of the plain predicated tile access iterator does scale it, but every other path applies the raw tile count:

`include/cutlass/transform/threadblock/predicated_tile_access_iterator.h`, residue path (correct):

```cpp
pointer_ += Shape::kContiguous * tile_offset.contiguous() * sizeof_bits<Element>::value / 8;
...
pointer_ += Shape::kStrided * tile_offset.strided() * sizeof_bits<Element>::value / 8;
```

same function, steady-state path a few lines below (unscaled):

```cpp
pointer_ += Shape::kContiguous * tile_offset.contiguous();
...
pointer_ += Shape::kStrided * tile_offset.strided();
```

So the same call arguments take differently-scaled code paths depending on `is_residual_tile_`. The same unscaled pattern appears in:

- `predicated_tile_access_iterator_2dthreadtile.h` (both paths)
- `ell_predicated_tile_access_iterator.h` (both paths)
- `predicated_tile_access_iterator_triangular_matrix.h` (both paths)
- `predicated_tile_access_iterator.h`, `AffineRankN<2>` specialization, which additionally ignores `stride_[0]` for the contiguous rank

I believe no in-tree caller currently trips this: every `add_tile_offset` call site on these global-memory iterators passes exactly one non-zero component (`{1,0}` / `{0,1}` / `{0,-1}` style), so the cross term is always zero and the missing scaling is invisible. It is nevertheless a broken API contract for any external code moving tiles diagonally with `Element` wider than one byte, and the intra-file inconsistency shows at least one of the two paths must be wrong.

### Steps to reproduce

Static: diff the two branches of `PredicatedTileAccessIterator::add_tile_offset` in the file above. A host-side demonstration needs only instantiating the iterator with a two-component tile offset, which no current example does.

### Expected behavior

Both paths should apply the same, correctly scaled cross-term (element size, and for the `AffineRankN<2>` case the layout stride).

### Environment details

- Current main, header-only observation
- Found while auditing the transform/threadblock iterator family; no functional failure observed in any in-tree kernel

items.title: GEMM profiler verification compares only batch 0 when batch-count > 1
items.author: VaggelisGian
items.body_excerpt:
### Description

The GEMM profiler's verification compares only the first batch when `--batch-count=N` with N > 1.

All gemm-family verify paths pass the per-batch stride as the element count:

```cpp
results_.back().verification_map[library::Provider::kCUBLAS] = compare_tensors(
  options,
  *gemm_workspace_.Computed,
  *gemm_workspace_.Reference,
  gemm_workspace_.Computed->batch_stride()      // <-- elements in ONE batch
);
```

(tools/profiler/src/gemm_operation_profiler.cu lines ~1369-1374 for cuBLAS and ~1542-1547 for the host reference; the same pattern appears in tools/profiler/src/block_scaled_gemm_operation_profiler.cu ~1357-1370 and blockwise_gemm_operation_profiler.cu ~1195-1200.)

`DeviceAllocation` allocates `capacity_ = batch_stride_ * batch_count_` (tools/profiler/src/device_allocation.cu ~350-356), so `Computed`/`Reference` hold all batches but `compare_tensors(..., count)` (tools/profiler/src/operation_profiler.cu ~630) only walks `batch_stride()` elements, i.e. batch 0. Batches 1..N-1 are never compared against either reference provider.

Consequence: a kernel bug that corrupts only later batches (wrong batch-stride advance in an epilogue or TMA descriptor) reports `Passed` under `--verification=true --batch-count=N`.

For contrast, the rank_k/rank_2k/symm/trmm/conv profilers compare with the full capacity, which is the conservative direction.

### Suggested fix

Either loop over batches comparing each `batch_stride()` slice at its offset, or compare the full capacity after ensuring padding regions are written deterministically. A one-line interim hardening is to compare `Computed->capacity()` instead of `batch_stride()` when `batch_count > 1`.

This is a static trace through allocation, stride computation, and the comparison call; I did not construct a deliberately-wrong kernel to demonstrate a false pass.

items.title: rank_2k_universal and symm_universal Arguments constructors discard batch_stride_B
items.author: VaggelisGian
items.body_excerpt:
### Description

The `Arguments` constructors of two kernels discard their `batch_stride_B` parameter and store 0 instead:

```cpp
// include/cutlass/gemm/kernel/rank_2k_universal.h:176
batch_stride_A(batch_stride_A), batch_stride_B(0),

// include/cutlass/gemm/kernel/symm_universal.h:173
batch_stride_A(batch_stride_A), batch_stride_B(0),
```

`trmm_universal.h:158` stores its parameter (`batch_stride_B(batch_stride_B)`), which makes the intent clear; these are copy-paste typos. Confirmed by constructing `Arguments` for both kernels in a host program and printing the stored field: passing 200 stores 0.

Consequences:

1. `Params` construction copies `args.batch_stride_B`, so downstream code always sees stride 0.
2. Both kernels' `transposed_problem()` does `std::swap(args.batch_stride_A, args.batch_stride_B)` on an `Arguments` built by that constructor (`rank_2k_universal.h:189`), so after the swap the *stored* `batch_stride_A` becomes the dead 0 too: for the transposed path both batch strides are wrong, not just B's.

Additional observation while tracing this: neither kernel body ever reads `params.batch_stride_A` or `params.batch_stride_B` (unlike `gemm_universal.h`, which advances both pointers per batch), so batched operation through these kernels keeps A and B fixed across batches regardless of the arguments. The typo is provable on its own; the unused-stride observation may deserve separate attention.

### Suggested fix

Store the parameter in both places:

```cpp
batch_stride_A(batch_stride_A), batch_stride_B(batch_stride_B),
```

items.title: F.threshold on integer tensors truncates a fractional threshold to the tensor dtype; eager and torch.compile disagree
items.author: the-Shallow
items.body_excerpt:
### 🐛 Describe the bug


`torch.nn.functional.threshold(input, threshold, value)` is documented as `y = x if x > threshold else value`.
For an integer `input` and a fractional `threshold`, the kernels cast `threshold` to the input dtype
(`threshold_scalar.to<scalar_t>()` in `aten/src/ATen/native/cpu/Activation.cpp` and
`cuda/ActivationThresholdKernel.cu`), which truncates it toward zero, so elements with `x > threshold`
are replaced. `torch.compile` compares in the promoted type and returns the documented result, so eager
and compiled code give different answers. A threshold outside the dtype's range raises instead of
thresholding every element. Other comparisons (`int_tensor > -0.5`, `torch.clamp(int_tensor, min=-0.5)`)
promote the scalar.



### Steps to reproduce

```python
import torch, torch.nn.functional as F
x = torch.tensor([-2, -1, 0, 1, 2])
print(F.threshold(x, -0.5, 99).tolist())                               # [99, 99, 99, 1, 2]
print(torch.where(x > -0.5, x, 99).tolist())                           # [99, 99, 0, 1, 2]
print(torch.compile(lambda t: F.threshold(t, -0.5, 99))(x).tolist())   # [99, 99, 0, 1, 2]
F.threshold(torch.tensor([1, 2], dtype=torch.int8), 1000.0, 0)         # RuntimeError: ... without overflow
```


### Expected

`[99, 99, 0, 1, 2]` in eager mode, as documented and as `torch.compile` returns; `[0, 0]` for the int8 case.


### Suggested fix

Compare in the promoted type (as the inductor lowering does), e.g. convert the input element to the scalar's type for the comparison, or check `x > threshold` with the scalar kept as double.


### Versions

### Environment

PyTorch 2.14.0 (the latest release, CPU wheel) and 2.12.0, Python 3.12, Ubuntu 24.04, x86_64


cc @albanD @mruberry @jbschlosser @walterddr @mikaylagawarecki @nairbv

items.title: Geometric.entropy() returns 0.0 for small probs in float32 (true entropy about 19.4 nats at probs=1e-8)
items.author: the-Shallow
items.body_excerpt:
### 🐛 Describe the bug


`torch.distributions.Geometric(probs=p).entropy()` returns `0.0` for small `p` in float32, starting around
`p = 1e-8` (`logits` about -18). The entropy of a geometric distribution is `(-(1-p) log(1-p) - p log p) / p`,
which tends to +inf as `p -> 0`; the implementation computes it as
`binary_cross_entropy_with_logits(logits, probs) / probs`, and the numerator underflows.

### Steps to reproduce

```python
import torch
G = torch.distributions.Geometric
print(G(probs=torch.tensor(1e-8)).entropy())                        # tensor(0.)
print(G(probs=torch.tensor(1e-8, dtype=torch.float64)).entropy())   # 19.4207 (correct)
```


### Expected

About 19.42 in float32 too (the float64 value).


### Suggested fix

Use a form without the cancellation, e.g. `-log(p) - (1 - p) / p * log1p(-p)` (with `log1p(-p)/p` evaluated stably), or compute from `logits`: `softplus(-logits) + softplus(logits) * exp(-logits)`-style expressions.


### Versions


### Environment

PyTorch 2.14.0 (the latest release, CPU wheel) and 2.12.0, Python 3.12, Ubuntu 24.04, x86_64


cc @fritzo @neerajprad @alicanb @nikitaved

items.title: torch.autograd.functional.jacobian(strategy='forward-mode', vectorize=True) fails for a 1-D input matmul'd with a matrix
items.author: the-Shallow
items.body_excerpt:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

torch.autograd.functional.jacobian(func, x, vectorize=True, strategy="forward-mode")` raises
`RuntimeError: Trying to set a forward gradient that has a different size than that of the original Tensor` for a
function that multiplies a 1-D input by a matrix and applies one more operation (an unbatched linear layer followed by
an activation). Reverse mode and `torch.func.jacfwd` compute the same Jacobian.

### Steps to reproduce

```python
import torch
from torch.autograd.functional import jacobian

W = torch.randn(3, 2)
x = torch.randn(2)
f = lambda t: (t @ W.T).exp()
print(jacobian(f, x).shape)  # torch.Size([3, 2])
jacobian(
    f, x, vectorize=True, strategy="forward-mode"
)  # RuntimeError: Trying to set a forward gradient ...
```


### Expected

`torch.Size([3, 2])`, equal to the reverse-mode result.


### Suggested fix

Build `_jacfwd` on `torch.func.jvp`/`vmap` (as `torch.func.jacfwd` is), or fix the legacy batching rule for `matmul` so the tangent gets the same rank reduction as the primal.


### Versions


### Environment

PyTorch 2.14.0 (the latest release, CPU wheel) and 2.12.0, Python 3.12, Ubuntu 24.04, x86_64

items.title: RDT: register_nixl_memory cache false-hits on a resized/recycled pointer, skipping registration of the new extent
items.author: BatshevaBlack
items.body_excerpt:
### Description

register_nixl_memory's cache is keyed on the storage's data_ptr(). If a tensor's storage is freed and a later allocation reuses the same address but with a larger size, the cache sees a hit on the pointer and skips re-registration. 
NIXL still only has the old, smaller extent [P, P+S1) registered. A subsequent transfer of that tensor will fail with NIXL_ERR_NOT_FOUND, since NIXL requires the full transfer range to be covered by a single registered region.

### Use case

1. On register_nixl_memory(tensor), when the cache has a hit on data_ptr(), also compare the previously-registered size against the current storage's nbytes():
   - Sizes match → current behavior (cache hit, skip registration).
   - Sizes differ → deregister the old registration and register the new extent as if fresh.
2. Add a docstring/comment on register_nixl_memory making explicit that resizing a preregistered buffer in place is inefficient and user should prefer allocating a big buffer size.

### What happened + What you expected to happen

### Description

Every replica start currently makes a blocking `ray.get(controller.get_tracing_config.remote())` call to fetch the `TracingConfig (replica.py:1192)`. This adds one extra controller task per replica start, putting avoidable load on the controller during large-scale deployments and scale-ups.

Pass the `TracingConfig` to the replica as a constructor argument instead of having each replica pull it from the controller at startup. The controller already builds replica init args, so the config can be threaded through there, hence eliminating the per-start RPC.

Follow-up to PR #65437 ([2/2] Propagate TracingConfig to proxies via long poll). This was deferred from that PR because it touches deployment_state / replica scheduling, which was out of scope.

items.title: [Serve] Tracing config changes don't take effect on live proxies/replicas (OpenTelemetry set-once provider)
items.author: suppagoddo
items.body_excerpt:
### Description

 ### Summary

After tracing has been initialized in a proxy (or replica) process, all the subsequent `TracingConfig` changes propagated via long poll do **not** take effect in that live process. For example, `enabled=True → enabled=False` will not disable tracing on an already-tracing proxy; changes to `sampling_ratio` or `exporter_import_path` are ignored too. The change only applies to proxies/replicas started afterward.

### Root cause

OpenTelemetry honors only the `first trace.set_tracer_provider()` call per process (t`racing_utils.py setup_tracing`). Once a provider (with its sampler + span processors) is installed, it is effectively immutable for the life of the process. The proxy's long-poll handler `_update_tracing_config (proxy.py)` detects this and logs a one-time warning rather than silently dropping the change.

### Current behavior (as of PR #65437)

-  serve deploy succeeds and the controller reports the new `TracingConfig`.
-  Live proxies keep their original sampler/exporter and log a warning that the update did not apply.
-  New proxies/replicas pick up the new config on startup.

###  Possible approaches to actually support runtime reconfig

 1. Indirection layer: Add a single stable TracerProvider with a mutable sampler wrapper and add/removable span processors, so runtime updates re-point sampling/export without installing a new provider. Requires a custom Sampler and span-processor lifecycle management.
 2. Restart proxies/replicas on tracing-config change: simpler but disruptive to in-flight requests.

###  Interim mitigation

 Document the constraint in user-facing Serve tracing docs and keep the loud log on attempted-but-ignored updates. (Note: the long-poll callback cannot raise an error because an exception will freeze route-table updates so this raises a WARN log, not an exception.)

###  Context

Follow-up from review on PR #65437 ([2/2] Propagate TracingConfig to proxies via long poll).

### Use case

_No response_

items.title: [Core] Worker SIGSEGV in PyTraceBack_Here when LocalGC arrives before worker.core_worker is assigned
items.author: Xargonus
items.body_excerpt:
### What happened + What you expected to happen

A worker segfaults (PyTraceBack_Here, <no Python frame>) if a LocalGC request reaches it during startup. The window is between the worker announcing its port to the raylet and Python assigning global_worker.core_worker. During that gap, gc_collect runs global_worker.core_worker.trigger_gc(), which raises AttributeError. The exception escapes a nogil callback and crashes the process, the same crash class as #54556 and #64558. Master has the same code.

We hit this in production. Frequent global GCs from WarnResourceDeadlock combined with high actor churn killed about 0.1% of new workers.

Expected: a GC request during startup is ignored instead of killing the worker.

Workaround: RAY_start_python_gc_manager_thread=0.

Suggested fix: in gc_collect, skip the call if core_worker isn't set yet, and wrap the body in try/except. Happy to send a PR.

### Versions / Dependencies

Ray 2.51.1, Python 3.12.7, Linux x86_64.

### Reproduction script

The sitecustomize delays the core_worker assignment by 0.5 s so the race always hits.
```
import os, sys, tempfile, time

d = tempfile.mkdtemp()
with open(os.path.join(d, "sitecustomize.py"), "w") as f:
    f.write(
        "import sys, time\n"
        "if 'default_worker.py' in ' '.join(sys.argv):\n"
        "    import ray._raylet as r\n"
        "    _Real = r.CoreWorker\n"
        "    def _slow(*a, **kw):\n"
        "        cw = _Real(*a, **kw); time.sleep(0.5); return cw\n"
        "    r.CoreWorker = _slow\n"
    )
os.environ["PYTHONPATH"] = d + os.pathsep + os.environ.get("PYTHONPATH", "")
os.environ["RAY_local_gc_min_interval_s"] = "0"

import ray
from ray._private.internal_api import global_gc

ray.init(num_cpus=4)


@ray.remote(num_cpus=0)
class A:
    def ping(self):
        return os.getpid()


deaths = 0
for _ in range(20):
    actors = [A.remote() for _ in range(8)]
    refs = [a.ping.remote() for a in actors]
    end = time.time() + 2
    while time.time() < end:
        global_gc()
        time.sleep(0.05)
    for ref in refs:
        try:
            ray.get(ref, timeout=60)
        except ray.exceptions.RayActorError:
            deaths += 1
    for a in actors:
        ray.kill(a)
print(f"actor deaths: {deaths} / 160", file=sys.stderr)
```
Output: actor deaths: 160 / 160, and every worker log shows the SIGSEGV. With RAY_start_python_gc_manager_thread=0: 0 / 160.

### Issue Severity

Medium: It is a significant difficulty but I can work around it.

items.title: [Train] STRICT_SPREAD runs can wait forever when the autoscaler packs coordinator bundles onto one node
items.author: justinvyu
items.body_excerpt:
### What happened + What you expected to happen

Since #66002, Train V2 waits for the AutoscalingCoordinator to reserve capacity before it creates the worker placement group, then pins each worker to a reserved node. For `placement_strategy="STRICT_SPREAD"` on an autoscaling cluster, that reservation may never cover the worker group, so the run never starts.

**Why**

- `_AutoscalingCoordinatorActor._merge_and_send_requests` (`python/ray/data/_internal/cluster_autoscaler/default_autoscaling_coordinator.py`) collapses `STRICT_PACK` bundles into a single summed bundle, so the autoscaler is asked for one big enough node. `STRICT_SPREAD` gets no equivalent treatment. Its bundles go to `ray.autoscaler.sdk.request_resources` as independent bundles, and that API can't express "one bundle per node".
- So for 8 workers × `{"GPU": 1}`, the autoscaler can satisfy the request with a **single 8-GPU node** if the cluster config offers that node type. After that, it considers the demand met and won't launch more nodes.
- `_compute_reservations` honors `STRICT_SPREAD` (at most one bundle per node), so that node yields **1 of 8** reserved slots.
- Train never creates the placement group, because it's still waiting for the reservation. So the strategy-aware pending placement group demand that used to drive autoscaling before #66002 never reaches the autoscaler.

**Result**

- `FixedScalingPolicy(num_workers=8)`: on master, it polls for 60s, raises `WorkerGroupStartupTimeoutError`, and retries indefinitely with the default `controller_failure_limit=-1`. With #66763, it waits in the controller loop indefinitely, logging "Waiting for reserved resources: 1/8 workers are covered…".
- `ElasticScalingPolicy` with `min_workers > 1`: waits indefinitely, since 1 < `min_workers`.

**Expected**

The autoscaler launches enough nodes to satisfy `STRICT_SPREAD`, as it did when the placement group itself drove autoscaling.

**Possible fixes**

1. Forward the strategy to the autoscaler for `STRICT_SPREAD`. This needs an autoscaler API that can express spread or anti-affinity, which `request_resources` can't.
2. Skip reservation pinning for `STRICT_SPREAD` in Train (`ScalingPolicy._should_pin_to_reservation`, or `can_pin_to_reservation` on master), letting the placement group drive autoscaling as before. The cost is losing protection from concurrent runs sharing capacity for that strategy only.
3. At minimum, detect a reservation stuck below what's needed and log that `STRICT_SPREAD` may not be satisfiable through autoscaling.

Related: the elastic policy requests `max_workers` bundles and the coordinator reserves `STRICT_PACK` all-or-nothing, so elastic + `STRICT_PACK` only starts once `max_workers` fit on one node, and `min_workers` has no effect.

### Versions / Dependencies

Ray master (`5808b33e30`), Train V2.

### Reproduction script

Not reproduced on a real autoscaling cluster yet. This was found by reading the code while reviewing #66601 / #66762. Expected repro:

```python
import ray
from ray.train import ScalingConfig
from ray.train.torch import TorchTrainer

# Cluster config whose only GPU worker node type has 8 GPUs, starting with 0 GPU nodes.
trainer = TorchTrainer(
    lambda: None,
    scaling_config=ScalingConfig(
        num_workers=8, use_gpu=True, placement_strategy="STRICT_SPREAD"
    ),
)
trainer.fit()  # expected: one 8-GPU node launches; the run never starts
```

### Issue Severity

Medium: It is a significant difficulty but I can work around it.

AI assistance (Claude Code) was used to find and write up this issue.

items.title: WSL2 + Windows setup notes: Nsight Compute whitespace bug, nvcc cross-boundary gotchas
items.author: ragulk143
items.body_excerpt:
Posting this in case it saves someone else time. Set up Triton via WSL2 on
Windows 11 this week (RTX 3050, CUDA 13.0 on Windows host). Confirmed the
docs are right that there's no official Windows wheel and WSL2 is the way
to go -- that part worked smoothly once PyTorch+CUDA was installed inside
WSL2.

Two friction points not covered in the docs that might be worth a mention
somewhere for Windows users specifically:

1. nvcc from the Windows-side CUDA install is visible through /mnt/c/ but
   calling it directly only works for --version/metadata, not actual .cu
   compilation, since it tries to invoke the Windows host compiler (cl.exe)
   which most WSL2-only setups won't have. Worth being explicit that Triton
   itself doesn't need this at all (PyTorch's bundled CUDA runtime is
   sufficient for pip install triton to work end to end) -- I lost some
   time assuming nvcc was a prerequisite before realizing Triton kernels
   compile fine without it.

2. If anyone also wants Nsight Compute profiling working inside the same
   WSL2 environment: the bundled Linux ncu binary (under
   target/linux-desktop-glibc_2_11_3-x64/ in the Windows install folder)
   works, but only if copied to a path with zero whitespace -- Nsight's
   launcher errors out on "Program Files" style paths even via WSL2's
   /mnt/c/ bridge. A symlink doesn't fix it since the resolved path still
   has spaces; needs an actual file copy to e.g. ~/tools/.

Happy to write this up more formally if it's useful for the install docs,
otherwise just leaving it here for searchability.

items.title: RayClusterFleet creates a new RayCluster before deleting the old one after a Pod failure
items.author: zhaizhch
items.body_excerpt:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

For a running `RayClusterFleet`, when one Pod inside the managed `RayCluster` is killed (e.g. force-delete a worker Pod), AIBrix treats the RayCluster as unrecoverable and should recreate it.

**Expected recreate semantics:** delete/tear down the unhealthy old `RayCluster` first, then create a new `RayCluster`.

**Actual behavior:** AIBrix creates a **new** `RayCluster` immediately while the **old** `RayCluster` (and remaining Pods) are still present. The old cluster is cleaned up later (or may linger), so old and new RayClusters coexist for a period of time.

This can cause temporary double resource usage (e.g. GPUs) and is inconsistent with a delete-then-create recovery path.

**Related code / analysis**

1. `RayClusterReplicaSet` marks a previously provisioned but no-longer-ready RayCluster as inactive (`isClusterActive` / `filterActiveClusters` in `pkg/controller/rayclusterreplicaset/rayclusterreplicaset_utils.go`), then scales up a new RayCluster because active replicas < desired.
2. The inactive old RayCluster is not necessarily deleted as part of that scale-up path, so a new RayCluster can appear first.
3. Separately, for `strategy.type: Recreate`, `oldPodsRunning` in `pkg/controller/rayclusterfleet/recreate.go` also appears incorrect vs upstream Kubernetes Deployment Recreate (it only waits when a cluster is deleting **and** still Ready), which can similarly allow create-before-delete during rollouts. The primary scenario reported here is **Pod failure recovery** on a running Fleet, not necessarily a template rollout.

### Steps to Reproduce

1. Deploy AIBrix `0.6.0` with RayClusterFleet / distributed-inference controllers enabled, and KubeRay installed.
2. Create a `RayClusterFleet` with `spec.replicas: 1` and a RayCluster template that has multiple Pods (e.g. 1 head + N workers). Wait until the Fleet is Available and the RayCluster is Ready.
3. Force-delete one Pod belonging to that RayCluster, e.g.:

```bash
kubectl delete pod <worker-or-head-pod> --force --grace-period=0
```

4. Watch RayClusters and Pods:

```bash
kubectl get raycluster -w
kubectl get rayclusterreplicaset -w
kubectl get pods -l ray.io/is-ray-node=yes -w
```

5. Observe that a **new** RayCluster is created while the **old** RayCluster is still present.

### Expected behavior

After a Pod in the RayCluster is killed and the RayCluster becomes unhealthy:

1. AIBrix should delete / tear down the old unhealthy `RayCluster` first.
2. Only after the old RayCluster is gone (or fully terminating in a controlled delete-first sequence), create a new `RayCluster` to restore desired replicas.
3. There should be no period where a healthy-path new RayCluster is started while the old RayCluster is still fully present and consuming resources.

### Actual behavior

1. After killing one Pod, the old RayCluster becomes not Ready / inactive from AIBrix's perspective.
2. AIBrix immediately creates a **new** RayCluster to satisfy desired replicas.
3. The old RayCluster is still present at that time (delete happens later or is incomplete from the user's perspective).
4. Result: create-new-first, rather than delete-old-then-create-new.

### Environment

```text
- AIBrix version: 0.6.0
- Deployment environment: Kubernetes 1.34.1
- Cloud provider (if applicable): N/A / private cluster
- KubeRay version: v1.2.1-patch-20250726
- Workload: RayClusterFleet managing 1 RayCluster (multi-Pod head/worker)
```

### Additional context

- User expectation for failure recovery: kill one Pod → AIBrix kills the whole RayCluster → then starts a new RayCluster.
- Observed: kill one Pod → AIBrix starts a new RayCluster directly (old one still around).
- Suggested fix direction:
  - On RayCluster becoming inactive/unhealthy, explicitly delete the old RayCluster (or scale down) **before** creating a replacement.
  - Ensure recreate / recovery paths never count an inactive-but-still-existing RayCluster as “gone” for the purpose of allowing a new create.
  - Add a test that force-deletes a worker/head Pod and asserts no second RayCluster exists until the first is deleted.

items.title: [Bug] Console-created deployments are not discoverable by the AIBrix data plane
items.author: Jeffwan
items.body_excerpt:
A deployment created from the Console can reach `Ready`, and its generated Service can handle requests directly, but the AIBrix Gateway does not discover it.

The generated Pod template currently has only the Console/application labels ([code](https://github.com/vllm-project/aibrix/blob/a40be9ba404730e4be2d2a0820942bca79275dc6/apps/console/api/deployment/provider/kubernetes.go#L633-L642)). It is missing the AIBrix model labels defined in [`pkg/constants/model.go`](https://github.com/vllm-project/aibrix/blob/a40be9ba404730e4be2d2a0820942bca79275dc6/pkg/constants/model.go#L23-L37), such as `model.aibrix.ai/name` and `model.aibrix.ai/port`. The [mocked app manifest](https://github.com/vllm-project/aibrix/blob/a40be9ba404730e4be2d2a0820942bca79275dc6/development/app/config/templates/deployment/deployment.yaml#L6-L23) shows the expected shape.

To reproduce:

1. Create a deployment in Console with the dev [`mock-vllm` template](https://github.com/vllm-project/aibrix/blob/a40be9ba404730e4be2d2a0820942bca79275dc6/apps/console/api/store/demo.go#L569-L590).
2. Wait for it to become ready.
3. Inspect the Pod labels with `kubectl get pods --show-labels`.
4. Port-forward the generated Service: `/v1/chat/completions` works.
5. Send the same request through the AIBrix Gateway: the model has no discovered backend.

A Console deployment reported as ready should also be callable through the AIBrix data plane.

The fix will likely need to map the Console Model's `serving_name`, the effective container port, and the template engine to the canonical AIBrix labels. Please reuse the existing label constants. If a different model-name mapping is intended, it should be documented as part of the change.

This is complete when the mock model can be deployed from Console and reached through the Gateway, with a small rendering test plus an end-to-end check.

Related: #2202, #2198
