items.title: [RFC]: Share the token_load decode ledger across gateway replicas
items.author: hengguangcui11-cyber
items.body_excerpt:
## Summary

The `token_load` decode policy (#2842, #2852) scores decode pods from a ledger kept in each gateway process. With several gateway replicas, each replica scores only the requests it routed itself, so it sees 1/N of the load it is meant to measure. This RFC proposes sharing the decode ledger across replicas through Redis, reusing the cross-gateway running-request counters (`pkg/cache/cache_running_requests.go`): each replica writes its own per-pod deltas, and the routing path reads the other replicas' sums in the same Redis round trip it already makes for running requests.

## Motivation

The `token_load` docs already state the limitation: "The ledger, like the prefill one, is local to each gateway replica: with several replicas, each scores only the requests it routed itself." Production deployments usually run more than one gateway replica, so this is the main gap between how the policy was evaluated and how it would be deployed.

Two consequences:

- **The policy's advantage shrinks as replicas are added.** A replica doesn't see the requests the others just routed, so bursts split across replicas pile up on the same decode pods again, which is what the ledger exists to prevent.
- **The growth term mixes scopes.** The per-request rate is the pod's throughput divided by its running requests, and the running count is already cross-gateway (`GetPodsRunningRequests`). That rate is multiplied by this replica's outstanding charges only.

In a simulation of the PD router (below), the local ledger with 4 replicas is about 3x worse than with one replica on short-output traffic, and with long outputs it falls back to roughly `load_balancing`'s level.

## Proposed Change

**Shared state.** For each decode pod, each gateway instance publishes three additive values:

- `tokens`: the prompt tokens it has charged to the pod and not yet released;
- `n`: its outstanding decode charges on the pod;
- `sum_at`: the sum of their charge times, in seconds since a fixed epoch on the Redis-synced clock (`redisNowMillis`), so the values from different gateways can be added.

The decode score becomes the local values plus the sum over the other live gateways: `tokens_total + rate × (n_total × now − sum_at_total)`. The local part stays exact and in memory, as today.

**Storage and writes.** One Redis hash per decode pod, with one field per gateway instance and value, following `cache_running_requests.go`:

- Every change to the local ledger (charge, release, re-acquire, TTL sweep) also queues a delta for its pod. A single writer goroutine per gateway applies them in order with a Lua script (`HINCRBYFLOAT` on the three fields, clamp at zero, refresh the key's hygiene TTL), off the request path.
- Field names use the existing per-process instance ID (`runningRequestsGatewayInstanceID`, salted with the process start time), so a restarted container doesn't inherit a crashed process's deltas.

**Reads.** `scoreDecodePods` already reads the live running-request counters for all decode candidates in one pipelined round trip. The ledger hashes go into the same pipeline, so no round trip is added. As for running requests:

- fields of gateways missing from the liveness set (3 s window) are excluded from the sum;
- this gateway's own field is replaced by its in-memory values;
- fields absent past the prune window are deleted.

**Failure behavior.**

- If Redis is not configured or a read fails, the score falls back to the local ledger: today's behavior.
- A crashed gateway's contribution drops out of the sum within the liveness window, without waiting for its charges' TTL.
- A write that fails leaves the remote view short by that delta. Clamping at zero bounds a lost acquire followed by its release.

**Configuration.** `AIBRIX_TOKEN_LOAD_SHARED_LEDGER`, on by default when Redis is configured (a deployment that uses `token_load` with several replicas wants it), and `false` to keep the ledger local. Only the `token_load` decode policy reads the shared state.

**Scope.** This covers the decode ledger. The prefill ledger (`token_load` and `hybrid_cache_load` prefill policies, #2681, #2682) has the same limitation and could use the same mechanism in a follow-up.

## Alternatives Considered

**Add the ledger to the periodic gateway pod snapshots** (`cache_gateway_snapshot.go`: written every 100 ms with a 500 ms TTL, read into memory every 100 ms). This needs no per-request Redis writes and recovers from crashes through the TTL, but the remote view is 0–200 ms old. In the simulation, a shared view that old helps little in steady traffic, and with bursts it is worse than not sharing (chat, bursty, 4 replicas: 21.4 vs 6.4 excess KV % at 200 ms). The reason: when every replica reads the same stale picture of the others, they all pick the same pod that looked free; with local ledgers, at least their choices differ.

**Keep the ledger local and document the limitation.** This is the status quo; the numbers below are what it costs.

## Evidence (simulation, not engine measurements)

The same simulation as #2849: it drives the real `filterPrefillDecodePods` against a per-pod KV model with load-dependent decode speed and a 1 s metric scrape. 8 decode pods with 160k KV tokens each, 10 seeds, `token_load` with output growth. Requests go to the gateway replicas round-robin; running requests and scraped metrics are shared, as in production. The shared variants publish each replica's ledger every 0 / 20 / 100 / 200 ms. The metric is excess KV: time-averaged demand above capacity as a % of one pod, lower is better.

| 4 gateway replicas | `load_balancing` | local ledger (today) | shared, live | shared, 20 ms | shared, 100 ms | shared, 200 ms |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| short outputs, steady (~70% KV) | 15.61 | 4.30 | 1.47 | 1.74 | 3.27 | 4.68 |
| short outputs, bursty | 53.15 | 6.36 | 2.32 | 4.17 | 9.42 | 21.37 |
| long outputs, steady (~48% KV) | 0.16 | 0.28 | 0.08 | 0.01 | 0.03 | 0.01 |
| long outputs, bursty (~57% KV) | 3.01

items.title: [Bug] Prefix cache delta sync drops blocks that change during a push
items.author: hmdsefi
items.body_excerpt:
## 🐛 Describe the bug

With `AIBRIX_STATESYNC_ENABLED=true`, each gateway pushes its prefix hash table changes to Redis in `pushDelta` (`pkg/plugins/gateway/statesync/redissync.go`). It calls `GetDelta`, writes the result to Redis, and then calls `ClearDirty`.

For `PrefixHashTable`, `GetDeltaForSync` copies the dirty blocks under the read lock and releases the lock before the Redis writes. Requests keep being routed during the push, and `AddPrefix` keeps marking blocks dirty. After the push, `ClearDirtyForSync` replaces the whole dirty set:

```go
c.dirtyIds = make(map[string]struct{})
```

So a block that `AddPrefix` adds or changes between `GetDeltaForSync` and `ClearDirtyForSync` loses its dirty mark without being pushed. This covers a new block, and also a new pod on a block that was already in the delta, because the delta holds a copy made before the change. The other replicas don't get that change unless a later request touches the same block again.

The `ClearDirty` doc in `pkg/utils/syncable/syncable.go` says it "marks all current dirty state as synced", and `PrefixHashTable` is the only implementation outside tests.

## Steps to Reproduce

This reproduces in a unit test, without Redis:

1. Create a table with `NewPrefixHashTable()`, call `EnableDeltaSync()`, and add a few blocks with `AddPrefix`.
2. Call `GetDeltaForSync`. It returns those blocks.
3. Call `AddPrefix` for a new block, and for one of the blocks from step 2 with another pod.
4. Call `ClearDirtyForSync`, as `pushDelta` does after a successful push.
5. Call `GetDeltaForSync` again. It returns nothing, so neither change from step 3 is pushed.

## Expected behavior

`ClearDirty` should clear only what the last `GetDelta` returned. Blocks that changed after that call should stay dirty and go out with the next push.

## Environment

- AIBrix version: main at e464454a
- Deployment environment: gateway plugin with `AIBRIX_STATESYNC_ENABLED=true` and more than one replica. Reproduced in a unit test.
- Cloud provider (if applicable): n/a
- LLM(s) being used: not model specific
- Client library version (if applicable): n/a

## Area

Gateway

I'd like to fix this. I have a change with a regression test ready and will open a PR.

items.title: [Feature][ModelClaim][Residency] Add declarative Wake Policy
items.author: googs1025
items.body_excerpt:
### Feature Description and Motivation

Related umbrella RFC: #2290.

#2880 implemented controller-driven wake admission and recovery after a request
for a sleeping model. This issue does not reimplement that mechanism. It defines
a declarative Wake policy under ModelClaim `residencyPolicy` and makes the
controller converge toward that desired state.

Today a ModelClaim cannot declare whether it should:

- retain the existing request-triggered Wake behavior;
- be proactively restored whenever it is observed Sleeping; or
- eventually be pre-warmed on a schedule before a known traffic window.

### Use Case

1. A long-tail model sleeps when idle and wakes on the next request; the client
   accepts `503 + Retry-After`.
2. An online model changes from a sleepable policy to always-on. If it is already
   Sleeping, the controller should wake it without waiting for user traffic.
3. A future workload may need scheduled pre-warming, but that should not block
   the first implementation.

### Proposed Solution

Add a Wake policy under `ModelClaimSpec.residencyPolicy`:

```yaml
spec:
  residencyPolicy:
    wakePolicy:
      mode: OnDemand
```

Proposed phases:

| Mode | Priority | Semantics |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `OnDemand` | P1 | Preserve the current request-triggered Wake behavior |
| `EnsureAwake` | P1 | When the controller observes the claim Sleeping, wake it and wait for readiness before restoring routing |
| `Scheduled` | P2/follow-up | Wake according to a schedule and time zone |

`Scheduled` does not need to be implemented in the first phase, but the umbrella
residency design should reserve it as a follow-up rather than mixing Cron and
time-zone semantics into the Sleep track.

### Interaction With Sleep Policy

Valid combinations:

| Sleep Policy | Wake Policy | Semantics |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `PoolDefault` | `OnDemand` | Preserve current behavior |
| `AfterIdle` | `OnDemand` | Sleep after idle, wake on request |
| `Never` | `EnsureAwake` | Do not sleep automatically; wake an already-sleeping instance |
| `AfterIdle` | `Scheduled` | Future: sleep after idle and pre-warm before a traffic window |

Combinations that create policy conflicts must be rejected. For example,
`AfterIdle + EnsureAwake` would sleep an idle engine and immediately wake it,
causing an endless oscillation.

When only Sleep Policy is configured, use compatibility defaults:

```text
PoolDefault / AfterIdle -> OnDemand
Never                  -> EnsureAwake
```

### EnsureAwake Convergence

When the effective Wake policy is `EnsureAwake` and the instance is Sleeping:

1. keep routing at `port=0`;
2. issue an idempotent Wake through the existing `RuntimeClient.Wake`;
3. do not treat a successful Wake call as readiness;
4. wait for the runtime snapshot to report Ready;
5. restore the real route port and converge the claim to Active;
6. on failure, keep the model non-routable, report an Event/Condition, and reuse
   the admission and recovery path implemented by #2880.

### Implementation Boundary

The first phase is primarily an API/controller change:

- define Wake modes and cross-policy validation;
- add an effective Wake-policy resolver;
- reconcile the `EnsureAwake` desired state;
- add idempotency, retry, Event, Condition, and test coverage.

No new Python runtime API is required; idempotent Wake and runtime snapshot state
already exist. `OnDemand` reuses #2880 and does not change the existing client
contract of `503 + Retry-After`.

### Priority

1. **P1: `OnDemand` compatibility semantics**.
2. **P1: `EnsureAwake` desired-state reconciliation**.
3. **P1: reject conflicting Sleep/Wake combinations**.
4. **P2: design and implement Scheduled Wake**.

### Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] An unset Wake policy uses compatibility defaults.
- [ ] `OnDemand` preserves the existing request-triggered Wake flow.
- [ ] `EnsureAwake` proactively restores a Sleeping claim to Active.
- [ ] The model remains non-routable until the runtime reports Ready.
- [ ] Wake operations and controller retries are idempotent.
- [ ] Conflicting Sleep/Wake combinations are rejected by CRD validation.
- [ ] No new Python runtime wire API is introduced.
- [ ] The capacity admission, failure handling, and replacement behavior from
      #2880 remain intact.
- [ ] Unit, integration, and E2E tests cover OnDemand and EnsureAwake.

### Area

Orchestration (controllers, CRDs)

items.title: GDN chunk_gated_delta_rule: much higher incomplete-generation rate on Hopper (SM90) vs Blackwell (SM120), same model/LoRA/config
items.author: anhngml
items.body_excerpt:
## GDN chunk_gated_delta_rule on Hopper (SM90): significantly higher rate of premature/incomplete generation vs Blackwell (SM100/SM120), same model/weights/config — suspect numerical difference, not a config issue

**flashinfer version**: `0.6.16.post3`
**Model**: `numind/NuExtract3` (Qwen3.5-family, hybrid Mamba/GDN attention) + a LoRA adapter, served via `vllm/vllm-openai:latest` (vLLM 0.28.0)
**GPUs compared**: NVIDIA H100 NVL (Hopper, SM90) vs NVIDIA RTX 5090 (Blackwell, SM120)

### Summary

Running the exact same model + exact same LoRA adapter (verified byte-identical, SHA256 match) + exact same serving config against the exact same input documents, we see a **~20-45% rate of incomplete generation** (model emits a natural stop token, `finish_reason='stop'`, before finishing valid JSON — output is missing a closing bracket at the very end) on an H100 (SM90), but **0/10 on an RTX 5090 (SM120)** in a matched test. We've ruled out every config-level variable we could think of and are left suspecting something in the GDN chunk_gated_delta_rule computation itself behaves differently (numerically) between SM90 and SM100/SM120.

### What we're doing

Structured extraction: model is prompted (via `chat_template_kwargs.template`, the NuExtract-style type-marker DSL) to fill in a JSON template for a large, deeply-nested schema (~19 repeating array/table fields, up to 5 levels of nesting, template itself ~8.6KB as JSON). Generation is **free-text** (no `response_format`/grammar constraint) — nothing enforces the model to close every bracket before stopping. `temperature=0.0`.

### The failure signature (confirmed by directly capturing raw model output + `finish_reason`)

For the majority of failures on H100:
- `finish_reason == "stop"` (NOT `"length"` — not a token-budget truncation; `completion_tokens` typically 1500-3700, nowhere near any configured ceiling)
- The resulting text fails `json.loads()` with `Expecting ',' delimiter` at a position exactly equal to `len(content)` — i.e. the model produced a fully well-formed JSON body but is missing exactly the outermost closing `}` (verified by manual bracket-depth counting: final depth = 1 on one captured example)
- The **same physical input document** reproducibly fails on some runs and succeeds on others (not a per-document deterministic thing) — confirmed directly: one specific document failed in one sequential run and succeeded in a later sequential run, same everything.

### What we ruled out (each tested directly, not assumed)

- **Not batching/preemption/concurrency**: fully sequential (1 request in flight at a time, `vllm:num_preemptions_total` stayed at 0 throughout) still reproduces the failure at the same rate (20-44% across several N=8-18 runs) as under concurrent load.
- **Not KV-cache size**: A/B test going from a 20G fixed KV cache pool (with heavy preemption under load) to a ~43GB auto-sized pool (zero preemption) left the failure rate unchanged (27.5% → 25%).
- **Not `--max-model-len`/token budget**: raised 65536 → 131072; a separate, distinct failure mode (genuine context overflow, `finish_reason='length'`) went away, but this premature-stop mode is unaffected (still ~20% after the change).
- **Not the vLLM version**: tried `0.26.1rc1.dev1046+gba07e4a48` (pinned via `pip install --no-deps` over the same base image, same torch 2.13.0/CUDA 13.0 — confirmed compatible, no start-up errors) on the H100 — failure rate was *higher* (45%), not lower.
- **Not `--gdn-prefill-backend`**: tried `triton` explicitly — same failure rate (20% over N=15) and same failure signature.
- **Not the LoRA adapter**: `sha256sum` of `adapter_model.safetensors` is byte-identical between the H100 and RTX 5090 hosts.
- **Not the prompt/template construction**: the reverse-derived `chat_template_kwargs.template` DSL we send matches, byte-for-byte (diffed programmatically), the template used to fine-tune the LoRA adapter in the first place.
- **Not the pipeline config**: identical JSON config (temperature, `pages_per_call`, all flags) on both hosts.

### The one variable we couldn't equalize: GPU architecture

| | H100 NVL (SM90) | RTX 5090 (SM120) |
|---|---|---|
| Failure rate, same 10-15 sequential requests, same documents | 20-45% (multiple runs) | **0/10** |
| `--gdn-prefill-backend` | default (`flashinfer`) and `triton` both tested, same result | default |

We traced flashinfer's own dispatch (`gdn_prefill.py`) and confirmed that on SM90 the default (non-CP) path already calls `chunk_gated_delta_rule_sm90` — i.e. we are *not* stuck on some older code path; this is the current SM90 kernel. We also found and briefly tried forcing vLLM's `--gdn-prefill-backend cutedsl`, but stopped immediately once we realized that vLLM's in-tree `cutedsl` GDN kernel (`vllm/model_executor/layers/mamba/ops/gdn_chunk_cutedsl/`) is a separate, SM100-specific implementation (`Sm100ChunkUWKernel`) — forcing it onto SM90 risks silently wrong results rather than a real fix, so we didn't pursue that path further or measure accuracy under it.

### Question

Is there a known numerical-precision or algorithmic difference between the SM90 and SM100/SM120 `chunk_gated_delta_rule` kernels that could plausibly manifest as occasional incorrect/divergent output for the *same* input at `temperature=0`? Or any pointers on how to get a tighter repro (we can build a minimal standalone script calling `flashinfer.gdn_prefill.chunk_gated_delta_rule` directly with saved intermediate tensors, if that would help — we currently only have this at the full vLLM-serving level; the exact input documents are real government records and can't be shared, but the schema shape and reproduction steps can be shared/generalized).

Happy to run any diagnostic you'd suggest — we have both a Hopper and a Blackwell machine available for A/B testing.
score_reasons: 匹配 KV 与存储、Serving 与评测、Kernel 与正确性

items.title: Descriptor stores write past the tensor's inner extent, up to the next 16-byte boundary
items.author: alepot55
items.body_excerpt:
`tensor_descriptor.store` documents that values outside the tensor bounds are ignored, and the interpreter clips them per element, but on an H100 (`e08ec196b`) a store of a block that ends beyond the inner extent `N` also writes the elements from `N` up to the next 16-byte boundary of the row. With a column slice of a larger tensor as the destination, that is another tensor's data.

```python
@triton.jit
def copy(out_d, a_d, N, BLOCK_M: tl.constexpr, BLOCK_N: tl.constexpr):
    off_m = tl.program_id(0) * BLOCK_M
    for ni in range(0, tl.cdiv(N, BLOCK_N)):
        v = a_d.load([off_m, ni * BLOCK_N])
        out_d.store([off_m, ni * BLOCK_N], v)

out = torch.full((32, 512), 7, dtype=dtype, device="cuda")
out_d = TensorDescriptor.from_tensor(out[:, :N], [32, 128])
copy[(1,)](out_d, a_d, N, BLOCK_M=32, BLOCK_N=128)
```

Columns of `out[:, N:]` no longer equal to 7 afterwards (same with a `tl.make_tensor_descriptor` built in the kernel with `shape=[M, N], strides=[512, 1]`):

```
int8   N=466: 14 columns written (466..479)      N=464: none
int16  N=470:  2 columns written (470..471)
int32  N=466:  2 columns written (466..467)      N=468: none
```

So the store clips at 16-byte granularity of the global address, and only inner extents that are a multiple of 16 bytes behave as documented. `TensorDescriptor` checks the base and the strides for 16-byte alignment but not `shape[-1] * itemsize`. Is the intended contract that the inner extent must be 16-byte aligned too (in which case the descriptor could assert it and the interpreter should match the device), or is this a lowering issue? Found with a differential fuzzer of descriptor kernels against `TRITON_INTERPRET=1`, where it shows up in about half of the programs with a ragged inner dimension.
score_reasons: 匹配 Serving 与评测、Kernel 与正确性、工程与测试

items.title: DeepSeek-V4: OpenAI `tools` field reorders the system prompt after the tool schemas
items.author: thorjohnsen
items.body_excerpt:
**Component:** `tensorrt_llm/tokenizer/deepseek_v4/tokenizer.py`
**Version:** TensorRT-LLM 1.3.0rc21
**Verified against:** `NVIDIA/TensorRT-LLM` **main** —
`tokenizer/deepseek_v4/tokenizer.py` is byte-identical to 1.3.0rc21; the
`messages.insert(0, ...)` at lines 441-442 is present on main. No existing
issue/PR found addressing this.
**Severity:** Medium — affects every `/v1/chat/completions` request that has both
a system message and tools
## Summary
`DeepseekV4Tokenizer.apply_chat_template` handles the OpenAI `tools` argument by
inserting a **synthetic** `{"role": "system", "tools": tools}` message at index
0. The DeepSeek-V4 reference format attaches tools to the *existing* system
message. When a request has both, the user's system prompt is emitted **after**
the tool schemas instead of before, with no separator between them and a stray
`\n\n` after BOS.
## Evidence
Reference implementation is `encoding/encoding_dsv4.py`, shipped inside the
DeepSeek-V4-Flash checkpoint. Comparing renderings of the same conversation
(system prompt "SYSTEM_PROMPT_HERE" + one tool + one user turn):
```
reference:  <BOS>SYSTEM_PROMPT_HERE\n\n## Tools\n...invoke tool calls.\n<｜User｜>Q<｜Assistant｜><think>
TRT-LLM:    <BOS>\n\n## Tools\n...invoke tool calls.\nSYSTEM_PROMPT_HERE<｜User｜>Q<｜Assistant｜><think>
```
Both strings are 1108 chars with an identical character multiset — it is a pure
transposition. The system prompt moves from offset 21 to offset 1061, landing
glued to the trailing `\n` of the tools block.
With `reasoning_effort: "max"` the effort preamble still lands first, so only
the system/tools pair is transposed.
## Scope
- **Affected:** requests where tools are passed via the OpenAI `tools` field
  *and* a `system` message is present. This is the normal serving path:
  `openai_server.py` builds `tool_dicts` and passes it to
  `async_apply_chat_template(tools=...)` then
  `inputs/utils.py:658-663` then `tokenizer.apply_chat_template(messages, tools=tools)`.
- **Not affected:** no system message (verified identical to reference);
  `developer` role instead of `system` (identical); tools attached directly to a
  message dict rather than passed as the `tools` argument.
The last case is why the checkpoint's own gold vector `test_output_1.txt` passes
— it attaches tools to `messages[0]` and never exercises the `tools=` path.
## Root cause
`tensorrt_llm/tokenizer/deepseek_v4/tokenizer.py:441-442`:
```python
conversation = kwargs.get("conversation", messages)
messages = list(conversation)
if tools:
    messages.insert(0, {"role": "system", "tools": tools})   # always a NEW message
```
The renderer's `system` branch (`tokenizer.py:307-312`) emits
`content` then `"\n\n" + render_tools(tools)`. With a synthetic message, index 0
has empty content, so it renders as `"" + "\n\n" + <tools>`, and the real system
message renders separately at index 1 — after it.
## Suggested fix
Merge into a leading system message when one exists:
```python
messages = list(conversation)
if tools:
    if messages and messages[0].get("role") == "system":
        messages[0] = {**messages[0], "tools": tools}
    else:
        messages.insert(0, {"role": "system", "tools": tools})
```
Verified against the checkpoint reference:
| case | current | proposed |
|---|---|---|
| system + tools | mismatch | matches |
| no system, tools | matches | matches (no regression) |
| developer + tools | matches | matches (no regression) |
## Suggested regression test
The existing gold vectors do not cover the `tools=` argument path. Add a case
that passes tools via the argument alongside a system message, asserting
equality with the reference encoding.
## Separately: the rest of the port is exact
For the record, the remainder of `tokenizer.py` matches
`encoding_dsv4.py` byte-for-byte. Verified:
- all 4 shipped gold vectors (`tests/test_output_{1..4}.txt`) reproduce exactly;
- a 36-case sweep of
  `{basic, multiturn, no-system} x {chat, thinking} x {None, high, max} x drop_thinking{T,F}`
  is byte-identical to the reference.
Two intentional and harmless divergences:
- `reasoning_effort` validation: the reference asserts membership in
  `['max', None, 'high']`; TRT-LLM silently coerces anything else to `None`.
  Reasonable for a server, but a typo'd value degrades quietly. Note only
  `"max"` has any effect — `"high"` is accepted but never read, in both
  implementations.
- TRT-LLM accepts `reasoning` as an alias for `reasoning_content` on input
  (`tokenizer.py:296`). This is *correct* — the server emits both fields in
  responses (`serve/openai_protocol.py:681-682`), so accepting both closes the
  round-trip. Strict superset of the reference.

comments.author: pbohannon
comments.body:
We measured the accuracy side of this on DeepSeek V4 Flash, and the reference order did not improve tool calling. The fix is still worth making to match the reference, but accuracy does not seem to hinge on it.

The test used a different server, [antirez/ds4](https://github.com/antirez/ds4), which renders the tools block before the client's system prompt on purpose (commit `7b68234`, for cache reuse). We built it twice from the same commit, once stock and once patched to match `encoding_dsv4.py` (system prompt, `\n\n`, then tools), with identical flags otherwise. Both ran a multi-call tool test (two scripted tasks needing 11 and 9 calls, under nine sampling settings, so 18 sequences per segment), alternating stock, patched, stock, patched, each on an empty cache.

| Build | Segment 1 | Segment 2 | Total calls correct |
|---|---|---|---|
| Tools before system (stock ds4) | 165 / 180 | 168 / 180 | 333 / 360 |
| System before tools (reference order) | 160 / 180 | 162 / 180 | 322 / 360 |

Stock came out slightly ahead, which we read as noise at 36 sequences per arm rather than a real advantage. The misses were the same two kinds in both arms. Grading call order strictly gives 313 and 306, the same picture.

Limits: this is a 2-bit quant (IQ2XXS) on Apple Metal, with thinking off, on one tool-calling test. A full-precision model could be more sensitive to the order.

items.title: Track experimental cuDNN variable-length Top-K backend for SM103/SM107
items.author: Anerudhan
items.body_excerpt:
Owner: @Anerudhan

Track an experimental `cudnn` backend for the existing `flashinfer.top_k_varlen` API, using the public cuDNN Frontend `IndexerTopKVarlen` plan introduced in NVIDIA/cudnn-frontend#1298. The use case is BF16 sparse-attention index selection on GB300 (SM103) and Rubin (SM107), including the DSv4.1 candidate-table shape T=512, N=16384, K=512.

The experimental path is appropriate because this is a new optional frontend/compiler integration with narrowly measured automatic dispatch coverage. It is not a new stable API. Explicit `backend="cudnn"` opts in; automatic selection requires `FLASHINFER_ALLOW_EXPERIMENTAL_AUTO_BACKENDS=1`. The implementation stays under `flashinfer/experimental/`, is JIT-only, and has no AOT registration.

Proposed automatic coverage is BF16 contiguous scores, contiguous Int32 lengths/output, indices-only, no hint, K=512, next_n=1 and compress_ratio=1, with these exact (T,N) pairs:

- SM103: (512,16384), (512,32768), (512,131072).
- SM107: (512,16384), (512,32768), (256,131072).

Every pair must pass the integrated comparison of automatic dispatch with the experimental gate disabled/enabled, including numerical, padding, graph replay and concurrent-stream checks and warm/cold GPU measurements. Standalone cuDNN results do not substitute for this dispatch-boundary validation. Other calls retain the existing automatic ranking. NaNs inside eligible prefixes remain outside the cuDNN backend contract; ignored storage is not read.

Graduation plan:

- [ ] Land and release the public cuDNN Frontend dependency, with a documented compatible CuTe DSL version and target architecture.
- [ ] Validate the actual FlashInfer API on both target GPUs, including optional-dependency containment, fresh tensor bindings, changed-input graphs and concurrent graphs.
- [ ] Publish absolute before/after timings and reproduction instructions for each automatic-dispatch pair; keep routing restricted to measured wins.
- [ ] Extend lifetime/allocator stress coverage and validate real serving consumers before recommending supported framework enablement.
- [ ] Complete stable documentation/trace requirements and the normal stable review before moving the backend out of experimental status.

Target: a graduation/removal review by 2026-10-28, with graduation in the first regular FlashInfer release following that review (release number assigned by maintainers). If dependency release, correctness or performance evidence is insufficient, remove the backend or obtain explicit maintainer approval for continued incubation with the remaining blockers documented here. Experimental enablement is not a default framework release recommendation.

items.title: Auto GID selection picks a non-routable link-local GID on routed RoCEv2 fabrics using RFC1918 (10.0.0.0/8)
items.author: Lzy17
items.body_excerpt:
### Summary
On a routed RoCEv2 fabric where the RoCE IPv4 addresses live in RFC1918 space
(e.g. 10.0.0.0/8), automatic GID selection (when no explicit GID index is set)
picks a non-routable link-local GID instead of the routable IPv4 GID. Cross-node
QPs then never reach RTR and every cross-node transfer fails.

### Environment
- Transport: RDMA (RoCEv2), auto-GID (no `MC_GID_INDEX` / `gid_index < 0`)
- Fabric: routed RoCEv2, RoCE NIC IPv4 in 10.102.0.0/16 (i.e. inside 10.0.0.0/8)

### GID table (per rdma0, representative)
| index | type    | GID                       | address      |
|-------|---------|---------------------------|--------------|
| 0     | RoCE v2 | fe80::0690:81ff:fe37:a9e8 | link-local   |
| 1     | RoCE v2 | ::ffff:0a66:0965          | 10.102.9.101 |

### Root cause
`isOverlayIPv4` flags 10.0.0.0/8 (and 172.16/12, 100.64/10) as an "overlay"
address, so the routable IPv4 GID (index 1) is classified as
`kNetworkDegraded`. A network-backed link-local GID (index 0) is also classified
as `kNetworkDegraded`. With both candidates in the same class, the stable
tie-break on ascending `gid_index` selects index 0 — the link-local GID. A
`fe80::` GID cannot route across subnets, so the QP never reaches RTR:

    Failed to modify QP to RTR ... timed out [110]

### Impact
Any routed RoCEv2 deployment using RFC1918 10/8 (etc.) addressing must currently
work around this by pinning `MC_GID_INDEX` manually. A flat-L2 fabric that
exposes a normal (non-overlay) routable IPv4 GID is unaffected.

### Proposed fix
Rank a network-backed link-local GID strictly below every network-backed IPv4
GID (routable and degraded/overlay alike), so link-local is only chosen when no
network-backed IPv4 GID exists. PR to follow.

items.title: [RFC]: OpLog Batch Record Ordered Writer and Durable Prefix
items.author: Icedcoco
items.body_excerpt:
## Introduction

Mooncake Store HA should do more than restart the Master process quickly. After a primary failure and failover, the new Master should preserve as much useful KV cache metadata, segment registry state, and object-location index state as possible.

The existing HA work has two complementary recovery paths:

1. **Snapshot** provides a coarse-grained baseline for restoring complete Master state.
2. **OpLog** provides incremental changes after the snapshot, so a standby can keep following the primary and catch up before promotion.

RFC #1200 proposed an etcd-backed hot-standby mechanism for Master metadata HA. The primary writes metadata mutations as OpLog entries, and the standby reads/watches those entries from etcd and applies them locally. RFC #1650 then introduced an `OpLogStore` / `OpLogChangeNotifier` abstraction to decouple the upper-layer replication logic from the etcd-specific implementation.

PR #2331 is the immediate baseline for this RFC. Although that PR was submitted by @Icedcoco, most of the HA hot-standby and OpLog implementation came from earlier work by @Libotry and @00fish0 in the `dev/snapshot_etcd_storage_integration_testing_fixbug` branch. The work in #2331 was mainly to rebase that legacy implementation onto the current `kvcache-ai/Mooncake:main`, adapt it to the current Mooncake Store architecture, and integrate recently added Store features such as tenant-aware object metadata, segment lifecycle replication, and the updated standby promotion / snapshot handoff paths.

This RFC builds on #2331 and proposes the next step for the OpLog write and replication protocol: **batch records**, an **ordered writer**, and a **durable prefix**. The goal is not to replace the business semantics that #2331 already adapted. Instead, this RFC keeps the current logical `OpLogEntry` semantics and replaces the underlying write and replay protocol to address lock-held durable waits, per-entry backend key amplification, and promotion boundary ambiguity.

Relevant links:

- Roadmap: https://github.com/kvcache-ai/Mooncake/issues/1035
- Hot Standby RFC: https://github.com/kvcache-ai/Mooncake/issues/1200
- OpLog Store Abstraction RFC: https://github.com/kvcache-ai/Mooncake/issues/1650
- Snapshot RFC: https://github.com/kvcache-ai/Mooncake/issues/1150
- etcd wrapper for HA: https://github.com/kvcache-ai/Mooncake/pull/1451
- initial hot-standby / OpLog implementation: https://github.com/kvcache-ai/Mooncake/pull/1515
- HA backend abstraction: https://github.com/kvcache-ai/Mooncake/pull/1678
- Redis leadership backend: https://github.com/kvcache-ai/Mooncake/pull/1722
- HA runtime / standby lifecycle refactor: https://github.com/kvcache-ai/Mooncake/pull/1777
- current rebase and adaptation PR: https://github.com/kvcache-ai/Mooncake/pull/2331

## Background

### Roadmap Context

The Mooncake Store V3 Roadmap (#1035) tracks HA under `Milestone 2: Master Service Enhancements`, specifically `Metadata Adaptation - HA`. That item has three related lines of work:

- **Snapshot**: #1150, #1431, #1465, #1381 and related work provide persistence and recovery for Master metadata, segment state, allocator state, and task-manager state.
- **OpLog**: #1200, #1451, #1515 and related work provide incremental metadata replication after a snapshot baseline.
- **HA refactoring**: #1648, #1678, #1722, #1777 and related work move leader coordination, standby runtime, snapshot bootstrap, and OpLog following into clearer runtime boundaries.

The relationship is straightforward: snapshot restores a complete baseline, OpLog catches the standby up from that baseline to a later primary state, and the HA runtime orchestrates snapshot bootstrap, OpLog following, promotion, and serving.

### Snapshot Baseline

RFC #1150 was motivated by a practical limitation of early HA mode: fast Master restart alone does not recover KV cache location metadata. If all metadata is lost after failover, upper-layer inference must rebuild cache state, and the recovery time can be much longer than the Master process restart time.

PR #1431 implemented Master snapshot and restore:

- fork + copy-on-write to reduce blocking during snapshot creation;
- background serialization and compression of metadata, segment state, allocator state, and task-manager state;
- local filesystem and S3 snapshot object stores;
- restore-time cleanup of incomplete metadata, non-ready segments, and expired leases.

PR #1465 added task-manager serialization/deserialization. PR #1381 designed an etcd snapshot object store so that snapshot data can also use the HA etcd deployment.

Snapshot is still periodic full-state persistence. It cannot recover mutations that happen after the latest snapshot. OpLog is therefore needed to reduce that loss window and let the standby catch up before promotion.

### RFC #1200: Initial OpLog Hot Standby

RFC #1200 proposed using etcd as a reliable intermediate component for primary-standby OpLog synchronization:

- On the primary, `OpLogManager` assigns a globally increasing `sequence_id` and creates `OpLogEntry` records for metadata mutations.
- `EtcdOpLogStore` persists each entry to etcd, for example under `/oplog/{cluster}/{sequence_id}`.
- `/oplog/{cluster}/latest` records the latest sequence.
- On the standby, `OpLogWatcher` receives real-time changes through etcd watch and reads historical entries during startup or reconnect.
- `OpLogApplier` checks ordering and applies entries to standby metadata.
- `HotStandbyService` manages standby lifecycle and promotion.

The main design points were correctness and RPO/RTO: global sequence ordering, etcd persistence, etcd watch, snapshot sequence recording, and OpLog cleanup.

### PR #1451 and PR #1515: Early Implementation

PR #1451 wrapped the basic etcd interface needed by Master HA.

PR #1515 implemented the early hot-standby and OpLog interface:

- `EtcdOpLogStore`
- `OpLogManager`
- `OpLogWatcher`
- `OpLogApplier`
- `HotStandbyService`
- `StandbyStateMachine`
- OpLog ty

items.title: TMA Store Non-deterministic results
items.author: jeromeku
items.body_excerpt:
Are there any footguns when using TMA store?

Are there still fenceproxy requirements when using TMA store?  It seems in the `release/3.3x` branch of triton that `tl.extra.cuda.experimental_tensormap_fenceproxy_acquire(desc)` was removed?

Reason I ask is I have a kernel that is using TMA store that works on the majority of test cases of varying shape, `seqlen x hidden_size` where `128 < seqlen < 1024` and `hidden_size` is `16-byte` aligned, but randomly fails, as in the output does not match that of a reference implementation.  

If I run the tests with the same random seed several times in a row (e.g., pytest --lf ...), it succeeds eventually.

I'm using the kernel TMA descriptor API since the shape of the tensor is determined at runtime based on the number of tokens assigned to an expert (MoE) in order to predicate stores to only that expert's tokens in a persistent kernel that loops over all experts.

I've thoroughly tested my kernel without TMA store enabled, and tests always pass so I'm absolutely certain that the kernel implementation is correct.  The fact that the kernel succeeds for the majority of test cases with TMA store enabled leads me to believe that the indexing for the descriptor is correct, but confused as to why it fails randomly?  FWIW, I'm also using kernel descriptor TMA loads, and these tests always pass for these configurations.

### The feature, motivation and pitch

Please add support for the community AdaLN-pruned MiniMax-H3 checkpoint ([multimodalart/MiniMax-H3-Pruned](https://huggingface.co/multimodalart/MiniMax-H3-Pruned)) in the VisualGen MiniMax-H3 pipeline.

**Motivation.** The pruned transformer is 40 GiB instead of 66 GiB (39% fewer parameters), and the text encoder is truncated from 66.7 to 52.5 GB. In diffusers this makes MiniMax-H3 fit one 80 GB H100 (see below), which the stock checkpoint cannot do in VisualGen today (weights alone are about 104 GiB with an FP8 transformer, and there is no CPU offload for H3; see #13893).

**Current behavior (1.3.0rc29, 1x H200).** `VisualGen(model=<dir>)` detects the MiniMax-H3 pipeline and reads the weights, then `MiniMaxH3Transformer.load_weights` fails:

```
ValueError: MiniMax-H3 checkpoint is missing 55 required tensors:
time_embedder.linear_1.weight, time_embedder.linear_1.bias,
time_embedder.linear_2.weight, time_embedder.linear_2.bias,
transformer_blocks.0.adaln_proj.linear.bias, ...
  tensorrt_llm/_torch/visual_gen/models/minimax_h3/transformer_minimax_h3.py:859
```

**Why.** The pruned checkpoint stores AdaLN differently:

| | Stock | Pruned |
|---|---|---|
| Time embedding | `time_embedder.linear_1/2` (MLP) | `time_embedder.table` (precomputed, 1025 entries) |
| `adaln_proj.linear.weight` | (96768, 2688) | (96768, 8) |
| `adaln_proj` bias | `adaln_proj.linear.bias` | `adaln_proj.folded_bias` |
| Extra tensors | none | `adaln_basis` [8, 2688], `adaln_mean` [2688] (in `transformer/adaln_affine.safetensors`) |
| Transformer config | stock | custom class `MiniMaxH3PrunedTransformer3DModel` (`auto_map`), `adaln_rank: 8`, `num_layers: 50` |

The reference implementation is `modeling_minimax_h3_pruned.py` in the pruned repo. Expanding the weights back to the stock shapes would make the loader pass but restores the 66 GiB transformer, so it does not help. The useful change is a rank-8 AdaLN and time-table path in the transformer.

**Reproduction.**
1. Build a model directory with the stock `vae`, `scheduler`, `audio_scheduler`, `audio_vae`, `tokenizer`, `processor` and `modular_model_index.json` from `MiniMaxAI/MiniMax-H3`, and the `transformer/` and `text_encoder/` from `multimodalart/MiniMax-H3-Pruned`.
2. Run `VisualGen(model=<dir>, args=VisualGenArgs.from_yaml("cfg.yaml"))` with `quant_config: {quant_algo: FP8, dynamic: true}`, `attention_config: {backend: FA4}`, resolution 480x832, 124 frames.

**Measured with the pruned weights in diffusers** (modular pipeline, 832x480, 124 frames, 28 steps, seed 42, 8 prompts, 1x H200):
- Cost: 9.5 GPU-s per video-s vs 20.9 for the stock checkpoint, both with CPU offload (2.2x). This is not a comparison with TensorRT-LLM.
- Quality vs stock: VBench composite +0.003 (95% paired-bootstrap interval -0.000 to +0.006); LPIPS 0.146, similar to the 0.149 between two stock runs on different engines. Only 8 prompts and one seed.
- Memory on an emulated 80 GB H100 (driver-reported free memory capped; real H100 not tested): peak 52.6 GiB at 960x544 and 53.4 GiB at 1344x768 with automatic CPU offload. The stock checkpoint peaks at 76.8 GiB there.

### Alternatives

- **CPU offload in VisualGen (#13893):** would also help H100 fit, but costs latency; pruning shrinks the weights themselves.
- **Quantized pruned variants** (SDNQ, GGUF, NVFP4 builds exist on Hugging Face) use formats VisualGen does not load.
- **Converter to the stock layout:** loads, but gives back the full transformer size.

### Additional context

- Related: #13893 (offloading for visual_gen) and the open PR #19772 (fuses MiniMax-H3 AdaLN RMSNorm with per-token modulation), which touches the same AdaLN code a pruned path would change.
- Open question: does the truncated 51-layer text encoder load in VisualGen? The failure occurs before that point.
- The FastH3 4-step adapter also expects the original AdaLN width, so we have not tested pruned + distilled in any engine.
- Environment: TensorRT-LLM 1.3.0rc29 (NGC image), 1x H200, includes the MiniMax-H3 support from #18733.

<details>
<summary>Trimmed log (TensorRT-LLM 1.3.0rc29, 1x H200)</summary>

```
[TensorRT-LLM] TensorRT LLM version: 1.3.0rc29
Loading transformer: 100%|██████████| 15/15
Loading MiniMax-H3 weights: ...
Traceback (most recent call last):

items.title: [BUG] [CuTeDSL] cute.coalesce doesn't do anything on dynamic shapes
items.author: lw
items.body_excerpt:
### Which component has the problem?

CuTe DSL

### Bug Report

**Describe the bug**
A mode with a dynamic shape doesn't get coalesced into previous modes, even though the stride is static and the previous modes are fully static too (and that's all that's needed to check whether the modes can be coalesced).

**Steps/Code to reproduce bug**
```py
import torch
import cutlass.cute as cute
from cutlass.cute.runtime import from_dlpack


@cute.jit
def repro(tensor: cute.Tensor):
    layout = cute.make_layout(
        (16, tensor.shape[1] // 128),
        stride=(8, 128),
    )
    expected = cute.make_layout(
        (16 * (tensor.shape[1] // 128),),
        stride=(8,),
    )

    print("input:    ", layout)
    print("coalesced:", cute.coalesce(layout))
    print("expected: ", expected)


tensor = from_dlpack(torch.empty((4096, 8192), device="cuda"))
tensor = tensor.mark_compact_shape_dynamic(mode=1)
repro(tensor)
```

Output:
```text
input:     (16,?):(8,128)
coalesced: (16,?):(8,128)
expected:  (?{div=16}):(8)
```

**Environment details (please complete the following information):**
Version 4.7.0 of CuTeDSL

items.title: numeric_limits< float_e2m3_t / float_e3m2_t >::lowest() returns a small negative value instead of the format minimum
items.author: VaggelisGian
items.body_excerpt:
### Description

`numeric_limits<cutlass::float_e2m3_t>::lowest()` and `numeric_limits<cutlass::float_e3m2_t>::lowest()` return values near -1.8 / -1.75 instead of the most negative finite value of each format. The same wrong constant is used in the `std::` specializations, the `cutlass::platform::` specializations, and the `float_e2m3_unpack8bits_t` / `float_e3m2_unpack8bits_t` variants, six call sites in total.

The type's own metadata disagrees with the hardcoded constant: `BitRepresentation::MIN_VALUE` for both formats is `0x3F`, and `max()` (which uses `MAX_VALUE = 0x1F`) is correct.

### Evidence

For E2M3 (bias 1) the most negative finite pattern is `0x3F` (`s=1, exp=11, man=111`, value -(1+7/8)*2^2 = -7.5). The code returns `bitcast(0x2f)`, which decodes to `s=1, exp=01, man=111` = -1.875.

For E3M2 (bias 3) the most negative finite pattern is `0x3F` (`s=1, exp=111, man=11`, value -(1+3/4)*2^4 = -28). The returned `0x2f` decodes to `s=1, exp=011, man=11` = -1.75.

Repro (g++ -std=c++17 -O2 against include/ only):

```cpp
#include "cutlass/float_subbyte.h"
#include <cstdio>
#include <limits>

int main() {
    printf("e2m3: max=%g lowest=%g\n",
        float(std::numeric_limits<cutlass::float_e2m3_t>::max()),
        float(std::numeric_limits<cutlass::float_e2m3_t>::lowest()));
    printf("e3m2: max=%g lowest=%g\n",
        float(std::numeric_limits<cutlass::float_e3m2_t>::max()),
        float(std::numeric_limits<cutlass::float_e3m2_t>::lowest()));
}
```

Actual output:

```
e2m3: max=7.5 lowest=-1.875
e3m2: max=28 lowest=-1.75
```

Expected: `-7.5` and `-28`. Note `lowest()` for `float_e2m1_t` (`0xf`) is correct, which shows the intent was sign bit | MAX_VALUE.

### Suggested fix

Replace `bitcast(0x2f)` with `bitcast(0x3f)` in all six places (include/cutlass/float_subbyte.h lines 628, 640, 715, 727, 738, and the e3m2_unpack8bits equivalent), or better, derive it as `type::bitcast(type::Base::BitRepresentation::MIN_VALUE)` so it cannot drift from the encoding again. `epsilon()` on these types checks out and needs no change.

No in-tree caller currently reads `lowest()` on these types, so the defect is latent but silently wrong for any external user relying on numeric_limits.

items.title: EpilogueDirectStore warp decomposition uses WarpShape::kN where WarpCount is meant
items.author: VaggelisGian
items.body_excerpt:
### Description

`EpilogueDirectStore`'s constructor computes the warp decomposition as:

```cpp
int warp_id_mn = warp_idx % (WarpCount::kM * WarpShape::kN);
```

(include/cutlass/epilogue/threadblock/epilogue_direct_store.h line 171)

The second factor is a typo: it mixes the warp shape's `WarpShape::kN` into what should be the warp count. `EpilogueBase` does this correctly (include/cutlass/epilogue/threadblock/epilogue_base.h lines 219-220):

```cpp
int warp_mn = warp_idx % (WarpCount::kM * WarpCount::kN);
```

When `WarpCount::kN > WarpShape::kN` the modulo truncates `warp_idx` early and two different warps receive the same `(warp_m, warp_n)` coordinates. For all currently instantiated direct-store configs `WarpCount::kN <= WarpShape::kN`, so nothing is observably wrong today; the defect surfaces only for shapes where `Shape::kN > WarpShape::kN^2`.

### Suggested fix

Use `warp_idx % WarpCount::kCount` (or `% (WarpCount::kM * WarpCount::kN)` to mirror `EpilogueBase`).

items.title: CuTeDSL: nested comprehension breaks staged control flow later in the outer comprehension (NameError on the generator variable)
items.author: VaggelisGian
items.body_excerpt:
### Description

`_visit_Comprehension` in `cutlass/base_dsl/ast_preprocessor.py` (~lines 2424-2428) sets `session_data.generator_targets` for the comprehension being visited, then unconditionally resets it to `[]` afterwards:

```python
self.session_data.generator_targets = targets
ele_visitor(node)
self.session_data.generator_targets = []
```

When the element expression contains a *nested* comprehension, the inner `_visit_Comprehension` overwrites `generator_targets` with the inner targets and resets it to empty on exit. The outer comprehension's remaining element processing then runs with no generator targets, so any later construct that synthesizes staged control flow (e.g. an `IfExp`) treats the outer generator variable as a free/global name and fails.

Minimal repro (verified against `nvidia-cutlass-dsl==4.7.0`; the control version without the inner comprehension compiles and runs):

```python
import cutlass
import cutlass.cute as cute

@cute.jit
def f(flag: cutlass.Boolean) -> cutlass.Int32:
    vals = [(len([0 for _ in range(2)]), (y if flag else -y)) for y in range(4)]
    return cutlass.Int32(sum(v[0] * v[1] for v in vals))

print(f(cutlass.Boolean(True)))
```

Actual error:

```
Caused exception: name 'y' is not defined
suggestion: Variables used inside staged control flow (for/if/while) must be defined before the
control flow region. Give the variable an initial value before the loop or branch.
```

The suggestion is misleading: `y` is the comprehension variable, not a user mistake.

### Suggested fix

Save the previous value of `session_data.generator_targets` before visiting and restore it after `ele_visitor(node)` returns (a `try/finally`, which also protects the session state on exception paths), instead of resetting to `[]`.

items.title: Conv2d/Conv3d output-size constructors use R*dilation instead of the effective filter size ((R-1)*dilation+1)
items.author: VaggelisGian
items.body_excerpt:
### Description

The output-size computing constructors in `include/cutlass/conv/conv2d_problem_size.h` (lines ~175-176) and `include/cutlass/conv/conv3d_problem_size.h` (~196 and ~224) subtract `R * dilation` instead of the effective filter extent `((R - 1) * dilation + 1)`:

```cpp
P = ((H + pad_h + padding[1] - R * dilation_h) / stride_h) + 1;
Q = ((W + pad_w + padding[3] - S * dilation_w) / stride_w) + 1;
Z = ((D + pad_d + ... - T * dilation_d) / stride_d) + 1;
```

The library's own profiler computes cuDNN-compliant sizes with the standard formula (tools/profiler/src/conv2d_operation_profiler.cu lines ~275-303):

```
output = div_up(input + 2*pad - ((filter - 1) * dilation + 1) + 1, stride)
```

For dilation == 1 the two agree (`R*1 == (R-1)*1+1`), which is why existing tests pass. For dilation > 1 the constructors undersize P/Q/Z: e.g. H=8, R=3, dilation_h=2, pad=0, stride=1 gives P = 8-6+1 = 3 instead of the correct 8-5+1 = 4. Degenerate combinations can even produce non-positive extents (H=1, R=1, dil=3, pad=0 gives P=-1).

Any caller constructing a problem via these Tensor4DCoord/Tensor5DCoord constructors with dilation > 1 gets wrong output extents; downstream kernels then truncate or mis-map the output.

### Suggested fix

Use `(R - 1) * dilation_h + 1` (and the S/T analogues) in all three places.

items.title: uint1b_t ReduceArray specializations are broken (logical_or never compiles / always true; logical_and tests bytes not bits)
items.author: VaggelisGian
items.body_excerpt:
### Description

The `uint1b_t` specializations of `ReduceArrayOperation` in include/cutlass/reduction/thread/reduction_operators.h (lines ~157-204) are broken in three independent ways.

#### logical_or: wrong parameter type AND constant-true result

```cpp
template <int N>
struct ReduceArrayOperation<logical_or<uint1b_t>, uint1b_t, N> {
  ...
  uint1b_t operator()(
    logical_and<uint1b_t> const &reduction_op,   // <-- copy-paste: accepts only logical_and
    ArrayType const &array) const {
    ...
    bool item = true;                            // <-- identity of OR is false
    for (...) { bits = ptr[byte]; item = (item || bits); }
    return uint1b_t{item};                       // <-- always true
```

Consequences, both verified against the current tree:

1. The public helper does not compile:
   `cutlass::reduction::thread::detail::ReduceArray(logical_or<uint1b_t>{}, array)` fails with *"operator() cannot be called with the given argument list"* because the parameter type names `logical_and`.
2. Even calling it directly with a `logical_and` argument compiles but ignores its input entirely: `item` starts `true` and is only ever OR-ed into, so the result is constant `true`.

#### logical_and: tests whole bytes, not bits

```cpp
bool item = false;
for (int byte = 0; byte < (N + 7) / 8; ++byte) {
  uint8_t bits = ptr[byte];
  item = (item || !bits);      // "some byte is entirely zero"
}
return uint1b_t{!item};
```

This returns "no byte is entirely zero", not "all elements are set". With `N = 8` and element 7 cleared, byte 0 is `0x7F`, no byte is zero, and the reduction reports true:

```
AND [1]*7+[0]: got=1 expected=0
```

There is also no masking of padding bits when N is not a multiple of 8.

Neither specialization has in-tree callers today, so both are latent public-API defects.

### Suggested fix

For logical_or: change the parameter type to `logical_or<uint1b_t>` and initialize `bool item = false;`.
For logical_and: loop over the ceil(N/8) bytes, mask the final byte's padding bits, and test per-byte zero as intended - or simply iterate elements via the array API.

items.title: SubbyteReference breaks its offset invariant for negative offsets (constructor and operator+=)
items.author: VaggelisGian
items.body_excerpt:
### Description

`SubbyteReference` (both the primary template and the `StorageVec` partial specialization in include/cutlass/subbyte_reference.h) mishandles **negative** offsets: the constructor and `operator+=` with a negative argument use truncating division without normalizing, leaving the object in a state that violates its own invariant.

Verified by execution on a minimal host build (Storage = uint8_t, Element = int4b_t):

```
control  -= (+3)  : storage_delta=-2 off=1   get=-3   correct
case B   += (-3)  : storage_delta=-1 off=-1            (invariant requires off in [0, 1])
FAIL: += negative breaks offset_ invariant
case C   ctor(ptr, -3): storage_delta=-1 off=-1        same broken state
```

Correct state for element -3 is one storage unit further back (`storage_delta == -2`, `offset_ == 1`). Instead `offset_ < 0`, and any subsequent `get()`/`set()` shifts by a negative bit count (undefined behavior) or reads the wrong nibble. The mirrored `operator-=` with a positive argument is correct - its borrow logic compensates - which is why only the negative-input paths were affected.

Reachability: `TensorRef::operator-(coord)` and negative `add_pointer_offset` feed this constructor through `ReferenceFactory` for sub-byte tensors. Nothing in-tree navigates sub-byte tensors backward across vector boundaries today, so this is latent public-API breakage.

### Suggested fix

Normalize negative deltas exactly like the positive path does: fold the current `offset_` in first, then use floor-style division/borrow so that the postcondition `0 <= offset_ < kElementsPerVector` always holds.

items.title: Collective operations do not work with `torch.BoolTensor`s on `gloo` and raise `Invalid scalar type`
items.author: sadra-barikbin
items.body_excerpt:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

Hi, collective operations do not work with `torch.BoolTensor`s on backend `gloo`. Actually `GENERATE_ALL_TYPES` macro in `torch/csrc/distributed/c10d/ProcessGroupGloo.cpp` seems to raise `RuntimeError: Invalid scalar type`.

To reproduce:
```python
import torch.distributed as dist

tensor = torch.empty((5,),dtype=torch.bool)
if dist.get_rank() == 0:
    gather_list = [torch.empty((5,),dtype=torch.bool) for _ in range(dist.get_world_size())]
else:
    gather_list = None
dist.gather(tensor, gather_list)
```
This is also the case for `all_gather`, `reduce`, `all_reduce` and `broadcast`. Changing `dtype=torch.bool` to `dtype=torch.uint8` resolves the error, while `torch.bool == torch.uint8` evaluates to `True`.

items.title: Nested nested_compile_region silently reuses a body specialized on the inner region's guards
items.author: aperson30
items.body_excerpt:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

An outer `nested_compile_region` can reuse a cached body that was specialized on a guard collected while tracing an *inner* region. The outer region's reuse condition never sees that guard, so it reuses a body traced under a branch the current call does not take, and the result is silently wrong. No indexing is involved.

```python
import torch

ncr = torch.compiler.nested_compile_region


class Layer(torch.nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, flag):
        super().__init__()
        self.flag = flag


@ncr
def inner(layer, x):
    if layer.flag:          # guard lands in the INNER region's trace
        return x.sin()
    return x.cos()


@ncr
def outer(layer, x):
    return inner(layer, x) + 1.0


layers = [Layer(True), Layer(False), Layer(True), Layer(False)]


def fn(x):
    return sum(outer(l, x) for l in layers)


x = torch.randn(8)
print(fn(x))
print(torch.compile(fn, backend="aot_eager", fullgraph=True)(x))
```

### Actual vs expected

```
eager   : [5.8224, 5.6067, 5.9738]
compiled: [3.6594, 3.2790, 3.9479]
```

Two speculate calls instead of four: the `flag=False` layers reuse the `flag=True` body, so every layer computes `sin`.

`SubgraphTracer.traced_sources` is per tracer and does not propagate outward, so `build_reuse_condition` for the outer region collects no guard for `layer.flag` even though the inner trace installed one.

Found while working on #191781 item 3, but unrelated to it: this needs no indexing and reproduces on a clean checkout.

### Versions

main at 98ebd10b379, CPU, `backend="aot_eager"`.

items.title: [Inductor][CPU/CUDA] torch.compile makes integer geometric_ return all ones
items.author: xyt66665000
items.body_excerpt:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

`torch.compile` with the Inductor backend incorrectly compiles `Tensor.geometric_` on integer tensors.

For `geometric_(0.3)`, eager execution produces samples from the expected geometric distribution, while the compiled version returns `1` for every element.

The issue reproduces on both CPU and CUDA.

## Reproduction

```python
import torch

def f(x):
    return x.geometric_(0.3)

for device in ["cpu", "cuda"]:
    x = torch.zeros(65536, dtype=torch.int64, device=device)

    torch.manual_seed(0)
    eager = f(x.clone())

    torch.manual_seed(0)
    compiled = torch.compile(f, fullgraph=True)(x.clone())

    print(device)
    print("eager:   ", eager.min().item(), eager.max().item(),
          eager.double().mean().item())
    print("compiled:", compiled.min().item(), compiled.max().item(),
          compiled.double().mean().item())
```

Log:

```text
cpu
eager:    1 29 3.335357666015625
compiled: 1 1 1.0
cuda
eager:    1 31 3.3436279296875
compiled: 1 1 1.0
```

For `p=0.3`, the expected mean is approximately `1 / 0.3 = 3.33`, so the compiled result does not satisfy the expected distribution.

### Versions

PyTorch version: 2.15.0.dev20260922+cu130
CUDA used to build PyTorch: 13.0
OS: Ubuntu 24.04.4 LTS (x86_64)

items.title: Gumbel.cdf raises ValueError for real values in the tails although Gumbel.support is constraints.real
items.author: the-Shallow
items.body_excerpt:
### 🐛 Describe the bug


`torch.distributions.Gumbel(loc, scale).cdf(x)` raises `ValueError` for ordinary real `x` in the tails
(for float32 `Gumbel(0., 1.)`: any `x < -4.47` or `x > 15.94`), under the default `validate_args=True`.
`Gumbel.support` is `constraints.real`, so these values are in the support. `Gumbel` is a
`TransformedDistribution` whose base is `Uniform(finfo.tiny, 1 - finfo.eps)`; the generic
`TransformedDistribution.cdf` inverts the transforms and validates the result against that truncated base
support, so tail values fail validation.

### Steps to reproduce

```python
import torch
g = torch.distributions.Gumbel(0.0, 1.0)
print(g.support)                    # Real()
g.cdf(torch.tensor(-5.0))           # ValueError: Expected value argument ... within the support (Interval(1.17e-38, 0.99999988))
g.cdf(torch.tensor(20.0))           # ValueError
```


### Expected

`cdf(-5.)` about 2e-65 (0 in float32) and `cdf(20.)` about 1, as `scipy.stats.gumbel_r.cdf` returns; no error for values in `Gumbel.support`.


### Suggested fix

Give `Gumbel` its own `cdf` (`exp(-exp(-(x - loc) / scale))`), or have `TransformedDistribution.cdf` validate against `self.support` rather than re-validating the transformed value against the base support.


### Versions


### Environment

PyTorch 2.14.0 (the latest release, CPU wheel) and 2.12.0, Python 3.12, Ubuntu 24.04, x86_64

items.title: torch.special.polygamma(1, x) (trigamma) and the gradient of digamma are accurate only to ~5e-10 in float64
items.author: the-Shallow
items.body_excerpt:
### 🐛 Describe the bug


`torch.special.polygamma(1, x)` in float64 has relative error about 5e-10, while `polygamma(0, x)` and
`polygamma(2, x)` are accurate to about 1e-16. The trigamma code shifts `x` up by only 6 and truncates its asymptotic
series after the `1/x^7` term. The gradient of `torch.digamma` is `polygamma(1, x)` and inherits the error.

### Steps to reproduce

```python
import math, torch
x = torch.tensor([1.0], dtype=torch.float64)
print(abs(torch.special.polygamma(1, x).item() - math.pi**2 / 6) / (math.pi**2 / 6))   # 4.8e-10
print(abs(torch.special.polygamma(2, x).item() + 2 * 1.2020569031595942) / 2.404)       # 1.8e-16
```


### Expected

Relative error near 1e-16 in float64, as for the other orders.


### Suggested fix

Shift the argument further (e.g. to x >= 10) and/or keep more Bernoulli terms of the asymptotic series, as Cephes' `zeta`-based evaluation does.


### Versions

### Environment

PyTorch 2.14.0 (the latest release, CPU wheel) and 2.12.0, Python 3.12, Ubuntu 24.04, x86_64

items.title: kl_divergence(Bernoulli, Bernoulli) returns wrong values or raises IndexError when the batch shapes broadcast
items.author: the-Shallow
items.body_excerpt:
### 🐛 Describe the bug


`_kl_bernoulli_bernoulli` fixes up the `probs == 0` and `probs == 1` cases with in-place boolean-mask assignment
(`t1[q.probs == 0] = inf`). When `p` and `q` have broadcast-compatible but different batch shapes, the mask has the
shape of one operand and the result the broadcast shape, so the correction lands on the wrong elements (silently
wrong values) or raises `IndexError`.

### Steps to reproduce

```python
import torch
from torch.distributions import Bernoulli, kl_divergence

p = Bernoulli(torch.full((3, 3), 0.5))
q = Bernoulli(torch.tensor([0.0, 0.5, 1.0]))
print(kl_divergence(p, q)[0])  # [inf, inf, inf]
print(
    kl_divergence(p, Bernoulli(q.probs.expand(3, 3).contiguous()))[0]
)  # [inf, 0.0, inf]
kl_divergence(Bernoulli(torch.rand(4, 3)), Bernoulli(torch.rand(1, 3)))  # IndexError
```


### Expected

The same result as with `q` expanded to the broadcast shape, and no error.


### Suggested fix

Use `torch.where` on broadcast masks instead of boolean-mask assignment.


### Versions


### Environment

PyTorch 2.14.0 (the latest release, CPU wheel) and 2.12.0, Python 3.12, Ubuntu 24.04, x86_64

items.title: `torch.ldexp` emits an `out=` resize warning when broadcasting without an `out` argument
items.author: the-Shallow
items.body_excerpt:
### 🐛 Describe the bug


`torch.ldexp(input, other)` emits the output-resize deprecation warning when an integer exponent broadcasts the input to a larger shape, even though the caller did not supply an `out` tensor.

This also occurs for the broadcasting example in `torch.ldexp`'s documentation:

```python
import warnings

import torch

with warnings.catch_warnings(record=True) as caught:
    warnings.simplefilter("always")
    result = torch.ldexp(
        torch.tensor([1.0]),
        torch.tensor([1, 2, 3, 4]),
    )

print(result)
for warning in caught:
    print(warning.message)
```


Output:

```text
tensor([ 2.,  4.,  8., 16.])
An output with one or more elements was resized since it had shape [1], which does not match the required output shape [4]. This behavior is deprecated, and in a future PyTorch release outputs will not be resized unless they have zero elements. ...
```

The warning tells the caller to resize an `out` tensor, but there is no user-provided `out` tensor in this call. It is also emitted on every invocation, so a broadcasting call in a loop can repeatedly produce the warning.

The integer-exponent path allocates its internal result with `at::empty_like(self)`. TensorIterator then resizes that result to the broadcast shape and emits the warning. The decomposition path broadcasts without this internal resize.

### Expected behavior

The functional overload should return the broadcast result without an `out=` resize warning. Its internally allocated output should begin empty or have the correct broadcast shape.



### Versions

PyTorch 2.14.0 and 2.12.0 CPU builds, Python 3.12, Ubuntu 24.04, x86_64.

items.title: torch.nn.functional.pad` reflect mode can restore values removed by negative padding
items.author: the-Shallow
items.body_excerpt:
### 🐛 Describe the bug


When a reflect pad combines negative padding (cropping) and positive padding on the same axis, PyTorch validates the positive reflect amount against the original axis size instead of the size remaining after the crop.

As a result, an oversized reflect pad can be accepted and copy data that the negative padding was supposed to remove:

```python
import torch
import torch.nn.functional as F

x = torch.tensor([[1.0, 2.0]])

print(F.pad(x, (-1, 0), mode="reflect"))
# tensor([[2.]])

print(F.pad(x, (-1, 1), mode="reflect"))
# tensor([[2., 1.]])  <- 1.0 was cropped but appears again

F.pad(F.pad(x, (-1, 0), mode="reflect"), (0, 1), mode="reflect")
# RuntimeError: Padding size should be less than the corresponding input dimension
```

The combined operation succeeds and produces `[[2., 1.]]`, while applying the crop first and then the reflect pad correctly rejects padding a length-one axis by one element.

The same behavior occurs on another axis:

```python
y = torch.arange(1.0, 7.0).reshape(1, 1, 2, 3)
print(F.pad(y, (0, 0, -1, 1), mode="reflect"))
# tensor([[[[4., 5., 6.],
#           [1., 2., 3.]]]])
```

The second output row is the row removed by the negative top padding. The reflect-padding checks compare the positive padding with the pre-crop dimension, allowing the kernel to index outside the surviving core while still remaining inside the original tensor.

### Expected behavior

Reflect padding should be validated against the axis size remaining after negative padding. The combined operation above should raise the same `Padding size should be less than the corresponding input dimension` error as the equivalent crop-then-pad sequence.


### Versions

PyTorch 2.14.0 and 2.12.0 CPU builds, Python 3.12, Ubuntu 24.04, x86_64.

items.title: [Serve] Allow app-defined health routes to bypass `max_ongoing_requests`
items.author: codechrl
items.body_excerpt:
### Description

Every request to a route on a `@serve.ingress` FastAPI app counts toward the deployment's `max_ongoing_requests`. A health route such as `GET /healthz` therefore waits for a free slot while the replicas are saturated. External health checkers (load balancers, Kubernetes probes) time out on it and mark a working application as down.

Repro on Ray 2.54.1 and FastAPI 0.116.0:

```python
import asyncio
import threading
import time

import requests
from fastapi import FastAPI
from ray import serve

app = FastAPI()


@serve.deployment(max_ongoing_requests=2)
@serve.ingress(app)
class Api:
    @app.get("/work")
    async def work(self):
        await asyncio.sleep(6)

    @app.get("/healthz")
    async def healthz(self):
        return "ok"


def timed_get(path):
    start = time.time()
    status = requests.get(f"http://127.0.0.1:8000{path}").status_code
    print(path, status, f"{time.time() - start:.2f}s")


serve.run(Api.bind())
timed_get("/healthz")

for _ in range(2):
    threading.Thread(target=timed_get, args=("/work",)).start()
time.sleep(1)
timed_get("/-/healthz")
timed_get("/healthz")
```

```text
/healthz 200 0.65s
/-/healthz 200 0.03s
/work 200 6.04s
/work 200 6.04s
/healthz 200 5.40s
```

The replica logs `GET /healthz 200 2.7ms` for the last call. The rest of the 5.40s is spent waiting for a free slot.

The built-in routes do not cover this case. The proxy's `/-/healthz` reports whether the proxy is draining, has a route table and, on worker nodes, knows a running replica. The replica's `/-/healthz` exists only with direct ingress, which `RAY_SERVE_ENABLE_DIRECT_INGRESS` leaves off by default. It returns the result of the controller's last `check_health` call. Neither runs a request through the application. #33979 asked for a per-application route that calls `check_health`. It was closed in a backlog sweep for inactivity.

Two possible shapes:

- An option on `@serve.ingress` or `@serve.deployment` that lists routes exempt from `max_ongoing_requests`, e.g. `exempt_routes=["/healthz"]`.
- A per-application `/{route_prefix}/-/healthz` that calls `check_health` outside the request semaphore.

Documented guidance on the recommended pattern would also work.

### Use case

A FastAPI ingress deployment forwards each request to model deployments through handles. Each forwarded call takes several seconds. A container health check calls the app's `/healthz`, which reports `serve.status()`. With the default `max_ongoing_requests=5`, five concurrent calls left `/healthz` unroutable. The health check failed. The container supervisor then restarted the service, which failed every in-flight request. Raising `max_ongoing_requests` to 200 only moves the threshold. A separate health deployment does not exercise the ingress deployment that serves the traffic.

items.title: [Core] GCS main thread wastes time copying redundant cluster resource data
items.author: dancingactor
items.body_excerpt:
## Description
On every RaySyncer update and every GCS load pull, the GCS main thread redundantly copies each node's resource data into `GcsResourceManager::node_resource_usages_`, even though the same data is already stored in `ClusterResourceManager` and `GcsAutoscalerStateManager`. On large clusters, these copies take a significant share of the GCS main thread.

## Performance Impact

I ran some performance tests.

Test configuration:
- Resources per node: 6
- Demand shapes per node: 10
- Busy cluster: both RaySyncer and GCS load pulls run at their maximum update rates
  - RaySyncer: 10 updates/node/s
  - GCS load pull: 1 pull/node/s

#### 1. In a large cluster (5,000 nodes), these redundant copies take an extra 26% overhead of the GCS main thread.

| Nodes | Main thread cost (with redundant copy) | Main thread cost (without copy) | Extra cost |
| ----- | -------------------------------------- | ------------------------------- | ---------- |
| 100   | 1.1%                                   | 0.8%                            | +0.3%      |
| 1,000 | 12.6%                                  | 9.1%                            | +3.6%      |
| 5,000 | 79.5%                                  | 53.7%                           | +25.8%     |

#### 2. Looking only at the resource data update work in GCS, the redundant copy makes it 34–48% more expensive.

| Nodes | Update cost (with redundant copy) | Update cost (without copy) | Extra cost |
| ----- | ----------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------- | ------------------------------ |
| 100   | 11.1 ms/s                                       | 8.3 ms/s                                 | +34%                           |
| 1,000 | 126.5 ms/s                                      | 90.8 ms/s                                | +39%                           |
| 5,000 | 795.0 ms/s                                      | 536.9 ms/s                               | +48%                           |

## Proposed Changes
Remove the extra copy of resource data in GCS, `GcsResourceManager::node_resource_usages_`. 

Proposed steps:

1. Migrate the consumers of `GcsResourceManager::node_resource_usages_` to other data sources.
   - **Autoscaler v1(#66633)**: it currently reads resource demand and placement group load from `GcsResourceManager::node_resource_usages_`.
     - **Resource demand:** `GcsAutoscalerStateManager` already exposes an equivalent field (`pending_resource_requests` in `ClusterResourceState`), so the v1 autoscaler can use it directly.
     - **Placement group load:** `GcsAutoscalerStateManager` only exposes the derived `pending_gang_resource_requests`, not the raw `PlacementGroupTableData` that the v1 autoscaler needs. Add a `placement_group_load` field to `ClusterResourceState` in `autoscaler.proto` so `GcsAutoscalerStateManager` can expose it directly.

items.title: [RLlib] MultiAgentEpisode marks the episode terminated when a new agent joins on the step the last registered agent terminates (despite __all__=False)
items.author: WiemKhlifi
items.body_excerpt:
### What happened + What you expected to happen

In a `MultiAgentEnv` if a new agent's **first** observation arrives on the **same step** the last already-registered agents terminate, `MultiAgentEpisode.add_env_step` declares the episode terminated, although the env returned `terminateds["__all__"] = False`. The new agent's observation is discarded, and under `batch_mode="truncate_episodes"` the `MultiAgentEnvRunner` then steps the still-live, un-reset env with an **empty action dict** (runner declares a new episode when it's still the same one). Envs that validate their actions crash the EnvRunner (`having_actions=set() does not cover all actions in needing_actions={...}` in our case).

**Expected:** the episode stays open (the env said so) and the new agent is registered.

**Why:** the "Case 2" check runs over agents that are **already registered** ([`multi_agent_episode.py#L413-L416`](https://github.com/ray-project/ray/blob/ray-2.58.0/rllib/env/multi_agent_episode.py#L413-L416); [`agent_ids`](https://github.com/ray-project/ray/blob/ray-2.58.0/rllib/env/multi_agent_episode.py#L1008-L1011) is `agent_episodes.keys()`):

```python
self.is_terminated = terminateds.get("__all__", False)       # False
...
if all(aid in set(agents_done) for aid in self.agent_ids):   # newcomer not registered yet
    self.is_terminated = True                                # overrides the env
```

The newcomer is only registered later in the same method ([`#L532`](https://github.com/ray-project/ray/blob/ray-2.58.0/rllib/env/multi_agent_episode.py#L532)), so it can't veto the check, and its first observation falls into the "already done" branch ([`#L509-L516`](https://github.com/ray-project/ray/blob/ray-2.58.0/rllib/env/multi_agent_episode.py#L509-L516)). 

`SyncVectorMultiAgentEnv` arms its autoreset from the env's own `__all__` ([`#L140-L145`](https://github.com/ray-project/ray/blob/ray-2.58.0/rllib/env/vector/sync_vector_multi_agent_env.py#L140-L145)), so the env is not reset, and the runner sends `{}` into it ([`multi_agent_env_runner.py#L389-L403`](https://github.com/ray-project/ray/blob/ray-2.58.0/rllib/env/multi_agent_env_runner.py#L389-L403)). 
In our case we were using the `batch_mode=complete_episodes` which only hides the crash.

This looks like the case the class's own TODO already anticipates ([`#L30-L31`](https://github.com/ray-project/ray/blob/ray-2.58.0/rllib/env/multi_agent_episode.py#L30-L31)): `# TODO (simon): Include cases in which the number of agents in an episode are shrinking or growing during the episode itself.`

**Suggested fix** (`multi_agent_episode.py#L415`): count agents that report an observation in this step as present.

```python
if all(aid in agents_done for aid in self.agent_ids | set(observations)):
```

This keeps the episode open at the handover and leaves the intended Case 2 behavior (every agent finished, some terminated, some truncated) unchanged. Happy to open a PR with the reproduction below as a test in `rllib/env/tests/test_multi_agent_episode.py`.


### Versions / Dependencies

- Ray 2.58.0 (also reproduced on 2.57.0)
- Python 3.13, gymnasium 1.2.2
- Tried it on both: Linux (Kubernetes) and macOS

### Reproduction script

```python
import numpy as np
from ray.rllib.env.multi_agent_episode import MultiAgentEpisode

eps = MultiAgentEpisode(agent_module_ids={"a0": "p", "a1": "p"})
eps.add_env_reset(observations={"a0": np.zeros(1, np.float32)}, infos={"a0": {}})

# One step: a0 terminates, a1 sends its FIRST observation, env says NOT done.
eps.add_env_step(
    observations={"a0": np.zeros(1, np.float32), "a1": np.ones(1, np.float32)},
    actions={"a0": 0},
    rewards={"a0": 1.0, "a1": 0.0},
    infos={"a0": {}, "a1": {}},
    terminateds={"a0": True, "__all__": False},
    truncateds={"__all__": False},
)
print(eps.is_terminated, sorted(eps.agent_ids), eps.get_terminateds())
```

Output on 2.58.0:

```
True ['a0'] {'a0': True, '__all__': True}
```

Expected:

```
False ['a0', 'a1'] {'a0': True, '__all__': False}
```

A full `MultiAgentEnvRunner` reproduction (PPO, `truncate_episodes`, a toy env that validates its action dict) that crashes on the empty action dict is available on request:

```
ActionsMissing: env step t=5: having_actions=set() does not cover all actions in needing_actions={'a1'} (live agents={'a1'})
```

### Issue Severity

Medium: It is a significant difficulty but I can work around it.

items.title: Autoscaler-driven elastic expert/data parallelism for MoE
items.author: Jeffwan
items.body_excerpt:
### Feature Description and Motivation

For large MoE models we only scale whole replicas, which is coarse and expensive. vLLM has elastic EP (`enable_elastic_ep`, `/is_scaling_elastic_ep`, the DP coordinator request-wave protocol in `vllm/v1/engine/coordinator.py`) to add/remove DP/EP ranks at runtime. The autoscaler doesn't drive it. Scaling EP width by load would right-size MoE serving without full-replica steps.

### Use Case

DeepSeek / Qwen-MoE style deployments where per-replica cost is high and traffic varies; scale expert parallelism up and down instead of adding or removing entire replicas.

### Proposed Solution

Let PodAutoscaler target EP/DP width for elastic-EP-enabled deployments and drive scaling via the engine's elastic-EP endpoints + the DP coordinator wave protocol. Start observe-only (read `/is_scaling_elastic_ep` and wave state) before acting on it.

## Summary

When an engine exhausts its local restart budget, reschedule the affected ModelClaim to another eligible warm pool Pod and restore routing after activation.

## Scope

- Reuse normal placement and activation; no live migration or in-flight request preservation.
