items.title: [RDT]: In-flight transfers race condition
items.author: BatshevaBlack
items.body_excerpt:
### What happened + What you expected to happen

`fetch_and_get_rdt_objects()` can call `remove_remote_agent()` while a sibling transfer on the same NIXL remote agent is still in-flight, causing crashes

## Summary

`RDTManager.fetch_and_get_rdt_objects()` in [rdt_manager.py](https://github.com/ray-project/ray/blob/master/python/ray/experimental/rdt/rdt_manager.py) posts multiple NIXL transfers before waiting on any of them, then waits for all of them to return. 
The version of remote metadata can change in between two transfers posted.
This can lead to a 'remove_remote_agent' call while previous in progress transfers that were posted are still inflight, this causes these inflight transfers to crash (`NIXL_ERR_REMOTE_DISCONNECT`).

## The mechanism

`fetch_and_get_rdt_objects()` [rdt_manager.py](https://github.com/ray-project/ray/blob/master/python/ray/experimental/rdt/rdt_manager.py) pipelines fetches for a list of object IDs:

```python
# Phase 1 - post every fetch, nothing waits between them
fetch_requests = {}
for object_id in object_ids:
    fetch_requests[object_id] = self._trigger_fetch(object_id, use_object_store)

# Phase 2 - only now does anything wait, after ALL are posted
while fetch_requests:
    result[object_id] = self._wait_fetch(object_id, fetch_request, ...)
```

`_trigger_fetch()` leads to `tensor_transport_manager.fetch_multiple_tensors()`

`fetch_multiple_tensors()` [nixl_tensor_transport.py](https://github.com/ray-project/ray/blob/master/python/ray/experimental/rdt/nixl_tensor_transport.py):
```python
if remote_agent_meta_version != self._remote_agents[remote_name]:
    nixl_agent.remove_remote_agent(remote_name)   # no in-flight check
```
## The race
In 'fetch_and_get_rdt_objects'
If there are two objects to transfer:
- Object A is posted
- The GC thread running in the background (from previous itterations) deregisters some memory and leads to a version change.
- Object B is posted,  (A is still in-flight) object B gets to the `fetch_multiple_tensors` check- sees the version has changed, and triggers- `remove_remote-agent`

The agent was removed while A was inflight- causes a NIXL error and crashes the application.

## Suggested fix: 
### Do not parallel transfers:
Don't proceed to next transfer tunill you get a completion from previous one in `fetch_and_get_rdt_objects`, this isn't the best solution for performance since we serialize transfers that can be parallelized.

### Prevent tearing down connections while requests are in flight
This suggest adding a tracking on inflight requests and preventing removing the remote agent while requests are inflight. 

**Can be treated as a reader-writer lock:**

The thread calling`remove_remote_agent()` will be treated as the **writer**.
Each transfer's lifetime - from `initialize_xfer()` through completion will be treated as a **reader**

The writer should not proceed while any reader holds the lock, readers should not be blocked by each other. 
This maps cleanly onto the existing call structure: acquire read-lock at `initialize_xfer()`, release at transfer completion (`wait_fetch_complete()`/cleanup); acquire write-lock before `remove_remote_agent()`, release after `add_remote_agent()`.

### Versions / Dependencies

**Environment**
- NIXL v1.4.0 @ c0a1102b
- Ray 3.0.0.dev0, TransferQueue (RDT) 0.1.7.dev0
- PyTorch 2.10.0+cu129, CUDA 12.9, Python 3.13.12
- 2×8 NVIDIA H100 80GB HBM3 (driver 535.216.03)

### Reproduction script

**Repro script:** 

[cpu_scatter_disconnect_race.py](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/31805047/cpu_scatter_disconnect_race.py)
python cpu_scatter_disconnect_race.py -N 16 --shape 3,2048,64000,128 --warmup 2 --iters 3

### Issue Severity

_No response_

shortlist.title: [Bug]: FP8 KV cache startup can OOM because CUDA graph memory is omitted from the cache budget
shortlist.author: the-Shallow
shortlist.body_excerpt:
### Your current environment
The output of python collect_env.py ```text vLLM 0.28.0 on Linux with an NVIDIA GPU ```
### 🐛 Describe the bug On a 24 GiB GPU, `LLM(..., kv_cache_dtype="fp8")` is accepted but fails during startup with an out-of-memory error, while the identical engine using the default KV cache dtype answers successfully. ```python from vllm import LLM, SamplingParams llm = LLM( model="Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B", kv_cache_dtype="fp8", ) print(llm.generate( ["Hello, my name is"], SamplingParams(max_tokens=8), )) ``` Observed failure: ```text torch.OutOfMemoryError: CUDA out of memory. Tried to allocate 150.00 MiB. GPU 0 has a total capacity of 23.49 GiB of which 122.00 MiB is free. ... RuntimeError: Engine core initialization failed. See root cause above. ``` The startup accounting allocates about 19.93 GiB to the KV cache after subtracting a near-zero CUDA graph estimate. CUDA graph capture happens afterwards and consumes about 0.80 GiB in the FP8 case, pushing actual usage beyond the memory reserved by `gpu_memory_utilization`. Reducing `gpu_memory_utilization` avoids the failure. ### Expected behavior KV cache sizing should reserve the actual CUDA graph memory so an accepted configuration does not exceed its memory budget during graph capture or the first sampling allocation. If vLLM cannot fit the configuration, it should fail early with an actionable error. ### Suggested fix Make `profile_cudagraph_memory()` account for the actual graph capture cost, including its dependence on the number of KV blocks, or adjust the KV cache after graph capture when measured use exceeds the requested budget. ### Before submitting a new issue... - [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.

shortlist.title: [good-first-issue] tests: make flaky vllm_bench throughput comparisons reproducible
shortlist.author: maobaolong
shortlist.body_excerpt:
Parent tracker: #5313 · Onboarding: #3372

## Confirmed flaky behavior

`k3-multiprocess-test / vllm / vllm_bench / zmq` changes its throughput verdict without a source update:

| Build #5340, September 29, 2026 (UTC) | Result |
| --- | --- |
| [Original job](https://buildkite.com/lmcache/k3-multiprocess-test/builds/5340#01a0eab1-a517-4a38-8163-b0ec7cfaff63) | LMCache throughput **7.34% slower** than baseline; fails the 5% limit |
| [Retry](https://buildkite.com/lmcache/k3-multiprocess-test/builds/5340#01a0eaba-4671-4f79-a910-4a02cfa0cadf) | LMCache throughput **0.62% faster** than baseline; passes |

Both are `dev` builds of **`9e8226dd49728769843bf6f586b00b33ab616125`**, with no PR-base merge, vLLM **`0.30.1rc1.dev244+g0da126676`**, and torch **`2.13.0+cu130`**. Both baseline and LMCache completed all 50 requests with 500400 input tokens. This is an intermittent benchmark verdict, not an installation failure.

The inputs are not reproducible across those attempts: the original uses seed `1790644335`, the retry `1790645482`. Each attempt uses the same seed for its own baseline/LMCache pair, but the default `RANDOM_SEED` comes from `date +%s`. The seed change is a confirmed confounder; it is **not proven to be the sole cause** of the throughput fluctuation.

## Bounded good-first task

Make this benchmark's inputs reproducible across retries, and make the comparison auditable. This is the first test-harness improvement for the confirmed flake, not a production performance optimization.

1. Replace the clock-derived default seed with a documented stable default; continue honoring an explicit `RANDOM_SEED` override.
2. Save a small comparison manifest next to `baseline.json` and `lmcache.json`: effective seed, model, request count and lengths, actual checkout SHA, installed vLLM/torch versions, and the two throughput values/verdict. Keep any new diagnostics local to this workload.

shortlist.title: [Performance]: spec-decode boot-to-boot throughput dispersion on L4 (CV up to 13.92%), resolved in 0.30.0
shortlist.author: akshathtiwari
shortlist.body_excerpt:
### Proposal to improve performance

Not a proposal so much as a measurement suggestion. Speculative-decoding throughput on this stack is boot-dependent to a degree a single-boot benchmark cannot see: on 0.29.0 / L4, twelve boots of a byte-identical configuration gave CV 13.92% in one container and 3.73% in another. Anything comparing speculative configurations from one boot each is partly measuring which boot it got.

0.30.0 looks much better on this axis (0.99% and 1.61% across two containers on different physical cards), so this may already be resolved. I am reporting it mainly because the mechanism is not what I assumed, and the protocol seems worth having on record either way.

### Report of performance regression

Reporting this because 0.30.0 appears to resolve it, and the obvious explanation turns out to be wrong, so something else changed and I would like to know what.

**Setup.** Qwen3-4B target, `z-lab/Qwen3-4B-DFlash-b16` drafter, 5 speculative tokens, bf16 weights, `--kv-cache-dtype auto`, FlashInfer pinned. GSM8K, concurrency 1, one fixed prompt set replayed on every boot. 12 boots per arm inside a single container, one physical GPU per session (UUID recorded). The harness speaks HTTP only and never imports vLLM.

Throughput at concurrency 1, output tokens/s:

| card | engine | session | default | --enforce-eager | ratio | default CV |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| L4 (SM89) | 0.29.0 | A | 39.2 | 80.5 | **0.487** | **13.92%** |
| L4 (SM89) | 0.29.0 | B | 61.2 | 79.7 | **0.768** | **3.73%** |
| L4 (SM89) | 0.30.0 | C | 82.8 | 81.6 | **1.014** | 0.99% |
| L4 (SM89) | 0.30.0 | D | 78.2 | 77.0 | **1.017** | 1.61% |
| A10 (SM86) | 0.29.0 | E | 132.6 | 138.3 | 0.959 | 2.08% |

Each ratio is the default arm divided by the eager arm measured in the same container, so session and card effects cancel. On 0.29.0/L4 the CUDA-graph path runs at 49% and 77% of the eager path; on 0.30.0 it reaches parity. Acceptance length is flat throughout (tau 4.11-4.15), so this is throughput rather than a change in what the drafter gets accepted.

### Misc discussion on performance

Two observations, one related issue, and a question.

**1. The CUDA-graph fallback still fires on 0.30.0.** I had assumed the improvement was the speculative path gaining full graphs. It is not. The warning is byte-identical on both versions and capture proceeds under PIECEWISE in each:

> CUDAGraphMode.FULL_AND_PIECEWISE is not supported with spec-decode for attention backend FlashInferBackend (support: AttentionCGSupport.UNIFORM_SINGLE_TOKEN_DECODE); setting cudagraph_mode=PIECEWISE

Backend selection is unchanged too: both versions log FLASHINFER for the target and FLASH_ATTN for the second selection. So neither graph mode nor backend choice explains the difference.

**2. On 0.29.0 the dispersion magnitude is itself not reproducible.** Two twelve-boot measurements of the identical configuration gave CV 13.92% and 3.73%, with means 39.2 and 61.2 tok/s. The effect is present in both; its size is not a property of the configuration. The eager arm is stable across every session measured (80.5, 79.7, 81.6, 77.0 on L4; 138.3 on A10), which is what makes it usable as a control.

**Related, but I do not think it is the same thing: #58677.** That reports the draft model's torch.compile cache identity flipping between exactly two values across restarts with byte-identical argv, attributed to the shared VllmConfig being mutated in-place during the main model's warmup and CUDA-graph-capture phase, before the draft head compiles. Two differences: the symptom there is startup recompile cost rather than steady-state throughput, and it reports 0.27.1 affected with 0.29 appearing immune, whereas what I measure is on 0.29.0.

Still, the shape is close enough that I would rather ask than assume: **if VllmConfig is mutated in place during graph capture and that mutation reaches what the draft compiles to, could the same mechanism produce a steady-state throughput difference and not only a cache-key difference?** My measurements begin after the server reports healthy, so any recompilation has finished by then.


**The question.** What changed between 0.29.0 and 0.30.0 on this path, given the fallback and the backend selection are identical in both? If a specific PR is responsible I would rather cite it than guess. I looked at #53867, #51700, #54646 and #52228 and could not attribute it from the release notes alone.

**Possibly relevant.** The effect is much weaker on an A10 (ratio 0.959) than on an L4 (0.487 and 0.768) at the same engine version. The A10 has 24 GiB against the L4's 22.03 GiB usable, and this configuration sits close enough to the memory ceiling that --enforce-eager alone decides whether an fp8_e4m3-KV variant boots at all. So capacity pressure may matter more here than architecture. I have not separated the two.

**Reproduction.** Harness, raw append-only records, analysis scripts and the engine logs are at https://github.com/akshathtiwari/spec-fp8-study (archived at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23033168). The boot-variance runs are one command each and the per-session numbers regenerate from the stored records. Happy to run further configurations if a specific one would help; the full sweep is a couple of GPU-hours.

### Your current environment (if you think it is necessary)

Not `collect_env.py` output: the engine runs in an ephemeral container on a rented GPU, so this machine's environment is not the one under test. These are the fields the harness records per measurement, read from nvidia-smi and from the running server.

```text
GPU         NVIDIA L4 (SM89, 22.03 GiB usable) and NVIDIA A10 (SM86)
            one physical card per session, gpu_uuid recorded per record
driver      580.95.05
CUDA        13.0
torch       2.13.0+cu130
vLLM        0.29.0 and 0.30.0, pinned by image digest. Version is read from
            the server's /version endpoint and checked against the declared
            value before any measu

comments.author: akshathtiwari
comments.body:
Correction to the "possibly relevant" paragraph in my original post.

I wrote that the A10 has 24 GiB against the L4's 22.03 GiB usable, and offered memory capacity as the likelier of two readings for why the deficit is weak on the A10. **That is wrong.** Both cards report **22.5 GiB** in my own records, and I had never checked the field before writing it. Capacity is not the difference between them.

What does differ, from the same records:

| | VRAM | arch | max SM clock | power limit |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| L4 | 22.5 GiB | SM8.9 | 2040 MHz | **72 W** |
| A10 | 22.5 GiB | SM8.6 | 1695 MHz | **150 W** |

So the card showing the deficit has less than half the power budget. That is a better fit for the symptom than capacity ever was: CUDA graphs run the work faster, faster work draws more power, and a 72 W part can hit its cap and clamp — variably, depending on thermal history, which would also explain why the dispersion magnitude itself does not reproduce between sessions. The eager arm runs slower, stays under the cap, and is stable in every session measured.

I want to be clear that this is a hypothesis and **my data cannot test it.** I was recording `clocks.max.sm` and `power.limit`, which are what the card is permitted to do, not what it did. A throttling explanation is precisely what configured limits cannot see.

I have since added sampling of achieved SM clock, power draw and `clocks_throttle_reasons.*` across the measurement window, and a run is in flight. If `sw_power_cap` is active during the default arm and not during the eager arm, that is the driver answering the question directly rather than me inferring it from a clock curve. I will post the result either way, including if it kills the hypothesis.

The throughput numbers and the ratio table in the original post are unaffected by this — they are measured, and the correction is to an explanation I attached to them.

shortlist.title: Restart-proof KV cache for llama-server: 40K-token TTFT 155s to 6s after reboot
shortlist.author: qqkzlm
shortlist.body_excerpt:
Every restart wipes your prefill. Server crash, box reboot, model reload — a 40K-token agentic prompt pays the full ~155s prefill again before the first token.

I patched llama-server to persist KV-cache prefix checkpoints to disk and auto-restore the longest matching prefix on boot. Same prompt after a restart: **first token in ~6s instead of ~155s** (2.1s disk read once + decode). No client changes, no re-architecture — the server just remembers.

Measured on GTX 1080 8GB, Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, `-c 92160`:

- Cold: 151s prefill → first token at ~155s
- Warm (post-restart): 2.1s disk read (first request only) → first token at ~6s
- Checkpoints keyed by model + ctx + KV quant (wrong config = ignored, never corrupted); disk-budget eviction included

Single-commit patch (86KB): https://github.com/qqkzlm/llama-cpp-prompt-disk-cache — `git am` onto the PrismML `prism` branch, four flags (`--slot-save-path`, `--checkpoint-min-step`, `--ctx-checkpoints`, `--prompt-cache-disk-budget`).

One MoE lesson from the same box: keep experts on GPU, let KV follow the layers — pushing 20 MoE layers to CPU collapsed prefill 265→30 tok/s, which no cache can fix.

Happy to upstream behind a flag if maintainers are interested.

comments.author: qqkzlm
comments.body:
Update to the README since this went up — three things worth calling out for anyone trying it:

**1. Prebuilt CUDA binaries exist for both platforms.** The `v0.2.3` release ships `llama-server-win-cuda-v0.2.3.zip` and `llama-server-linux-cuda-v0.2.3.tar.gz`. The Linux package is built for `sm_61`/Pascal, so it also runs on GTX 10-series. No build needed:

```bash
./llama-server -m model.gguf -c 32768 --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8000 \
  --slot-save-path /var/tmp/kvstore/model \
  --prompt-cache-disk-budget 20 --checkpoint-min-step 2048 --ctx-checkpoints 64
```

**2. Only one flag is actually required.** `--slot-save-path` is the only one you must pass — `--prompt-cache-disk-budget` and `--prompt-cache-disk-path` are silently ignored without it, and entries land in `<slot-save-path>/pdcache`. `--prompt-cache-disk` is **enabled by default**, so passing it is optional; use `--no-prompt-cache-disk` to turn the cache off.

**3. Cache hits require a byte-identical prompt prefix.** Only the common prefix from token 0 onward is reused. If you prepend a timestamp or a random ID, everything after it misses and the cache is effectively unused. Put stable content first (system prompt, tool definitions, long docs) and per-turn content last — opencode / Claude Code already do this, so it works out of the box.

The README now has a "when does the cache hit / when does it miss" section covering this, a flag-duty table, and a Chinese-first three-step guide (the repo README is now Chinese-primary). A Windows `start-llama-server.bat` is included in the zip if you want a prompt-driven launcher instead of a command line.

Still happy to upstream this behind a flag if maintainers are interested — the whole feature is one commit touching `tools/server/server-prompt-disk.cpp` (~900 lines) plus slot/task integration.

shortlist.title: GGUF convert support for Vibevoice
shortlist.author: amin-jhn
shortlist.body_excerpt: Hey there! I am trying to convert my fine-tuned vibevoice into a gguf format for inference but cant find proper code or converter any where. The architecture is currently unsupported to any known converter like llama.cpp but I have already seen many variation of gguf-formated vibevoice. Can anyone help me with that?

comments.author: pwilkin
comments.body:
So the status currently is that there's no support for VibeVoice in llama.cpp (but llama.cpp *does* support TTS architectures, it's a question of somebody adding support for that specific model). 

What you have seen are probably repacks done by calcuis in his weirdly named "gguf-org project", but that project is not affiliated with ggml-org nor with llama.cpp in any way and from what I've analyzed the contents of those files, they are simply direct repacks of the original SafeTensors files, but with layers that are known to be quantizable by GGML converted to the respective quant format (with a side effect being that only a small percentage of the tensors that *should* be quantizable are really quantized, since the GGUF library does not know that for example `model.acoustic_tokenizer.decoder.stages.0.0.ffn.linear1.weight` should be a quantizable tensor). He then converts them back to F32 before running, so it's not a real GGML architecture, just a repack - not a very efficient one at that, since he unpacks all the quants to F32, so the memory usage will be the same as with the original model, just the quality will be lower (for example, the ComfyUI-GGUF solution, which supports GGUF quantization, does it by properly patching methods and dequantizing tensors on the fly as they're being used, so even though it does not utilize native quantized kernels for MAT_MUL like GGUF does, it actually allows to run those quants with a lower memory footprint).

TL;DR: You can try doing a repack in the same way, using `quantize` from the `gguf-py` library (a decent LLM coder will probably write that for you), but real VibeVoice support requires adding a proper MTMD model.

comments.author: amin-jhn
comments.body: Thank you so much for your detailed response!

comments.author: Ra5hidIslam
comments.body:
Hey @amin-jhn and @pwilkin,

Following up on pwilkin's suggestion, I went ahead and wrote a Python script using gguf-py that successfully repacks and quantizes the VibeVoice SafeTensors into a Q8_0 GGUF file.

While I know this doesn't close the issue (since it still needs the native C++ MTMD model support mapped out for llama.cpp), this script should fully solve the repackaging hurdle for anyone trying to run a compressed version through custom frontends like ComfyUI in the meantime.


```python

import argparse
import numpy as np
import torch
from safetensors.torch import load_file
import gguf
from gguf.quants import quantize
from gguf.constants import GGMLQuantizationType

def pad_tensor(tensor_np: np.ndarray, block_size: int = 32) -> np.ndarray:
    """Pads the last dimension of a 2D tensor to be a multiple of block_size."""
    rows, cols = tensor_np.shape
    if cols % block_size == 0:
        return tensor_np
    
    padding_needed = block_size - (cols % block_size)
    print(f"  --> Padding tensor: {cols} -> {cols + padding_needed} columns")
    return np.pad(tensor_np, ((0, 0), (0, padding_needed)), mode='constant', constant_values=0)

def vibevoice_repack_with_padding(path_input: str, path_output: str):
    print(f"Loading Safetensors from {path_input}...")
    try:
        tensors_loaded = load_file(path_input)
    except Exception as e:
        print(f"Error loading file: {e}")
        return
        
    print("Initializing GGUF writer...")
    writer_gguf = gguf.GGUFWriter(path_output, arch="vibevoice")
    writer_gguf.add_string("general.name", "vibevoice")

    tensor_count = 0
    quantized_count = 0
    BLOCK_SIZE = 32 

    for tensor_name, tensor_data in tensors_loaded.items():
        tensor_np = tensor_data.cpu().float().numpy()
        
        is_2d_weight = len(tensor_np.shape) == 2 and "weight" in tensor_name
        
        if is_2d_weight:
            # 1. Pad to multiple of 32
            tensor_padded = pad_tensor(tensor_np, block_size=BLOCK_SIZE)
            
            # 2. Quantize into a structured array
            q_type = GGMLQuantizationType.Q8_0
            quantized_struct = quantize(tensor_padded, q_type)
            
            # 3. Cast the structured array to raw bytes
            quantized_bytes = quantized_struct.view(np.uint8)
            
            # 4. Add to GGUF using ONLY the raw bytes
            writer_gguf.add_tensor(
                name=tensor_name,
                tensor=quantized_bytes,
                raw_dtype=q_type,
            )
            quantized_count += 1
        else:
            # Standard F32 for 1D tensors
            writer_gguf.add_tensor(tensor_name, tensor_np)

        tensor_count += 1
        if tensor_count % 50 == 0:
            print(f"Processed {tensor_count} tensors...")

    print(f"Writing {tensor_count} tensors to disk...")
    writer_gguf.write_header_to_file()
    writer_gguf.write_kv_data_to_file()
    writer_gguf.write_tensors_to_file()
    writer_gguf.close()

    print(f"Successfully converted to GGUF at {path_output}.")
    print(f"Total: {tensor_count} | Quantized (Q8_0): {quantized_count}")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(description="Repack VibeVoice to GGUF with Q8_0 Fix.")
    parser.add_argument("--input", required=True)
    parser.add_argument("--output", required=True)
    args = parser.parse_args()
    vibevoice_repack_with_padding(args.input, args.output)
```

Hope this helps anyone trying to get the file size down while we wait for native C++ support!

shortlist.title: [RFC]: Explicit Context Caching — Guaranteed KV Cache Eviction Protection
shortlist.author: Colors-111
shortlist.body_excerpt:
### Changes proposed

#  Explicit Context Caching — Guaranteed KV Cache Eviction Protection

## Summary

Introduce a `guaranteed_until` timestamp mechanism in Mooncake Store to implement Explicit Context Caching:

1. **Eviction protection**: Users mark `cache_control: {"type": "ephemeral"}` in `messages`, and the corresponding prefix KV Cache is marked as guaranteed (non-evictable within TTL) in the Store. After expiration, objects automatically degrade to regular objects
2. **Passive expiration**: Uses an absolute `guaranteed_until_` timestamp — BatchEvict naturally skips unexpired objects; expired objects automatically become eviction candidates. Zero new RPCs, crash-safe by design
3. **Zero state on inference engine side**: All guaranteed lifecycle management resides on the Master side. Inference engines (SGLang, vLLM, etc.) do not track or manage guaranteed cache; radix tree nodes require no new fields

## 1. Background and Motivation

### Problem 1: High-Value Prefixes Lack Eviction Protection

Mainstream inference engines (SGLang, vLLM, etc.) reuse KV Cache through prefix matching (RadixAttention / Automatic Prefix Caching). Shared prefixes (system prompts, RAG documents, few-shot examples) are frequently hit. The current eviction strategy in Mooncake Store sorts purely by lease timeout — least recently accessed objects are evicted first. This means:

- Under memory pressure, high-value long prefixes (e.g., a 4K-token system prompt) may be evicted first (because they may not have recent writes)
- After eviction, the next request requires full recomputation, causing P99 latency spikes and GPU compute waste

### Problem 2: OpenAI-Compatible cache_control Semantics Have No Backend Support

The OpenAI API introduced `cache_control: {"type": "ephemeral"}` markers, allowing users to declare "this prefix is important, don't evict it" in message content blocks. Frontend frameworks (e.g., LangChain, VLLM) widely support this semantic, but Mooncake Store has no corresponding eviction protection mechanism, rendering the marker effectively inert.

### Problem 3: Design Gap Between Explicit and Implicit Caching

Alibaba Bailian adopts a standalone CacheIndex + 20-block lookback window approach (multi-tenant cloud service), but this introduces a complex indexing system and inference-engine-side lifecycle management. For single-cluster self-deployment scenarios, we need a lighter approach.

**Goals**: Provide deterministic eviction protection (hard guarantee) for prefixes marked with `cache_control`. After TTL expiry, objects automatically degrade to regular objects. Zero new state on inference engine side. Zero regression risk.

## 2. Core Design

### Tiered Architecture

| Tier | Location | Role in Explicit Caching | Guarantee Level |
|------|----------|-------------------------|-----------------|
| L1 (GPU) | Inference engine Worker (local) | Temporarily held during inference, normal eviction | No guarantee |
| L2 (CPU) | Inference engine Worker (local) | Speedup on same-engine hit (bonus) | No guarantee |
| L3 (Mooncake Store) | Distributed storage | **Deterministic guarantee tier** | Hard guarantee |

L1/L2 do not participate in guarantees: requests may be routed to any engine instance, and L2 is only available on the local instance. Binding guarantees to L2 would require forced routing to a specific instance, breaking load balancing. L3 is shared across all engines, naturally supporting cross-engine reuse.

### Architecture Diagram

```
  Client (messages with cache_control markers)
       │
       ▼
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Inference Engine API Server          │
  │  - Parse cache_control → token offsets│
  └──────────────┬───────────────────────┘
                 │
                 ▼
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Inference Engine Worker Instance     │
  │  ┌──────────────────────────────┐    │
  │  │ HiCache Controller (no change)│   │
  │  │ - radix tree normal prefix   │    │
  │  │   matching                   │    │
  │  │ - On write: check cache_     │    │
  │  │   control → write_through    │    │
  │  │   with guaranteed param      │    │
  │  │ - On read: check cache_      │    │
  │  │   control → GetReplicaList   │    │
  │  │   with guaranteed param      │    │
  │  └──────────────────────────────┘    │
  └──────────┬───────────────────────────┘
             │
  ┌──────────▼───────────────────────────┐
  │  Mooncake Store (L3)                │
  │  - guaranteed_until_ timestamp guard │
  │  - BatchEvict skips unexpired objs  │
  │  - GrantLease auto-renewal          │
  │  - Guaranteed capacity limit+fallback│
  │  - SSD Offload priority protection  │
  └─────────────────────────────────────┘
```

### Design 1: guaranteed_until_ Timestamp Scheme

Add `guaranteed_until_` (`SteadyClock::time_point`) to `ObjectMetadata`, defaulting to epoch (no guarantee). At PutStart, if `ReplicateConfig.guaranteed_until_ms > 0`, the Master converts it to an absolute timestamp.

**Core semantic**: `guaranteed_until_` unexpired → object is non-evictable (equivalent to hard pinned); expired → automatically degrades to a regular object.

**Why timestamps over reference counting / lease renewal**:

| Approach | New RPCs | Crash recovery | Complexity |
|----------|----------|----------------|------------|
| Reference counting | Requires ReleaseGuaranteed | Must clean residual counts | High |
| Lease renewal | Requires RenewGuaranteed | Depends on TTL patches | Medium |
| **guaranteed_until timestamp** | **Zero** | **Natural expiration, no orphans** | **Low** |

### Design 2: Zero State on Inference Engine Side

Inference engines (SGLang, vLLM, etc.) hold no guaranteed state. All lifecycle management is on the Master side:

- **Write path**: HiCache checks whether the current block falls within `cache_control`-marked token range → if yes, write_through to L3 with `guaranteed_until_ms`
- **Read path**: When a request carries `cache_control`, pass `guaranteed_ttl

shortlist.title: [good-first-issue] tests: retain L2 diagnostics when flaky TTFT checks fail
shortlist.author: maobaolong
shortlist.body_excerpt:
Parent tracker: #5313 · Onboarding: #3372

## Confirmed flaky behavior

`k3-multiprocess-test / vllm / long_doc_qa_l2 / zmq` changes its L2 time-to-first-token (TTFT) verdict on a same-source retry:

| Build #5287, September 26, 2026 (UTC) | Query speedup | TTFT speedup | Verdict |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [Original job](https://buildkite.com/lmcache/k3-multiprocess-test/builds/5287#01a0db08-cd08-4819-aafd-3b1599eed368) | 1.46x | **1.49x** | Fails the 1.5x TTFT requirement |
| [Retry](https://buildkite.com/lmcache/k3-multiprocess-test/builds/5287#01a0db28-e4d4-4a86-96f8-6923e870be90) | 1.43x | **1.54x** | Passes |

Both jobs test `dev` commit **`002693d8aa5ba8ead0d67922540e4ad4ba6fb3d3`**, without a PR-base merge, and install vLLM **`0.30.1rc1.dev142+g3a58aeb1a`** and torch **`2.13.0+cu130`**. The retry additionally reports 1190 successful L2 stores, 95 prefetch lookups, 2340 prefix hits, and 2340 loaded keys.

The failed attempt exits before the L2 data-flow checks, so we cannot tell from those checks whether it exercised the same successful cache path. That diagnostic gap must not be treated as evidence of broken L2 retrieval, or as proof that the fluctuation is harmless noise.

## Bounded good-first task

Ensure a performance-threshold failure still captures and checks L2 data-flow evidence before the workload exits.

In `long-doc-qa-l2.sh`, `set -e` is active. Step 3's Python threshold verifier exits nonzero, so Step 4's Prometheus scrape and L2 store/prefetch validation never run on the failing path. This is a small shell control-flow and test-diagnostics task.

1. Retain the performance verification status instead of immediately exiting. Run the existing bounded metrics collection while the L2 server is still alive.
2. Report **both** performance and data-flow outcomes, save the metrics snapshot, then return failure if either outcome fails. A metrics timeout/missing snapshot must remain visible and must not mask the original performance failure.
3. Make the snapshot and summary accessible in the public job log or a job artifact. Keep the change local to the L2 workload and any narrowly needed artifact rule.
4. Add CPU-only coverage with stubbed verifier/scrape commands for: both pass, only performance fails, only metrics/data-flow fails, and both fail. Assert bounded behavior, metrics collection after a performance failure, and the final exit status.

Keep the existing 1.3x query-speedup, 1.5x TTFT-speedup, 1.2x warmup-overhead limits and positive L2 data-flow assertions. Do not add blanket retries, reduce thresholds, or redesign storage policy. This completes the missing diagnostics for a confirmed flake; it does **not** by itself establish that the GPU timing instability is fixed. Keep the L1 wrapper outside this task.

Starting points, checked at `42be9c7439a1eb0b17bf6b7565a894a9743fd052`:

- [L2 workload: threshold verifier followed by metrics checks](https://github.com/LMCache/LMCache/blob/42be9c7439a1eb0b17bf6b7565a894a9743fd052/.buildkite/k3_tests/multiprocess/scripts/workloads/common/long-doc-qa-l2.sh#L229).
- [Result cleanup/copying](https://github.com/LMCache/LMCache/blob/42be9c7439a1eb0b17bf6b7565a894a9743fd052/.buildkite/k3_tests/multiprocess/scripts/cleanup.sh).
- [Buildkite workload step](https://github.com/LMCache/LMCache/blob/42be9c7439a1eb0b17bf6b7565a894a9743fd052/.buildkite/k3_tests/multiprocess/pipeline.yml#L173).

## Acceptance

- [ ] A forced performance failure still collects bounded L2 diagnostics before cleanup.
- [ ] All four outcome combinations have regression coverage and correct final exit status.
- [ ] A failed GPU comparison exposes the available store/prefetch counters, or an explicit collection error, in public output/artifacts.
- [ ] Existing thresholds and data-flow assertions remain effective.
- [ ] The PR reports remaining timing instability separately from completed diagnostic hardening.

## Reproduce the CI workload

The evidence below comes from CI; this issue does not claim a local GPU reproduction. Use a dedicated Linux x86_64 GPU test host with Docker and NVIDIA Container Toolkit, two available CUDA GPUs capable of running separate `Qwen/Qwen3-14B` servers, sufficient host RAM for the default 80 GiB LMCache buffer (plus the mock L2 storage for the L2 case), and disk/network access for the image, wheels, and model. CI uses CUDA 13.0, Python 3.12, and a 1 GiB `/dev/shm`. A maintainer can run the GPU validation for a contributor who only has a CPU machine.

These commands build the public CI image recipe, explicitly start Bash, and pin the historical LMCache and vLLM revisions. They are a reproduction recipe, not a fully locked copy of every historical dependency or GPU scheduling condition. Run from a fresh directory; make the actual PR against current `dev`.

```bash
git clone https://github.com/LMCache/LMCache.git
cd LMCache
git checkout 002693d8aa5ba8ead0d67922540e4ad4ba6fb3d3
docker build -t lmcache-flake-ci \
  -f .buildkite/k3_harness/ci-base.Dockerfile .
docker run --rm --gpus '"device=0,1"' --shm-size=1g \
  --entrypoint bash \
  -v "$PWD:/workspace/LMCache" -w /workspace/LMCache \
  -e MAX_JOBS=1 \
  -e INFERENCE_ENGINE=vllm \
  -e LMCACHE_REQUEST_TRANSPORT=zmq \
  -e LMCACHE_PR_BASE_MERGE=never \
  -e PINNED_VLLM_VERSION=0.30.1rc1.dev142+g3a58aeb1a \
  -e PINNED_VLLM_ARCHIVE_INDEX_URL=https://wheels.vllm.ai/3a58aeb1a13e7447da3037608d6489da7e7f22a2/cu130 \
  lmcache-flake-ci -c '
    set -e
    source /opt/venv/bin/activate
    command -v git uv python3 nvcc gcc g++
    nvidia-smi
    git config --global --add safe.directory /workspace/LMCache
    .buildkite/k3_tests/multiprocess/run.sh long_doc_qa_l2
  '
```

Use the linked failed and passed jobs as the initial reproduction pair. For subsequent GPU runs, record the actual checkout SHA, installed package versions, GPU model, input settings, and first-attempt result. A green retry alone does not show that the underlying fluctuation was fixed.

shortlist.title: [good-first-issue] examples: convert token_dropping experiment logging to %-format
shortlist.author: maobaolong
shortlist.body_excerpt:
Follow-up for #5118 after #5125.

#5125 enabled Ruff `G004` repo-wide and added temporary `per-file-ignores` for the files/directories that still build logging messages with f-strings. This issue is one small slice of that cleanup queue.

Claiming: please comment `/claim` and wait for assignment so we avoid duplicate PRs.

## Scope

Convert only the logging f-strings in:

- `examples/token_dropping/rkv_token_dropping.ipynb` (7 G004 findings)
- `examples/token_dropping/snapkv_token_dropping.ipynb` (3 G004 findings)

Counts above were measured on `dev` at `dd5dfca` with `ruff check --isolated --select G004`.

## Expected change

- Replace logging f-strings with lazy `%`-style logging arguments, for example `logger.info("loaded %s tokens", num_tokens)`.
- Preserve the rendered log text and behavior.
- Do not change non-logging f-strings or unrelated control flow.
- Remove the matching `G004` ignore entry/entries from `pyproject.toml` once the listed paths are clean.

Matching ignore entry/entries:

- `"examples/token_dropping/rkv_token_dropping.ipynb" = ["G004"]`
- `"examples/token_dropping/snapkv_token_dropping.ipynb" = ["G004"]`

For a `**` directory ignore, delete the directory entry only when the whole listed directory is clean. If a merge conflict leaves other unmigrated files in that ignored directory, replace the broad `**` entry with explicit file-level entries for the leftovers.

## Verification

shortlist.title: Assertion in TritonAMDGPUCanonicalizePointers: "expected then yield to report fat ptr indices" on a pointer select inside a runtime scf.if
shortlist.author: O1iveira7
shortlist.body_excerpt:
### Describe the bug

Compiling a legal Triton kernel fails with a C++ assertion in the AMD `TritonAMDGPUCanonicalizePointers` pass. The kernel merges two pointer bases with `tl.where` under a tensor condition inside a runtime `if`; the pass then hits a mixed representation between the two `scf.if` arms and aborts compilation.


**Error log**
```
CanonicalizePointers.cpp:1445: ... ConvertSCFIfOp::matchAndRewrite_(scf::IfOp, OneToNOpAdaptor, ...):
Assertion ifOp.thenYield()->hasAttr(kSCFIfOpYieldFatPtrOffsets) &&
          "expected then yield to report fat ptr indices" failed.
note: Pipeline failed while executing [TritonAMDGPUCanonicalizePointers` on 'tt.func' operation: @kernel]
RuntimeError: PassManager::run failed

Failure is in `make_ttgir` (MLIR), before LLVM codegen; exit code 1.
```

The generated TTGIR is:

```
%5 = scf.if %4 -> (tensor<2x!tt.ptr<f32>>) {
  %11 = tt.addptr %10, %0          // base = splat(arg1)
  %12 = arith.select %9, %11, %2   // tensor condition, different bases
  scf.yield %12
} else {
  scf.yield %2                     // base = splat(arg2)
}
%8 = tt.load %5
```
TritonAMDGPUCanonicalizePointers is a 1:N conversion to fat pointers (scalar base, tensor offset). scf.if is only rewritten after both scf.yields are rewritten (tracked via internal then/else-rewritten attributes). ConvertSCFYieldOp sets kSCFIfOpYieldFatPtrOffsets on a yield only when one of its remapped operands is a 2-element fat pointer, while ConvertSCFIfOp unconditionally asserts that the then-yield has that attribute.

Here ConvertArithSelectOp takes its special case for a tensor condition with differing scalar bases and materializes both arms into full tensor pointers instead of a (base, offset) pair. So the then-yield carries a single materialized pointer and gets no fat-pointer index attribute, while the else-yield (a plain tt.addptr) converts to a fat pointer pair and does get the attribute. Both yields are marked rewritten, the scf.if becomes illegal, ConvertSCFIfOp fires, and the assertion fails on the inconsistent arms.

**Reproducer**
```
import os

import torch
import triton
import triton.language as tl


@triton.jit
def kernel(sw, a_ptr, b_ptr, BLOCK: tl.constexpr):
    offs = tl.arange(0, BLOCK)
    p = b_ptr + offs
    if tl.load(sw) == 0:
        p = tl.where(offs >= 0, a_ptr + offs, b_ptr + offs)
    tl.store(a_ptr + offs, tl.load(p))


def _main() -> None:
    device = "cuda"
    N = 2
    a = torch.randn(N, device=device)
    b = torch.randn(N, device=device)
    sw = torch.tensor([0], dtype=torch.int32, device=device)
    print(f"REPRO_START N={N} buffer_ops={os.environ.get('AMDGCN_USE_BUFFER_OPS', 'default')}", flush=True)
    kernel[(1,)](sw, a, b, BLOCK=N, num_warps=1)
    torch.cuda.synchronize()
    print("REPRO_DONE (no crash)", flush=True)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    _main()
```

### Environment details

- AMD Instinct MI308X (gfx942), ROCm 7.2.3
- triton-rocm 3.8.0, torch 2.14.0+rocm7.2, Python 3.12.13

shortlist.title: [RFC]: Radix Tree Index — Prefix-Aware KV Cache Management and Cascading Eviction
shortlist.author: Colors-111
shortlist.body_excerpt:
### Changes proposed

## Summary

Introduce a Radix Tree auxiliary index for the Mooncake Store Master Service to enable:
1. **Prefix queries**: O(1) lookup of all objects sharing a blake3 hash prefix
2. **Parent-child-aware eviction**: Evict leaf nodes first; when space is still insufficient, cascade upward to evict parent nodes — preserving RadixAttention inference path integrity
3. **Zero invasion of primary storage**: Implemented as an auxiliary index layer on top of the existing `unordered_map<string, ObjectMetadata>`, with no impact on hot paths

## 1. Background and Motivation

Mooncake Store stores KV Cache objects in 1024-sharded `unordered_map<string, ObjectMetadata>`. Keys are opaque strings — the Master never parses their internal structure. This leads to three core problems:

**Problem 1: No prefix queries**

SGLang's RadixAttention needs to check whether all keys under a given hash prefix exist (batch_is_exist). Currently this requires scanning all 1024 shards — an O(N) operation that becomes prohibitively slow at million-object scale.

**Problem 2: Eviction is parent-child-unaware**

In RadixAttention, a parent node's KV Cache is the prefix of its children. If a parent is evicted while its children remain, the children lose their context (inference requires a complete root-to-leaf path). Current `BatchEvict` sorts purely by lease timeout, completely ignoring parent-child dependencies.

**Problem 3: Diverse key formats but uniform prefixes**

Key formats vary across model configurations (MLA: `<hash>`, MHA: `<hash>_<layer>_<k|v>`, MHA+TP: `<hash>_<layer>_<k|v>_tp_<rank>`), but the first 64 characters are always a blake3 hex digest identifying a RadixAttention node.

**Goals**: Prefix queries O(N) → O(1), eviction guarantees "children alive implies parent alive", zero invasion of primary storage, progressive enablement via `enable_radix_tree` flag.

## 2. Core Design Decisions

### Design 1: Auxiliary Index, Not a Replacement

The Radix Tree is an auxiliary index layer on top of primary storage. Primary storage (MetadataShard[1024]) remains unchanged; a new RadixTreeShard[256] stores only relationship metadata (parent_prefix_hash, children, registered_keys) — not ObjectMetadata itself.

Rationale: ObjectMetadata is non-copyable/non-movable; hash table O(1) lookup is a critical hot path; the Radix Tree only stores string references with minimal overhead.

```
struct RadixTreeNode {
    // The prefix hash (blake3 hex digest), e.g.
    // "13b825898e41332c2beeae39b161d50994fd2ea4af86f4b95fb5dd0e66893882"
    std::string prefix_hash;

    // Parent node's prefix hash, or "" for root nodes
    std::string parent_prefix_hash;

    // Child nodes' prefix hashes
    std::unordered_set<std::string> children;

    // Full object keys registered under this prefix hash.
    //   MLA models:  {"<hash>"}
    //   MHA models:  {"<hash>_0_k", "<hash>_0_v", "<hash>_1_k", ...}
    //   MHA+TP:      {"<hash>_0_k_tp_0", "<hash>_0_k_tp_1", ...}
    std::unordered_set<std::string> registered_keys;

    bool IsLeaf() const { return children.empty(); }
};
```

```
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                  Master Service                         │
│                                                        │
│  Primary Store (unchanged):                            │
│    MetadataShard[1024]                                 │
│      key → ObjectMetadata (replicas, lease, ...)      │
│                                                        │
│  Relationship Index (NEW):                             │
│    RadixTreeShard[256]                                │
│      prefix_hash → RadixTreeNode                       │
│        ├── parent_prefix_hash                          │
│        ├── children: {child1_hash, child2_hash}       │
│        └── registered_keys: {full_key1, full_key2}    │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

### Design 2: Sharding by prefix_hash

Consistent with MetadataShard's 1024-shard pattern, but with fewer shards. Rationale: Radix Tree node count is far smaller than object count (MLA ~1:1, MHA ~1:2×num_layers), so 256 shards provide sufficient granularity while reducing the number of shards to scan during eviction.

### Design 3: String References Instead of Pointers

`RadixTreeNode` uses `string` for parent/children references rather than `shared_ptr/weak_ptr`. Rationale:

| | Pointer approach | String approach (current) |
|---|---|---|
| Cross-shard safety | `weak_ptr::lock()` produces `shared_ptr` without guaranteeing target shard lock is held | `nodes.find(hash)` operates under shard lock protection |
| Lock ordering | Cannot predict which shards need locking during traversal | Can pre-compute shard indices and lock in ascending order |
| CascadeCleanup | Acquiring new shard locks per level cannot guarantee ascending order | Per-level `find` + shard lock acquisition, implemented and safe |
| Memory overhead | 16-byte pointers | 64-byte strings, but node count is far smaller than object count |

### Design 4: Prefix Extraction via blake3 Fixed Length

blake3 hex digest is always 64 characters. If the first `_` in a key falls at position 64, the first 64 characters are the prefix; otherwise the entire key serves as the prefix (MLA or non-standard formats). O(1) time.

### Design 5: Two Registration Paths

- **Path A**: Inline via `ReplicateConfig.parent_block_hash` at `PutStart` time, registered through the Deferred Pattern
- **Path B**: Standalone `RegisterRadixTreeNode` / `BatchRegisterRadixTreeNode` RPCs, for scenarios like Indexer batch registration

### Design 6: Shell Node Mechanism

When a child node is registered before the parent's `PutStart` arrives, a shell node is created — with `children` populated but `registered_keys` empty. When the parent's `PutStart` arrives later, `registered_keys` is filled in. This ensures correct relationship establishment regardless of registration order.

## 3. Multi-Round Leaf-to-Root

comments.author: zxpdemonio
comments.body:
Hi @Colors-111, thanks for the thoughtful RFC! I'd like to flag that we just opened **#2009 — `[Store] Add chained-prefix LPM lookup (QueryPrefixMatch RPC)`**, which I believe is **complementary** to your design rather than overlapping.

### Where each fits

|                       | **#2009 — LPM**                                                                            | **#1998 — Radix Tree**                                                                          |
| --------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Consumer              | **Router** (read-side)                                                                     | **Master internals** (write-side + eviction)                                                    |
| Question              | "How many leading blocks of *this request's* hash chain are cached, and where?"            | "What's the parent/child topology, and how to evict without breaking inference paths?"          |
| Write-path invasion   | **Zero**                                                                                   | Adds `parent_block_hash` + deferred register/unregister across ~18 functions                    |
| Eviction              | Untouched                                                                                  | Multi-round leaf-to-root cascading                                                              |
| RPC                   | `QueryPrefixMatch(chain[]) → (matched_blocks, candidates, lease_ms)`                       | `RegisterRadixTreeNode`, `GetKeysByPrefix`, …                                                   |

The only apparent overlap is `GetKeysByPrefix` vs `QueryPrefixMatch`, but the consumer model is different: `GetKeysByPrefix` is for callers that already know the exact prefix hash, whereas `QueryPrefixMatch` is for routers that have a token sequence and need **LPM length + segment owners in one round-trip**. Emulating the latter on top of the former would cost N RPCs per request.

### How they integrate cleanly

If your RFC lands, `QueryPrefixMatch` becomes a thin facade on the radix tree — walk down the chain `O(N)` under shared locks, do **one** metadata lookup at the deepest match. Public RPC signature unchanged; the `__pfx__<hash>` convention in #2009 quietly retires. We picked the chain-based input shape precisely so the backend could be swapped.

One coupling point: the `query_lease_ms` we return is a static value today; once cascading eviction lands it should track the **deepest matched leaf's remaining lease** so routers don't hold stale hints.

### Proposal

1. **Land #2009 independently** — zero-invasion, scoped to one read RPC, unblocks SGLang routing now.
2. **Land #1998 on its own merits** — solves a problem #2009 doesn't attempt (path-integrity-preserving eviction).
3. **Follow-up issue** to swap the LPM backend onto the radix tree and unify the two enable-flags (`--enable_prefix_query` + `enable_radix_tree`) into a single mode.

Really like the deferred register/unregister pattern and the watermark-based exit — the lock-ordering analysis is excellent. Happy to coordinate timelines.

comments.author: adolphinvx
comments.body:
Thanks for writing this RFC. This direction looks well aligned with the prefix-preservation problem in RadixAttention / HiCache-backed KV reuse.

We have been building a Mooncake-style KV cache scheduling simulator to evaluate eviction and tiering policies under controlled workloads. It is not a production implementation of Mooncake Store, but it can help quantify the trade-offs in this RFC before the Store-side API and locking design are finalized.

A few observations that may be useful:

1. The parent-child invariant is important. In particular, the guarantee that `children alive => parent alive` seems to be the core value of radix-aware eviction. One thing worth clarifying is the fallback path: if cascading radix eviction cannot reclaim enough memory and the system falls back to traditional eviction, it may still evict a parent while children remain unless the fallback path is also guarded.

2. It may be safer to make radix relationships explicit through `parent_block_hash` / registration APIs rather than relying only on parsing the first 64 characters of opaque Store keys. Key parsing works for current conventions, but explicit metadata would keep Mooncake Store less coupled to a specific upper-layer key format.

3. HA restore / index rebuild semantics may need a precise mode definition. If objects survive restore but the radix index is temporarily missing, the system should either rebuild the index before enabling radix-aware guarantees or clearly degrade to a mode where those guarantees are disabled.

4. This may be worth aligning with existing Store lifecycle mechanisms such as object grouping, leases, soft pin, and hard pin. A radix node often maps to multiple physical objects, so reusing existing group/pin semantics where possible may reduce API surface and edge cases.

5. We can contribute simulation results comparing approximate LRU, radix-aware LRU, and cost-aware radix eviction under multi-turn / agentic workloads. Useful metrics could include cache hit rate, orphaned-suffix ratio, memory reclaimed per eviction round, number of cascade rounds, and TTFT / transfer-latency proxy.

If maintainers think this evidence would be useful, I am happy to share the workload assumptions and results, or help turn them into a small benchmark/design-study PR linked to this RFC.

comments.author: adolphinvx
comments.body:
Followed up a small Mooncake-Sim study for the eviction part of this RFC, mostly to check whether preserving `children alive => parent alive` buys enough to justify the extra radix bookkeeping.

The setup is simple: replay the Mooncake FAST'25 conversation, toolagent, and synthetic traces, preserving `hash_ids` as prefix/cache block IDs, then compare LRU, `radix_lru`, and decayed `radix_cost_aware`. This is not a Store benchmark. It does not measure Master lock contention, metadata memory, HA replay, or `GetKeysByPrefix` latency.

The result is mixed. The invariant does what it is supposed to do: orphaned suffixes go to zero, and the live radix index is smaller. On the full conversation trace, eviction-induced prefill drops from 1178 with LRU to 335 with the radix policies.

Toolagent is the more interesting case. Plain `radix_lru` is worse than LRU: strict hit 0.587 vs 0.611, eviction-induced prefill 1673 vs 1200. Decayed `radix_cost_aware` is better shaped there: strict hit 0.616 vs 0.611, prefill 969 vs 1200. But it still does not show a TTFT win, and the overhead proxy is not cheap, about 591 candidate scans per saved eviction-induced prefill on toolagent.

My read is: keep approximate LRU as the default. If radix-aware eviction moves forward, make it cost-aware and gated by workload signal, then validate the Store-side lock, memory, and prefix-query cost separately. I can share the tables, simulator patch, and commands if helpful.

comments.author: YEXINGZHE54
comments.body: I think it's just a difference between  long-time metric and short-time peak metric. From the perspective of bench_serving, estimating token throughput using TPOT (Time Per Output Token) provides a comprehensive evaluation over the entire testing period. On the other hand, the throughput printed in the engine log refers to the number of tokens generated within a single logging interval (which can be understood as the time for 40 consecutive decodes) divided by the time taken. Clearly, the data in the engine log is influenced by various factors, including: the potential interleaving of the prefill phase between decodes, which extends the total time; additionally, the amount of remaining memory also affects the number of tokens output per decode. Of course, the core issue here is that the engine log records short-term peak throughput, and similar results might be obtained if using the P25 (25th percentile) of TPOT for estimation.

I think I've found the cause. In multiple tests, when the backend is specified as "sglang," the `flush_cache` function is called to clear the cache.

 If `flush_cache` is executed successfully, there will be an inconsistency in the Decode Throughput between `bench_serving` and `engine logs`, specifically, `bench_serving` will be lower than `engine logs`. 

If `flush_cache` fails, the difference in Throughput between the two is within an acceptable range.

I speculate that the time loss caused by the successful execution of `flush_cache` might be the reason. The Decode Throughput in `engine logs` is not affected by this, but `bench_serving` is. I'm still not sure how to fix it. Does anyone have any suggestions?

```python
# Flush cache
if "sglang" in backend:
    requests.post(base_url + "/flush_cache")
```

    if len(self.waiting_queue) == 0 and (
        self.running_batch is None or len(self.running_batch.reqs) == 0
    ):
        self.tree_cache.reset()
        self.tree_cache_metrics = {"total": 0, "hit": 0}
        if self.grammar_backend:
            self.grammar_backend.reset()
        self.req_to_token_pool.clear()
        self.token_to_kv_pool.clear()

        if not self.spec_algorithm.is_none():

            self.draft_worker.model_runner.token_to_kv_pool.clear()

        self.num_generated_tokens = 0

        self.spec_num_total_accepted_tokens = 0
        self.spec_num_total_forward_ct = 0
        torch.cuda.empty_cache()
        logger.info("Cache flushed successfully!")
        if_success = True
    else:
        logging.warning(
            f"Cache not flushed because there are pending requests. "
            f"#queue-req: {len(self.waiting_queue)}, "
            f"#running-req: {0 if self.running_batch is None else len(self.running_batch.reqs)}"
        )
        if_success = False
    return if_success
```

comments.author: ptimizeroracle
comments.body:
I went through both sides of this with the current code (main @ 99b9109). Happy to turn any of it into a fix if wanted, but evidence first.

**The two numbers are different estimators, not two measurements of the same thing:**

| | bench_serving | engine log |
|---|---|---|
| definition | TPOT-derived, per request: `(latency − ttft)` over `output_len − 1`, averaged across the whole run, client-side | `num_generated_tokens / gap_latency` where `gap_latency` is the time since the previous log line (`scheduler_components/metrics_reporter.py:799,894`) |
| window | entire run: queueing, any cold start, `[DONE]` tail included | one reporting interval, near-instantaneous |

So bench < engine is expected whenever the run has any ramp-up: the engine line reads close to a short-window peak, the bench number is a whole-run average.

Three smaller things verified along the way (all `python/sglang/benchmark/serving.py` unless noted):

1. TPOT arithmetic is the standard upstream vLLM formula (`(latency − ttft)/(output_len − 1)`, `:1136`): sound.
2. `itl` is recorded per stream **event**, not per token (`:334-337`, `:466+`). Events carrying several tokens (stream-interval batching, speculative decoding) contribute one itl sample, so `len(itl) < output_len − 1` and ITL percentiles conflate event latency with token latency. A retokenized correction already exists, but only for the `sglang-oai` backends (`:1131-1135`, `:1145-1155`); the completions/chat paths don't get it. I wrote CPU unit tests pinning this behavior (sum(itl) + [DONE]-tail == latency − ttft exactly; mean(ITL) > TPOT for the same request from denominators alone). Happy to PR them.
3. `should_flush_cache` is `("sglang" in backend AND SGLANG_IS_IN_CI) or --flush-cache` (`:1467-1471`), not default-on, so the cold-start mechanism discussed earlier in this thread needs CI or the explicit flag to apply to a default run.

If it's useful, the options I see: (a) a note in the bench output clarifying the window difference vs engine logs, (b) an engine-side long-window average for apples-to-apples runs, (c) extending the retokenized ITL path to the other backends. Which, if any, would you want?

shortlist.title: [Feature] Expose the effective `max_running_requests` (after the mamba/linear-attention state-cache cap) in `/get_server_info`
shortlist.author: fredchu
shortlist.body_excerpt:
### Checklist
- [x] This is a feature request, not a general question.
- [x] English.

### Motivation
On hybrid (mamba / Gated DeltaNet) models, `KVCacheConfigurator.resolve_max_num_reqs` (`python/sglang/srt/mem_cache/kv_cache_configurator.py`, v0.5.19) can cap concurrency well below the CLI value and only says so in the log:

```
max_running_requests is capped to 9 by the mamba state cache (max_mamba_cache_size=47, 5 state slots per request). To raise it: increase --mamba-full-memory-ratio or --max-mamba-cache-size, or halve the state size with --mamba-ssm-dtype bfloat16.
```

`GET /get_server_info` keeps returning the CLI value (`"max_running_requests": 32` in our runs), and the ready-summary line (`max_total_num_tokens=... max_running_requests=9 ...`) is again log-only.

Concrete impact: we drove a concurrency benchmark through the OpenAI-compatible API on `Jackrong/Qwopus3.6-27B-v2-FP8` (Qwen3.5-27B hybrid, RTX 6000 Ada 48 GB, `--max-running-requests 32`, default radix cache) across three rentals, believing the server ran 16–32 concurrent requests. It ran 9 and queued the rest. Every "N=16/24/32" number measured the queue, not the engine, and the inflated per-request latency looked like retraction until we read the container log. With `--disable-radix-cache` the per-request slot count drops from 5 to 1 (`_calculate_mamba_ratio`) and the cap disappears — again only visible in the log.

Proposal:
- Add `effective_max_running_requests` to `/get_server_info` (keep the CLI value as-is for compatibility), populated from the value `resolve_max_num_reqs` returns.
- Optionally expose the inputs (`max_mamba_cache_size`, mamba slots per request) so clients can explain the cap, and a gauge in `/metrics` (e.g. `sglang:max_running_requests_effective`).

### Related resources
- `kv_cache_configurator.py::resolve_max_num_reqs` (warning text above) and `_calculate_mamba_ratio` (ratio 3 + 2 with radix cache + overlap schedule; 1 with `--disable-radix-cache`).
- Ready-summary log line: `max_total_num_tokens=... chunked_prefill_size=... max_prefill_tokens=... max_running_requests=<effective> ...`.

shortlist.title: llama-quantize: GGML_ASSERT(size mismatch) when quantizing mmproj files containing 3D conv tensors (gemma4v audio conv1d)
shortlist.author: mrBenBern
shortlist.body_excerpt:
Quantizing the gemma-4-E2B combined mmproj (vision+audio, gemma4v/gemma4a projectors) from F16 to Q8_0 aborts with:

  llama-quant.cpp:1365: GGML_ASSERT(gguf_get_tensor_size(...) == new_size) failed

Repro:
  llama-quantize --allow-requantize mmproj-F16.gguf out.gguf Q8_0

Fails at tensor `a.conv1d.0.weight` — shape [3,3,1,128] (3D conv1d from the audio encoder). The f32→f16 conversion changes the tensor size, and the split-output writer asserts on the mismatch. Every subsequent 3D tensor fails the same way (a.conv1d.1.weight [3,3,128,32], ...).

Workaround (verified): keep 3D tensors in f32 via tensor-type overrides —
  llama-quantize --allow-requantize \
    --tensor-type "a.conv1d.0.weight=f32" \
    --tensor-type "a.conv1d.1.weight=f32" \
    mmproj-F16.gguf mmproj-F16-q8_0.gguf Q8_0

This works and the resulting Q8_0 mmproj is functionally correct on-device (Android, llama.cpp 4ebdf2c): vision outputs verified same-in-quality as F16 (sign-text reading), encode on a Helio G99 CPU improved 6.4x vs BF16 (37s -> 5.8s for a 91-token image).

Expected behavior: either skip/conversion-preserving handling for N-D tensors whose element count doesn't allow requantization, or a clean error message listing the offending tensors instead of an assert.

shortlist.title: Performance comparison for dense shared prefix + block-diagonal local mask: custom mask in BatchPrefillWithPagedKVCacheWrapper vs MultiLevelCascadeAttentionWrapper
shortlist.author: catnanami
shortlist.body_excerpt: I am trying to evaluate the best way to implement an attention pattern with a dense shared/global prefix plus a local block-diagonal suffix. The mask pattern is shown below: I am considering two implementations: BatchPrefillWithPagedKVCacheWrapper with a custom mask MultiLevelCascadeAttentionWrapper Questions: 1. For this pattern, is cascade attention expected to be faster than paged prefill with a custom mask? 2. Or is this pattern better handled by a custom kernel/backend? My use case is speculative decoding, where all verification tokens share the same prefix KV, but each local block should only attend to its own block.

comments.author: VectorPeak
comments.body:
For the mask in the image - a dense shared prefix on the left plus independent block-diagonal local regions on the right - `MultiLevelCascadeAttentionWrapper` is usually the better fit than `BatchPrefillWithPagedKVCacheWrapper` with one large custom mask.

The reason is that the custom-mask prefill path does not really exploit this structure as well: it still treats the problem like one masked attention problem over the full layout, so the block-diagonal sparsity mostly becomes masking overhead. Cascade attention lets you model this as:

- shared/global prefix KV: attended by all verification tokens
- local suffix KV: split into independent blocks/requests
- final result: merge prefix-attention state with each local block’s attention state

For speculative decoding, this is exactly the kind of case where cascade can help, especially when the shared prefix is large and the local verification blocks are relatively small. Each local block can be represented as a separate batch item sharing the same prefix. If the local part also needs causal masking inside each block, use the normal causal/local mask for that per-block suffix attention.

shortlist.title: Vulkan: ~45% prompt processing regression on RDNA1 (gfx1010) between b10455 and b11429 (v0.6.0) with a GDN-hybrid model; TG unchanged
shortlist.author: unfallen-314
shortlist.body_excerpt:
## Environment

- GPU: AMD RX 5700 XT 8GB (gfx1010, RDNA1) — no coopmat, no `v_dot4_i32_i8`
- OS: Windows 10 19045, Vulkan backend
- Model: Qwen3.5-9B hybrid fine-tune (24 GDN / 8 full-attention layers, GQA 16/4), Q4_K_M GGUF, `-fa on -ctk q4_0 -ctv q4_0 -ngl 99`
- Both builds are the **official release binaries** (also reproduced with a self-built Vulkan binary, `GGML_VULKAN_USE_COOPMAT=OFF`)

## Results

Identical single request (10,890-token prompt, 8 generated tokens), server cold start, first request:

| build | PP (tok/s) | TG (tok/s) |
|---|---:|---:|
| b10455-37a215c9e (2026-08-17) | 269.7 | 44.5 |
| b11429-d81235049 (v0.6.0, 2026-10-05) | 151.6 | 44.3 |

**PP regressed ~45%, TG unchanged.** Reproduced across 4 controlled rounds (152.0 / 145.6 / 143.0 vs old build 252.6-269.7).

## Ruled out

- **Context size**: 128K -> 32K with the new build: 145.6 t/s (no change) — not a memory/workspace sizing issue; no allocation or "fit params" warnings in either build's log
- **-ub 256**: 143.0 t/s (no change)
- **Thermal / test order**: old build re-tested *last* in the session, still 252.6 t/s
- 4 rounds were interleaved cold-start runs; each server instance was freshly started and killed after one request

## Suspects (in the b10455..b11429 window)

- #29476 "vulkan: Tune GDN kernel" — measured on Intel Arc (+26-38% PP) and AMD Pro VII (neutral); the regressed workload here is exactly GDN-hybrid prefill
- ggml v0.26.0 buffer allocation API rework
- Vulkan FA fixes #29591 / #29988

Happy to bisect the per-day builds (b10455..b11429) or run patches/benchmarks on this hardware if useful.

shortlist.title: [RFC]: EPD Disaggregation and Cooperative Scheduling for Agentic Multimodal Inference（CCF 赛题四）
shortlist.author: Pinoeer-kingxi
shortlist.body_excerpt:
### Changes proposed

<!-- GitHub-safe plain Markdown. Copy from the raw .md text, not from Word or a rich-text preview. -->

# RFC: EPD Disaggregation and Cooperative Scheduling for Agentic Multimodal Inference

| Field | Content |
|---|---|
| RFC | RFC-EPD-Agent-Multimodal-2026 |
| Status | Draft |
| Date | 2026-07-05 |
| Target Project | Mooncake / Mooncake Transfer Engine / MooncakeStore |
| Target Integrations | vLLM, SGLang, Qwen-VL/Qwen3-VL-style multimodal models |
| Scope | Encoder-Prefill-Decode disaggregation, Agent state cloning, cross-step KV reuse, evaluation protocol |
| Primary Audience | Mooncake maintainers, serving-system contributors, vLLM/SGLang integration reviewers |
| Implementation Horizon | One-month prototype milestone, followed by staged hardening |
| Compatibility Target | Preserve existing PD and colocated serving paths; new features must be gated by configuration |

---

## Summary

This RFC proposes an extension to Mooncake for **agentic multimodal inference**. The core idea is to generalize Mooncake's KVCache-centric disaggregated serving capability from a two-stage Prefill-Decode model into a broader **Encoder-Prefill-Decode (EPD)** architecture, while also supporting:

- **Agent state cloning** for multi-branch reasoning;
- **visual feature caching** for repeated image/document contexts;
- **cross-step KV reuse** for repeated workflow prefixes;
- **tool-call offload/restore** to release GPU memory during blocking I/O;
- **A2A handoff** for state transfer among planner, executor, verifier, and domain agents;
- **coordinated scheduling** across Encoder, Prefill, Decode, and storage resources.

The proposal introduces a unified `MultimodalState` abstraction that represents visual feature bundles, textual/multimodal KV pages, workflow metadata, state versions, fork branches, TTL, and ownership.

The design intentionally avoids a single global strongly-consistent KV registry. Instead, it uses:

1. **KV Directory** for eventually consistent metadata lookup;
2. **Workflow Shards** for per-workflow strong consistency, refcount, CAS, fork, release, and CoW;
3. **Decentralized Scheduler** for admission control, priority scheduling, offload/restore, and A2A-aware routing.

For KV reuse correctness, the RFC uses a conservative default:

> **Exact Prefix Reuse by default; Approximate Reuse only behind validation gates and feature flags.**

Approximate reuse is never required for correctness. If any validation step fails, the system falls back to exact prefix reuse or full Prefill.

---

## Motivation

### Multimodal inference is naturally EPD-shaped

Multimodal inference contains three computationally different stages:

1. **Encoder**: image/video/audio features are produced by a modality encoder.
2. **Prefill**: the language model processes the full multimodal prompt and builds KV cache.
3. **Decode**: autoregressive generation produces output tokens.

Traditional PD disaggregation couples Encoder with Prefill. This becomes inefficient when the same multimodal context appears repeatedly across turns, agent steps, or branch candidates. Separating Encoder from Prefill enables:

- independent scaling of visual encoder workers;
- reuse of visual features across turns and workflows;
- lower repeated prefill cost for multimodal prompts;
- more flexible routing for prefill-heavy versus decode-heavy workloads.

### Agent workflows require persistent state

Agent workloads are not simple one-shot requests. They involve:

- multi-turn conversations;
- external tool calls and long I/O waits;
- multi-branch reasoning such as Tree-of-Thought, beam search, and verifier branches;
- A2A handoff between planner, executor, retriever, tool agent, and verifier;
- repeated prefixes across workflow steps.

These patterns make KV state a first-class runtime object rather than a temporary per-request artifact.

### Mooncake is well positioned for this extension

Mooncake already focuses on disaggregated KVCache management and high-performance transfer. Extending it to EPD and agentic workflows is a natural next step because the same core primitives are needed:

- cross-node tensor transfer;
- distributed KVCache pooling;
- offload and restore;
- memory ownership;
- scheduling across heterogeneous workers;
- efficient movement of large intermediate states.

This RFC defines a practical architecture that can be implemented incrementally and reviewed in stages.

---

## Goals

This RFC has the following goals.

### G1. Support EPD disaggregation

- Separate Vision Encoder, Prefill, and Decode into independently schedulable workers.
- Transfer Encoder outputs to Prefill and Prefill KV pages to Decode through Mooncake Transfer Engine.
- Preserve fallback paths to normal colocated or PD-only execution.

### G2. Introduce a unified multimodal state abstraction

- Represent FeatureBundle, KVPage, workflow metadata, state versions, fork branches, leases, and TTL.
- Support snapshot-based state reads, page-level refcount, and Copy-on-Write.
- Provide clear lifecycle transitions for active, shared, offloaded, restored, released, and aborted states.

### G3. Support Agent State Cloning

- Enable low-cost fork for multi-branch reasoning.
- Avoid deep-copying full KV state for each branch.
- Make branch writes safe through page-level CoW.
- Make refcount correctness testable and observable.

### G4. Support cross-step KV reuse

- Use exact prefix reuse as the safe default.
- Add approximate or non-contiguous reuse behind validation gates and feature flags.
- Always preserve fallback to full Prefill.

### G5. Reduce control-plane bottlenecks

- Avoid a globally locked GDKR-style metadata service.
- Move refcount and CAS to workflow-local shards.
- Keep cross-workflow metadata eventually consistent with bounded staleness.
- Prevent a single hot workflow or global registry from throttling unrelated workflows.

### G6. Provide a reproducible evaluation protocol

- Define datasets, workload construction, ba

shortlist.title: [Misc]: CMake Clean-up / Refactor Tasks
shortlist.author: LucasWilkinson
shortlist.body_excerpt:
In an effort to make the CMake more readable, stable and easy to use we have a few tasks we'd like to work on, creating a GitHub issue here to track that progress, some planned changes/investigations:

- [ ] Rename `define_gpu_extension_target`, currently this is used for CPU extensions too so the name is now misleading
- [ ] Add a CI test of local builds, i.e. `pip install -e .`
- [ ]  Warn that PTX builds are not currently supported (post https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/8845), currently if there is a `+PTX` in `TORCH_CUDA_ARCH_LIST` this will be ignored. We should warn when this is the case. Alternatively we can add support for PTX builds although this is generally not desirable since PTX increases the wheel size by quite a bit (PTX is larger than SASS), and we already build for all currently supported arches.
- [ ]  Have vllm-flash-attn use [ExternalProject](https://cmake.org/cmake/help/latest/module/ExternalProject.html) currently vllm-flash-attn uses the parent CMake scope which creates many footguns since it is in a separate repo, using `ExternalProject` will mean that the vllm-flash-attn will be run in a separate CMake scope/process
  - [ ] It might be even better to revert to the FlashMLA approach, where CMake code lives in vllm.
- [ ] Look into removing early returns in CMakeLists.txt (potentially move backends into its own files)
- [ ] Potential build both C++ and CUDA extensions when building for CUDA and using torch dispatcher to dispatch between the two, https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/8424

2. Should it run on every PR, or only when build-related files change? I'm thinking we could use `source_file_dependencies` to trigger only on changes to CMakeLists.txt, cmake/*, csrc/*, setup.py, etc.
